intro:
**The Sūrah of the Heights**

Al-Aʿrāf, "the Heights," is the seventh chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 206 verses, and it stands as one of the great mid-length Makkan sūrahs whose structure resembles a vast architectural plan: a broad statement of the Law, then a series of rooms — narrative suites in which the sacred history of the prophets is told again and again, each time widening the circle of warning. The name comes from the word *al-aʿrāf* in verses 46 and 48, the "heights" from which certain men will look across a partition between the Garden and the Fire, identifying the people of both sides "by their marks." Classical commentators differ on what these heights are: some say a ridge or terrace between Paradise and Hell, others say a level of Paradise from which its inhabitants survey all that is below. Whatever the precise identification, the image gives the sūrah its name and one of its deepest psychological tones: the standing, unresolved middle — the place of those whose outcome is not yet the reward they hoped for, who can see the blessed and the damned, and who must watch. It is a name that keeps the sūrah, and everyone who reads it, out of comfort.

**The Shape of the Sūrah**

The opening verses (1–10) state the case of the Book: it is sent down for the Prophet's breast, for warning, and for the remembrance of the believers; it is followed by the fate of destroyed towns, by the questioning of messengers and their peoples, and by the weighing of deeds. Then the first great narrative begins (11–28): the creation of Adam, the refusal of Iblīs, the temptation in the Garden, the descent, and the clothing that follows. From the clothing the sūrah moves to adornment and temperance (31–33), to the appointed term of every nation (34–39), and then to the famous passage of the Hereafter in which the people of the Garden call out to the people of the Fire, and the men on the Heights call to those they know by their marks (44–50). A brief discourse on the signs of God in creation (52–58) introduces the long procession of the destroyed peoples (59–93): Noah, the people of the well and the palm-grove (Hūd), the she-camel of Ṣāli, the transgression of the people of Lūt, and the commerce and religion of Shuʿayb. The Mūsā narrative (103–156) is the sūrah's longest and most detailed suite: the staff and the white hand, the confrontation with Pharaoh, the magicians, the plagues, the parting of the sea, the drowning, the mountain, the golden calf, and the covenant of the elders. A verse identifies the Prophet as the "unlettered" Muḥammad ﷺ written in the Torah and the Gospel (157). The sūrah then returns to Israel's later history — the breach of the covenant, the punishment of the Sabbath-breakers, the city in the land (161–67) — and closes, after a passage on the character of the Prophet and his mission (158–188), with the great verses of the Covenant of the Looms (172), the story of the two brothers and the field (176–77), the parable of the dog in the Cave (178–81). The final, serene vision of the angels in the Presence of God, who are not too proud to worship Him, glorifying Him and prostrating to Him (206).

**The Method of Its Warning**

What distinguishes al-Aʿrāf from its neighbors is the patience of its method. It does not once say "you Makkans will be destroyed" in so many words in the narrative sections; it simply tells the case files and lets the listener recognize himself. This is a warning designed to bypass the defender's defenses: when a man is told directly that he is wrong, he prepares his answer; when he is told a story of a people he knows, he watches it, and in the watching, he confesses. The sūrah trusts its evidence and its order. It also pairs the narratives with the present address constantly — "O Children of Adam" (7:26–35) — so that every story is also a mirror.

verses.1:
> Alif-Lãm-Mĩm-Ṣãd

**Four Letters, and Only These, Before This Book**

The seventh sūrah of the Qur'an does not begin with a word, a name, a blessing, or a story. It begins with four letters of the Arabic alphabet, recited by their own names in that order: *Alif, Lām, Mīm, Ṣād* — a combination that belongs to this sūrah alone. Of the twenty-nine sūrahs that open with the so-called "separated letters" (*al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿāt*), no other carries precisely this quartet. Alif, Lām, Mīm together open the second, third, and twenty-ninth chapters; Mīm alone opens others; and ṣād opens chapter thirty-eight. But the four-letter sequence *ʾalif lām mīm ṣād* stands in the muṣḥaf exactly once, and that once is here, at the gate of al-Aʿrāf. The repetition of the formula across the Book establishes that the letters are not a scribal accident but a standing feature of Divine speech in the Qur'an. The singularity of this particular combination then marks this sūrah with its own signature, as though the Book announced, before a single sentence was spoken, that what follows is a specific and unrepeatable message.

**A Signature of Mystery**

The commentators' first instinct was the same as it was for every set of the separated letters: to acknowledge that the letters are true, real, and weighty, and to acknowledge that their precise meaning is one of the points in which God has concealed knowledge from us. It is transmitted among the early authorities that the meaning of the letters is a *munkarat* — a mystery that the Prophet ﷺ did not explain and that therefore was not to be forced. Some of the later reporters, as the sources gather them, held that the opening letters are a name of God, and that this particular sequence may stand for the "Greatest Name" (*al-Ism al-Aʿẓam*), the name by which God is known to Himself before He is known to creation.
verses.2:
> ˹This is˺ a Book sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺—do not let anxiety into your heart regarding it—so with it you may warn ˹the disbelievers˺, and as a reminder to the believers

**The Book Named at Its Own Gate**

The four letters of the opening are not left hanging in the air. And it is immediately qualified with the passive participle *anẓala* — "sent down" — which does two things at once: it declares the Book's origin (it is not produced, compiled, or composed by any hand in this world) and its direction (it descends, it comes from above, it is addressed downward to the human level). The combination — "˹This is˺ a Book sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺" — is the Qur'an's own self-introduction in miniature, and it is the first complete sentence of the sūrah. Everything that follows in al-Aʿrāf — the destroyed towns, the prophets, the Hereafter — is the unfolding of a single claim that is made in this verse: that a Book has come from God, and that it has come to one man first, and through him to the rest of the world.

**The Constriction in the Breast**

The address now turns to the Prophet ﷺ, and it turns to the most sensitive place in him: *do not let anxiety into your heart about it*. The word is *ḥaraj* — so the translation's "anxiety into your heart" (7:2) — or, in the common reading, the sense of *ḍayq*: a narrowing, a tightening, a closing-in, as when a chest constricts under fear or grief so that the breath grows short. The Qur'an elsewhere places the *ṣadr*, the breast or chest, precisely as the organ of this kind of distress: it is where the word that is too heavy to bear "weighs down" (2:255, where the recitation of the signs is a *ṣadr ḍīq* — "a narrow breast"), and it is where the heart sits. The Qur'an's psychology is bodily before it is abstract: the distress of the messenger is not a thought but a physical tightening, the kind of compression a person feels in the pit of the chest when he sees his own people turn away from the very thing that could save them.

This is not a hypothetical. The history of the first years of the mission is a history of constriction. The Prophet ﷺ had come down from the cave of Ḥirā with a breast that, by his own account to Khadija, was afraid for itself. He had stood before the Quraysh and seen the faces of men he loved harden against him; he had been stoned, insulted, and blocked in the streets of Makkah. The constriction this verse speaks of is not doubt about the Book — that question never troubled him — it is the sorrow and fear of the messenger who carries a warning his people will refuse. And the command *“do not let anxiety into your heart”* (7:2) is not a command to stop feeling; it is a command to locate the feeling correctly. The Qur'an elsewhere treats exactly this kind of messenger's distress with the same medicine: *do not grieve over them* (16:127), *do not be in distress* (28:21, 56). The famous prayer taught for the very condition — when a believer's heart tightens, he is taught to say, "O God, Lord of the Throne, Lord of the Might, Lord of the Greatness" — a dhikr whose name in the sources is the *dhikr al-ḍiqq*, the remembrance for constriction. The cure for a constricted breast is not less feeling but the transfer of the feeling to its proper object: the One who owns the constriction and can open it.

**A Book Named at Its Own Gate: The Same Opening in al-Baqarah**

7:2 opens the sūrah by naming the thing the reader holds, and al-Baqarah opens in the same way: *“This is the Book! There is no doubt about it—a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺”* (2:2). The two openings agree on three points.

The second function named at 7:2 has a rule stated elsewhere: *“But ˹continue to˺ remind. For certainly reminders benefit the believers.”* (51:55).
verses.3:
> Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not take others as guardians besides Him. How seldom are you mindful

**The Address Widens**

The previous verse spoke to the Prophet in the singular. This verse speaks in the plural, and the shift is deliberate: the command now reaches the community, and beyond the community, all people. *Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord* — the "you" is the collective "you" of every person who has received the Book and stood in the light of it. The object of the command is the revealed Book, the very Book named in the preceding verse. The verb is *ittabiʿū*, "follow," from the root *ṭ-w-y*, which pictures walking behind someone on a path: to follow is to place oneself on the same track as the one you follow, to let his footfall set your pace. To "follow" a revealed Book is therefore not an abstract approval of its truth but a practical alignment: one makes the Book the route of one's life, the direction of one's choices, the standard by which one measures what to take and what to leave. The Qur'an uses the same verb for the following of the prophets and the following of the law, and the pattern is constant: faith in the Book without following it is like knowing the map and walking a different road.

**Protectors Besides God**

The negative half of the verse is the one that carries the weight: *and do not take others as guardians besides Him*. The word is *awliyāʾ*, the plural of *walī*, from the root *w-l-y*, which means closeness — a wali is literally a close one. The word has grown in Arabic to cover the whole family of relations: the guardian, the patron, the ally, the protector, the friend who has authority over a person or a cause. To *take* (*ittakhadhū*) protectors other than Allah is to place oneself in a relation of closeness, dependence, and loyalty toward something or someone other than God, such that one's security, direction, and love are attached to that other thing. For the disbelievers, *“their guardians are false gods”* (2:257). Whoever *“turns a blind eye to the Reminder of the Most Compassionate”* is given *“a devilish one as their close associate”* (43:36). And Iblīs and his descendants are taken *“as patrons instead of Me”* (18:50); and in this very sūrah, a few verses later, the same sentence is repeated with the subject made explicit: *“They have taken devils as their masters instead of Allah— thinking they are ˹rightly˺ guided”* (7:30).

> *"The parable of those who take protectors other than Allah is that of a spider spinning a shelter. And the flimsiest of all shelters is certainly that of a spider, if only they knew."* (29:41) The verse closes with a rebuke that is short and very old in the Qur'an: *How seldom are you mindful!* The word is *taʿqilūn*, from the root *ʿ-q-l*, the same root as *ʿaql*, the intellect, and the word *taʿqīl* — to reason, to judge, to grasp, to hold a thing in the mind and weigh it. The Qur'an repeats this rebuke in the same short form in several places — "Yet you are hardly mindful!" (27:62, 40:58; 69:42, and dozens of close variants) — and the repetition is itself a teaching: the central failure of the human heart is not a lack of intelligence but a refusal to apply it to the things that matter.

**Follow What Is Revealed: The Command to the Messenger**

7:3 issues two commands in one sentence, the first directed at following: follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord. The Book puts the same command to the Prophet: *“Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord. Surely Allah is All-Aware of what you ˹all˺ do.”* (33:2)

The second command forbids taking others as guardians beside Him, and the Book states the same prohibition in a social form: *“Believers should not take disbelievers as guardians instead of the believers—and whoever does so will have nothing to hope for from Allah”* (3:28)
verses.4:
> ˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed! Our torment took them by surprise ˹while sleeping˺ at night or midday

**The Rhetoric of the Many**

The verse opens with a rhetorical plural in the form of a question: *˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed!* The Arabic word is *kaẓīr*. The figure is the one the grammarians call the *mabnāʾ li-ḍamīr al-kathīrah* — a form that does not expect an answer, because the answer is not a number but a volume: many, so many that counting has stopped being possible. The construction is deliberate. The Qur'an does not say "I destroyed your town" or "I destroyed one town"; it says *how many*, and the listener's mind is immediately placed in front of a procession of cities, a city after a city, each one with its own name and its own end. This is the sūrah announcing its own method. The long narrative suite that follows — the people of Noah, the people of Hud, the people of Salih, the people of Lot, the people of Shuayb, and then the people of Pharaoh — is the gallery that this single verse opens. The verse is the door: step in, and the walls are lined with the cases of the destroyed towns.

**The Hour of the Strike**

The Qur'an's own narratives keep the two hours in view. Lot's people are told to *“travel with your family in the dark of night”* (15:65) and *“the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook them at sunrise”* (15:73). Sūrat al-Qamar states the same dawn from the side of the punished — *“by the early morning they were overwhelmed by an unrelenting torment”* (54:38); the flood of Noah rose in the hour of their deepest security. The pattern is constant and it is the pattern of this verse: the destruction does not come with a second notice, and it does not come at a convenient hour. It comes when the people is at rest, because the people that has rejected the messenger has already made the rest its religion.

The suddenness of 7:4 is put as a question elsewhere: *“who would be destroyed other than the wrongdoers?”* (6:47), asked of a punishment that would overwhelm a people with or without warning.
verses.5:
> Their only cry—when overwhelmed by Our torment—was, “We have indeed been wrongdoers.”

**Why the Confession Cannot Help Them**

The word rendered "wrongdoers" is *ẓālimūn*, from *ẓ-l-m*. Its primary sense is not cruelty but displacement: to put a thing where it does not belong. A man is a *ẓālim* in this Qur'anic sense when he installs himself in a station that is not his — when he sits in judgment over what belongs to God, treats his own desire as the standard, and answers for an account that was never his to settle. The confession in the verse is therefore exact. The townspeople do not confess a list of crimes; they confess a mislocation, a life spent in a place that was not theirs.

The tragedy is that the words are true and the time is gone. The Qur'an draws the line between two confessions with unmistakable clarity. Repentance belongs to the living hour: *“repentance is not accepted from those who knowingly persist in sin until they start dying, and then cry, ‘Now I repent!’”* (4:18). Pharaoh made this confession with the water at his throat — *“I believe!”* — and the answer still echoes: *“Now you believe? But you always disobeyed and were one of the corruptors”* (10:90–91). The dead cry out for a second term: *“My Lord! Let me go back, so I may do good in what I left behind”* — and the door answers: *“Never!”* (23:99–100).

**The Clock Inside the Verse**

Read this way, 7:5 stops being a report about vanished nations and becomes a measurement of the reader's own position. The sentence *we were wrongdoers* has two lives. Spoken inside the season of the open door, it is the beginning of the turning; spoken after the closing, it is the final entry in a ledger already sealed. The same words, one hour apart, are two different acts — and the two verses before this one established that no one controls the hour, since the torment came at night or at midday, unannounced.

*“Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves then seeks Allah’s forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”* (4:110) is what the townspeople could have said and did not, in the years when saying it would have worked. The Prophet ﷺ described God's reception of such a turning in terms that make this verse's warning land: *“God is more joyful at the repentance of His servant than one of you who finds his camel that he had lost in the desert.”* (Muslim 2747, from Anas ibn Mālik).

**The Ruins the Sūrah Tells Its Readers to Read**

The sūrah does not leave the destroyed towns in the past tense of a report. It tells its audience that the evidence is still lying around them. *“Say: Travel throughout the land and see the fate of the deniers”* (6:11; see also 16:36; 27:69; 29:20; 30:42), and Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ makes the same point with the remains in view: *“˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed that had been spoiled by their ˹comfortable˺ living! Those are their residences, never inhabited after them except passingly.”* (28:58).

The traders of Makkah rode north and south every season, and the caravan routes of the peninsula ran through the territories of peoples the Qur'an names as examples: ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lot, the people of the ditch. The sūrah's argument in these first verses is not that God is capable of punishing nations; it is that He already has, in the neighbourhood, and that the ruins are readable to anyone who stops. Verse 96 will state the law that explains the ruins: *“Had the people of those societies been faithful and mindful of Allah, We would have overwhelmed them with blessings from heaven and earth”* (7:96). The verse of the cry, then, is not a piece of ancient history.

Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ reports the cry and then the mowing: *“Woe to us! We have surely been wrongdoers.”* (21:14), *“They kept repeating their cry until We mowed them down, ˹leaving them˺ lifeless.”* (21:15).
verses.6:
> We will surely question those who received messengers and We will question the messengers ˹themselves˺

**What the Messengers Are Asked**

The Qur'an describes the messengers' interrogation, and it is narrow: *“the Day Allah will gather the messengers and say, ‘What response did you receive?’”* (5:109). The question is not whether they were eloquent or successful — success was never theirs to engineer — but whether the message was delivered. The Book states their commission in the same short form again and again: *“your duty is only to deliver the message”* (13:40); *“then your duty ˹O Prophet˺ is only to deliver ˹the message˺ clearly.”* (16:82). A messenger's account is settled by the delivery, and the delivery is what leaves the community without an excuse.

**Why the People Are Questioned at All**

The classical commentators took seriously a difficulty that other verses create: some passages seem to say the guilty will not be questioned. *“On that Day there will be no need for any human or jinn to be asked about their sins”* (55:39). A witness will be brought from every faith-community (4:41; 16:84), the record will be laid open (39:69). How can there be interrogation if there is nothing to ask?

The answer the commentators gave is the key to this verse: the questioning is not an investigation. God does not ask to learn; the account is already complete. The very next verse says so — *“Then We will give them a full account with sure knowledge—for We were never absent.”* (7:7) The questioning of 7:6 is the arraignment: the moment the evidence is put to the person and the person is made to stand inside it. That is why 16:84 ends with the disbelievers allowed neither to plead nor to appeal — the interrogation exposes the excuse; it does not discover the fact.

**The Question That Will Be Put to the Messengers**

The interrogation of verse 6 runs in two directions at once, and the Qur'an returns to it at several points in the Book. *“And watch for the Day He will call to them, asking, 'What response did you give to the messengers?'”* (28:65). Sūrat al-Naḥl adds that a witness will be produced from every faith-community (16:84), and the Prophet himself is told that he is one of them: *“So how will it be when We bring a witness from every faith-community and bring you ˹O Prophet˺ as a witness against yours?”* (4:41).

**Voices Hushed Before the Questioning**

The sūrah describes an interrogation; the Book describes the sound of the Day. Ṭāhā: *“On that Day all will follow the caller for assembly, and none will dare to deviate. All voices will be hushed before the Most Compassionate. Only whispers will be heard.”* (20:108). An-Nabaʾ: *“on the Day the holy spirit and the angels will stand in ranks. None will talk, except those granted permission by the Most Compassionate and whose words are true.”* (78:38).

The two verses supply what 7:6 leaves unstated: the questioning occurs in a silence, and speech on that Day is licensed. 20:108 describes voices hushed and whispers only; 78:38 adds the condition — permission, and truth in what is said. Read together with 7:6 they explain why the verse says nothing about answers. The interrogation is not a debate; it is a proceeding in which the right to speak is granted and the content is fixed.

**No Interpreter on That Day**

The Prophet ﷺ described the encounter this verse anticipates: "There is none among you except that Allah will speak to him, with no interpreter between Him and him. He will look to his right and see nothing except what he has sent forth. To his left nothing except what he has sent forth. Ahead of him nothing but the Fire — so protect yourselves from the Fire even with half a date" (al-Bukhārī 7443; the command to ward off the Fire with half a date is at al-Bukhārī 1413 and Muslim 1016 — all three from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim). Human courts have secretaries, advocates, and patrons between ruler and ruled. This one has none, which is why the smallest offering sent ahead still counts for something.
verses.7:
> Then We will give them a full account with sure knowledge—for We were never absent

**The Reading of the Record**

The sequence of this sūrah — question, recounting, weighing — matches the courtroom imagery the Qur'an uses for the final accounting. The record is brought out and opened: *“And the record ˹of deeds˺ will be laid ˹open˺, and you will see the wicked in fear of what is ˹written˺ in it”* (18:49). Each person is handed his own book: *“We have bound every human's destiny to their neck, and on the Day of Judgment We will bring forth to each person a record which they will find laid open”* (17:13) — and is told: *“Read your record. You alone are enough this Day to take account of yourself”* (17:14). Before the prophets and witnesses are brought forward, the earth shines with the light of its Lord and judgment is passed (39:69).

**The Account Written by Observers Who Never Left**

The clause *with sure knowledge* — *ʿalā ʿilm* — rests on a doctrine the sūrah assumes but states elsewhere: the deed was never unobserved. *“He reigns supreme over all of His creation, and sends recording-angels, watching over you”* (6:61). *“Not a word does a person utter without having a vigilant observer ready to write it down”* (50:18). *“While you are certainly observed by vigilant, honourable angels, recording ˹everything˺. They know whatever you do.”* (82:10–12). Sūrat al-Zukhruf adds that not even an unspoken thought escapes the record: *“Or do they think that We do not hear their ˹evil˺ thoughts and secret talks? Yes ˹We do˺! And Our messenger-angels are in their presence, recording ˹it all˺.”* (43:80).

**Simultaneous Rather Than Retrospective**

The verse grounds the recounting in God’s presence: *“for We were never absent.”* (7:7). The Book states the same presence at length in Yūnus: *“There is no activity you may be engaged in ˹O Prophet˺ or portion of the Quran you may be reciting, nor any deed you ˹all˺ may be doing except that We are a Witness over you while doing it.”* (10:61). The verse enumerates three cases — an affair, a recitation, a deed — and puts the witnessing inside each of them, with the participle *īdh tafīḍūna fīh*: while you are engaged in it.

Al-Mujādilah states it in the form the commentators quote most often: *“If three converse privately, He is their fourth. If five, He is their sixth. Whether fewer or more, He is with them wherever they may be. Then, on the Day of Judgment, He will inform them of what they have done.”* (58:7). The verse runs from the smallest private gathering to the Day on which it is reported, and its final clause is 7:7’s clause: informing follows from presence.

**The Sūrah’s Own Method Stated**

7:6 and 7:7 together give the procedure of the Day: questioning, then recounting with knowledge by a Witness who was never absent. The same two verbs govern the sūrah’s own procedure. It questions its readers through its histories — every town’s exchange is a question put to the one reading — and it narrates with knowledge, in the first person plural, of events none of its audience saw.

The Qur'an expresses the same fact elsewhere in images the imagination can hold: *“We are closer to them than their jugular vein”* (50:16); *“Not even a leaf falls without His knowledge, nor a grain in the darkness of the earth or anything—green or dry—but is ˹written˺ in a perfect Record.”* (6:59).

**The Questions That Will Be Put**

The Prophet ﷺ supplied what the recounting will ask: the feet of the servant will not move on the Day of Judgment until he is asked about his life and how he spent it, his body and how he wore it out, his wealth and how he earned it and where he spent it. His knowledge and what he did with it (al-Tirmidhī 2417, from Abū Barzah al-Aslamī; al-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ). The point of the report is the point of this verse: the account is itemised, and nothing spent is left unrecorded.
verses.8:
> The weighing on that Day will be just. As for those whose scale will be heavy ˹with good deeds˺, ˹only˺ they will be successful

**The Scale That Weighs What Scales Cannot**

The Qur'an describes the operation of this balance with mechanical precision: *“We will set up the scales of justice on the Day of Judgment, so no soul will be wronged in the least. And even if a deed is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth”* (21:47). It will register an atom's weight (4:40; 99:7–8), and its verdicts are given in the very phrasing used here: *“As for those whose scale is heavy ˹with good deeds˺, it is they who will be successful. But those whose scale is light, they will have doomed themselves, staying in Hell forever”* (23:102–103); and in Sūrat al-Qāriʿah, *“So as for those whose scale is heavy ˹with good deeds˺, they will be in a life of bliss”* (101:6–7).

What, then, is weighed? The Prophet ﷺ answered with an image no arithmetic can hold. A man is brought before God with ninety-nine scrolls of sins, each stretching as far as the eye can see, and a single card bearing the witness *there is no god but God*. The scrolls are placed on one pan and the card on the other: the scrolls rise, the card descends — *“nothing is heavier than the Name of God”* (al-Tirmidhī 2639, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr; graded ḥasan gharīb by al-Tirmidhī and ṣaḥīḥ by Dār al-Salām; Ibn Mājah 4300 records it as well).

That image is this verse's commentary. The scales of the hereafter do not weigh quantity, so that whoever piles up the most acts wins; they weigh reality — the actual worth of what a life was aimed at. A mountain of activity performed for display can rise like chaff, while one sincere confession of the One God can descend with the weight of a lifetime. This is why the Day can be called *the truth*: it is the moment when things are measured as they are, and not as they were advertised. The Book states elsewhere the arithmetic that gives the weighing its relief: *“Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold. Whoever comes with a bad deed will be punished for only one”* (6:160), and the atom of good and evil each appears on the record of the one who did it (99:7–8). But the sūrah's wording is not that deeds are counted; it is that they are *weighed*. The Prophet ﷺ said of two short phrases that *they are light on the tongue, heavy in the balance, and dear to the Most Merciful: Subḥān Allāh wa biḥamdih, Subḥān Allāh al-ʿAẓīm* (al-Bukhārī 6406, from Abū Hurayrah).

**Successful Indeed Are the Believers**

The verse’s second clause names the outcome of heaviness: *“As for those whose scale will be heavy ˹with good deeds˺, ˹only˺ they will be successful.”* (7:8). Al-Muʾminūn opens with the same word: *“Successful indeed are the believers: those who humble themselves in prayer.”* (23:1–2).

The restriction in both verses is the same — *ʾulāʾika hum al-mufliḥūn*, those, they are the successful — and the list that follows in al-Muʾminūn gives the conduct the word is attached to. The heaviness of 7:8 is not a quantity deposited but a life described, and 23:1–9 is the Book’s own description of it.

This is why the verse is placed at the head of the sūrah’s account of the Day. 7:8–9 states the weighing and its two outcomes before any narrative begins, and the histories that follow show the two classes in the towns. The word for success is the sūrah’s positive term throughout, and its definition is given in the verses that describe what the successful do.

Ar-Raḥmān describes the balance as something set in place before any weighing occurs: *“As for the sky, He raised it ˹high˺, and set the balance ˹of justice˺ so that you do not defraud the scales. Weigh with justice, and do not give short measure.”* (55:7–9).
verses.9:
> But those whose scale is light, they have doomed themselves for wrongfully denying Our signs

**The Exactness That Spares No One**

The verses around this one guard the verdict from despair. *“We will set up the scales of justice on the Day of Judgment, so no soul will be wronged in the least”* (21:47). *“Indeed, Allah never wrongs anyone — even by an atom's weight”* (4:40). *“So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it”* (99:7–8). The lightness of this verse is therefore no accident of arithmetic, and no one will be condemned for a gram that was never his to supply: the same Book that weighs a mustard seed also declares that God does not require of any soul more than it can bear (2:286).

What follows in the sūrah — the settlement of humanity on the earth, its brief tenure, and the return (7:10 onward) — reads as the practical conclusion of this weighing. If the scale is real, then the days in which a pan may still be loaded with something of weight are exactly the days being lived now. Verse 9 closes the ledger with a warning whose force lies in its tense: those who *were* wronging Our signs made their own lightness, one deliberate and unremarkable moment at a time.

**"They Have Doomed Themselves"**

The phrase is one of the Qur'an's most concentrated statements of what sin does, and the Book repeats it with a variety of emphasis. *“And by the soul and ˹the One˺ Who fashioned it, then with ˹the knowledge of˺ right and wrong inspired it! Successful indeed is the one who purifies their soul, and doomed is the one who corrupts it!”* (91:7–10). *“The ˹true˺ losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on Judgment Day. That is indeed the clearest loss.”* (39:15), a sentence Sūrat al-Shūrā echoes for the wrongdoers exposed to the Fire (42:45). Sūrat al-Baqarah uses the same vocabulary for the small-scale version of the crime in this world: the hypocrites think they are deceiving God and the believers, *“yet they only deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive it”* (2:9).

The sūrah itself returns to this ending later, in the mouths of the condemned: *“They will have certainly ruined themselves, and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them”* (7:53).

**The Scales of Justice: The Word for Weighing**

The verse’s subject is the scale — *mīzān*, from the root *w-z-n*, which gives *wazn* (weight), *wazana* (to weigh) and *mīzān* (the instrument by which weight is known). The plural in this verse and in 21:47 is *mawāzīn*. The root is the Book’s ordinary vocabulary for commercial weighing, which is why its use for deeds is so deliberate: the sūrah that condemns short measure in Midian (7:85) describes the Day in the language of the market the Midianites corrupted.

**Wronging the Self: The Reflexive in the Sūrah**

The sūrah has already used this formula at its opening, in the first confession it records: *“Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers.”* (7:23). Between 7:23 and 7:9 the same words describe two outcomes, and the difference is the request that follows the admission. Ādam said it and asked; the people of the light scales said it in practice and did not ask. 10:44 explains why the second case is final: the wrong was never inflicted from outside, so there is no injustice to appeal against.
verses.10:
> We have indeed established you on earth and provided you with a means of livelihood. ˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks

**makkannākum: The Verb of Being Settled**

The verb is *makkanā*, from *m-k-n*, the root of place and of power. *Tamkīn* is not only to drop someone somewhere; it is to give him a firm place, the ability to act from it, and the security to remain. The Qur'an uses the same root for the establishment of the believers in the land (22:41; 24:55) and for the power given to Joseph in Egypt (12:56). Here it is granted to humanity as such, without distinction of nation or creed.

The Qur'an describes the earth with the vocabulary of a house prepared for a guest: *“Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy”* (2:22). *“It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you”* (40:64); *“He is the One Who smoothed out the earth for you, so move about in its regions and eat from His provisions”* (67:15). The last of these is the closest twin to this verse: the earth is *smooth*, *tamed*, *made traversable* — a planet whose gravity holds instead of crushing, whose atmosphere filters instead of burning, whose soil yields food when a seed is placed in it. None of that was arranged by the person who benefits from it.

**The Ingratitude Clause**

The verse closes with *qalīlan mā tashkurūn* — “little is it that you give thanks.” The construction (*qalīlan mā* + imperfect) is one of the Arabic forms of emphatic rebuke, and the translation’s rendering of this verse, “˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks” (7:10), carries it. The wording is careful: the verse does not say that human beings are never grateful. It says that gratitude is *little* — occasional, partial, easily displaced by complaint. The Qur'an returns to this diagnosis repeatedly: *“If you tried to count Allah's blessings, you would never be able to number them”* (14:34; 16:18), with 14:34 ending in the same verdict — *“Indeed humankind is truly unfair, ˹totally˺ ungrateful.”*

The Qur'an also states the law that governs the relationship: *“If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more. But if you are ungrateful, surely My punishment is severe”* (14:7). The logic deserves to be stated plainly, because it is not a bargain in the manner of a merchant. Gratitude is not a payment that purchases increase; it is a *seeing* that makes increase bearable and fruitful. The person who acknowledges the Giver receives the same gift and is enlarged by it; the person who credits himself receives it and is narrowed by it, because everything he has becomes a monument to himself — and monuments have to be defended forever.

**A Place of Settlement: The Same Gift Described in Ghāfir**

40:64 ends where 7:10 begins its complaint: the arrangement is described, and then the blessing is named. The sūrah’s own summary of it is shorter — *“˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks.”* (7:10) — and the word for seldom, *qalīlan*, quantifies the response rather than denying it. The gift is plural in both verses; the thanks are few in both.

**Blessings That Cannot Be Numbered**

The provision named in this verse is *maʿāyish*, the plural of *maʿīshah* — a means of living, what a life is lived on. An-Naḥl states the scale of what the plural contains: *“If you tried to count Allah’s blessings, you would never be able to number them.”* (16:18).

**Look Downward, Not Upward**

The Prophet ﷺ trained his companions to compare downward rather than upward in the things of this world: "Look at those below you and not those above you, for that is more likely to keep you from belittling the favour of God upon you" (Muslim 2963, from Abū Hurayrah). Ingratitude rarely announces itself as denial of God; it arrives as an eye fixed on the one thing missing in a life that has received a thousand things. Gratitude is trained by looking down, where the gift becomes visible again — and *qalīlan*, the verse's word for how seldom thanks are given, is the exact diagnosis of eyes trained the other way.
verses.11:
> Surely We created you, then shaped you, then said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused to prostrate with the others

**Two Verbs: Created, Then Formed**

*Khalaqnākum thumma ṣawwarnākum* — We created you, then shaped you. The two verbs are not synonyms. *Khalaqa* names the bringing into being of what was not; *ṣawwara* names the giving of shape — proportion, features, the arrangement that makes a thing recognizable as itself. The Qur'an uses the second verb for the human form with evident pleasure: *“He shaped you in the womb, perfecting your form”* (40:64); *“He created the heavens and the earth for a purpose. He shaped you ˹in the womb˺, perfecting your form.”* (64:3); *“Who has perfected everything He created”* (32:7); and the summary statement of Sūrat al-Tīn, *“Indeed, We created humans in the best form”* (95:4).

**The Prostration and What It Confers**

Then God addressed the angels: *“Prostrate before Adam.”* (7:11) The angels obeyed, and the Qur'an states their obedience without qualification. The command requires religious care, because prostration appears to be an act of worship and worship belongs to God alone. The classical commentators resolve this by distinguishing the *act* from its *object of worship*: the prostration was commanded by God, performed for God, and directed at Adam as a *qiblah* of honor — a salute, in the manner of a subject greeting a king. Al-Qurṭubī cites the analogy of Jacob and his sons prostrating before Joseph (12:100), which the Qur'an records without censure: the prostration of greeting was a known courtly form, and its permissibility or prohibition is set by the divine command. What the angels performed was obedience to God expressed in the direction He chose.

That the direction was a human being is the astonishing part. The angels are described elsewhere as creatures of uninterrupted worship — *“who never disobey whatever Allah orders—always doing as commanded”* (66:6) — and here they are told to bow to dust that has been shaped and animated by God. The honor of humanity, in this scene, is not intrinsic but *conferred*, and it is conferred by the very act that Iblīs will refuse. Dignity, in the Qur'an's account, is always a grant; the moment it is treated as a personal possession, it becomes the occasion of a fall.

**Iblīs and the Grammar of the Exception**

*Illā Iblīs* — except Iblīs. The verse's final clause is unusual: *but not Iblîs, who refused to prostrate with the others* — the Arabic (*lam yakun min al-sājidīn*) states the refusal as an absence, *he was not among those who prostrated*. The Qur'an distributes the facets of his act across sūrahs: he *refused and was arrogant* (2:34); he *was one of the jinn, but he rebelled* (18:50); he *protested* (17:61); he *said, “It is not for me to prostrate to a human You created from sounding clay”* (15:33). Each wording adds a detail. From 18:50 we learn that he was not an angel at all but a jinn, whose free will was the very test the command was designed to exercise. From 2:34 we learn that the refusal was accompanied by *istikbār* — the attribution of greatness to oneself. And from this verse we learn that his non-prostration was a settled state: he did not merely miss the moment; he placed himself outside the ranks of the obedient and remained there.

**The Order of the Two Verbs**

The verse opens on two acts in sequence — We created you, then We shaped you — and the Book keeps that sequence wherever it states it. Sūrah al-Muʾmin lists the same pair among the grounds of gratitude: *“It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy. He shaped you ˹in the womb˺, perfecting your form. And He has provided you with what is good and lawful.”* (40:64). Sūrah al-Infiṭār compresses it into a question addressed to the human being: *“Who created you, fashioned you, and perfected your design, moulding you in whatever form He willed?”* (82:7–8).
verses.12:
> Allah asked, “What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?” He replied, “I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay.”

**The First Analogy in the Tradition's Telling**

*“I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay.”* (7:12) The classical scholars read these words as the first act of reasoning by analogy (*qiyās*) in the history of the creation, and they examined its form with the care of logicians. Al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī set out the objections in sequence.

First, the premise is asserted, not established. Iblīs claims a nobility of fire above clay as though the proposition were self-evident. It is not; it is a claim about material substances whose ranking Iblīs had no revelation to support. The Qur'an, for its part, treats the composition of both as dust-bound and God-given: *“He created humankind from ˹sounding˺ clay like pottery, and created jinn from a ˹smokeless˺ flame of fire”* (55:14–15), and the human being is *“We created man from sounding clay moulded from black mud”* (15:26). Arranging these ingredients in a hierarchy of superiority is a human projection, not a scriptural datum.

Second, even a true premise could not have produced that conclusion. The value of a thing before God is not set by what it is made of, but by its obedience and its reverence: *“Surely the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous among you.”* (49:13). Iblīs reasoned from origin to rank, and the Qur'an's entire moral architecture refuses that move. A creature of fire and a creature of clay stand equally as creatures; only the command of God differentiates their duties.

**The Lie in the Phrase “I Am Better”**

The comparative carries its own refutation. Iblīs accepted God's act of creation and even cited it as an argument; what he refused was God's authority to command. He was, in practice, a theist in metaphysics and an atheist in ethics, dividing lordship into departments so that the department that inconvenienced him could be reserved for himself. The Qur'an will answer the posture directly in another sūrah: *“Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Surely those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, fully humbled”* (40:60).

And the final irony is the criterion he chose. *“I am better than he is”* (7:12) — better in substance, by a material comparison. The Book's answer is that the creature he despised would receive what he lost: *“Indeed, We have dignified the children of Adam”* (17:70). Rank in the divine court is not a property of matter; it is a matter of response. It is the one measurement Iblīs never applied, because applying it would have cost him the argument — and it is the same measurement this sūrah put before its readers four verses earlier, when it asked who among the settled, provided, and shaped would give thanks.

**The Same Question in Three Other Places**

The interrogation is not told once. Sūrah al-Ḥijr records it with the addressee named: *“O Iblîs! What is the matter with you that you did not join others in prostration?”* (15:32). The answer given there omits the comparison and states the refusal as a matter of what is fitting: *“It is not for me to prostrate to a human You created from sounding clay moulded from black mud.”* (15:33). Sūrah Ṣād gives the answer in the words this sūrah gives it: *“I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay.”* (38:76). Sūrah al-Isrāʾ compresses the protest into a question: *“Should I prostrate to the one You have created from mud?”* (17:61).

When God announced the creation of a deputy on earth and the angels asked their question, the answer given for them — and given by them — was: *“Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise”* (2:32).
verses.13:
> Allah said, “Then get down from Paradise! It is not for you to be arrogant here. So get out! You are truly one of the disgraced.”

**The Verdict and Its Exact Fit**

Iblīs had offered an argument; the verse answers with a sentence. *Fa-hbiṭ* — get down. The command is abrupt, and its brevity is part of its meaning: the case is closed, and no further exchange is permitted. What precedes it in the sūrah is now visible as a whole: a command was given, a creature measured himself against another, a rationale was produced, and the answer is a two-word eviction.

The proportionality is worth pausing over. The punishment is not an arbitrary penalty attached to a rule; it is the *reversal* of the thing he did. He placed himself above his station, so his station is lowered. He judged himself great, so he is told he is small — *min al-ṣāghirīn*, of the humbled, the reduced. The Qur'an states this correspondence elsewhere as a settled law: *“Is Hell not a fitting home for the arrogant?”* (39:60), and *“Surely those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, fully humbled”* (40:60). The grammar of the hereafter is the grammar of a mirror.

**ṣāghirīn: The Weight of Smallness**

For human beings the Qur'an keeps the door open to the very end, and it does so explicitly: the same Adam who will slip in the verses that follow receives words from his Lord and is forgiven (2:37).

**Get Down: One Verb, Three Addressees**

The command is *ihbiṭ*, from *h-b-ṭ*, to descend or to go down. The sūrah uses it three times and to three different addressees: to Iblīs here (7:13), to the pair later in the same narrative (7:24), and — in the Book’s other account — to the two together with their enemy. Al-Baqarah records the third: *“Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other.”* (2:36)

The verb is therefore not a punishment addressed to one party but a relocation addressed to all of them. The descent is common, and the enmity is what distinguishes the parties inside it. 7:13 states the descent and the disgrace; 2:36 and 20:123 state the descent and the enmity; and 20:123 adds the condition that follows — guidance will come, and whoever follows it will not go astray.

This is why the expulsion in the sūrah is stated twice rather than once. The first expulsion removes Iblīs from a rank (7:13); the second fills a place with him and with his followers (7:18)

**Disgraced Here, Rejected There**

The verdict ends with a single word: *“You are truly one of the disgraced.”* (7:13). Five verses later the same case is closed with two: *“Get out of Paradise! You are disgraced and rejected!”* (7:18). The second expulsion adds the rejection and the oath about Hell, and the first states the rank that has been lost.

The two verses also differ in what they name. 7:13 names the place — it is not for you to be arrogant *here* — and makes the incompatibility the ground of the expulsion. 7:18 names the consequence: Hell filled with him and whoever follows. The sūrah therefore states the verdict and then the sentence, and between them the descent that puts both into effect.
verses.14:
> He appealed, “Then delay my end until the Day of their resurrection.”

**anẓirnī: The Language of a Debtor**

The verb *anẓirnī* comes from *n-ẓ-r* in its second form, *inẓār*: to grant a delay, to let a term run on. It is the vocabulary of the creditor who gives a debtor more time, and the Qur'an uses it precisely there: *“If it is difficult for someone to repay a debt, postpone it until a time of ease. And if you waive it as an act of charity, it will be better for you, if only you knew” (2:280)* (2:280). Iblīs, then, phrases his demand in the technical language of a man who owes and asks for an extension.

The wording exposes him. He has just been sentenced as the wrongdoer; he speaks as though he were a debtor with a claim to accommodation. And the extension he requests is not for the purpose a debtor asks for time — to gather means and repay. It is time to work against the creditors. The vocabulary of the verse is therefore doing two things at once: it shows the formal courtesy of the request, and it shows that the courtesy is the outer layer of a plan he will announce in two verses.

**The Respite as a Workshop**

The request is granted — the next verse is the answer — and the granting is not a concession to his will but the opening of the test. That is the pattern the Qur'an states as law: *“Do not think ˹O Prophet˺ that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only delays them until a Day when ˹their˺ eyes will stare in horror”* (14:42), and *“Those who disbelieve should not think that living longer is good for them; they are only given more time to increase in sin”* (3:178). The same delay that is a workshop of repentance for one person is a workshop of accumulation for another; the clock itself is neutral, and time is what the human being is made of.

There is a mercy folded into this verse that its words do not advertise. Al-Ḥijr and Ṣād report the same exchange, and there the answer adds a refinement: the respite runs *“until the appointed Day”* (15:38; 38:81) — the known time whose knowledge belongs to God alone, not the Day of Resurrection as such. The Qur'an leaves that ambiguity in place, and the effect is instructive. No one — not the believer, not the rebel, not the one who asks for time — ever knows how much time he has. Every term is fixed, as the sūrah itself will state later: *“For each community there is an appointed term. When their time arrives, they can neither delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it”* (7:34; see also 10:49; 63:11).

The verse so hands the reader the one thing that no creature can negotiate. Iblīs was given his extension because the trial required it; the human being is given his days for the same reason. The difference is what the two build with them.

The Qur'an's own diagnosis in another sūrah names this posture exactly: *“When it is said to them, ‘Fear Allah,’ pride carries them off to sin.”* (2:206).
verses.15:
> Allah said, “You are delayed ˹until the appointed Day˺.”

**"Delayed Until the Appointed Day"**

The phrasing is partitive: *min al-munẓarīn*, *among* the deferred, a member of a class. Iblīs is not handed an unique exemption; he is enrolled in a standing law. Everything mortal lives on borrowed time: *“No soul can ever die without Allah's Will at the destined time”* (3:145); *“For each community there is an appointed term”* (7:34); *“Allah never delays a soul when its appointed time comes”* (63:11). The indefinite plural is the point. He had asked to be made an exception to the general rule of ends; the answer tells him that he has been given a longer rope, not a different rope.

**The Delay That Builds Two Different Men**

The Qur'an treats delay as a moral substance, and it divides its users. For the wrongdoer it is accumulation: *“Those who disbelieve should not think that living longer is good for them. They are only given more time to increase in sin”* (3:178). For the rebellious community it is a trap that feels like kindness: *“When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired. But just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise”* (6:44). And against that, the same delay is the space in which a person returns: *“Say, ˹O Prophet, that Allah says,˺ ‘O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy”* (39:53).

The three verses describe one clock with three faces. Iblīs' respite produced a strategy against humanity (vv. 16–17). A human being's respite can produce either the same ruthless accumulation or the quiet correction of a life. Nothing in the calendar tells the difference; only the use does.

**istidrāj: The Respite That Looks Like Generosity**

Arabic gives this delay a technical name, and the Qur'an builds a doctrine on it. *Istidrāj* is the drawing-on of a person stage by stage, so that he is led further while believing he is being blessed. *“So leave to Me ˹O Prophet˺ those who reject this message. We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot understand.”* (68:44), and the verse that follows seals it: *“I only delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless”* (68:45). The sūrah of the Heights says the same thing in its own voice: *“I only delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless”* (7:183), immediately after describing those who reject the signs and are given increase.

The psychological mechanism is what makes the doctrine so uncomfortable, and the Qur'an states it without softening: *“When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired”* (6:44). The gifts keep arriving; the warnings stop feeling urgent; the recipient concludes that the silence of heaven is approval. This is why the Qur'an repeatedly forbids the interpretation of prosperity as a verdict — the wealthy denier's comfort is not a certificate, and the sufferer's hardship is not a sentence. The delay granted to Iblīs, extended to the end of time, is the purest case of *istidrāj* in the Book: an unlimited opportunity, mistaken for an endorsement.

In the other accounts of this exchange the granting is given with the same economy, and in al-Ḥijr and Ṣād it is completed by the clause *“until the appointed Day”* (15:37–38; 38:80–81).
verses.16:
> He said, “For leaving me to stray I will lie in ambush for them on Your Straight Path

**The Ambush on the Road**

Then the vow: *la-aqʿudanna lahum ṣirāṭaka al-mustaqīm* — I shall surely *sit* for them on Your straight path. The verb *qaʿada* gives the picture of a seated watcher, a highwayman at his post; the emphatic *nūn* of *la-aqʿudanna* matches the certainty of the divine oaths, as though the creature were claiming the same decisiveness for his vendetta.

**The Exception He Cannot Breach**

The other accounts complete the vow with a limit Iblīs was forced to concede: *“except Your chosen servants among them”* (15:40; 38:83). And the Qur'an states the boundary as a standing law: *“you will certainly have no authority over My servants, except the deviant who follow you”* (15:42). *“He certainly has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord”* (16:99); *“You will truly have no authority over My faithful servants”* (17:65). Even the permission given to the tester is bounded by the freedom of the tested. His weapon is suggestion (*waswasah*), and suggestion works only on a will that agrees with it.

That is why the sūrah's own remedy is not a wall or a weapon but a turning: *“If you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah”* (7:200). And the verse that follows it describes the escape precisely — *“when Satan whispers to those mindful of Allah, they remember their Lord, then they start to see things clearly”* (7:201). The ambush in 7:16 is real. So is the road's protection, and the protection is that the traveler keeps looking at where he is going.

The Book's readers are meant to notice the difference between the two confessions: Iblīs attributes his ruin to God, while Adam and Eve attribute theirs to themselves. The sūrah places the two sentences a few verses apart, and the contrast is the whole doctrine of responsibility in miniature.

**My Path, Perfectly Straight**

The verse names the object of the ambush: *“For leaving me to stray I will lie in ambush for them on Your Straight Path.”* (7:16). The path is described as God’s, and al-Anʿām describes the same path as a single one against many: *“Indeed, that is My Path—perfectly straight. So follow it and do not follow other ways, for they will lead you away from His Way.”* (6:153).

The commentators read 7:16 as the reason the path is named straight. Straightness here is not simplicity but singularity: there is one, it is identifiable, and it is where the ambush is set. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the sūrah forbids the same practice to people two thirds of the way through, at 7:86, using the image of sitting on a road.

**Trust as the Ground of the Exception**

The verse states an intention; an-Naḥl states its limit. The next verse defines the authority that remains: *“His authority is only over those who take him as a patron and who—under his influence—associate ˹others˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺.”* (16:100).

This is the ground on which 7:16 can be read as a declaration rather than as a threat. The ambush is set on the path, and the sūrah’s answer is not that the path is cleared but that the one who walks it in reliance is outside the ambusher’s jurisdiction. 7:200 states the same position as an instruction to the individual: seek refuge when the goading touches you.

**A Lord Who Forgives and Takes Account**

The Prophet ﷺ pictured repentance in terms that answer this verse's refusal: a man who says, "My Lord, forgive me my sin," and is answered by a God who says, "My servant committed a sin and then came to know that he has a Lord who forgives the sin and takes account of it" — and at the third turning, "do what you like, I have forgiven you" (Muslim 2758, from Abū Hurayrah). Iblīs' announcement here is the opposite disposition: a creature who blames God and asks for nothing. Adam's story ends with "our Lord, we have wronged ourselves" (7:23) and hope; this one ends with a promise to mislead.
verses.17:
> I will approach them from their front, their back, their right, their left, and then You will find most of them ungrateful.”

**His Verdict on Humanity — and the Remnant**

The Qur'an confirms the statistic without confirming his conclusion. *“Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most of them are ungrateful”* (10:60; see also 27:73; 16:83) — and the same Book says of the divine bounty that it reaches the grateful and the ungrateful alike, since *“He has granted you all that you asked Him for”* (14:34). The word *most* is where the hope lives. The enemy's sentence leaves a remainder, and the remainder is the company he himself was forced to acknowledge and exclude from his reach: *“except Your chosen servants among them”* (15:40; 38:83). Gratitude, in this sūrah's architecture, is not a virtue added to faith. It is the door the ambush was designed to block, and the shield that shuts it is a single remembered favour at the right moment.

**The Siege and Its Psychology**

The Prophet ﷺ described the siege from the inside, as a condition of every human life: *“Each one of you has a devil-companion from the jinn over him.”* When the companions asked whether this included him, he answered: *“Even me, yet Allah helped me against him until he submitted. He does not order me to do anything but good.”* (Muslim 2814, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd).

**Sitting in Wait on the Straight Path**

The verse before this one contains Iblīs’s first declaration: *“For leaving me to stray I will lie in ambush for them on Your Straight Path.”* (7:16). 7:17 then lists four directions from which he will come. The two verses describe the same operation from two positions — stationary and mobile — and the sūrah’s own prohibition names the first of them.

For the sūrah has already forbidden exactly this practice, in its account of Shuʿayb: *“And do not lie in ambush on every road—threatening and hindering those who believe in Allah from His Path and striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked.”* (7:86). The same phrase — lying in ambush on a road — is used of the enemy at 7:16 and of the corrupters of Midian at 7:86. The Book so reports the practice as both the method of Iblīs and the method of the men who cut the roads, and forbids it to the believers in the same sūrah.

**The Proclamation That Answers the Forecast**

The sūrah tests the prediction in its own histories, and the test is documented rather than asserted. Every town given a sign responds with denial; every people given respite responds with security; the sūrah’s summary of the pattern is that the few who were grateful were the remnant (7:10). Sabaʾ records the same estimate inside God’s charge to the family of David — *“˹Only˺ a few of My servants are ˹truly˺ grateful.”* (34:13) — and it is the reason the prediction is not treated as a boast in the interpretive tradition but as a statement of fact.

The counter-statement is also in the sūrah. *“And remember when your Lord proclaimed, ‘If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more. But if you are ungrateful, surely My punishment is severe.’”* (14:7). The proclamation answers the prediction by making gratitude a matter of increase rather than of numbers: what Iblīs forecast about the majority is true, and what the proclamation offers is available to anyone who performs it. 7:17 states the enemy’s expectation and leaves the reader with the verse that defeats it.
verses.18:
> Allah said, “Get out of Paradise! You are disgraced and rejected! I will certainly fill up Hell with you and your followers all together.”

**The Oath of the Filling**

*La-amlaʾanna jahannama minkum ajmaʿīn* — I will certainly fill up Hell with you and your followers all together. The first-person oath-pronoun is God's, and the same declaration is repeated at three other places in the Book: *“I will surely fill up Hell with jinn and humans all together”* (11:119). *“My Word will come to pass: I will surely fill up Hell with jinn and humans all together”* (32:13); and the address to Iblīs, *“I will surely fill up Hell with you and whoever follows you from among them, all together”* (38:85).

The sūrah also states the population of that sentence with precision in the verse following al-Ḥijr's parallel: *“and surely Hell is their destined place, all together. It has seven gates, to each a group of them is designated”* (15:43–44). The imagery of gates and groups is not a decoration of the threat; it is a refusal to describe the Fire as a mass. Those who enter are not a crowd but named categories of a chosen road.

**"Whoever Follows You" — the Condition That Keeps It Just**

The threat is conditional, and the condition is doing the work: *man ittabaʿaka minhum* — literally, *whoever among them follows you*; the translation names them simply as *your followers*. What is threatened is not humanity but the *following*. The Qur'an states the same boundary as a law of the enemy's power: he has *no authority* over the sincere (15:42; 16:99; 17:65), and his capacity to lead is itself part of the test — *“He does not have any authority over them, but Our Will is only to distinguish those who believe in the Hereafter from those who are in doubt about it”* (34:21). The tempter tempts; he does not compel. A man who enters the Fire has walked there, however subtly the walking was arranged.

Read with 32:13 the oath at 7:18 is not a threat against a particular group but a statement about the outcome of a choice that both orders share.

**Disgraced and Rejected, and the Followers Named**

The two passives describe a status: *madhʾūman*, blamed and held in contempt, from *dhaʾama*; *madḥūran*, banished and driven away, from *daḥara*. Neither is a description of feeling. The sūrah has already recorded the reason — the refusal to prostrate and the claim of superiority (7:12) — and the two words are its consequence stated as a condition.

The verse then names who shares it: *“I will certainly fill up Hell with you and your followers all together.”* (7:18). The Book describes those followers elsewhere as more than human: *“And so We have made for every prophet enemies—devilish humans and jinn—whispering to one another with elegant words of deception.”* (6:112). The verse explains the mechanism by which a refusal becomes a following — decorative speech passed between two kinds of creature — and it makes the same point 32:13 makes by naming both orders.

The sūrah’s own account of the following is more precise still: at 7:20 it records that the whispering was addressed to a pair, and at 7:27 that the devils see the people from where they cannot be seen. 7:18 therefore states the end of a chain the sūrah describes link by link — a refusal, a whisper, a following, and a filling that includes both.
verses.19:
> ˹Allah said,˺ “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat from wherever you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”

**The Generosity of the Command**

The narrative returns to Adam with a command that is almost all permission. *Uskun* — dwell, take up residence — and then *fa-kulā min ḥaythu shiʾtumā*: eat from wherever the two of you wish. The Qur'an's fuller account in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā fills in what the permission covers: *“Here it is guaranteed that you will never go hungry or unclothed, nor will you ˹ever˺ suffer from thirst or ˹the sun's˺ heat”* (20:118–119). Food, clothing, water, shade — the four anxieties that organize most human labor — are declared settled in advance. The Garden is presented not as a reward to be earned but as a home to be inhabited, and the single prohibition is set inside a field of open permissions.

**One Tree, Deliberately Unnamed**

*Wa-lā taqrabā hādhihi al-shajarah* — and do not come near this tree. Two details of the wording carry the teaching. The first is *lā taqrabā*, do not approach, rather than *lā taʾkulā*, do not eat. The Qur'an uses the same construction for adultery — *“Do not go near adultery”* (17:32) — and for the orphan's property — *“do not come near the wealth of the orphan”* (6:152). The prohibition is a fence placed around the act, not merely a line at the act itself, and the jurisprudence of *sadd al-dharāʾiʿ* — blocking the pathways to what is forbidden — is read by the jurists out of exactly this phrase.

**Both of Them, and the Silence About Hawwāʾ**

The verse addresses the pair: *dwell, you and your wife* — and the wife is not named anywhere in the Qur'an. The Book has kept her identity from the text, though the commentators transmit the name Hawwāʾ from the older reports.

That silence is worth noticing, because of what the surrounding verses do with the pair. In 7:20–22 the tempter addresses *them*, both of them act, and both are exposed together. The Qur'an never assigns the first initiative to the woman. Where the older scriptural narrative presents a sequence in which the woman is deceived and then leads the man, this sūrah presents a single act of two people. The responsibility is shared and equal: *“Then their Lord called out to them, ‘Did I not forbid you from that tree and ˹did I not˺ tell you that Satan is your sworn enemy?’”* (7:22) The point matters because a long tradition of misogynist preaching has drawn from the story a doctrine of female culpability for the first sin. The Qur'an's own text does not support it, and the careful reader of this verse has already been given the corrective: the warning was addressed to both, the command was given to both, and the failure was theirs together.

**The Command in al-Baqarah and Ṭā Hā**

The command is given twice elsewhere with different emphases. Sūrah al-Baqarah states it in almost the same words: *“O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”* (2:35). Sūrah Ṭā Hā states the provision in the four needs it meets: *“Here it is guaranteed that you will never go hungry or unclothed,”* (20:118), *“nor will you ˹ever˺ suffer from thirst or ˹the sun’s˺ heat.”* (20:119).
verses.20:
> Then Satan tempted them in order to expose what was hidden of their nakedness. He said, “Your Lord has forbidden this tree to you only to prevent you from becoming angels or immortals.”

**Two Promises: Transcendence and Permanence**

His argument is preserved in the fuller account: *“Shall I show you the Tree of Immortality and a kingdom that does not fade away?”* (20:120). Here it is given in its compressed form: your Lord has forbidden you this tree *“Then Satan tempted them to expose what was hidden of their nakedness. He said, ‘Your Lord has forbidden this tree to you only to prevent you from becoming angels or immortals.’”* (7:20).

**The Whisper: A Method, Not an Announcement**

The previous episode showed the tempter declaring war openly — the vow to sit in ambush on the straight path (7:16), the four-sided approach (7:17). Here he changes his register completely. *Fa-waswasa lahumā al-shayṭān*: he whispered to them. The Arabic *waswasah* names a sound at the edge of hearing — the rustle of a garment, a step half-made, the murmur that a person cannot quite attribute to anyone. The word is used in the Qur'an for the work of *al-waswās al-khannās*, the retreating whisperer who works in the breast (114:4–5).

**Clothing Provided Before the Whisper**

The whisper’s aim is stated in the verse’s first clause: to expose what was hidden of their nakedness. The sūrah has already described what covered it: *“O children of Adam! We have provided for you clothing to cover your nakedness and as an adornment. However, the best clothing is righteousness.”* (7:26).

The verse distinguishes two functions of clothing — covering and adornment — and then names a third thing that deserves the word better. Read against 7:20, the exposure the enemy intends is the removal of the first function, and the sūrah’s own answer is that the covering that matters is not the one that can be removed.

The placement of 7:26 is deliberate. It stands inside the sūrah’s address to the children of Ādam, before the histories begin, and it describes a provision already made. The whisper at 7:20 therefore operates against a background of provision, which is why the sūrah can describe its aim as exposure of something hidden rather than as the creation of a new shame.

**The Garden’s Terms**

The verse reports a prohibition attributed to a motive. Al-Baqarah records the terms as they were given: *“O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”* (2:35).

The three terms are a dwelling, an open permission, and one exception with its consequence named. Nothing in them suggests a motive for the exception beyond the warning attached to it — *fa-takūnā min al-ẓālimīn*, or else you will be wrongdoers. The whisper at 7:20 supplies the missing motive by inventing one: that the tree was withheld to withhold something else.

Adam is blamed for his act and named as the one who forgot (20:115) and disobeyed (20:121).

The Book will say in Sūrah al-Zumar that *no soul bears the burden of another* (6:164; 39:7), and in al-Najm that *the human being has only what he strives for* (53:39).

**Nearness Without Compulsion**

The Prophet ﷺ described how close the tempter works: "Satan circulates in the body of man like the circulation of blood" (Muslim 2175; the same report appears in al-Bukhārī 3281, both from Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyayy). The image is exact about what it claims. It claims nearness — the whisper has no distance to cross. It does not claim force; the blood is inside the man, and the choice stays his. That is why the whisper in this verse can supply a false motive for the tree, and why Adam is still named as the one who forgot and disobeyed.
verses.21:
> And he swore to them, “I am truly your sincere advisor.”

**The First Perjured Oath**

*Wa-qāsamahumā* — and he swore to them. The verb is from *qasam*, the oath, and it is chosen for its weight in a society where an oath was the ultimate instrument of trust. The tempter had no standing to be believed on his word, so he manufactured standing by appealing to the one thing the Arabs of the sūrah's audience treated as beyond manipulation: the sworn word.

The commentators note the formal completeness of the deception. He did not assert; he promised. He did not persuade with evidence; he offered a guarantee. And in doing so he produced the first false oath in the moral history of the creation — a detail the sūrah does not dwell on but the reader should notice, because the Book will later make oath-taking by the divine name a matter of severe account: *“Do not use Allah’s Name in your oaths as an excuse for not doing good”* (2:224). *“those who trade Allah’s covenant and their oaths for a fleeting gain will have no share in the Hereafter”* (3:77). The ancestor of all swearing-away of the truth is the oath of Iblīs.

**The Theft of a Religious Word**

The word is not accidental; the sūrah has been using it of the prophets. Each of the five messengers of Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ opens with the same claim: *“I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you”* (26:107; 26:125; 26:143; 26:162; 26:178), and the sūrah's own messengers speak in the same register: *“conveying to you my Lord’s messages. And I am your sincere advisor”* (7:68), *“conveying to you my Lord’s messages and giving you ˹sincere˺ advice”* (7:62), and the farewell Shuʿayb addresses to his people, *“I have delivered to you the messages of my Lord and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice. How can I then grieve for those who chose to disbelieve?”* (7:93). The tempter takes the signature phrase of the prophetic office and wears it. This is a deliberate arrangement by the sūrah: it teaches the reader that the counterfeit of a category is not the absence of that category but its imitation, and that the imitation will sound exactly like the original.

**The Sincerity That Keeps Its Address**

One further note belongs here, because it is the difference between the tempter's *nāṣiḥ* and the prophets' *nāṣiḥ*. The messengers of this sūrah never demand to be trusted for their own sake; each of them says, in the same breath, *“I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds.”* (26:109; 26:127; 26:145; 26:164; 26:180). Sincere counsel in the Qur'anic sense is counsel that can name where it is going — to the commanded good, and to God. The oath of the tempter names nothing beyond itself. The safest question a person can put to any adviser, including the advice that rises inside his own chest, is the one this verse leaves unspoken but answers: toward whose good does this counsel actually point?

A person cannot verify sincerity by tone; the perjurer is often warmer than the truthful man, and the Qur'an says so of the very people who oppose religion: *“When you see them, their appearance impresses you. And when they speak, you listen to their ˹impressive˺ speech.”* (63:4).

**Speech That Borrows Religion's Authority**

The Prophet ﷺ warned his community about counsel that wears the language of piety while serving something else: he described a people who would recite the Qur'an but whose recitation would not pass their throats. Whose speech would be more pleasing than it deserved (al-Bukhārī 3344; Muslim 1064, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, describing the Khawārij). The oath of this verse — "I am surely one of your sincere advisers" — is the archetype. Words alone cannot verify a counsellor, which is why the Book trains the reader to ask where the advice points, not how warm it sounds.
verses.22:
> So he brought about their fall through deception. And when they tasted of the tree, their nakedness was exposed to them, prompting them to cover themselves with leaves from Paradise. Then their Lord called out to them, “Did I not forbid you from that tree and ˹did I not˺ tell you that Satan is your sworn enemy?”

**The Descent into Delusion**

*Fa-dallāhumā bi-ghurūr* — so he brought them down by delusion. Beside it stands *ghurūr*, the noun of deception, formed from the same root the Qur'an uses for the deceitful world (*al-ghurūr*) and for the delusion of the one who trusts it — *“So do not let the life of this world deceive you, nor let the Chief Deceiver deceive you about Allah.”* (31:33; 35:5).

That is the anatomy of the first temptation, and it is the one the reader of the sūrah will meet again in the surah's own warnings about wealth, adornment, and appetite (7:26–32): a slow gradualism in which each step is justified by the promise of the next.

**The Call in the Garden**

The sūrah has, in fact, already delivered that warning to the reader — *“Do not let Satan deceive you as he tempted your parents out of Paradise”* (7:27). Sūrat Ṭāhā records the warning given to Adam himself: *“O Adam! This is surely an enemy to you and to your wife.”* (20:117). The call therefore closes no gap of information. It exposes a gap of attention: the enemy was named in advance, the boundary was pointed out in advance, and both were held in the same hand. The wording *ʿaduww mubīn* — an open, manifest enemy — is one of the Qur'an's recurring formulas about Satan. It recurs so often (2:168; 2:208; 6:142; 7:22; 12:5; 17:53; 28:15; 36:60; 43:62) because the Book is teaching a single habit of mind: whereas a person's dealings with enemies in the visible world are conducted with caution, the enemy who works through the inner suggestion is regularly treated as a friend.

**Deceived and Made to Fall: The Other Account**

The verse names the instrument: *“So he brought about their fall through deception.”* (7:22). Al-Baqarah describes the same act with its result: *“But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in”* (2:36). The two verses agree on the deception and on the fall, and al-Baqarah adds the state they were left.

The noun the sūrah uses for the deception is *ghurūr*, from a root meaning to make a thing appear other than it is.
