The commentators note that *ghurūr* is not lying but misleading by appearance, which is what the whisper at 7:20 consisted of — a prohibition given a motive it did not have, and two benefits promised that the tree could not contain.

2:36’s addition matters for the sūrah’s argument. The sūrah’s own account of the descent (7:24–25) adds the enmity and the guidance that will come, so that the fall is never described as the last term of the narrative.

**Enemies to Each Other: What the Descent Establishes**

The verse’s second half describes the exposure and the first covering; the command that follows establishes a relation. Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray ˹in this life˺ nor suffer ˹in the next˺.”* (20:123).

The enmity is what makes the sūrah’s later instructions intelligible. Refuge is commanded at the moment of provocation (7:200), reliance is described as the ground on which the enemy has no authority (16:99), and the histories report town after town taking him as a patron instead.

**The Tree Named, and Not Named**

The tree is never identified. This sūrah’s command gives a boundary and no species: “do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers” (7:19). Al-Baqarah’s version varies the permission — “eat as freely as you please” (2:35), where al-Aʿrāf has “eat from wherever you please” (7:19) — and keeps the prohibition word for word. The only name it ever carries in the Qurʾān is the one given to it inside the whisper: “Shall I show you the Tree of Immortality and a kingdom that does not fade away?” (20:120).

The Prophet ﷺ stated the principle in a hadith that has been memorized in the same spirit — *“Beware of minor sins; they pile upon a man until they ruin him”* (Musnad Aḥmad 3808, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, graded ṣaḥīḥ by Aḥmad Shākir).
verses.23:
> They replied, “Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers.”

**"Our Lord" — The Address That Survives the Fall**

The sentence opens with *rabbanā*. It would have been possible for a shame-stricken creature to address God by the Name of power, of judgment, of wrath; the pairing chosen is the Name of nurture and cultivation. The first word after the failure is therefore a claim on the relationship, not a renunciation of it. The Qur'an's model of repentance begins here, and this is why the same opening recurs on the lips of the returning: *“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves”* (7:23), *“Our Lord! We have believed, so forgive our sins and protect us”* (3:16), *“Our Lord!”

**"We Have Wronged Ourselves"**

*Ẓalamnā anfusanā.* Three words, and the whole architecture of Islamic accountability is inside them. The object of the wrong is the self — *anfusanā* — not the majesty of God in the abstract, and not another party. The verse so contains a diagnosis before it contains a request: sin is first of all an injury to the one who commits it, and the Qur'an uses this self-directed language consistently. *“And whoever commits a sin—it is only to their own loss. Allah is AllKnowing, All-Wise.”* (4:111); *“Indeed, whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has clearly gone ˹far˺ astray”* (33:36); *“Surely you have wronged yourselves”* (2:54).

The verb is in the perfect tense, with the *nā* of the first person plural. It reports a finished act and accepts it as one's own. Now compare it with the sentence spoken by Iblīs eleven verses earlier — *“He said, ‘For leaving me to stray I will lie in ambush for them on Your Straight Path.”* (7:16) — and the contrast the sūrah has built becomes unavoidable. One creature files the blame upward; the other files the blame inward. The Book does not present both as mistakes with different flavors. It presents one as a position from which no return was ever sought, and the other as the exact posture from which return always begins.

**The Master Formula**

The Prophet ﷺ gave this pattern its most complete written form in the *sayyid al-istighfār*, the master supplication: *“O God, You are my Lord; there is no god but You. You created me and I am Your servant, and I abide by Your covenant and promise as much as I am able. I seek refuge with You from the evil I have done. I acknowledge before You Your favour upon me and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.”* (al-Bukhārī 6306, from Shaddād ibn Aws). The components are exactly those of 7:23 — lordship addressed, fault owned, mercy requested, credit given to God alone — and the hadith adds the detail that makes the earlier scene intelligible: the one who says this in the morning and dies that day enters the Garden.

The Book's verdict on that turning is given in the verse that follows in Sūrah al-Baqarah — *“Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful”* (2:37) — and the sūrah of the Heights will spend the rest of its length teaching the children of Adam to use the same door.

**The Same Confession From a Different Servant**

The words of 7:23 are a confession with two requests attached, and the Book records the same confession from a servant in a different situation. Mūsā, after the blow that killed, pleads: *“My Lord! I have definitely wronged my soul, so forgive me.”* (28:16), and the verse reports the outcome in three words: *“So He forgave him”* (28:16). The structure is the one 7:23 uses — an address, an admission in the first person, a request — and the admission in both cases is placed on the speaker rather than on a circumstance.
verses.24:
> Allah said, “Descend as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”

**"Descend as Enemies to Each Other"**

*Baʿḍukum li-baʿḍin ʿaduww* — some of you are enemies to others. The plural is broad and the commentators read it widely: Iblīs and the human race; the human being and his own kind; the human being and the demons; and, in the reading al-Qurṭubī reports, the two members of the couple about a domestic strife the temptation had opened. The Book returns to this condition repeatedly, because it is the structure of life in the world the descent created: *“But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in, and We said, ‘Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.’”* (2:36); *“Surely Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy”* (35:6); *“Do not follow Satan's footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy”* (2:168).

**mustaqarr and matāʿ: Dwelling and Provision**

Two nouns are given for the earthly condition. *Mustaqarr* — a place of settlement, from the root *qarra*, to settle, to remain still — is the word the Qur'an uses elsewhere for the stability of created things: *“The sun travels for its fixed term”* (36:38). *“And He is the One Who created the day and the night, the sun and the moon—each travelling in an orbit”* (21:33). The earth is given to the human being as something firm enough to build a life on. Beside it stands *matāʿ*, provision or enjoyment — with the nuance of a thing borrowed and used for a while, since the same word describes the goods of this life generally: *“Know that this worldly life is no more than play, amusement, luxury, mutual boasting, and competition in wealth and children.”* (57:20).

**"Until a Time"**

*Ilā ḥīn* — until a time. The phrase is deliberately indefinite, and the indefiniteness is one of the Book's recurring devices: the term is fixed *“When their time arrives, they can neither delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it”* (7:34) and unknown. It is the unknown part that produces the moral seriousness of a life. The same phrase appears at the end of Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt's account of the people of Jonah: *“who then believed ˹in him˺, so We allowed them enjoyment for a while.”* (37:148; see also 2:36).

**The Earth Laid Out: A Residence Described as a Place**

The sentence at 7:24 gives the pair a place to go and a thing to live on, and it does both in one breath: descend as enemies, and find in the earth a residence and a provision for an appointed stay. The two nouns the verse supplies are the ground of the whole human story that follows in the sūrah, and the Book describes that ground elsewhere in language that is almost administrative. *“Who has laid out the earth for ˹all of˺ you, and set in it pathways for you”* (20:53), and *“We made in it means of sustenance for you and others, who you do not provide for”* (15:20)

The enmity named in the same sentence is therefore set inside a provisioned place. This is why the human story in al-Aʿrāf is a story of towns rather than of individuals: the earth given to the pair is the earth the towns inhabit, the earth whose blessings the sūrah enumerates at 7:10 and whose destruction it reports at 7:4 and 7:97–99.
verses.25:
> He added, “There you will live, there you will die, and from there you will be resurrected.”

**Three Clauses, One Place**

The verse is built on a single repeated pronoun. *Fīhā* — "in it", "in it", the "there" of the translation — governs all three clauses, and the antecedent is the earth named in the command to descend that precedes it. Life is in it, death is in it, and the coming forth is from it. Nothing in the sequence happens anywhere else.

> *He added, “There you will live, there you will die, and from there you will be resurrected.”* (7:25)

> *"An act of disobedience that bequeaths humility and need is better than an act of obedience that bequeaths might and pride."* (Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh, al-Ḥikam 96)

**The Second Account**

This verse closes the second telling of the Adam narrative in the order of the muṣḥaf. The first is at 2:30–39; later accounts run at 17:61–65 and 20:115–24, and at 15:28–43 and 38:71–85 the same story is told of the first human being without naming him.

The repetition is not redundancy, and the differences are where the meaning lies. Each account closes differently, and this one closes on the earth: on where the story's descendants will actually live, die and rise. The telling in Sūrah Ṭā Hā closes on the warning not to forget; this one closes on a geography.

**The Verb That Both Sends and Raises**

That is why the clause stands as the Book’s answer to an objection it records in the objector’s own words: *“Who will give life to decayed bones?”* (36:78). The question assumes that what has decayed is finished; the verse assumes that the same ground is the instrument of the return. Sūrah al-Nāziʿāt gives the objection in fuller form — *“Will we really be restored to our former state, even after we have been reduced to decayed bones?”* (79:10–11) — and adds the objector’s own conclusion, *“Then such a return would be a ˹total˺ loss ˹for us˺!”* (79:12). Verse 25 does not argue with that conclusion. It states the itinerary, and leaves the loss to be calculated by whoever walks it.

**The Same Three Prepositions in Ṭā Hā and Nūḥ**

Two other passages lay out the same itinerary, and both bind it to the same ground. In the address that follows Mūsā’s commissioning, Sūrah Ṭā Hā says: *“From the earth We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you back again.”* (20:55). Nūḥ preaches it to his people in the language of cultivation: *“Allah ˹alone˺ caused you to grow from the earth like a plant.”* (71:17), *“Then He will return you to it, and then simply bring you forth ˹again˺.”* (71:18).

**The Earth as the Place of Return in Law**

The jurists read the third clause as the ground of burial. If the coming forth is *from* the earth, the staying is *in* it, and the return of a body to the soil is not a local custom but the shape the verse describes. Sūrah al-Mursalāt states the arrangement as a provision made for the creature: *“Have We not made the earth a lodging for the living and the dead”* (77:25–26). Sūrah ʿAbasa puts the two acts in a single line — God *“then causes them to die and be buried”* (80:21) — the verb *qabara*, from which the word for grave derives.
verses.26:
> O children of Adam! We have provided for you clothing to cover your nakedness and as an adornment. However, the best clothing is righteousness. This is one of Allah’s bounties, so perhaps you will be mindful

**"Sent Down": Clothing as a Divine Gift**

The verb *anzalnā* is the same verb the Qur'an uses for rain, for the Book, and for iron (*“We sent down iron, in which is great might and benefits for people”*, 57:25). Clothing is placed in that company deliberately. The wool of sheep, the strength of flax, the growth of cotton, the shade of a tree — none of these were manufactured by the human being who wears them; what the human being contributes is knowledge of how to use what was supplied. The same point is made in Sūrah al-Naḥl, where garments and their purposes are traced to the Creator: *“He has also provided you with clothes protecting you from the heat ˹and cold˺, and armour shielding you in battle” (16:81)* (16:81). For the mercantile Makkans, whose cloth trade was a livelihood, the verse quietly relocates the origin of their merchandise: the wealth of their caravans was borrowed.

**rīsh: The Case for Beauty**

This is the verse that Muslim tradition cites against a spirituality of self-neglect. The Prophet ﷺ, when a man came to him looking disheveled, remarked that God is beautiful and loves beauty, and that the display of God's favour upon a servant is part of what is due to Him. The Qur'an's own term for the good things of life is *ṭayyibāt*, and it treats their enjoyment as worship when gratitude accompanies it (2:172; 7:32). *rīsh* is the licence for that enjoyment, written into the earliest instruction given to the human race after the fall.

**libās al-taqwā: The Garment That Cannot Be Bought**

Then the verse introduces its comparative: *wa-libāsu al-taqwā dhālika khayr* — the best clothing is righteousness. The *khayr* is not a dismissal of the earlier garments; it is a ranking. Cloth covers a body that will decay; *taqwā* covers a soul that will be presented to God. The Qur'an elsewhere names *taqwā* as the thing that survives when all provisions are counted: *“Take ˹necessary˺ provisions ˹for the journey˺—surely the best provision is righteousness.”* (2:197). The metaphor works because it shares the function of clothing exactly. Taqwā hides what ought not to be seen — the faults, the appetite that has not yet been disciplined — and it protects its wearer from exposure. In the sūrah's own story, the first thing sin produced was exposure; the remedy offered to the children of Adam is a covering that cannot be lost by taste or theft.

**How Clothing Is Sent Down**

The verse says that clothing was sent down — *anzalnā lakum libāsā* — and the commentators have always had to meet the obvious objection, since garments are woven rather than revealed. Their answers are levels rather than alternatives. At the first level the material is literally sent down: nothing reaches the loom that did not begin as water, and the water falls. Sūrah al-Naḥl lists the finished products in the same register of provision: *“And out of their wool, fur, and hair He has given you furnishings and goods for a while.”* (16:80), *“He has also provided you with clothes protecting you from the heat ˹and cold˺, and armour shielding you in battle.”* (16:81).

At the second level what is sent down is the knowledge, since the covering that distinguishes the human being is a practice that had to be taught — and the sūrah’s own narrative has just shown the first couple learning it under the compulsion of shame (7:22). It is under that heading that the sūrah will shortly forbid anyone to declare provision unlawful (7:32).

From this verse and the command at 7:31 they drew the rulings on covering: the obligation to cover the *ʿawrah* in prayer, the recommendation of the best of one’s clothing at the places of worship. The rejection of the ascetic who declares adornment forbidden to be more devout than the law requires.
verses.27:
> O children of Adam! Do not let Satan deceive you as he tempted your parents out of Paradise and caused their cover to be removed in order to expose their nakedness. Surely he and his soldiers watch you from where you cannot see them. We have made the devils allies of those who disbelieve

**The Asymmetry of Vision**

Then comes the sentence that makes the whole passage practical: *innahu yarākum huwa wa-qabīluhu min ḥaythu lā tarawanahum* — surely he and his soldiers watch you from where you cannot see them. The word *qabīl*, rendered here "his soldiers", is kinship language: a clan, a tribe, an organized body. The jinn are described as a community with forces, and the Qur'an elsewhere names their orders and ranks — infantry and cavalry, incursion and collaboration (17:64) — and the four-sided approach of 7:17.

The verse so removes from the reader the comfort of an even fight. And this is precisely why the sūrah's remedy for the ambush is not intelligence-gathering but refuge — *“If you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah”* (7:200) — and why the Book supplies the missing visibility by naming the enemy's techniques in advance.

The hadith tradition handles the same reality with a metaphor that has stayed in the Muslim imagination: *“Satan circulates in the human being as blood circulates in him”* (al-Bukhārī 3281, from Ṣafiyyah). The Prophet ﷺ said it while warning one of his wives that the enemy might throw a suggestion into her heart — a remark that tells the reader this is not a subject for those who consider themselves immune.

**"We Have Made the Devils Allies of Those Who Disbelieve"**

The final clause is the verse's theology. *Innā jaʿalnā al-shayāṭīn awliyāʾa li-lladhīna lā yuʾminūn* — We have made the devils allies of those who disbelieve. *Walī* is the nearest of relations: protector, patron, the one to whom loyalty is given and from whom protection is expected. The Qur'an uses the term for the divine guardianship over the believers (*“Allah is the Protector of those who believe”*, 2:257) and here for its inversion.

The construction *jaʿalnā*, We made, has drawn the attention of theologians: is this a decree or a consequence? The alliance is a settlement that the person's own movement has produced — the same law stated in Sūrah al-Zukhruf, *“And whoever turns a blind eye to the Reminder of the Most Compassionate, We place at the disposal of each a devilish one as their close associate”* (43:36) — and once settled, it is administered by God's decree.

**The Word for Garment, and What Else It Covers**

The covering the verse says was stripped is *libās*, the ordinary word for a garment — but the Book uses it of persons as well as cloth. Of spouses it says: *“Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them.”* (2:187).

The root *l-b-s* splits into two verbs, and the split is worth holding. *Labisa* is to wear; *labasa* is to confound, to mix a matter until it can no longer be read. From the first comes *libās*, garment; from the second comes *labs*, the confusion of a thing with what it is not. The temptation in this verse does both at once: it uncovers the body and it obscures the case. That is why the sūrah’s next addresses to the children of Adam concern dress at the places of worship (7:31) and the refusal to let anyone declare forbidden what God has produced for them (7:32–33). Clarity about what covers a person and clarity about what is permitted to him are the same discipline.

**The Garment That Cannot Be Stripped**

The verse before this one provides; this one warns that the provision can be removed. 7:26 names two garments and then a third — clothing “to cover your nakedness and as an adornment”, and then “the best clothing is righteousness” (7:26). The first two are given, the third is practised, and it is the only one of the three called best. This verse takes up the first: Satan “caused their cover to be removed to expose their nakedness” (7:27), which is the loss of a covering that can be taken off. The warning to the children of Adam is therefore about a sequence and not only about an event.
verses.28:
> Whenever they commit a shameful deed, they say, “We found our forefathers doing it and Allah has commanded us to do it.” Say, “No! Allah never commands what is shameful. How can you attribute to Allah what you do not know?”

**Taqlīd: The Qur'an's Sustained Objection**

This is not an isolated complaint. The Qur'an returns to the ancestral argument again and again and rejects it in nearly identical words: *“When it is said to them, ‘Follow what Allah has revealed,’ they reply, ‘No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.’ ˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance?”* (2:170; see also 5:104; 31:21; 43:22–24). The rejoinder in al-Baqarah is the sūrah's own rejoinder here, sharpened into a question about the competence of the ancestors to be followed.

The point is not hostility to tradition. Islam is, in its own self-description, the religion of Abraham and of the prophets before Muhammad ﷺ, and the sūrah will spend a great part of its length appealing to the inheritance of the Children of Israel. What the Book rejects is not inherited practice but inherited practice used *as a proof*. A custom can be a legitimate vehicle of a genuine command, but its antiquity is not the reason the command binds; the command binds because God commanded it, and the command must be traceable to Him. The moment a practice is defended by the fact that it is ancestral, it has been removed from the jurisdiction of revelation altogether.

**The Worse Claim: "Allah Has Commanded Us to Do It"**

The principle underneath is fundamental to Islamic belief. God's commands are not arbitrary; they are consistent with His names and His revealed law. A command to commit what revelation names *fāḥishah* — an obscenity, a thing the sound conscience recoils from — cannot come from God, because God has already declared such things forbidden in the Book and in the innate disposition He created (7:157; 16:90; 30:30). Any claim of a divine command that contradicts the divine law has just refuted itself. This is the criterion the tradition later used to sift an enormous body of purported reports and rulings, and it begins here.

**The Epistemic Sins**

Speaking about God without knowledge is treated in this sūrah as a distinct and grave category of offense. Verse 33 will list it among the five things God has forbidden — indecencies, sin, wrongful aggression, and *“associating ˹others˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺—a practice He has never authorized—and attributing to Allah what you do not know”* (7:33). Sūrah al-Baqarah warns that the same enemy who incites indecency also urges *“to claim against Allah what you do not know”* (2:169). Sūrah al-Naḥl condemns the fabrication of permissions and prohibitions by the tongue alone: *“Do not falsely declare with your tongues, ‘This is lawful, and that is unlawful,’ ˹only˺ fabricating lies against Allah.”* (16:116).

**Fāḥishah as a Technical Term**

The word this verse reports is *fāḥishah*, and the Book applies it to acts of very different kinds. Lūṭ puts it to his people as a deed without precedent: “Do you commit a shameful deed that no man has ever done before?” (7:80). The prohibition list makes it the first of five (7:33). Al-Nisāʾ uses the same word of a married woman’s offence, “unless they are found guilty of adultery” (4:19). The range is not looseness in the term but one sense — what exceeds a recognised limit — which is why the argument can move from a sexual charge to a claim about God without changing its vocabulary. That continuity is what makes this verse’s second claim graver than its first: the ancestors defended a *fāḥishah*, and an attribution to God is an excess of the same kind, committed in speech.

The same act is attributed elsewhere to the opposite agent — “The Devil threatens you with ˹the prospect of˺ poverty and bids you to the shameful deed ˹of stinginess˺” (2:268) — and one act cannot be commanded by both, which is the form of the argument the verse leaves the reader to complete.
verses.29:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “My Lord has commanded uprightness and dedication ˹to Him alone˺ in worship, calling upon Him with sincere devotion. Just as He first brought you into being, you will be brought to life again.”

**Justice First**

The first item is *qisṭ*, and the choice of the word is deliberate. Arabic has several words for justice — *ʿadl* for balance and equity, *ḥukm* for judgment, *qisṭ* for the fair share that is due. *Qisṭ* is the word of the scale, and its use here, in a sūrah that has just placed a balance on the Day of Judgment (7:8–9), ties the ethics of this life to the accounting of the next. Justice is not one virtue among many in the Qur'an; it is the first thing named when a prophet is asked to describe what his Lord commands. The Book reinforces this repeatedly: *“Indeed, Allah commands justice, grace, as well as courtesy to close relatives.”* (16:90); *“when you judge between people, judge with fairness”* (4:58); *“Be just — that is closer to righteousness”* (5:8), the verse that commands justice even toward those one hates.

**Faces Set Toward Him**

*Wa-aqīmū wujūhakum ʿinda kulli masjid* — literally, "set your faces at every place of worship"; the translation carries the clause as *dedication ˹to Him alone˺ in worship*. The verb *aqāma* is from *q-w-m*, the root of standing upright, and the Qur'an uses it for establishing prayer (*aqāma al-ṣalāh*) throughout. The commentators give several readings of the phrase. Al-Ṭabarī takes it as a command to direct oneself wholly to God in every act of worship, whatever place one is in. The word *wajh*, face, in the Qur'an's phrase carries the sense of the whole directed self, which is why *aslamtu wajhī* is not to be rendered word-for-word as *I have turned my face* but carries the sense *“I have submitted myself to Allah”* (3:20; see also 2:112).

**Sincerity as the Definition of Religion**

*Wa-dʿūhu mukhliṣīna lahu al-dīn* — and call upon Him with sincere devotion. The phrase *mukhliṣīn lahu al-dīn* recurs through the Book as the definition of the religion Abraham founded — in the call of 10:22 and 29:65, in the supplication of 31:32. In the two addresses of 40:14 and 40:65 — and it is given its final summary in Sūrat al-Bayyinah: *“even though they were only commanded to worship Allah ˹alone˺ with sincere devotion to Him in all uprightness, establish prayer, and pay almstax. That is the upright Way”* (98:5).

The verse closes with the resurrection, and the argument it uses is one of the Qur'an's most persistent: the appeal to the beginning as proof of the return. *Kamā badaʾakum taʿūdūn.* Sūrat al-Rūm states it with the reasoning spelled out — *“And He is the One Who originates the creation then will resurrect it—which is even easier for Him.”* (30:27) — and the same proof is pressed in 21:104, 29:19, 27:64, and 10:4. Al-Anbiyāʾ puts it as a promise: *“Just as We produced the first creation, so shall We reproduce it”* (21:104). And when the Makkans posed the challenge in its hardest form, asking who would restore bones to life, the answer given was the same: *“The One Who created you the first time.”* (17:51).

There is a second layer in the phrase, and the sūrah exploits it immediately. *Just as He first brought you into being* — the human being began as nothing, without property, without name, without a tribe. The verse is a reminder that this is also how the account will be resumed: as the Qur'an says elsewhere, *“˹Today˺ you have come back to Us all alone as We created you the first time”* (6:94). *“You have surely returned to Us ˹all alone˺ as We created you the first time”* (18:48).

The Book states elsewhere who owns those locations, in a verse that reads as a rule rather than a description: *“The places of worship are ˹only˺ for Allah, so do not invoke anyone besides Him.”* (72:18)
verses.30:
> He has guided some, while others are destined to stray. They have taken devils as their masters instead of Allah—thinking they are ˹rightly˺ guided

**Two Parties on One Road**

*Farīqan hadā wa-farīqan ḥaqqat ʿalayhimu al-ḍalālah.* The verse divides humanity into two groups, and the two verbs are not symmetrical. For the first, guidance is something done *to* them — *hadā*, He guided, with God as the subject. For the second, straying is something that has *settled upon* them — *ḥaqqat*, from a root meaning to be due, to fall upon a person as a right or a consequence.

The asymmetry is the Qur'an's careful position on one of its most discussed questions. The Book never says that God *made a party stray* in the way it says He guided a party; at most it says He *left* them, *turned away* from them, or *did not guide* them — and it never allows these statements to be detached from the condition of those concerned. Sūrat al-Ṣaff states the sequence explicitly: *“So when they ˹persistently˺ deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate.”* (61:5). The same law appears in 2:26, where straying happens to *“the rebellious”*; in 6:125, where the chest of the one left astray is constricted because of what he chose; and in 42:44, where the one left astray has no protector after Him.

**"They Took Devils as Their Masters Instead of Allah"**

The cause is then named: *ittakhadhū al-shayāṭīn awliyāʾa min dūni Allāh*. The verse is not speaking of a formal cult of the jinn, though such cults existed and are addressed elsewhere (72:6; 6:100).

The second sūrah of the Qur'an states the outcome of the two guardianships in one verse: *“Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness and into light. They will be there forever.”* (2:257).

**"And They Think They Are Guided"**

Then the clause that makes the verse frightening: *wa-hum yaḥsabūna annahum muhtadūn*. Not merely lost — lost while convinced of the opposite. The Qur'an treats this as a distinct condition with its own vocabulary. Sūrat al-Kahf describes people *“whose efforts are in vain in this worldly life, while they think they are doing good”* (18:104). Sūrat Fāṭir asks the question the sūrah of the Heights has been building toward: *“Are those whose evil-doing is made so appealing to them that they deem it good like those who are rightly guided?”* (35:8). And Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn shows it operating at the social level: a group swearing oaths of loyalty while the Qur'an names them liars (63:1; 58:18).

The psychology of this sentence is the reason the verse pairs it with the ancestral argument of 7:28 and the enemy of 7:27. There are three roads into the same ditch: blaming one's failure on God, as Iblīs did; defending a practice because one's fathers did it; and taking the enemy as a protector while believing one has taken God.

**An Enemy to Be Taken as an Enemy**

The verse’s second sentence reports an exchange that did not happen: people took devils as protectors *besides* Allah while supposing themselves guided. He only invites his followers to become inmates of the Blaze.”* (35:6).

7:30 supplies the case the instruction is aimed at. The sūrah has already described the mechanism: the devils see people from where they cannot be seen (7:27), the whisper is answered by a remembrance (7:201), and refuge is commanded at the moment of provocation (7:200). What 7:30 adds is the state of mind in which all of this is accepted as guidance — which is why the verse ends where it does, with the supposition rather than with the punishment.

The third sūrah of the Qur'an states the point about misguidance and its victims in one line that preserves hope: *“Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us”* (3:8).

An-Nisāʾ describes the same movement as a consequence of a prior choice: *“And whoever defies the Messenger after guidance has become clear to them and follows a path other than that of the believers, We will let them pursue what they have chosen, then burn them in Hell—what an evil end!”* (4:115)
verses.31:
> O Children of Adam! Dress properly whenever you are at worship. Eat and drink, but do not waste. Surely He does not like the wasteful

**"Eat and Drink, But Do Not Be Prodigal"**

The Book repeats the prohibition as a settled principle: *“Eat from the fruit they bear and pay the dues at harvest, but do not waste. Surely He does not like the wasteful.”* (6:141); *“Do not spend wastefully; surely the wasteful are like brothers to the devils, and the Devil is ever ungrateful to his Lord”* (17:26–27); *“They are those who spend neither wastefully nor stingily, but moderately in between”* (25:67). The last verse describes the servants of the All-Merciful, and the standard it gives — neither the open hand of the wastrel nor the clenched fist of the miser — is the balance this sūrah has been teaching since it placed a scale on the Day of Judgment.

**Worship and Dignity**

The word *zīnah* is the same word used in 7:32, where God defends the adornments He has brought forth for His servants — the two verses are a pair, one granting and one commanding. Taken together they form the Qur'an's refusal of two opposite errors. The first is the ascetic error: the notion that God is honored by the rejection of the good things He gave, that piety is measured in shabbiness and self-denial.

**The Hadith of the Stomach**

The Prophet ﷺ gave the ethic of 7:31 its most concrete expression. From Miqdām ibn Maʿdī Karib, he said: *“The human being does not fill any vessel worse than his stomach. It is enough for the son of Adam to eat a few morsels to keep his back straight. But if he must eat more, then a third for his food, a third for his drink, and a third for his breath.”* (al-Tirmidhī 2380, from al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib; graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ by al-Tirmidhī and ṣaḥīḥ by Dār al-Salām). The tradition read this hadith as a rule of bodily discipline with spiritual consequences: the full stomach produces a sluggish heart, and the appetite that is never denied becomes the door through which every other appetite enters.

The verse's final clause makes the prohibition religious rather than hygienic: *innahu lā yuḥibbu al-musrifīn* — He does not love the extravagant. The Quranic formula of God's love and its absence is the Book's way of ranking conduct on the scale of relationship rather than of legality. Extravagance is not only unwise; it is the kind of conduct a person engages in when he has stopped seeing the One who provided. That is why the verse appears where it does, after a chapter on provisioning (7:10), a chapter on covering (7:26), and a chapter on the enemy who strips cover away (7:27). Ingratitude, exposure, excess — three names for the same misplacement — and the remedy offered is one: to take, deliberately and gratefully, what God has sent down, and not one measure more.

**Isrāf and Tabdhīr**

The word for the excess forbidden here is *isrāf*, and the Book distinguishes it from a second word for waste, *tabdhīr*. The commentators draw the line by direction: *isrāf* is excess in what is itself permitted, spending past the measure on a lawful thing. *tabdhīr* is spending on what ought not to be spent on at all — the word used where the wasteful are assigned a company: *“Surely the wasteful are ˹like˺ brothers to the devils. And the Devil is ever ungrateful to his Lord.”* (17:27).

Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather ʿAbdullāh b. ʿAmr, in Sunan Ibn Mājah at 3600 and 3605, has the Prophet ﷺ command eating, drinking, giving charity and wearing clothes so long as that involves no extravagance and no vanity; al-Bukhārī carries it in suspended form, Aḥmad in his Musnad, and it is graded good.
verses.32:
> Ask, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought forth for His servants?” Say, “They are for the enjoyment of the believers in this worldly life, but they will be exclusively theirs on the Day of Judgment. This is how We make Our revelations clear for people of knowledge.”

**The Long History of Pious Prohibition**

The verse is addressing a pattern, not a single practice. The commentators attach it to several: the Arabs who set aside certain livestock and crops as *baḥīrah*, *sāʾibah*. *waṣīlah*, declaring them forbidden by religious vow (5:103; 6:138–139); the People of the Book who forbade themselves foods that God had never forbidden (3:93; 4:160; 6:146); and the ascetics, referred to in the Qur'an's own words about monasticism: *“As for monasticism, they made it up—We never ordained it for them—only seeking to please Allah, yet they did not ˹even˺ observe it strictly.”* (57:27).

The Book's attitude to all of them is consistent. Self-denial is not a virtue in itself, and legislation that God did not issue is not worship but a claim upon His authority. The Prophet ﷺ made the principle explicit when he heard that some of his companions had resolved to fast continuously, to stand all night in prayer. To abstain from marriage: he refused to have anything to do with such a discipline and said, *“But I fast and break the fast, I pray and sleep, and I marry — so whoever turns away from my practice is not of me”* (al-Bukhārī 5063; Muslim 1401). The response is not a rebuke of devotion; it is the rejection of devotion conducted by a law that God did not write.

Al-Ṭabarī records the readings. The dominant one is that in this world the good things are shared — the rain falls on everyone, the fields of the ungrateful yield as well as those of the grateful — and in the Hereafter the good things will be pure, reserved. Without the mixing that characterizes a world in which the righteous and the wicked live side by side. This is what the Book means elsewhere when it says of the Garden that its reward is past imagining — *“No soul can imagine what delights are kept in store for them”* (32:17) — and that its people *“will have whatever they desire”* (50:35; 16:31; 39:34; 42:22; see also 41:31, *“There you will have whatever your souls desire”*). The promise is not that the believer will be repaid in kind; it is that the enjoyment of the good will finally be untroubled.

**Two Pieties the Verse Rejects by Name**

The question *who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought out for His servants?* answers two opposite errors, and the Book answers each of them elsewhere in its own terms. The first is the piety that treats the good things of the world as inherently defiling: Sūrat al-Māʾidah commands, *“Do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not like transgressors”* (5:87), and Sūrat al-Aʿrāf itself had laid the foundation two verses earlier: *“Eat and drink, but do not waste. Surely He does not like the wasteful”* (7:31). The second error is the licence that reads the verse as permission for excess, and the same clause rules it out: the lawful is *ṭayyib*, good, and the Book's command is to eat it with gratitude (2:172; 16:114), not to gorge on it.

The Prophet came out and said, *“Are you the ones who said such and such? By Allah, I am the most God-fearing and pious among you, yet I fast and I break my fast, I pray and I sleep, and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me”* (al-Bukhārī 5063; Muslim 1401).
verses.33:
> Say, “My Lord has only forbidden open and secret indecencies, sinfulness, unjust aggression, associating ˹others˺ with Allah ˹in worship˺—a practice He has never authorized—and attributing to Allah what you do not know.”

**The Five Forbidden Things**

The list that follows has a considered order.

*Al-fawāḥish* — indecencies, *mā ẓahara minhā wa-mā baṭan*: what is open of them and what is hidden. The word *fāḥishah* covers sexual immorality in the broadest Qur'anic sense — the act that is shameful by nature and that every sound tradition has recognized as such. The phrase *outward and inward* is the verse's own insistence that the prohibition is not only about conduct. It reaches the intention, the imagination, the private arrangement, and the intention that never reaches conduct. The Book repeats the same pairing elsewhere — *“Shun all sin—open and secret”* (6:120) — and the Prophet ﷺ summarized the whole doctrine in a single sentence: *“Verily, Allah does not look at your faces or your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds.”* (Muslim 2564, from Abū Hurayrah).

*Wa-l-ithm* — and sin. Commentators differ on the specific extension: some read it as the class of sins generally, others as intoxicants by a well-attested usage of *ithm* in the Arabic of the Qur'an (2:219; see also 5:90), others as the inward malice that leads to wrong.

*Wa-a tushrikū bi-Allāh mā lam yunazzil bihi sulṭānā* — and that you associate others with Allah, a practice He has never authorized. The word is *sulṭān*: evidence, warrant, authorization. The Qur'an does not merely say that idolatry is incomplete; it says that the classes of things worshiped besides God are, without exception, unsupported by any evidence. This is a challenge to produce a warrant, and it is issued repeatedly in the Book with the same confidence (10:68; 16:116; 34:22; 46:4).

**The Parallel Lists**

This verse sits inside one of the Qur'an's most systematic treatments of the divine moral law. Sūrat al-Anʿām gives the longer version: *“Come! Let me recite to you what your Lord has forbidden to you: do not associate others with Him ˹in worship˺. ˹Do not fail to˺ honour your parents. We provide for you and for them. Do not come near indecencies, openly or secretly. Do not take a ˹human˺ life—made sacred by Allah—except with ˹legal˺ right. This is what He has commanded you, so perhaps you will understand.”* (6:151), continuing through the orphan's property, honest measure, and truthful speech (6:152). Sūrat al-Isrāʾ gives a third version in a passage of some thirty verses (17:22–39).

**No Authority Sent Down**

The fourth item in the list carries a clause of its own: associating others with God, *a practice He has never authorized*. The qualification states the ground of the prohibition — not the practice’s offensiveness but the absence of warrant — and the Book puts the same criterion to work in its argument: *“Or do they have associate-gods who have ordained for them some ˹polytheistic˺ beliefs, which Allah has not authorized?”* (42:21).

The word behind the clause is *sulṭān*, an authority that can be produced, and this sūrah has already used it of the names given to idols (7:71). Its appearance inside the list is what makes the list a legal text rather than a moral one.

**The Default the Pair of Verses Establishes**

This verse is preceded by a question that carries as much of a ruling as the list does: *“Who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought forth for His servants?”* (7:32). The two together give the jurists the principle they state as the default: things are permitted until a prohibition is established, and prohibitions are established by warrant rather than by preference.

The Book states the principle from inside a ruling on food, where the list is explicitly closed: *“I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to eat except carrion, running blood, swine—which is impure—or a sinful offering in the name of any other than Allah.”* (6:145). The form of that sentence is the point — a search of what has been revealed, an exception, and nothing beyond it.

The report stands in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim at 1499a.
verses.34:
> For each community there is an appointed term. When their time arrives, they can neither delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it

**Neither Delayed nor Advanced**

The clause is echoed almost word for word in Sūrah al-Naḥl, where the same rule is given first as a mercy and then as a limit: *“If Allah were to punish people ˹immediately˺ for their wrongdoing, He would not have left a single living being on earth. But He delays them for an appointed term. And when their time arrives, they cannot delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it.”* (16:61).

**The Same Sentence, Repeated in the Book**

The verse's second half is one of the most repeated formulas in the Qur'an: *lā yastaʾkhirūna sāʿatan wa-lā yastaqdimūn*. It appears in the sūrah of Yūnus, in Sūrat al-Naḥl, in al-Muʾminūn, and elsewhere with the same insistence (10:49; 16:61; 23:43; 7:34; 34:30). The repetition is not a stylistic habit; the Book repeats what its audience is most inclined to forget.

*Sāʿah* means a hour, and the verse's point is its smallness: not that a community may not receive an extension of years, but that not even a hour can be negotiated. The two verbs are the crucial ones — *yastaʾkhirūn*, to put off, and *yastaqdimūn*, to bring forward. The first closes the hope of the procrastinator, who assumes that the deadline can be renegotiated. The second closes the door on the anxious, who fears that his hour may come too soon and who tries to make his arrangements as though he could hurry or delay the decree. Neither is possible, and the verse's grammar states the symmetry exactly: the term can neither be delayed for a moment nor advanced.

Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn restates the law at the level of the individual soul: *“Allah never delays a soul when its appointed time comes”* (63:11). And Sūrat Āl ʿImrān says the same thing from the opposite angle, as a comfort: *“No soul can ever die without Allah's Will at the destined time”* (3:145) — no one dies early, no one is cheated of a moment that was his.

**The Use of the Doctrine**

The Islamic tradition drew two practical conclusions from this verse and its parallels. The first is that urgency belongs to the individual and not to the world. A person cannot know whether his own term will end today; the Book's counsel is that this uncertainty is the structure of moral seriousness, which is why it says that *no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow* (31:34) and *no soul knows in what land it will die* (31:34). The Prophet ﷺ reinforced it with an instruction reported from Ibn ʿUmar: *“Be in this world as a stranger or a traveler”* (al-Bukhārī 6416, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar) — a saying that turns the teaching about the term into a way of carrying one's possessions.

The sūrah's placement of the doctrine in the middle of its prohibitions gives it a practical edge: a community that knows its term is being addressed is a community that cannot pretend its choices are weightless, and the Book's address to the Prophet's city works exactly that way.

The word for the appointed term is *ajal*, and the Book distinguishes two terms under that name: *“He is the One Who created you from clay, then appointed a term ˹for your death˺ and another known only to Him ˹for your resurrection˺”* (6:2).
verses.35:
> O children of Adam! When messengers from among yourselves come to you reciting My revelations—whoever shuns evil and mends their ways, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**Messengers From Among You**

The verse returns to the address that has organized this whole passage: *O children of Adam.* And this time the subject is the arrival of revelation in human form: *immā yaʾtiyannakum rusulun minkum* — should there come to you messengers from among yourselves. The phrase *min anfusikum*, from your own selves, is the sūrah's standing answer to the Makkans' most persistent objection.

That objection is recorded in the Qur'an's own words in at least four places. The Makkans said, *“What kind of messenger is this who eats food and goes about in market-places?”* (25:7). They said that a messenger should be accompanied by an angel (17:92–93). They asked why the Qur'an had not been given to some great man of influence (43:31). The Book's answer is consistent and this verse is part of it: the messenger is *from among you*, because a revelation addressed to human beings must reach them through a channel that shares their condition. The Book states the underlying principle more than once: *“We did not send ˹messengers˺ before you ˹O Prophet˺ except mere men inspired by Us”* (16:43; 21:7; see also 12:109, *“We only sent before you ˹O Prophet˺ men inspired by Us”*).

**The Two Conditions**

The promise that follows has two conditions: *fa-mani ittaqā wa-aṣlaḥa* — then whoever shuns evil and mends their ways. The pair deserves to be examined, because it is the sūrah's summary of what is demanded of the hearer of a prophet, and it names the two dimensions of a life that is being renewed.

*Ittaqā* is the verbal form of *taqwā* — the reverent caution that guards against the divine displeasure, the inward disposition the sūrah named two verses ago as the best of all garments (7:26). It is the vertical axis, and it comes first, because the horizontals of religion are parasitic on it.

*Wa-aṣlaḥa* is the form of *iṣlāḥ*, to repair. Its object is deliberately unspecified, and the commentators have drawn the silence out: the person who is reverent repairs whatever in his condition needs repair — the wrong he has done, the harm he has caused, the property he has taken, the relationship he has broken. The Qur'an uses the word for the making of peace between people (49:9–10), for the improvement of one's own conduct (4:128), and in the mouth of Shuʿayb as the banner of his mission: *“I only intend reform to the best of my ability”* (11:88).

**Where the Formula Recurs Across the Book**

The verse closes with a phrase that recurs in the Qur'an in almost identical form: *fa-lā khawfun ʿalayhim wa-lā hum yaḥzanūn* — there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve. It appears in al-Baqarah for the followers of guidance (2:38), for the believers in the broadest sense (2:62; 5:69), for those who reform (6:48), for the friends of God (10:62), and for those who remain steadfast (46:13). The tradition's commentators found a distinction in its two halves: no fear for what lies ahead, and no grief for what is behind — the two directions in which human anxiety runs, closed by one clause.
verses.36:
> But those who receive Our revelations with denial and arrogance will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever

**The Echo of Iblīs**

The word *istakbara* is the same word the sūrah used for Iblīs in verse 12 — *abā wa-stakbara*, he refused and was arrogant — and in al-Baqarah's account of the same scene, *“who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful”* (2:34). The echo is structural. The sūrah opened its narrative with a creature destroyed by arrogance against a command; here, at the end of the passage addressed to the children of Adam, the same word describes the fate of those who meet the signs of God with disdain. The chapter's answer to its own opening story is that arrogance is not a historical curiosity in the biography of one jinn. It is the recurring disposition that turns rejection into final loss.

Narrative aside, the Book treats *istikbār* as a category of its own with a specific destination. *“Your Lord has proclaimed: Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Surely those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, fully humbled”* (40:60). *“On the Day of Judgment you will see those who lied about Allah with their faces gloomy. Is Hell not a fitting home for the arrogant?”* (39:60). *“The Messiah would never be too proud to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels nearest to Allah. Those who are too proud and arrogant to worship Him will be brought before Him all together.”* (4:172). The last verse is notable for who is included: even the highest created beings are said never to be too proud, which leaves the human arrogance of 7:36 with no model to imitate and no company.

**The Definition the Prophet Gave**

The sūrah's readers would have understood the word, but the Prophet ﷺ defined it, and the definition is a small masterpiece of precision: *“Arrogance is rejecting the truth and belittling people”* (Muslim 91, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd). A single sentence, two halves, and both are present in this verse.

*Rejecting the truth* is the denial: *kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā*. *Belittling people* is what the arrogant posture does to the messenger and to the community of the weak whom the message gathers — and the sūrah's own account of the Makkan leadership is a study in exactly that (see 7:75–76, where the proud ask whether they should believe as the poor do). The Prophet's definition leaves no room for the self-flattering interpretation of arrogance as dignity. In his sentence, it is not a feeling about oneself at all; it is a pair of actions, one toward God's truth and one toward His creatures.

**Residents of the Fire: The Same Sentence in al-Baqarah**

The addition is the verse’s own contribution. Denial alone describes a judgment about the signs; arrogance describes a posture toward them. The sūrah has just given the posture its archetype in Iblīs, whose refusal was stated as a claim of superiority (7:12), and 2:39 is therefore the general rule of which 7:36 is the qualified case.

The commentators read the qualification as decisive. Al-Ṭabarī notes that the verse is placed before the description of the parties at the Heights (7:46–49), so that the reader knows what separates them: not the record of deeds alone but the manner in which the signs were received.

**Endless Ages**

The two verses belong together because neither is a threat addressed to an opponent. 7:36 is a description of a class, given before the histories begin; 78:23 is part of a description of the Day. Both state permanence as a property of the place rather than as a sentence pronounced on an individual, which is why the sūrah can use the statement to frame its narratives.

Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn's image of the arrogant is that they turn their heads aside (63:5); Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own image, six verses later, will be the camel and the needle's eye.
verses.37:
> Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His revelations? They will receive what is destined for them, until Our messenger-angels arrive to take their souls, asking them, “Where are those ˹false gods˺ you used to invoke besides Allah?” They will cry, “They have failed us,” and they will confess against themselves that they were indeed disbelievers

**The Two Crimes That Head the List**

*Fa-man aẓlamu mimman iftarā ʿalā Allāh kadhiban aw kadhdhaba bi-āyātihi* — who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His revelations? The interrogative is rhetorical in form and absolute in force: the question has no answer other than the one the verse has just named. The sūrah has been circling this pair for ten verses. The lie against God was committed by those who said *God has commanded us so* (7:28) and by those who forbade what God had made lawful (7:32). The denial of the signs was the disdain of verse 36.

The Book repeats this superlative with striking consistency. *“Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed”* (6:21). *“Who does more wrong than the one who fabricates lies against Allah or claims, ‘I have received revelations!’—although nothing was revealed to them”* (6:93). *“Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah? They will be brought before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, ‘These are the ones who lied against their Lord’”* (11:18). *“Who then does more wrong than those who lie about Allah and reject the truth after it has reached them?”* (39:32).

**The Messenger-Angels Who Arrive to Take Their Souls**

*Ḥattā idhā jāʾathum rusulunā yatawaffawnahum* — until Our messenger-angels arrive to take their souls. The messengers here are the angels of death, and the Qur'an gives their work a vocabulary of precision. Sūrat al-Sajdah names the office: *“Your soul will be taken by the Angel of Death, who is in charge of you. Then to your Lord you will ˹all˺ be returned.”* (32:11). Sūrat al-Anʿām describes the process of the *tawaffī*, the taking of the soul: *“He reigns supreme over all of His creation, and sends recording-angels, watching over you. When death comes to any of you, Our angels take their soul, never neglecting this duty.”* (6:61). And where the death is a punishment, the account is harsher: *“If only you could see when the angels take the souls of the disbelievers, beating their faces and backs”* (8:50; see also 47:27).

**"They Will Confess Against Themselves"**

The verse closes with self-condemnation: *wa-shahidū ʿalā anfusihim annahum kānū kāfirīn* — and they will confess against themselves that they were indeed disbelievers. The courtroom that has stamped the whole sūrah now gets its confession, and it is not extracted by the prosecutor. Sūrat al-Anʿām has the same formula: *“˹Today˺ you have come back to Us all alone as We created you the first time”* (6:94), and the interrogation of the jinn and humans ends with their own admission — *“We confess against ourselves!”* (6:130; see also 41:21, where the skin itself testifies). Sūrat al-Qiyāmah puts the principle as a general law of the human constitution: *“In fact, people will testify against their own souls, despite the excuses they come up with”* (75:14–15).

**The Messenger-Angels Who Arrive: The Same Scene in an-Naḥl**

7:37 moves from a charge to a scene. The arrival is described in al-Anʿām's account of the same moment, with a detail 7:37 leaves out: *“Those whose souls the angels seize while they wrong themselves will then offer ˹full˺ submission”* (16:28). The submission offered at the gate is the confession that 7:37 reports a few words later, and the two verses describe one event from two angles.

**Where Are Those You Called: The Question Put at the Gate**

The question the angels ask in 7:37 has a parallel in al-Qaṣaṣ, where it is put by Allah Himself on the Day: *“Where are those you claimed were My associate-gods?”* (28:62). The answer given there is the same in substance as the confession in 7:37. The verse that follows it records the disowning that the sūrah describes from the other side: *“Those ˹misleaders˺ against whom the decree ˹of torment˺ is justified will cry”* (28:63) that they led their followers astray and disassociate themselves from them.
verses.38:
> Allah will say, “Enter the Fire along with the ˹evil˺ groups of jinn and humans that preceded you.” Whenever a group enters Hell, it will curse the preceding one until they are all gathered inside, the followers will say about their leaders, “Our Lord! They have misled us, so multiply their torment in the Fire.” He will answer, “It has already been multiplied for all, but you do not know.”

**The Plea of the Last for the First**

*Ḥattā idhā iddārakū fīhā jamīʿan qālat ukhrāhum li-ūlāhum* — until they are all gathered inside, the followers will say about their leaders: *“Our Lord! They have misled us, so multiply their torment in the Fire.”* (7:38) The plea is precisely the one the Qur'an records in four other passages, in almost identical words. Sūrat al-Aḥzāb has the condemned in the Fire saying, *“Our Lord! We obeyed our leaders and elite, but they led us astray from the Right Way. Our Lord! Give them double our punishment, and condemn them tremendously”* (33:67–68). Sūrat Ṣād has the same petition (38:61). Sūrat Sabaʾ records the exchange in full (34:31–33). And Sūrat al-Baqarah states the outcome: those who misled others disown their followers, the bonds between them are cut, and the followers cry out for a second chance (2:166–167).

**"For Each Is Double"**

The "double" is not a doubling of torture; it is the doubling that the Book attaches to whoever combines two offenses. The leader who sinned *and* caused others to sin carries both; the follower who sinned and who imitated another's authority carries what he earned. The same arithmetic is stated as a law of the Book: *“Let them bear their burdens in full on the Day of Judgment as well as some of the burdens of those they mislead without knowledge. Evil indeed is what they will bear!”* (16:25). And it is balanced by the verse of the same Book that says every soul will receive only what it earned: *“No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another”* (35:18; 53:38).

**An Assembly of Jinn and Men**

The verse’s company is mixed: *“Enter the Fire along with the ˹evil˺ groups of jinn and humans that preceded you.”* (7:38). Al-Anʿām describes the same mixed assembly at the gathering: *“˹Consider˺ the Day He will gather them ˹all˺ together and say, ‘O assembly of jinn! You misled humans in great numbers.’”* (6:128).

The charge in 6:128 is addressed to the jinn first and names the number of those misled as great. The reply that follows in that verse is the one 7:38 dramatises: the human associates say that they benefited from one another’s company and have now reached their term. The two verses describe the same relation from the two sides — leading and benefiting — and both end inside the Fire.

**The Acknowledgement Inside the Fire**

The reply fixes what 7:38 assumes. The cursing, the plea and the request for a doubled punishment all occur after the term has been reached, and the sūrah has already stated that no soul is asked to make amends once its term is up (7:53). 35:37 supplies the missing premise in the form of a question: a life long enough had been given, and a warner had come.

Sūrah al-Aḥqāf has the leaders of the people saying, *“We found our forefathers following a particular way, and we are following in their footsteps”* (43:22), and Sūrat al-Zukhruf has the warners anticipate the objection (43:24).
verses.39:
> Then the leaders will say to their followers, “You were no better than us! So taste the torment for what you used to commit.”

**No Advantage Over Us: The Bonds Cut Off**

The leaders' reply at 7:39 is a denial of superiority. The Book records the same denial in a verse that describes what happens to the relation between the two parties, beginning from the Day *“when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off”* (2:166). The disowning and the cutting are two descriptions of one event, and 7:39 gives the words spoken inside it: you were no better than us, so taste the torment for what you used to commit.

**"You Have No Favour Over Us"**

*Fa-mā kāna lakum ʿalaynā min faḍl* — you have no superiority over us. The word *faḍl* is the vocabulary of rank, merit, and advantage; it is the same word the Qur'an uses for God's bounty and for the distinctions He grants among people. The first community's reply is a claim of strict equality: whatever we did, you did; whatever we taught, you accepted; the ledger carries no favour of yours over ours.

The sentence reverses the whole social logic of the world. The Qur'an's earlier verses in this sūrah had shown the same logic operating in religion and being applied to the believers — the arrogant chiefs asking, *“Are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord?”* while the lowly answered, *“We certainly believe in what he has been sent with.”* (7:75–76).

The Book pronounces the same verdict as a general law of the Hereafter. *“No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another”* (35:18; 53:38; 6:164). *“Whoever chooses to be guided, it is only for their own good; and whoever chooses to stray, it is only to their own loss. No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another”* (17:15). The plain meaning of the doctrine is that the moral architecture of this life — rank, influence, dependency, the ability to make others carry one's cost — does not extend across the threshold. Every one of those arrangements which the previous verse showed collapsing is here denied the last consolation it might have claimed.

**The Argument That Fails Everywhere**

The exchange between the leaders and the followers belongs to a family of scenes in which the Qur'an rehearses, in advance, every alibi a human being might carry into the reckoning. Sūrat al-Baqarah's account of the same dispute ends with the followers saying, *“If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us”* (2:167) — that is, the regret is not that they were misled but that they obeyed. In fact, you were wicked on your own”* (34:32).

And the reason the argument fails is that the guidance was never held hostage by any human being. Did messengers not come from among you, proclaiming My revelations and warning you of the coming of this Day of yours?”* (6:130).

The verse that follows in al-Baqarah records the wish that the level produces: *“If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.”* (2:167). The wish is not for a different act in the world but for a second act in the Fire, which is precisely what 7:53 denies when it asks whether there is any intercessor. The leaders at 7:39 are not offering a defence; they are refusing one.

The equality asserted in the Fire is the sūrah's own standard applied to the leaders. The weighing at 7:8–9 measures what each person carried, and no one's record can be transferred to another; the verse at 7:39 is the leaders' acknowledgement of that rule at the moment it operates against them.

The second half of the leaders' reply states the ground of the torment, and the Book states that ground as a rule of the Day: *“Today every soul will be rewarded for what it has done. No injustice Today!”* (40:17)

**Obedience Only in What Is Right**

The Prophet ﷺ drew the line that keeps this verse from becoming a licence for rulers or teachers: "No obedience in disobedience to Allah; obedience is only in what is right" (al-Bukhārī 7257; Muslim 1840, from ʿAlī). Whatever rank a person holds, his command stops where God's command begins. That is why the powerful cannot hide behind the weak, and the weak cannot hide behind the powerful. The obligation to obey is conditional, and the responsibility for a wrong act is personal — which is precisely the acknowledgement the leaders make here.
verses.40:
> Surely those who receive our revelations with denial and arrogance, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle. This is how We reward the wicked

**The Gates That Do Not Open**

*Inna alladhīna kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā wa-stakbarū ʿanhā lā tufattaḥu lahum abwāb al-samāʾ* — surely those who receive Our revelations with denial and arrogance, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them. The verse is a mirror of the one before it, with a single phrase exchanged: where verse 36 said *they are the inhabitants of the Fire*, this verse says what the Fire means in architectural terms. The gates do not open.

The image of the gates of heaven is a Qur'anic constant, and its use here is precise. In Sūrat al-Zumar, the gates are opened for the blessed: *“And those who were mindful of their Lord will be led to Paradise in ˹successive˺ groups. When they arrive at its ˹already˺ open gates, its keepers will say, ‘Peace be upon you! You have done well, so come in, to stay forever.’”* (39:73) — while the disbelievers, driven in groups to the Fire, also find gates, and are told: *“Enter the gates of Hell, to stay there forever. What an evil home for the arrogant!”* (39:72). The Book's heavens are gate-able: Sūrat al-Nabaʾ describes the sky split open, *becoming many gates* (78:19), and Sūrat al-Qamar records the sky’s gates opened with pouring rain (54:11). To say that the gates will not be opened for this group is therefore to say that the entire architecture of access — ascent, acceptance, entry — is closed to them, and the reason given is the one this sūrah has been developing since its first narrative: *disdain*.

**"Until the Camel Passes Through the Eye of the Needle"**

The Prophet ﷺ used the same register for the destination this verse denies, describing the entry of the blessed in terms no camel could satisfy: *“The first group to enter Paradise will be like the full moon”* (al-Bukhārī 3245, from Abū Hurayrah; Muslim 2834 records the same in fuller form). It is not the possession of wealth that bars the gate — the sūrah's own verses on lawful enjoyment (7:31–32) forbid that reading — but the swelling self that makes a person's entry physically impossible.

**What the Verse Says About Divine Exclusion**

Read together with the garden imagery of the whole Book, the verse makes a claim that many modern readers find startling: heaven has a policy. The Qur'an is not vague about who is inside. It names the qualities that enter — reverence and reform in verse 35, faith and right action throughout — and it names the qualities that do not. The early sūrahs of the Makkan period repeat the point in dozens of images, from the balance of al-Qāriʿah (101:6–9) to the books handed right and left (69:19–25).

And yet the Book is careful not to make the gate a function of a single category of person. The verse's own clause requires two acts — denial *and* disdain — and the two together describe a settled character rather than a momentary lapse. The distinction has practical consequences, and the tradition drew them. It is the difference between the person who sins and the person who has decided; between the soul that falls and the soul that has taken up a position against the signs. The sūrah's earlier verses about repentance (7:23) and divine acceptance (2:37) remain available to everyone whose disdain has not become a permanent structure. What the camel-and-needle proverb states is what happens when it has.
verses.41:
> Hell will be their bed; flames will be their cover. This is how We reward the wrongdoers

**The Wrongdoers and the Rule That Spares No One**

The verse ends: *“This is how We reward the wrongdoers.”* (7:41). *Ẓālim* is the sūrah’s standing term, and its uses mark the shape of the argument: the first confession admits it of itself (7:23), the gate of heaven is closed to those who deny and are *ẓālimūn* (7:40), the calf-worshippers are named by their invention (7:152), and the towns are destroyed under the same word.

**The Same Architecture, Elsewhere in the Book**

The image recurs because the Qur'an wants it to. Sūrat al-Zumar states it to the believers as a threat aimed at their own complacency: *“They will have layers of fire above and below them. That is what Allah warns His servants with. So fear Me, O My servants!”* (39:16). Sūrat al-Kahf encloses the wrongdoer in a *muḥīṭ*, a thing that surrounds and from which there is no direction of escape (18:29). Sūrat Ibrāhīm clothes the rebels in tar and covers their faces with flame (14:50), and Sūrat al-Ḥajj cuts garments of fire for the deniers (22:19). Sūrat al-Raʿd's contrast uses the same logic in the other direction: the good word is a tree whose shade and fruit are available to all (14:24–25).

Read next to the paradise verses of the same sūrah — rivers, garments, thrones (7:43; 18:31) — the point becomes plain. The afterlife in the Qur'an is described as a *place* with furniture, because the human beings it addresses are embodied creatures who understand the moral state of a life through the conditions of a home. The pride of verse 36 chose a posture; this verse gives the posture a room.

**"This Is How We Reward the Wrongdoers"**

*Wa-kadhālika najzī al-ẓālimīn* — and this is how We reward the unjust. The phrase closes the verse on a note of exactness, and the vocabulary carries it. *Jazāʾ*, requital, is the Qur'an's term of payment in kind: the wage returned for work done. *“Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it”* (99:7–8). *“Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold. But whoever comes with a bad deed will be punished for only one. None will be wronged” (6:160)* (6:160). The formula *this is how We reward* appears throughout the sūrahs of warning, and in every appearance it forecloses one specific objection — that the punishment of God is arbitrary, or excessive, or born of wounded pride in the way human punishment so often is.

The sūrah has already given the court where the accounting is done: *“The weighing on that Day will be just”* (7:8). This verse names the currency. What is repaid is what was spent, and the recompense is not a change of direction in God's disposition but the arrival of a bill already written.

**A Covering: The Same Noun at al-Baqarah’s Opening**

The two uses describe one covering at two stages. In 2:7 the *ghishāwah* is over the sight and belongs to the present; in 7:41 it is over the body and belongs to the Fire. The commentators read the pair as the same condition completed — what covered the faculties becomes what covers the person — and al-Ṭabarī notes that the verse’s furnishings are named so that no part of the inhabitant is left outside them.

7:41 therefore reports a furnishing and a verdict in the same breath. The verdict is not that the wrongdoers have been treated harshly but that they have been treated exactly, and 10:44 explains why exactness here is not severity: the wrong was self-inflicted, so the return is a measurement rather than an addition.

Sūrat al-Nabaʾ uses it for the earth itself: *“Have We not smoothed out the earth like a bed?”* (78:6), and Sūrat al-Baqarah uses its sibling *firāsh* for the same idea: *“˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you”* (2:22).
verses.42:
> As for those who believe and do good—We never require of any soul more than what it can afford—it is they who will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever

The promise of 7:42 is stated in al-Baqarah in almost identical words: *“And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever.”* (2:82).

**The Sentence That Turns the Page**

Verse 41 ended with a formula: *and so do We recompense the wrongdoers* (7:41). Verse 42 opens with the same construction and the opposite content: *wa-lladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāti* — and those who believed and did righteous deeds.

The closing clause returns the vocabulary of verse 36 to its rightful owners: where the arrogant were *aṣḥāb al-nār*, the residents of the Fire, these are *aṣḥāb al-jannah*, the residents of Paradise, and the abiding is stated in the identical word — *khālidūn*, there forever. In a sūrah that has arranged its arguments in pairs since the first page — the guided and the misguided (7:30), the reverent and the disdainful (7:35–36), the bed of fire and the rivers of the garden — this symmetry is not ornament.

**The Parenthesis That Answers Two Questions**

The Qur'an states it three times in this form and several more in substance: *“Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford”* (2:286), *“We never require of any soul more than what it can afford”* (23:62), *“Allah does not require of any soul beyond what He has given it”* (65:7). It is embedded in the practical legislation of the Book — in the concession for the traveller who cannot fast (2:184–185), in the prohibitions against burdening the nursing mother or the father beyond means (2:233), in the declaration, *“He deserves. ˹it is˺ He ˹Who˺ has chosen you, and laid upon you no hardship in the religion—the way of your forefather Abraham”* (22:78). The tradition drew from it the whole discipline of *taklīf*, the assignment of obligation according to ability, and the jurists built on it the principle that no duty is imposed where it cannot be performed.

The Prophet ﷺ gave the doctrine its practical shape in a hadith the sūrah's readers have always paired with this verse: *“The deeds of any one of you will not save him” — they said, “Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?” — he said, “Not even me, unless Allah envelops me in His mercy. So be moderate and do what you can”* (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816, from Abū Hurayrah — the clause *and give glad tidings* belongs to the report of ʿĀʾishah at al-Bukhārī 6099 and Muslim 2818). Neither the despair nor the presumption survives that sentence.

**The People of the Garden**

The verse then states the destination with a possessive that the sūrah has already used twice: *ulāʾika aṣḥāb al-jannah*. *Aṣḥāb* is the vocabulary of belonging and company — the owner of a house, the companion of a road. The Qur'an does not say the righteous will be admitted to the Garden, though it says that too elsewhere (16:32; 39:73); here it says they *are its people*, and the clause *hum fīhā khālidūn* settles the tenure.

Verse 41 furnishes the Fire. Verse 42 furnishes the Garden with the simplest inventory the Qur'an has: belief, action, and a measure that fits the soul. Verse 43 will give the Garden its voice.
verses.43:
> We will remove whatever bitterness they had in their hearts. Rivers will flow under their feet. And they will say, “Praise be to Allah for guiding us to this. We would have never been guided if Allah had not guided us. The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth.” It will be announced to them, “This is Paradise awarded to you for what you used to do.”

**"We Will Remove Whatever Bitterness They Had in Their Hearts"**

*Wa-nazaʿnā mā fī ṣudūrihim min ghill* — and We shall strip out whatever rancour was in their hearts. The verb *nazaʿa* is the verb of drawing a thing out that has sunk in: a nail from wood, a spear from a wound, a root from soil. *Ghill* is the particular vice it removes — not anger of the moment but the sediment of old grievance, the grudge that has been carried so long it has become part of a person's furniture.

The promise is repeated almost word for word in Sūrat al-Ḥijr, and the following clause there explains the purpose: *“We will remove whatever bitterness they had in their hearts. In a friendly manner, they will be on thrones, facing one another”* (15:47). Facing one another. The Qur'an's Garden is a place where assembly is possible without the history that makes assembly dangerous, and the Book has prepared the reader for why this matters. The sūrah's own account of Ṣāliḥ's people (7:75–76) was a scene of division: the arrogant chiefs on one side, the lowly believers on the other, and a social order in which one group's rank was the other group's humiliation. The Muslim community receiving these verses had come out of a tribal world in which a man's grievance against a clan could last three generations.

What the verse promises is not amnesia but surgery. The memory stays; the poison is extracted. And the phrase is only one of several in which the Book describes the moral hygiene of the Garden: purified spouses (2:25), speech in which no idle talk or falsehood is heard (56:25), a place whose only sound is peace (19:62). The world to come is drawn not as a bigger version of this world's societies but as one whose members have had the thing removed that made society a contest.

**"It Will Be Announced: This Is Paradise Awarded to You"**

*Wa-nūdū a tilkumu al-jannatu ūrithtumūhā bimā kuntum taʿmalūn* — and it will be announced to them: "This is Paradise awarded to you for what you used to do." (7:43) Two grammatical details carry the theology.

The first is the passive *nūdū*: it is announced, and the announcer is unnamed. The sūrah used the same device four verses later, where a nameless caller pronounces condemnation on the wrongdoers (7:44). The message is what matters; the voice belongs to the place.

The second is the verb *ūrithtumūhā*, you have been made its heirs. The Book could have said you have been paid it, or awarded it, or admitted to it. It says inherited — the term of a transfer that no one earns in the ordinary sense. The clause continues *bimā kuntum taʿmalūn*, for what you used to do, and both halves are necessary.
