The sūrah's parenthetical in verse 42 insisted that no soul is burdened beyond capacity; this clause insists that the Garden is not the wage a soul's capacity could ever produce. Sūrat al-Zukhruf speaks of the same place in the same register: *“That is the Paradise which you will be awarded for what you used to do”* (43:72), and Sūrat Āl ʿImrān calls the whole arrangement *an accommodation from Allah* (3:198). The Prophet ﷺ stated the balance in one sentence: the deeds do not entitle anyone, and the deeds are the road. What the verse establishes is that the road and the destination have the same owner.
verses.44:
> The residents of Paradise will call out to the residents of the Fire, “We have certainly found our Lord’s promise to be true. Have you too found your Lord’s promise to be true?” They will reply, “Yes, we have!” Then a caller will announce to both, “May Allah’s condemnation be upon the wrongdoers

**The Call Across the Divide**

*Wa-nādā aṣḥābu al-jannati aṣḥāba al-nār* — and the residents of Paradise will call out to the residents of the Fire. The sūrah's next six verses are built on the verb *nādā*, to call from a distance: here, and again at 7:48, and again at 7:50 where the residents of the Fire cry out to the residents of the Garden. The Book is describing a landscape in which the two populations are within sight and voice of one another, and in which nothing can be exchanged between them but words.

That is a deliberate design, and the sūrah has prepared the reader for it. In this world, the two groups are intermingled and indistinguishable to the outer eye; the sūrah's earlier narratives showed them arguing across a social distance that could still be crossed — the proud chiefs and the lowly believers of Ṣāliḥ's town (7:75–76). Sūrat al-Aʿrāf will make that plain three verses later, when the condemned beg for a drop of water and receive a doctrinal answer instead (7:50).

**The Question That Is the Punishment**

Sūrat al-Aʿrāf records the same admission in another key seven verses later: the day the warning is fulfilled, those who ignored it will say, *“The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth”* (7:53). Sūrat al-Anʿām closes the door on its usefulness: *“On the Day your Lord’s signs arrive, belief will not benefit those who did not believe earlier or those who did no good through their faith”* (6:158).

**The Hope That Lives Inside the Verdict**

The curse of verse 44 is stated in the absolute, and the tradition of the Prophet ﷺ read it within a larger mercy that the Book states in a hundred places. The Messenger of God described what will happen after the reckoning in a report from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī: when the people of the Garden and the people of the Fire have entered their homes, God will say, *“Take out whoever has faith equal to a mustard seed in his heart”* — and they will come out blackened like coal. They will be cast into the river of al-Ḥayyāt, and they will sprout green as a seed does on the bank of a torrent (al-Bukhārī 6560, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī).

**The Greeting the Book Gives Three Times**

This verse is a call across the barrier with no greeting in it, and the absence is what makes the Book’s other crossings worth counting. Wherever the greeting appears it is spoken by angels, and it appears three times in one shape — salutation, then the ground for it. At the taking of the soul: “Peace be upon you! Enter Paradise for what you used to do.” (16:32). At the gates: “Peace be upon you! You have done well, so come in, to stay forever.” (39:73). Inside the Garden, to those who endured: “Peace be upon you for your perseverance. How excellent is the ultimate abode!” (13:24). The exchange here runs the other way: the residents of Paradise call to the residents of the Fire and the Fire calls back, and what crosses is information and reproach rather than peace. The only greeting in the whole passage comes two verses later, from the people on the heights, who greet a party they have not yet joined and are still hoping to enter (7:46).

*Laʿna* in the Qur'an is not profanity but the opposite of mercy: the expulsion of a creature from the radius within which God's special favour operates (2:161; 4:52).

The Book records the same finding as a prayer made before it, in the words of those who ask for what was promised: *“Grant us what You have promised us through Your messengers and do not put us to shame on Judgment Day—for certainly You never fail in Your promise.”* (3:194)

Satan addresses his followers after the judgment: *“Indeed, Allah has made you a true promise. I too made you a promise, but I failed you.”* (14:22)
verses.45:
> those who hindered ˹others˺ from Allah’s Way, strived to make it ˹appear˺ crooked, and disbelieved in the Hereafter.”

**A Catalogue, Not an Insult**

The herald of verse 44 has just pronounced the curse of God upon the unjust. Verse 45 tells the reader whom the word describes: *alladhīna yaṣuddūna ʿan sabīli Allāh* — those who hindered others from Allah’s Way — *wa-yabghūnahā ʿiwajan* — strived to make it appear crooked — *wa-hum bi-l-ākhirati kāfirūn* — and disbelieved in the Hereafter.

The sentence is a three-part diagnosis, and the order of the parts is the order of a process. First a person is turned away from a road. Then the road itself is misrepresented — the seeker is told that it bends this way and does not reach where it claims to reach. Then, at the root, the one who does the misrepresenting has already decided that the destination does not exist. The Qur'an repeats the trio almost verbatim in four other places. The repetition establishes it as a definition rather than a description of a particular historical group: *“who hinder ˹others˺ from Allah’s Path, striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked. Disbelieve in the Hereafter”* (11:19); *“Why do you turn the believers away from the Way of Allah—striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked. You are witnesses ˹to its truth˺?”* (3:99); *“˹They are˺ the ones who favour the life of this world over the Hereafter and hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah, striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked”* (14:3; see also 16:88, where added punishment is promised because of the corruption they spread).

**The Verb That Presupposes a Traveller**

*Ṣadda ʿan* is one of the Qur'an's most sociable verbs: it cannot be used without a second person. You cannot *block* in the abstract; the grammatical form of the sin requires somebody who was walking and was turned back. This is the crime that the sūrah's Makkan leadership is, in the reading of the commentators, most directly charged with: barring the way to the Sacred Mosque, pressuring the new believers of the town, forbidding access to the recitation of the Prophet ﷺ. The Book states that charge at length elsewhere: *“they hinder pilgrims from the Sacred Mosque”* (8:34); *“They are the ones who persisted in disbelief and hindered you from the Sacred Mosque”* (48:25); *“But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque”* (2:217). The Makkan leadership's real offense, on this reading, was not merely unbelief but blockade.

And the verse's principle reaches further than Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ stated the two directions of the traffic in a hadith from Abū Hurayrah: *“Whoever calls others to guidance will have a reward equal to that of those who follow, without anything being diminished from their reward”* — and its mirror, the one who calls to misguidance, carries the load of those who follow (Muslim 2674, from Abū Hurayrah).

**The Engine Underneath**

The last clause supplies the motive: *wa-hum bi-l-ākhirati kāfirūn*. The denial of the Hereafter is not tacked onto the verse as an unrelated item of unbelief; it is offered as the reason the rest of the sentence is possible. In fact, you love this fleeting world, and neglect the Hereafter”* (75:20–21), and it puts the same confession about the Fire in the mouth of the deniers themselves (74:42–46).

The verse therefore closes the circle opened at 7:8, where the scale of the Day was described as just. The people who are cursed in verse 44 are, at bottom, people who removed the scale from their world.

**Ambush on Every Road: The Sūrah's Own Parallel**

The description at 7:45 is a catalogue of three acts, and the sūrah states the same acts as a prohibition addressed to a living community. Shuʿayb tells the people of Midian: *“do not lie in ambush on every road—threatening and hindering those who believe in Allah from His Path and striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked”* (7:86)

The path of God is described by the Book's own opening prayer as *al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm*, the straight way (1:6).
verses.46:
> There will be a barrier between Paradise and Hell. And on the heights ˹of that barrier˺ will be people who will recognize ˹the residents of˺ both by their appearance. They will call out to the residents of Paradise, “Peace be upon you!” They will have not yet entered Paradise, but eagerly hope to

**The Barrier**

*Wa-baynahumā ḥijāb* — and between them a barrier. The word *ḥijāb* is the Qur'an's term for a screen that divides while allowing perception through or across it: the partition that shielded Maryam from her people (19:17), the barrier God placed before the disbelievers so that they cannot grasp the revelation while it is being recited (17:45), the veil that belongs to God's own transcendence (42:51). Here it is a physical feature of the Hereafter, and the Book describes it in another sūrah with a detail this one assumes: *“Then a ˹separating˺ wall with a gate will be erected between them. On the near side will be grace and on the far side will be torment.”* (57:13).

**"They Will Recognize Both by Their Appearance"**

*Yaʿrifūna kullan bi-sīmāhum* — they recognize each group by their marks. The word *sīmā* is the brand a man puts on his cattle, the characteristic by which a tribe is identified in the dark. The Qur'an uses it three times for the Hereafter and the world, and in each place it makes the same claim: the moral quality of a person becomes visible. *“The wicked will be recognized by their appearance, then will be seized by their forelocks and feet”* (55:41). In this world the mark is often invisible — the Book tells the Prophet that he will know the hypocrites *by the tone of their speech* (47:30), and it tells him that the impoverished believers who give in secret are known only *by their mark* to those who look carefully (2:273). On the Day, the recognition becomes the universal reading of a face.

**"Peace Be Upon You"**

*Wa-nādaw aṣḥāba al-jannati a salāmun ʿalaykum.* The verb of the previous verse returns: they call out, and the content of the call is the greeting of Paradise itself. *Salām* is the first word the Book's own liturgy places in the mouths of the redeemed — *“in which their prayer will be, ‘Glory be to You, O Allah!’ and their greeting will be, ‘Peace!’”* (10:10) — and the greeting the angels will give the blessed at the gates: *“Peace be upon you! Enter Paradise for what you used to do”* (16:32; 39:73).

What makes this a moment of high composition is that the greeting is offered by people who have not yet entered. They stand on the wall, they see the gardens, they salute their inhabitants, and their own case is still pending. The Prophet ﷺ spoke of the community's faces being bright with the marks of the worship they performed in the world — *“My community will be called on the Day of Resurrection al-ghurr al-muḥajjalūn, radiant from the traces of ablution”* (al-Bukhārī 136. Muslim 246, from Abū Hurayrah) — and the verse of the Heights shows a group identified by marks and greeting those who have arrived.

**"And They Have Not Entered It, Yet They Hope"**

The verse's last clause is the hinge of the whole scene: *lā yadkhulūnahā wa-hum yaṭmaʿūn* — they have not entered it, but they are eager in hope. The Arabic *ṭamaʿa* means desire tinged with confidence, and the Qur'an uses it for the hope a believer has of forgiveness: Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ places in Ibrāhīm's prayer the words, *“And He is ˹the One˺ Who, I hope, will forgive my flaws on Judgment Day.”* (26:82).

**A Barrier They Never Cross**

7:46 opens with a barrier between the two abodes, and the Book describes a barrier of the same kind in the created world: *“between them is a barrier they never cross”* (55:20), said of the two seas whose waters meet without mixing. The barrier of 7:46 has people standing on it, which the barrier of ar-Raḥmān does not, and that addition is the verse's own contribution.

The greeting of 7:46 is spoken before entry, and the Book records the same greeting at the moment of arrival: *“Peace be upon you for your perseverance. How excellent is the ultimate abode!”* (13:24).
verses.47:
> When their eyes will turn towards the residents of Hell, they will pray, “Our Lord! Do not join us with the wrongdoing people.”

**The Prayer of the Almost-Saved**

*Rabbanā lā tajʿalnā maʿa al-qawmi al-ẓālimīn* — “Our Lord! Do not join us with the wrongdoing people.” (7:47) The petition is not for a rank and not for a gift. It is a request to be kept out of a *company*. *Lā tajʿalnā maʿa* — do not make us *with* — is the vocabulary of placement, and the Book uses it consistently in the mouth of those who understand that the company is the consequence.

The Qur'an's most exact rendering of the sentiment appears in the prayer of the family of ʿImrān, which the sūrah of Āl ʿImrān reports in full: *“Our Lord! We have heard the caller to ˹true˺ belief, ˹proclaiming,˺ ‘Believe in your Lord ˹alone˺,’ so we believed. Our Lord! Forgive our sins, absolve us of our misdeeds, and allow us ˹each˺ to die as one of the virtuous.”* (3:193), preceded by the plea *“Our Lord! Indeed, those You commit to the Fire will be ˹completely˺ disgraced!”* (3:192). Sūrat al-Furqān attributes to the servants of the Merciful the habit of praying, *“Our Lord! Keep the punishment of Hell away from us, for its punishment is indeed unrelenting” (25:65)* (25:65), and Sūrat al-Muʾminūn teaches the same petition in the present life: *“My Lord! I seek refuge in You from the temptations of the devils, and I seek refuge in You, my Lord, that they even come near me”* (23:97–98).

**Why the Fear Is of Company, Not of Pain**

Verse 38 described the communities entering the fire and cursing one another; verse 39 had the first saying to the last, *you have no superiority over us*; verse 40 closed the gates; verse 44 recorded the accusation; verse 45 defined the accused. Sūrat al-Zukhruf states the principle for the whole Day: *“Close friends will be enemies to one another on that Day, except the righteous”* (43:67). Sūrat al-Furqān records the regret of the one who took a bad companion: *“I wish I had never taken so-and-so as a close friend.”* (25:28). And Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt tells the story of a man in the Garden who looks down and sees his old comrade in the Fire (37:51–57).

**Three Groups and Their Three Calls**

7:47 sits inside a scene the sūrah divides into three parties, each of which speaks. The people of Paradise call to the people of the Fire: *“We have certainly found our Lord’s promise to be true. Have you too found your Lord’s promise to be true?”* (7:44). The people of the Heights call to men they recognise by their marks: *“Your large numbers and arrogance are of no use ˹today˺!”* (7:48).

The three calls also carry three different tenses of knowledge. 7:44 reports a promise found true, in the past perfect of a completed discovery; 7:48 reports a reckoning already known to the speakers, who recognise the men they address; 7:47 reports nothing known, only a fear about company. The people of the Heights are therefore described as the party that has found and the party that recognises, while the speakers of 7:47 are described by the direction of their eyes.
verses.48:
> Those on the heights will call out to some ˹tyrants in the Fire˺, who they will recognize by their appearance, saying, “Your large numbers and arrogance are of no use ˹today˺

**Recognized by Their Appearance: The Marks in ar-Raḥmān**

The marks are what the two abodes have in common. The people of the heights recognise the residents of both by their appearance at 7:46, and at 7:48 they recognise particular men among the residents of the Fire.

**"Your Numbers Have Availed You Nothing"**

*Mā aghnā ʿankum jamʿukum* — your multitude has not enriched you in anything. *Aghnā* is the verb of sufficiency: to make someone need nothing more. *Jamʿ* is the mass — the assembled following, the party, the coalition, the mob, the congregation of clients and dependents, the crowd a man can produce when he wants to show that he matters. The sentence declares that the entire apparatus has been weighed and found to have no purchasing power.

This is one of the Book's most persistent themes and one of its least welcome. *“If you were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead you away from Allah's way”* (6:116). *“Most of them do not believe in Allah without associating others with Him in worship”* (12:106). *“Competition for more ˹gains˺ diverts you ˹from Allah˺, until you end up in ˹your˺ graves.”* (102:1–2). *“We are far superior ˹to the believers˺ in wealth and children. We will never be punished.”* — this is the speech of the affluent of Sabaʾ (34:35), and the answer comes in the next verses: *“It is not your wealth or children that bring you closer to Us”* (34:37). Sūrat al-Baqarah records an army that fled its homes in the thousands for fear of death and was told to die (2:243). The Qur'an mentions the size of the crowds that followed the truth and the size of the crowds that opposed it, and it refuses, in either case, to treat the number as an argument.

**"Nor What You Used to Be Arrogant About"**

*Wa-mā kuntum tastakbirūn* — and neither has the arrogance you used to practise. The phrase returns to the sūrah's single diagnosis. Verse 36 described those who *denied Our signs and treated them with disdain*; verse 40 closed the gates of heaven against the same people; verse 48 now names what the disdain was, and whom it was for. The arrogant elite of the sūrah's narratives had defined themselves by the lowliness of the people who believed: the chiefs of Ṣāliḥ's town asking *“Are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord?”* while the lowly answered, *“We certainly believe in what he has been sent with.”* (7:75–76). The disbelieving chiefs of Noah's people telling him that only *the lowliest* follow him (11:27); the people of Shuʿayb lying in ambush on the road to turn back those who believed (7:86).

The Prophet ﷺ gave the two populations their portraits in a single hadith, and no commentary improves on it. Harithah ibn Wahb heard the Messenger of God say: *“Shall I tell you of the people of Paradise? They comprise every poor humble person, and if he swears by Allah to do something, Allah will fulfil it; while the people of the fire comprise every violent, cruel, arrogant person”* (al-Bukhārī 6657, from Ḥārithah ibn Wahb). The verse of the Heights has staged that hadith as a conversation between two populations who can see one another.

**Wealth and Children Do Not Bring Nearness**

What this adds to 7:48 is the measure that replaces the removed one. Numbers avail nothing, and belief joined to good works is multiplied; the arithmetic of the world is replaced by an arithmetic of the record. The sūrah states the same replacement at 7:8–9, where the weighing decides and no soul is wronged, and the verse at 7:48 reports the replacement from inside the Fire, addressed to men whose numbers had been their argument in life.
verses.49:
> Are these ˹humble believers˺ the ones you swore would never be shown Allah’s mercy?” ˹Finally, those on the heights will be told:˺ “Enter Paradise! There will be no fear for you, nor will you grieve.”

**The Question That Names the Mockery**

*A-hāʾulāʾi alladhīna aqsamtum lā yanāluhum Allāh bi-raḥma* — are these the ones you swore would never be shown Allah’s mercy? The verse is a question addressed to the tyrants of verse 48, and it closes the longest single argument the sūrah has constructed: the exchange between the proud and the lowly that began, in the world, with a sneer and now ends in the Hereafter with a demonstration.

The oath in the question is the point of it. *Aqsamtum* is the verb of a solemn sworn claim, and the claim is a denial of God's mercy to specific people — the poor, the dependent, the unimpressive believers who had attached themselves to the messengers. The sūrah's own account of that sneer has already appeared: the arrogant chiefs asking the lowly whether they were sure their prophet was really from God (7:75–76). The Qur'an preserves the same scene in the histories of other prophets. The chiefs of Noah's people said, *“We see you only as a human being like ourselves, and we see that no one follows you except the lowliest among us”* (11:27). The people of Shuʿayb's town asked the prophet, *“How can we believe in you, when you are followed only by the lowest of the low?”* (26:111). And the sūrah of the Cave records the instruction given to the Prophet in the middle of a Makkah that made precisely this calculation: *“And patiently stick with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure. Do not let your eyes look beyond them, desiring the luxuries of this worldly life”* (18:28; see also 6:52).

**The Answer Nobody in the Verse Gives**

*Lā khawfun ʿalaykum wa-lā antum taḥzanūn* — no fear will be upon you, and you will not grieve. The formula is one of the most repeated promises in the Book: it is given to the followers of guidance in the first descent from the Garden (2:38), to all who believe in God and the Last Day and do good (2:62; 5:69), to those who submit themselves to God (2:112), to the friends of God (10:62), and to those who say, *Our Lord is Allah*, and remain steadfast (46:13). Its two halves are exhaustive by design. *Lā khawfun ʿalaykum* — nothing to fear ahead, no threat still in the pipeline, no sentence pending, no loss still possible. *Wa-lā antum taḥzanūn* — nothing to grieve behind, no ache for what was lost, no regret for the years, no memory doing damage. Sūrat Fāṭir gives the residents of the Garden the same sentiment in their own words: *“Praise be to Allah, Who has kept away from us all causes of sorrow”* (35:34), and Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own verse 43 will say that God has removed what was bitter in their hearts.

**The Sūrah's Last Word on the Two Crowds**

The passage ends, as it began in verse 36, on the question of who gets in. It began with a word — *istakbarū*, they disdained — and it ends with a door. Along the way, the sūrah showed the dishonest question (7:37), the community cursing its sister (7:38), the leaders and followers trading blame (7:39), the camel and the needle (7:40), the bed and its covers (7:41), the capacity of the soul (7:42), the song of the grateful (7:43), the call and its answer (7:44), the definition of the unjust (7:45), the people who recognize (7:46), the prayer of the almost-saved (7:47), the useless crowd (7:48), and this command. Every one of those verses made the same distinction in a different register, and the last of them makes it by pointing: these, whom you discounted, are told to enter.
verses.50:
> The residents of the Fire will then cry out to the residents of Paradise, “Aid us with some water or any provision Allah has granted you.” They will reply, “Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers

**What the Condemned Ask For**

*Afīḍū ʿalaynā mina al-māʾi aw mimmā razaqakum Allāh* — pour out on us some water, or any of what Allah has provided you. The request is remarkable for how little it asks. These are the residents of the Fire, and they do not ask to be released, nor to have their punishment reduced, nor even to enter the Garden. They ask for water — for a share of the *provision* of the Garden, in whatever amount, in whatever form. The Book's portrait of damnation at its most concrete is a request for a mouthful.

Sūrat al-Sajdah describes them saying, *“Our Lord! We have now seen and heard, so send us back and we will do good.”* (32:12). Sūrat Fāṭir has them crying, *“Our Lord! Take us out ˹and send us back˺. We will do good, unlike what we used to do. ˹They will be told,˺ ‘Did’”* (35:37). And the sūrah's own verse 53 will record the same plea.

The Gospel gives the same scene in its own phrase: the rich man in torment looks across the chasm and begs that Lazarus might dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his tongue (Luke 16:24).

**Why Water?**

The choice of water as the subject of this final deprivation is not incidental to the sūrah. Water is the Book's standing emblem of mercy and of life: *“We split them apart? And We created from water every living thing.”* (21:30); *“Have you considered the water you drink? Is it you who bring it down from the clouds, or is it We Who do so?”* (56:68–69); *“Say, ‘Consider this: if your water were to sink ˹into the earth˺, then who ˹else˺ could bring you flowing water?’”* (67:30). The sūrah of al-Aʿrāf itself had opened its meditation on God's provision with the rain: *“He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy. When they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land”* (7:57).

**Water in the Fire: The Same Element in al-Ḥajj**

The request at 7:50 is for water or for any provision, and the reply forbids both to the disbelievers. The Book describes water inside the Fire in terms that explain why the request is refused rather than merely denied: *“garments of Fire will be cut out for them and boiling water will be poured over their heads”* (22:19), *“melting whatever is in their bellies, along with their skin”* (22:20)

The verse of al-Ḥajj sets this scene inside a dispute: two opposing groups that disagree about their Lord. The request at 7:50 is made across the same divide as the call at 7:44, and it is the fourth of the sūrah's calls between the two abodes.

The specificity of water is what makes the scene intelligible to the sūrah's reader. The towns of al-Aʿrāf are destroyed in part by water — the flood at 7:133, the rain at 7:84 — and the deliverance of the believers is also by water at 7:160.

**What Landed You: The Category Answer**

The reply at 7:50 names a category rather than the persons asking, and the Book records the same kind of answer given by the condemned themselves. They are asked *“What has landed you in Hell?”* (74:42) and they answer in what they were not: *“We were not of those who prayed”* (74:43), *“nor did we feed the poor.”* (74:44)

The symmetry is not a coincidence of vocabulary; the sūrah has been building to it since verse 32. The point is the teaching about requital in kind that the Book states repeatedly: *“Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it”* (99:8); *“This is the reward for what your hands have done, and Allah is never unjust to His creation”* (3:182).
verses.51:
> those who took this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere amusement and play and were deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life.” ˹Allah will say,˺ “Today We will ignore them just as they ignored the coming of this Day of theirs and for rejecting Our revelations.”

**The Religion Taken as a Hobby**

*Alladhīna ittakhadhū dīnahum lahwan wa-laʿiban* — those who took this faith as mere amusement and play. The construction is worth pausing on. The object of the taking is *dīnuhum* — their own religion, the thing that should have been the organizing axis of their days, the affair to which they belonged. What they made of it was *lahw*, distraction, and *laʿib*, game. The two nouns are the Qur'an's standard pair for whatever occupies a person while having no consequence: the entertainment and the sport, the pastime and the joke.

*“And leave those who take this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere play and amusement and are deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life”* (6:70). And in Sūrat al-Ḥadīd, the divine description of the world's own texture: *“Know that this worldly life is no more than play, amusement, luxury, mutual boasting, and competition in wealth and children.”* (57:20).

The sūrah itself forbade the men who banned God's adornments (7:32) and defended the lawful enjoyment of food, drink, and clothing (7:31). The Book's objection is never to delight; it is to the *demotion* of the highest concern to the level of a trifle.

**"Deluded by ˹Their˺ Worldly Life"**

*Wa-gharrat-humu al-ḥayāt al-dunyā* — and they were deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life. The verb *gharra* is the verb of the mirage: to make a thing look like what it is not, to promise what it will not deliver. The Book uses it constantly and always with the same target: *“So do not let the life of this world deceive you, nor let the Chief Deceiver deceive you about Allah”* (31:33; 35:5); *“the life of this world is no more than the delusion of enjoyment”* (3:185, 57:20).

**"Today We Will Forget Them"**

The verse passes from description to sentence: *fa-l-yawma nansāhum kamā nasū liqāʾa yawmihim hādhā* — so today We will ignore them, just as they ignored the coming of this Day of theirs. The phrase of God "forgetting" is one the Book uses with care, and it never means a lapse of knowledge — the Qur'an's God is the One from whom nothing is hidden (40:16; 2:284). *Nisyān* here is the vocabulary of abandonment: the withdrawal of attention, the cancellation of the relationship. Sūrat al-Sajdah states the same sentence in the same words: *“So taste ˹the punishment˺ for neglecting the meeting of this Day of yours. We ˹too˺ will certainly neglect you.”* (32:14); Sūrat al-Jāthiyah repeats it (45:34); and Sūrat al-Tawbah applies it to the hypocrites who forgot God and were forgotten in turn (9:67).

The word *yajḥadūn* is not the general verb for disbelief. *Juḥūd* is denial of what one knows to be true — the refusal to acknowledge a thing whose evidence is already in hand. Sūrat al-Naml describes the people of the signs as rejecting them *“And, although their hearts were convinced the signs were true, they still denied them wrongfully and arrogantly.”* (27:14), and the sūrah of al-Aʿrāf's own account of Iblīs's fall supplies the pattern: he did not doubt God's existence; he declined to obey. The men of verse 51 are not being condemned for an intellectual failure. They are being condemned for a habit of ignoring what they had already been shown — which is precisely why the verse says *they forgot*, and not *they never heard*.

The Aʿrāf's Makkah was a place where the Prophet's recitation was treated as an entertainment: *“The disbelievers say, ‘This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but a fabrication which he made up with the help of others.’”* (25:4). *“they hear ˹you recite˺ the Reminder, and say, ‘He is certainly a madman.’”* (68:51); *“Indeed, the wicked used to laugh at the believers”* (83:29–30).

The second is stated in al-Ḥadīd as an instrument with an operation of its own: *“You chose to be tempted ˹by hypocrisy˺, ˹eagerly˺ awaited ˹our demise˺, doubted ˹the truth˺, and were deluded by false hopes”* (57:14).
verses.52:
> We have certainly brought them a Book which We explained with knowledge—a guide and mercy for those who believe

**"We Explained It in Detail"**

The verb *faṣṣala* means to separate a thing into its parts so that each one is distinct: the cutting of a text into clear statements, the articulation of a body of teaching into chapters, commands, stories, warnings, and promises. The Qur'an uses it to describe its own composition at its opening pages: *“a Book whose verses are well perfected and then fully explained. It is from the One Who is All-Wise, All-Aware”* (11:1); *“a Book whose verses are perfectly explained”* (41:3). And it uses the same verb for what the Book's opponents demand: *“If only its verses were made clear ˹in our language˺”* — the sūrah of Fuṣṣilat records the objection and answers it (41:44).

The claim *ʿalā ʿilm*, with knowledge, is the one that distinguishes this Book from the other things the Makkans classed it with. The audience of 7:52 had poets, soothsayers, genealogists, and story-tellers, and all of them produced texts out of talent and memory. Sūrat Yā-Sīn denies the poet label outright — *“We have not taught him poetry, nor is it fitting for him.”* (36:69) — and Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah lists the alternatives and rejects them one by one: it is not the word of a poet, not the word of a soothsayer, not the word of a soothsayer-like jinn (69:40–42).

**"A Guide and Mercy for Those Who Believe"**

*Hudan wa-raḥmatun li-qawmin yuʾminūn* — guidance and mercy for those who have faith. Indeed, there has come to you a warning from your Lord, a cure for what is in the hearts, a guide, and a mercy for the believers.”* (10:57). *“We send down the Quran as a healing and mercy for the believers, but it only increases the wrongdoers in loss.”* (17:82).

The promise is generous and the qualifier is exact. The Book is not described as a source of mercy in the abstract. It is *a guide and mercy for those who believe*, and Sūrat Fuṣṣilat explains what it does to those who will not: *“As for those who disbelieve, there is deafness in their ears and blindness to it ˹in their hearts˺”* (41:44). The sūrah of al-Aʿrāf states the law bluntly a few verses later: God will turn away from His signs those who treat them with arrogance (7:146).

**The Explanation Requires Students**

If a Book is explained in detail, its hearers have an obligation that those who receive oracles do not have: the obligation to study. The Qur'an expects its audience to look things up — *“Had they referred it to the Messenger or their authorities, those with sound judgment among them would have validated it.”* (4:83) — and the sūrah of Muḥammad instructs them to reflect on it directly: *“Do they not then reflect on the Quran? Or are there locks upon their hearts?”* (47:24). Sūrat al-Nisāʾ goes further and makes recitation, memorization, and teaching the identifying work of a community (4:82; 9:122).

The Prophet ﷺ summarized the resulting status in a sentence the tradition has never stopped repeating: *“The best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it”* (al-Bukhārī 5027, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān). Verse 52 is the doctrinal ground under that hadith.

**What the Sūrah Does With the Book**

Al-Aʿrāf returns to revelation as its anchor verse after verse. It opened with the letters *alif lām mīm ṣād* and the announcement of a Book revealed so that its Prophet might warn (7:2). It told its readers, *“Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not take others as guardians besides Him”* (7:3). It will say of itself that it is *“˹This is˺ a Book which We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ so that you may lead people out of darkness and into light”* (14:1). It will close the section on the people of the Heights with the reminder that those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer are not forgotten (7:170).

Verse 52 therefore sits in the sūrah as the answer to every scene that has preceded it. The mockers of 7:51 treated the revelation as entertainment; the condemned of 7:50 had nothing to drink; the people of the Heights recognized everyone by their marks.

7:52 describes a Book brought with knowledge, and the description has a close parallel at the opening of Fuṣṣilat: *“a revelation from the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful”* (41:2), *“a Book whose verses are perfectly explained—a Quran in Arabic for people who know”* (41:3).
verses.53:
> Do they only await the fulfilment ˹of its warning˺? The Day it will be fulfilled, those who ignored it before will say, “The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth. Are there any intercessors who can plead on our behalf? Or can we be sent back so we may do ˹good,˺ unlike what we used to do?” They will have certainly ruined themselves, and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them

**The Question of the Waiting**

*Hal yanẓurūna illā taʾwīlahu* — do they only await its fulfilment? The verb *yanẓurūn* here is not the word for looking but the word for waiting in suspense, and the noun is one of the Qur'an's most interesting technical terms. *Taʾwīl* is the coming-to-be of a statement: the point at which a proclamation stops being a prediction and becomes a fact. Sūrat Yūsuf uses it for the fulfilment of the dream (12:100); Sūrat Yūnus uses it for the fulfilment of a warning that the mockers had asked to be hurried (10:39).

The question is so a rebuke in the form of an observation. Sūrat al-Zukhruf puts the same question to the mockers — *“Are they waiting for the Hour to take them by surprise when they least expect ˹it˺?”* (43:66) — and Sūrat al-Anʿām adds the warning that belief on the morning of arrival will be of no use (6:158).

**"Or We Could Be Sent Back"**

*Aw nuraddu fa-naʿmala ghayra alladhī kunnā naʿmal* — or be sent back so we may do ˹good,˺ unlike what we used to do. The request for return is the Book's most repeated final plea: *“Our Lord! Take us out ˹and send us back˺. We will do good, unlike what we used to do. ˹They will be told,˺ ‘Did’”* (35:37); *“My Lord! Let me go back, so I may do good in what I left behind.”* (23:99–100); *“If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us”* (2:167); *“Our Lord! We have now seen and heard, so send us back and we will do good.”* (32:12). Sūrat al-Zumar records the same request in the first person: *“If only I had a second chance, I would have been one of the good-doers”* (39:58) — and the Book states elsewhere the ransom such a speaker would offer: *“Even if the wrongdoers were to possess everything in the world twice over, they would certainly offer it to ransom themselves”* (39:47; see also 13:18; 3:91).

And the Book's refusal is equally consistent, and it is not cruelty. Sūrat al-Anʿām has already given the reason with a precision that makes the plea collapse: if they were returned they would return to exactly what was forbidden them (6:28). The sūrah of Yūnus puts the same anatomy of repentance on record: the repentance of the drowning is not counted as faith (10:90–91).

**"They Have Ruined Themselves"**

The verse's last sentence ends the scene with an accounting: *qad khasirū anfusuhum* — they will have certainly ruined themselves — *wa-ḍalla ʿanhum mā kānū yaftarūn* — and whatever they fabricated will fail them. The word *khasira* is the trader's word for losing his capital. The Book uses it for those whose capital was the self: *“But those whose scale is light, they have doomed themselves for wrongfully denying Our signs.”* (7:9); *“The ˹true˺ losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on Judgment Day. That is indeed the clearest loss.”* (39:15). The parable is exact.

**The Request to Be Sent Back, Elsewhere**

The request the verse records is made in the same words at two different moments, and the Book reports both. At death: *“My Lord! Let me go back,”* (23:99), and the answer is immediate — *“It is only a ˹useless˺ appeal they make. And there is a barrier behind them until the Day they are resurrected.”* (23:100). At the judgment the request returns with the same two grounds, sight and hearing: *“Our Lord! We have now seen and heard, so send us back and we will do good. We truly have sure faith ˹now˺!”* (32:12).

The second of the verse’s two wishes asks for intercessors, and the Book has already told its readers what the Day will contain in that respect: *“before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining, friendship, or intercession”* (2:254).
verses.54:
> Indeed your Lord is Allah Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days, then established Himself on the Throne. He makes the day and night overlap in rapid succession. He created the sun, the moon, and the stars—all subjected by His command. The creation and the command belong to Him ˹alone˺. Blessed is Allah—Lord of all worlds

**"In Six Days"**

The phrase *sittati ayyām* has drawn the attention of every commentator, and two lines of reading are worth preserving. The first concerns the measure: a "day" in the Qur'an's own usage is not necessarily a solar day. Sūrat al-Ḥajj states that *“But a day with your Lord is indeed like a thousand years by your counting.”* (22:47), and Sūrat al-Maʿārij gives the measure of a day as fifty thousand years (70:4). What the verse tells the reader, therefore, is not a schedule but a manner: the creation was brought about in ordered stages, not in a single stroke.

The second line concerns the purpose of the number. Sūrat Hūd's version of the verse continues, *“to test which of you is best in deeds”* (11:7), connecting the six days to a moral project rather than to a mechanics. And the Book is emphatic about one implication the number has been misused to draw: *“We created the heavens and the earth and everything in between in six Days, and We were not even touched with fatigue”* (50:38).

**"Then He Rose over the Throne"**

*Thumma istawā ʿalā al-ʿarsh.* The Throne — *al-ʿarsh* — is the Book's image of the seat of universal authority: the angels carry it (69:17), circle it (39:75), and glorify God around it (40:7); God's All-Encompassing Seat, the *Kursī*, extends over the heavens and the earth (2:255). The verse's claim is that the One who made the world governs it from that authority, and the sūrah later adds its practical consequence: *“Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly.”* (7:55) — the God being addressed is the owner, not a distant first cause.

What is not disputed is the point being made. The Prophet ﷺ tested the belief of a slave girl whom her master intended to free, asking her, *“Where is Allah?”* She answered, *“In the heaven,”* and he ruled that she was a believing woman and ordered her freed (Muslim 537, from Muʿāwiyah ibn al-Ḥakam).

**"His Is the Creation and the Command"**

*Tabāraka Allāh rabbu al-ʿālamīn* — blessed is Allah, Lord of all worlds. *Tabāraka* is the Book's formula of exalted generosity, used at the openings of Sūrat al-Furqān and Sūrat al-Mulk over precisely the same doctrine — the One who sent the Criterion, the One in whose hand is dominion (25:1; 67:1). *Rabb al-ʿālamīn*, the Lord of all worlds, is the appellation with which the Book's own opening sūrah names Him (1:2). The phrase *al-ʿālamīn* includes every order of creation — the angels, the jinn, humanity, and every species and system the reader does not know.

The next verses will explain what a person is supposed to do about that: call on Him, in humility, in secret, with hope and fear, and not corrupt the earth after it has been set right (7:55–56).

**The Bearers of the Throne**

The connection to 7:54 is one of rank. 7:206 closes the sūrah with those nearest to God not too proud to worship Him; 40:7 describes them at the Throne, glorifying and asking forgiveness for people on the earth.

**Creation and Command, Then Supplication**

This is also why the verse is placed where the sūrah places it. The preceding section has described the Day and its parties (7:36–53); 7:54 turns from the hereafter to its Maker, and 7:55 turns from the Maker to the act by which a person addresses Him.

**Seven Verses, One Formula**

The formula is not local to this verse. Counted from this repository’s translations, the establishment on the Throne is stated seven times: here, at 10:3, 13:2, 20:5, 25:59, 32:4 and 57:4. Yā-Sīn states it with no sequence marker at all: “the Most Compassionate, ˹Who is˺ established on the Throne.” (20:5).

The word *musakhkhar* is the term for a thing compelled into service, and the Book uses it of everything in the natural order that serves human life: the day and the night, the sun and the moon, the ships at sea, the rivers, the winds, the clouds (16:12; 14:33; 45:13).

The Qurʾān’s own support is the answer about the spirit — “Its nature is known only to my Lord, and you ˹O humanity˺ have been given but little knowledge.” (17:85) — the spirit being named as belonging to the Lord’s *amr*.
verses.55:
> Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly. Surely He does not like the transgressors

**From the Throne to the Supplication**

Verse 54 ended with the claim that the creation and the command belong to God, and the next two verses explain what a creature is supposed to do about that claim. The doctrine moves immediately into practice: the One who made the heavens and the earth is the One who is asked. Sūrat al-Baqarah states the same proximity in its own way — *“When My servants ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about Me: I am truly near. I respond to one’s prayer when they call upon Me”* (2:186) — and Sūrat Ghāfir supplies the command with a warning attached: *“Your Lord has proclaimed: Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Surely those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, fully humbled”* (40:60).

**Teacharrruʿan wa-Khufyatan: The Two Adverbs**

The sūrah returns to the same instruction in its own later verse, in a line that is the practical commentary on this one: *“Remember your Lord inwardly with humility and reverence and in a moderate tone of voice, both morning and evening. And do not be one of the heedless.”* (7:205) — that is, the same two adverbs, applied to remembrance rather than request. Sūrat al-Isrāʾ takes the pulse of the regulation from the other side, in the middle of an argument with the pagans about the manner of their prayer: *“Do not recite your prayers too loudly or silently, but seek a way between.”* (17:110).

The two clauses answer the two clauses of 7:55 — an invitation with a promised response, and a fate for those too proud to accept it.

**Hope and Fear: The Posture Named in al-Anbiyāʾ**

The three verses agree on the components: a call, two motives held together, and a humility stated in the body — humbling before God, abandoning the bed. 7:55 supplies the manner of the voice; 21:90 and 32:16 supply the manner of the heart and of the limbs. Read together they describe the act the sūrah commands as a whole.

The commentators note that hope and fear are named together everywhere the Book describes an accepted call, because either alone distorts it: hope without fear is the transgression of presumption, fear without hope is the transgression of despair. That is the same balance the sūrah states at 7:56, where the two terms appear again in the verse that follows this one.

The same root names the boundary-crossers of verse 55's legal context throughout the Book: *“O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder— a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. But if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian, then bloodmoney should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously.”* (2:178), *“do not exceed the limits. Surely Allah does not like transgressors.”* (2:190).

Sūrat al-Furqān puts the last piece in place: it is not the volume of the prayer or the standing of the suppliant that determines the answer. The fact that the one calling is calling the One who responds — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘You ˹all˺ would not ˹even˺ matter to my Lord were it not for your faith ˹in Him˺. But now you ˹disbelievers˺ have denied ˹the truth˺, so the torment is bound to come.’”* (25:77).
verses.56:
> Do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order. And call upon Him with hope and fear. Indeed, Allah’s mercy is always close to the good-doers

**The Command to Repair What Is Set Right**

*Wa-lā tufsidū fī al-arḍ baʿda iṣlāḥihā* — and do not spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order. The verse sits immediately after the command to call upon God humbly, and its placement makes a religious point that the Qur'an never leaves in doubt: the disorder that the Book calls *fasād* is not only a civic nuisance. It is damage done inside a repair.

The word *iṣlāḥ* — the setting right — is the sūrah's own term for what the messengers came to do. Verse 35 described the saved as those who *reform*; the first command of the sūrah's opening address was to follow what has been sent down (7:3). Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's prophets are consistently described as *nāṣiḥ* — sincere, repairing counsellors (7:62, 7:68, 7:79). *Fasād*, its opposite, covers the whole field of ruin: the destruction of crops and livestock (2:205), the breaking of treaties, the exploitation of the weak, and the corruption of religion, which the sūrah has been cataloguing since verse 28.

**Corruption With a History**

The Book uses this verse's vocabulary consistently in its accounts of ruined nations. Sūrat al-Baqarah describes the mischief-maker who is told not to corrupt the earth and answers that he is merely a reformer: *“Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it.”* (2:11–12). Sūrat al-Rūm states the general law: *“Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people’s hands have done, so that Allah may cause them to taste ˹the consequences of˺ some of their deeds and perhaps they might return ˹to the Right Path˺”* (30:41). And Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ records Shuʿayb's prohibition in the same terms: *“And do not follow the command of the transgressors — who spread corruption throughout the land, never setting things right”* (26:151–152).

The sūrah's own use of the verb will arrive twice within a few verses: once in Hūd's reminder to ʿĀd (7:74) and once in Shuʿayb's to his people (7:85). Its presence here, before the first prophet appears, makes it a footnote under the whole succeeding narrative: the towns the sūrah is about to describe did not fall for a single crime, they fell for the systematic undoing of what had been set in place.

**"Call Upon Him With Hope and Fear"**

*Wa-dʿūhu khawfan wa-ṭamaʿan.* The verse returns to supplication and now gives it its emotional content. *Khawf* is fear of the consequence and the judgment; *ṭamaʿ* is the eager hope of recompense and forgiveness. Sūrat al-Sajdah describes the believing worshippers as *“invoking their Lord with hope and fear”* (32:16); Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ states that the prophets *“in doing good. Call upon Us with hope and fear”* (21:90); Sūrat al-Zumar asks, with a touch of rebuke, whether the one who *“hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of their Lord?”* is equal to the heedless (39:9). Sūrat al-Isrāʾ places the same fear in the prayer of every sincere suppliant (17:57).

The doctrinal effect of the pair is a balanced religion. Fear without hope curdles into despair, and the Book condemns it explicitly (12:87; 39:53); hope without fear curdles into presumption, and the Book condemns that too — *“Did they feel secure against Allah’s planning? None would feel secure from Allah’s planning except the losers.”* (7:99). The one supplication that is forbidden by 7:55 is the one that has lost the fear; the one that is sterile is the one that has lost the hope.

**"Mercy Is Near"**

The verse closes: *inna raḥmata Allāhi qarībun mina al-muḥsinīn* — indeed, Allah’s mercy is always close to the good-doers. Sūrat al-Baqarah's verse about the divine response says simply, *“I am near”* (2:186), and the Qur'an speaks of God's help in the same phrase when it reassures a besieged community: *“Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy”* (39:53).

The qualifier concentrates the promise on conduct. *Muḥsinūn* — those who do good, who do a thing well — carries in the Book the sense of a life with quality in it: the Book's first mention of the term at 2:195 attaches it to generous spending, and 4:125 to the religion of Abraham.

What *iḥsān* means is fixed by the only report that defines it: in the ḥadīth of Jibrīl the angel asks the Prophet ﷺ to state it. He answers that it is to worship God as though you see Him, and that if you do not see Him, He sees you (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 8; Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 50, on the authority of ʿUmar b. Al-Khaṭṭāb).
verses.57:
> He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy. When they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land and then cause rain to fall, producing every type of fruit. Similarly, We will bring the dead to life, so perhaps you will be mindful

**The Winds That Herald the Mercy**

*Huwa alladhī yursilu al-riyāḥa bushrā bayna yaday raḥmatihi* — He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy. The winds go before the rain the way a messenger goes before a king. The Book adopts the imagery in several places with the same term: *“And He is the One Who sends the winds ushering in His mercy. We send down pure rain from the sky”* (25:48). *“And one of His signs is that He sends the winds, ushering in good news ˹of rain˺ so that He may give you a taste of His mercy”* (30:46); *“He is the One Who shows you lightning, inspiring ˹you with˺ hope and fear, and produces heavy clouds”* (13:12).

*Bushrā* is the announcement given to a person awaiting news; *raḥma* here is specifically rain, the sustenance that keeps a desert population alive from one season to the next.

**The Argument From the Dead Land**

*Ḥattā idhā aqallat saḥāban thiqālan suqnāhu li-baladin mayyitin* — until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land. The progression is careful: the winds, the clouds, the journey of the clouds by a movement the verse attributes to God (*suqnāhu*, We drove it), the rainfall, and then the fruit. What is emphasized is the destination. The clouds are not sent to the sea, where the rain would be wasted, or to the fertile mountains; they are driven to the *mayyit* — the corpse-land, the dust that has no green on it.

Then comes the application: *kadhālika nukhriju al-mawtā laʿallakum tadhakkarūn* — similarly, We will bring the dead to life, so perhaps you will be mindful. The comparison is drawn in the Book repeatedly and with a consistent structure: rain revives a dead land, and that revival is the closest thing in the experience of the Book's audience to the resurrection. *“And We send down blessed rain from the sky, bringing forth gardens and grains for harvest”* (50:9), followed a verse later by *“˹as˺ a provision for ˹Our˺ servants. And with this ˹rain˺ We revive a lifeless land. Similar is the emergence ˹from the graves˺.”* (50:11). Sūrat al-Rūm makes the inference explicit: *“See then the impact of Allah’s mercy: how He gives life to the earth after its death! Surely That ˹same Creator˺ can raise the dead” (30:50)* (30:50; 16:65; 45:5; 22:5).

**The Resurrection Argument in Its Own Register**

The Book's readers have often noted that its proofs of the resurrection are drawn overwhelmingly from agriculture and gestation rather than from philosophy. *“You sow? Is it you who cause it to grow, or is it We Who do so?”* (56:63–64). *“O humanity! If you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then ˹know that˺ We did create you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then ˹developed you into˺ a clinging clot ˹of blood˺, then a lump of flesh —fully formed or unformed—to show ˹Our power˺ to you.”* (22:5). *“And it is Allah Who sends the winds, which then stir up ˹vapour, forming˺ clouds, and then We drive them to a lifeless land, giving life to the earth after its death. Similar is the Resurrection.”* (35:9).

Sūrah Yā Sīn: *“There is a sign for them in the dead earth: We give it life, producing grain from it for them to eat.”* (36:33).
verses.58:
> The fertile land produces abundantly by the Will of its Lord, whereas the infertile land hardly produces anything. This is how We vary ˹Our˺ lessons to those who are thankful

**The Parable of Two Soils**

*Wa-l-baladu al-ṭayyibu yakhruju nabātuhu bi-idhni rabbihi* — the good land brings forth its vegetation by the permission of its Lord — *wa-lladhī khabutha lā yakhruju illā nakidan* — and the land that is bad brings forth nothing but with difficulty. The verse applies the rain of verse 57, and it is stated as an observation of nature that any farmer in the audience could test. Two plots of ground receive the same rain. The good soil answers with a crop; the exhausted, salty or stony ground, though it receives the same water, gives back little.

The Qur'an builds a whole doctrine on this image, and the sūrah of Ibrāhīm has the most developed version: *“Do you not see how Allah compares a good word to a good tree? Its root is firm and its branches reach the sky, ˹always˺ yielding its fruit in every season by the Will of its Lord.”* — and immediately, the bad counterpart: *“And the parable of an evil word is that of an evil tree, uprooted from the earth, having no stability.”* (14:24–26). Sūrat al-Raʿd adds the element of foam: the torrent carries away the dross while the water that is useful stays for people, and the Book concludes the image with a sentence that reads like an interpretive note: *“This is how Allah sets forth parables.”* (13:17).

**"This Is How We Vary ˹Our˺ Lessons"**

*Kadhālika nuṣarrifu al-āyāt li-qawmin yashkurūn* — this is how We vary ˹Our˺ lessons to those who are thankful. The verb *ṣarrafa* is the Book's word for turning a thing through its aspects: to put a subject in different lights so that each angle is exhausted, to rotate an argument. The Qur'an uses it repeatedly as a description of its own method: *“And so We vary our signs to the extent that they will say, ‘You have studied ˹previous scriptures˺,” and We make this ˹Quran˺ clear for people who know.’* (6:105). *“We have surely varied ˹the signs˺ in this Quran so perhaps they may be mindful, but it only drives them farther away. Other Gods?”* (17:41).

**The Rain Parables Elsewhere in the Book**

This parable belongs to a family, and the family is worth reading together because each member varies a different term. Sūrah al-Raʿd makes the water the variable: *“He sends down rain from the sky, causing the valleys to flow, each according to its capacity.”* (13:17). Sūrah al-Zumar makes time the variable: *“then produces with it crops of various colours, then they dry up and you see them wither, and then He reduces them to chaff”* (39:21). Sūrah al-Baqarah makes the giver’s intention the variable, in the image of the garden on the height: *“when heavy rain falls, it yields up twice its normal produce. If no heavy rain falls, a drizzle is enough.”* (2:265).

**The Prophet’s Own Parable of Three Grounds**

The commentators set beside this verse a parable the Prophet ﷺ gave of his own mission, and the comparison is instructive because it adds a third ground. *“The example of guidance and knowledge with which Allah has sent me is like abundant rain falling on the earth, some of which was fertile soil that absorbed rain water and brought forth vegetation and grass in abundance”* (al-Bukhārī 79, from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, in the Book of Knowledge). The report continues with a second portion that is hard and holds the water for people to drink and irrigate from. A third that is barren, holding nothing and growing nothing; the first ground is the one who understands the religion and teaches it, the last the one who takes no notice of it at all.
verses.59:
> Indeed, We sent Noah to his people. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous Day.”

**The First of the Five Towns**

*Laqad arsalnā Nūḥan ilā qawmihi* — indeed We sent Noah to his people. With this verse the sūrah begins the longest sequence of prophetic narratives in the Qur'an: Noah (7:59–64), Ḥūd and ʿĀd (7:65–72), Ṣāliḥ and Thamūd (7:73–79), Lot (7:80–84), Shuʿayb and Madyan (7:85–93), followed by Moses and the children of Israel in the longest installment of all (7:103–171). Each of the five pre-Mosaic accounts follows a recognizable architecture: the calling, the accusation by the town's elite, the messenger's defense, the warning, and the end. The reader who has received the parable of the two soils in verse 58 is now shown the same rain falling five times on the same kind of ground.

**"I Fear for You the Torment of a Tremendous Day"**

*Innī akhāfu ʿalaykum ʿadhāba yawmin ʿaẓīm* — I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous Day. The formula is the sūrah's own and its speakers' — Ḥūd and Ṣāliḥ will speak in the same register, and Sūrat al-Zumar's prophet uses the identical phrase (39:13). The *tremendous Day* is the Day of Judgment, and the sūrah has already defined it three times in its own voice (7:14, 7:51, 7:53). What is distinctive in Noah's sentence is the verb: *I fear for you*, not *I warn you of what is about to happen to you*.

The pastoral vocabulary of the messengers — *my people*, *I fear for you*, *sincere advice* — is set against the vocabulary of the towns — *misguided*, *fool*, *liar* — and the sūrah's reader is invited to compare the two dictionaries at his leisure.

**Noah in the Book's Larger Portrait**

The Qur'an gives Noah the longest continuous treatment of any pre-Mosaic prophet, and the details of the other passages fill out what the sūrah assumes. Sūrat Nūḥ preserves his private reasoning with his Lord over the centuries of his calling: *“My Lord! I have surely called my people day and night, but my calls only”* (71:5–6). Sūrat Hūd records the elite's argument that he is merely a man like themselves and that only the lowest follow him (11:27), and Noah's response that he will not drive the believers away (11:29–30). Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt gives the duration: *“Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, and he remained among them for a thousand years, less fifty.”* (29:14).

**Sent in the Language of His People**

Ibrāhīm states the rule that governs the sending: *“We have not sent a messenger except in the language of his people to clarify ˹the message˺ for them. Then Allah leaves whoever He wills to stray and guides whoever He wills.”* (14:4)

The pairing explains what the five towns’ cycle is for. The message is delivered in terms the hearers cannot claim to have misunderstood, which is why each refusal in the sūrah is a refusal of something understood. 14:4’s second sentence removes the last available excuse, and the sūrah’s refrain — *fa-kayfa kāna ʿāqibat al-mukadhdhibīn* — is the demonstration of it town by town.

**A Thousand Years Less Fifty**

Both verses name the Day early. 7:59 has it as *“the torment of a tremendous Day”* (7:59); Shuʿayb’s address in Hūd has the same structure: *“I truly fear for you the torment of an overwhelming Day.”* (11:84). The formula belongs to the messengers rather than to the narrators, and it appears in the mouth of the first and of the last of this sūrah’s five.
verses.60:
> But the chiefs of his people said, “We surely see that you are clearly misguided.”

**The Verdict of the Elite**

*Qāla al-malaʾu min qawmihi innā la-narāka fī ḍalālin mubīn* — the chiefs of his people said: we surely see you in clear misguidance. The sentence is short and it does three things at once, and all three are the standard operating procedure of the sūrah's towns.

First, it identifies the speakers: *al-malaʾ*, the assembled notables — the men whose standing gives them the authority to pronounce. The Qur'an uses this term for the elite of every ruined city in this sūrah, and it uses it as a diagnosis. Noah's town (7:60), ʿĀd (7:66), the court of Pharaoh (7:103), Madyan's affluent leaders (7:88) — in each case the first voice raised against the messenger is the voice of established power. The ordinary people of the towns are not the ones who speak; the sūrah will later show them believing (7:75) and being silenced.

Second, the sentence is not an argument but a classification. Noah has just delivered a message about the worship of the One God and a warning about the Day; the response says nothing about either. What the chiefs supply instead is a label, *ḍalāl mubīn*, clear misguidance — one of the two verdicts the sūrah's narratives will trade in, the other being *liar*, which ʿĀd will use of Ḥūd (7:66) and Thamūd of Ṣāliḥ (7:77). The Qur'an's actors prefer the label because the label requires no reasoning: it moves the discussion from what was said to who is saying it.

**The Word Turned Around**

The label's irony is the sūrah's own. *Ḍalāl* — misguidance, straying — is the Qur'an's technical term for the condition of those who reject revelation, and the sūrah's earlier verse 30 had already used it in the divine voice: *“He has guided some, while others are destined to stray”* (7:30). From the chiefs' mouths, the word is a verdict on Noah; from the Book's, it is a verdict on them. Sūrat al-Naḥl records the same inversion at the Day of Judgment, where the followers of the misleaders say, *“For those who disbelieve and hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah, We will add more punishment to their punishment for all the corruption they spread.”* (16:88; see also 33:67–68).

**The Elite as a Category in the Qur'an**

The Qur'an's analysis of the *malaʾ* deserves attention because it is one of the Book's most consistent social observations. Sūrat al-Muʾminūn's version of Noah's narrative has the chiefs say, *“But the disbelieving chiefs of his people said ˹to the masses˺, ‘This is only a human like you, who wants to be superior to you. Had Allah willed, He could have easily sent down angels ˹instead˺. We have never heard of this in ˹the history of˺ our forefathers.”* (23:24). Sūrat Hūd's has them argue that only *the lowliest* follow him (11:27). Sūrat Sabaʾ has the affluent of a town explain their superiority in wealth and children (34:35). Sūrat al-Zukhruf has the Makkans object that the Qur'an should have been sent to *a great man of the two cities* (43:31).
verses.61:
> He replied, “O my people! I am not misguided! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds

**"Lord of All Worlds"**

The title Noah uses is the one the sūrah used a few verses earlier in its own voice: *Tabāraka Allāh rabbu al-ʿālamīn* (7:54). The echo is deliberate. The chiefs of the town have just measured a man by the standards of their settlement; the man has just named the authority he represents as the Lord of every world. Makkah, for all its importance as a sanctuary, was one town among thousands; the message being proclaimed in it belonged to a jurisdiction that has no boundary.

Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ puts this contrast at the head of every one of its prophets' speeches: *“I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you. So fear Allah, and obey me. I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds.”* (26:107–109; 26:127; 26:145; 26:164; 26:180). The phrase is the Qur'an's shorthand for the universality of the prophetic claim and the total absence of a local interest in it. Noah is not asking for the ḥimā of a clan or a share of the caravan traffic; he is announcing a message that has no patrons.

**"I Am Not Misguided" — Prophetic Self-Definition**

The Books of the prophets in the Qur'an show a consistent reticence: the messenger never defends his own spiritual attainment, and he never claims personal authority. Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's Shuʿayb answers a similar charge by pointing to what is *with Allah* (7:89); Hūd says less than Noah does here (7:67); and Ṣāliḥ's rebuke of his people in verse 79 places the whole affair in the category of *counsel delivered*. The Book's only claim on behalf of its messengers is the message: *“Your fellow man is neither misguided nor astray. Nor does he speak of his own whims.”* (53:2–3), and *“Say, ‘I am not the first messenger ever sent, nor do I know what will happen to me or you. I only follow what is revealed to me. And I am only sent with a clear warning.’”* (46:9).

The reticence is doctrinal, not modest. Sūrat Fuṣṣilat states the same position in the Prophet's own voice: *“I am only a man like you, ˹but˺ it has been revealed to me that your God is only One God”* (41:6).

**The Familiar Address**

The verse's opening words are worth keeping in view: *yā qawmi*, O my people. Noah has been pronounced misguided, and he answers by calling the accusers his own. The Book's prophets never sever the relationship while the argument continues, and the sūrah's five narratives show this address surviving every stage short of the destruction: Noah uses it here, Hūd in his replies (7:65, 7:68), Ṣāliḥ at the end of his town's history, when he turns away saying, *“O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice”* (7:79), and Shuʿayb in the last speech of the sequence (7:89).

**Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn**

The title with which the denial is followed is the Book’s first word about God: *“All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds,”* (1:2). The word *ʿālam* is derived by the classical lexicons from the root for a sign or a mark, so the worlds are everything that functions as a sign of its Maker — a derivation that makes the title a claim about evidence as well as about ownership.

The prophets use the title when they state their commission, and Mūsā defines it for a court that has just asked who the Lord of the worlds might be: *“˹He is˺ the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, if only you had sure faith.”* (26:24). In this sūrah the same title carries Nūḥ’s reply, Hūd’s, Ṣāliḥ’s and Shuʿayb’s, and it is the first thing the magicians say when they fall down believing (7:121–122).
verses.62:
> conveying to you my Lord’s messages and giving you ˹sincere˺ advice. And I know from Allah what you do not know

**"And I Know From Allah What You Do Not Know"**

*Wa-aʿlamu mina Allāh mā lā taʿlamūn* — and I know from Allah what you do not know. The sentence is the epistemological edge of the prophetic claim, and the Book's messengers keep it sharp. The knowledge in question is not information about the future or mastery of hidden things; Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own Ḥūd will declare no such possession, and Sūrat Hūd records Noah saying explicitly that he does not claim the treasures of God or knowledge of the unseen (11:31). What the messengers do have, in the Book's consistent account, is something received: *“Nor does he speak of his own whims. It is only a revelation sent down ˹to him˺.”* (53:3–4).

The verse's audience is being asked to entertain the possibility that a human being might have access to facts about the moral structure of reality that they have not been given — and that this access is not a rank but a burden. Say, ‘I am not a keeper over you’”* (6:66; see also 6:107).

**The Two Ways of Hearing the Verse**

The classical commentators read the pair of duties as a division of labour that answers two very different impulses in the messenger's audience. I will soon show ˹all of˺ you the home of the rebellious.”* (7:145), and the Book's final prophet is instructed simply to recite (96:1). The Qur'an's messengers are not allowed to become authorities over conscience — *“You are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺.”* (88:22), *“Had Allah willed, they would not have been polytheists. We have not appointed you as their keeper, nor are you their maintainer.”* (6:107) — but they are required to be sincere.

The combination protects both the message and the messenger's humanity. Noah's century of calling, in the Book's telling, is filled with both duties: he explains and he pleads (71:5–20).

**Conveying: The Verb of Reaching**

Hūd describes his office with two participles: *uballighukum* — conveying to you — and *anṣaḥu lakum*, advising you. A *balāgh* is a message delivered to the point where nothing remains undelivered, which is why the Book uses the same root for the completion of a term (7:142) and of a life.

Al-Māʾidah states the office in the imperative: *“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and beware! But if you turn away, then know that Our Messenger’s duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺ clearly.”* (5:92). The verse separates obedience from delivery and makes the second the whole of the messenger’s charge — the same separation 13:40 states as delivery on one side and judgment on the other.

**Disclosed Only to a Messenger of His Choice**

The verse’s second clause is a claim about knowledge: *“And I know from Allah what you do not know.”* (7:62). Then He appoints angel-guards before and behind them.”* (72:26–27).

The two verses answer the charge Hūd’s people have just made — that he is in clear error and foolishness (7:66). A knowledge disclosed only to a chosen messenger and guarded by appointed angels is not a knowledge a man invents, and the sūrah’s formulation is careful: he knows *from Allah*, *min Allāh*, which names the source rather than the extent.

This is why the clause follows the two duties rather than preceding them. 72:27 adds the guardians because the disclosure is the point at which the enemy would intervene, and the sūrah has already described that intervention (7:27).

The Book uses it for the man of Madyan who warned Moses of a plot against him (28:20) and for the brother of Yūsuf, and it is the standard term for the religious duty of giving good counsel to those who are open to it.

*“And it was revealed to Noah, ‘None of your people will believe except those who already have. So do not be distressed by what they have been doing’”* (11:36) — the disclosure arrives after the centuries of argument and confirms what the messenger had learned from God rather than from the town.

In the account of Noah to come, the town's answer to a century of speech is a decision to wait and see: *“O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky”* (8:32 is Makkan rhetoric; Noah's own version is 71:23–24).
verses.63:
> Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own, warning you, so you may beware and perhaps be shown mercy?”

**"Do You Wonder?"**

*A-wa-ʿajibtum a jāʾakum dhikrun min rabbikum ʿalā rajulin minkum* — do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own? The question is the sūrah's answer to the towns' real objection, and it is stated with an incredulity that turns the tables. The chiefs find it *astonishing* that God would send a human being; the verse asks what else they expected.

The Qur'an records the objection in several forms and answers it in kind. *“And they say ˹mockingly˺, ‘What kind of messenger is this who eats food and goes about in market-places ˹for a living˺? If only an angel had been sent down with him to be his co-warner,”* (25:7). *“And nothing has prevented people from believing when guidance comes to them except their protest: ‘Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?’”* (17:94). The Book's reply to the last one is the most elegant: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Had there been angels walking the earth, well settled, We would have surely sent down for them an angel from heaven as a messenger.’”* (17:95). The choice of messenger follows the nature of the addressee; revelation comes in the tongue of the people who must receive it, and the Qur'an says so directly elsewhere: *“We have not sent a messenger except in the language of his people to clarify ˹the message˺ for them. Then Allah leaves whoever He wills to stray and guides whoever He wills.”* (14:4).

**The Argument From Human Ordinariness**

Behind the objection sits an assumption the sūrah is dismantling: that divine speech requires a superhuman vehicle, that a creature who eats and sleeps and dies cannot be a conduit for something eternal. Do you not understand?’”* (10:16).

The Book returns to this protection in its accounts of the messengers' humanity. They are men who eat food (25:20), who marry and have children (13:38), who grieve and get angry, who die. Sūrat al-Kahf instructs the Prophet to declare, *“I am only a man like you, ˹but˺ it has been revealed to me that your God is only One God.”* (18:110). The humanity is not a compromise; it is the design.

**"A Reminder From Your Lord"**

*Dhikr* — the key word of the verse — is the Qur'an's own name for revelation: a reminder, not a new invention. The Book's self-presentation is that it restores what the human being already knows and has let slip. *“It is certainly We Who have revealed the Reminder, and it is certainly We Who will preserve it.”* (15:9). *“So, ˹continue to˺ remind ˹all, O Prophet˺, for your duty is only to remind.”* (88:21).

The sūrah's own audience had the same reminder in the same form: *“This is a blessed Book which We have revealed—confirming what came before it—so you may warn the Mother of Cities and everyone around it.”* (6:92). Its Prophet was told to say that his message and the earlier ones share a single source (41:43; 46:9). Verse 63's use of the word places Noah's preaching on the same continuum as the Book being recited in Makkah.

**A Mercy for the Whole World**

Read against 7:63 the verse explains the structure of the question’s clauses. Warning is first, then wariness, then mercy — the order of a process whose end is not the warning. 21:107 states the end without the process, and the two together describe an office whose form is severe and whose content is not.

Sūrat al-Anʿām puts the principle in a single line: *“and ‘If Allah touches you with harm, none can undo it except Him. And He is the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.’”’* (10:107).

Sūrat al-Mulk's question answers it across the whole world: *“Have they not seen the birds above them, spreading and folding their wings? None holds them up except the Most Compassionate.”* (67:19).
verses.64:
> But they rejected him, so We saved him and those with him in the Ark, and drowned those who rejected Our signs. They were certainly a blind people

**The Ending of the First Town**

*Fa-kadhdhabūhu fa-anjaynāhu wa-lladhīna maʿahu fī al-fulki* — but they rejected him, so We saved him and those with him in the ark. The sūrah has compressed the entire flood into a single sentence, and the compression is the point. What the town did is stated first and in one word, *kadhdhabūhu*: they declared him a liar. What God did follows immediately: the rescue and the drowning. Between the two clauses stands the whole of a civilization's history, and the sūrah gives it the length of a comma.

The reader of the Qur'an knows the details from the other accounts: the sign given to Noah about the oven (11:40), the pairs of every species loaded into the vessel (11:40), the ark riding on waves like mountains (11:42), the son who would not board (11:42–43), the call from the ship to a world that had mocked it for a century (11:42), the waters that rose until the vessel came to rest on al-Jūdī (11:44). The command to the sky and the earth, *“O earth! Swallow up your water. And O sky!”* (11:44). Sūrat al-Qamar gives the whole event four verses and a purpose: *“We certainly left this as a sign. So is there anyone who will be mindful?”* (54:15).

**The Ark as the Sūrah's Image**

In the architecture of the sūrah, the ark carries more than its cargo. Ḥūd's people are saved by mercy (7:72), the believers in Thamūd are named as the lowly who spoke up (7:75), and Lot's family leaves in the night (7:83).

The vessel itself is described elsewhere in the Book with a vocabulary that makes it the prototype of the Hereafter's escape routes. *“And it was said, ‘O earth! Swallow up your water. And O sky! Withhold ˹your rain˺.’ The floodwater receded and the decree was carried out. The Ark rested on Mount Judi, and it was said, ‘Away with the wrongdoing people!’”* (11:44). Sūrat al-Qamar, as noted, preserves the ship as a permanent sign (54:15), and Sūrat al-Muʾminūn adds the teaching about *taskhīr*: the ark rides by God's command (23:27). The Book's use of the flood as a model of the resurrection is explicit in Sūrat al-Qamar: *“So We opened the gates of the sky with pouring rain, and caused the earth to burst with springs, so the waters met for a fate already set.”* (54:11–12).

Sūrat al-Qamar describes the vessel — *“We carried him on that ˹Ark made˺ of planks and nails”* (54:13) — and states its purpose: *“We certainly left this as a sign. So is there anyone who will be mindful?”* (54:15).
