Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah addresses the drowned generation directly: *“Indeed, when the floodwater had overflowed, We carried you in the floating Ark ˹with Noah˺, so that We may make this a reminder to you, and that attentive ears may grasp it”* (69:11–12).

The sequence is the same one the reader met in the Hereafter scenes: the refrain that began with the question *who is more unjust than the one who invents a lie about God?* (7:37) reaches its first historical instance here. The next four towns will run the experiment again with different people, different gods, and identical results.

The Qur'an's vocabulary of blindness is used consistently for the failure of perception rather than of eyesight — *“They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb. Blind, so they will never return”* (2:18); *“whoever is blind ˹to the truth˺ in this ˹world˺ will be blind in the Hereafter”* (17:72) — and the Book's most complete statement of the doctrine appears in this very sūrah, eleven verses later: *“They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with.”* (7:179).

The Book records the same deliverance elsewhere and adds what was made of it: *“But We delivered him and those in the Ark, making it a sign for all people.”* (29:15)
verses.65:
> And to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. Will you not then fear Him?”

**ʿĀd and Their Brother**

*Wa-ilā ʿĀdin akhāhum Hūdan* — and to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd. The sūrah's second city is introduced with a phrase that carries more weight than its brevity suggests. *Akhāhum* — their brother — is the Qur'an's way of locating the messenger inside the community he addresses. Hūd is not a stranger sent from elsewhere with a warrant; he is a man of ʿĀd, known to its families, sharing its water, its grazing, and its ancestors. The Book uses the same word for every pre-Mosaic messenger in this sequence: the brother of ʿĀd, the brother of Thamūd, the brother of Madyan (7:65, 7:73, 7:85).

The effect is an intensification of the towns' responsibility rather than a softening of the message. The Qur'an's classic statement of the point appears in Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ, where the townsmen are told that their messenger's credentials are local: *“when their brother Hûd said to them, ‘Will you not fear Allah?’”* (26:124, with the same opening for Ṣāliḥ, Lūṭ, and Shuʿayb at 26:142, 26:161, 26:177), and the Prophet's own community is reminded that there *“certainly has come to you a messenger from among yourselves”* (9:128). The Book's summons is never exotic. It arrives in the voice of a neighbour, and the towns' decision to reject it is a decision about someone they could have questioned any day of the week.

**The People of Iram**

ʿĀd is not a footnote in the Qur'an; it is the Book's standing example of a civilization destroyed by strength. Sūrat al-Fajr names their city with a grandeur the Book reserves almost exclusively for it: *“˹the people˺ of Iram—with ˹their˺ great stature, unmatched in any other land;”* (89:7–8). Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ lists their monuments and asks whether they built them for eternity: *“˹Why˺ do you build a landmark on every high place in vanity, and construct castles, as if you are going to live forever”* (26:128–129). Sūrat Fuṣṣilat records the boast that the sūrah turns into their epitaph: *“As for ’Ȃd, they acted arrogantly throughout the land with no right, boasting, ‘Who is superior to us in might?” Did they not see that Allah ˹Himself˺, Who created them, was far superior to them in might? Still they persisted in denying Our signs.’* (41:15).

**"Worship Allah; You Have No God Besides Him"**

Hūd's message is Noah's message, word for word, and the sūrah does not vary it. *“He has ordained for you ˹believers˺ the Way which He decreed for Noah, and what We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what We decreed for Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, ˹commanding:˺ ‘Uphold the faith, and make no divisions in it.’”* (42:13).

The verse then adds the ending that the sūrah gives to Hūd alone: *a-fa-lā tattaqūn* — will you not then fear Him? The sūrah's own opening used the same construction to open the whole sūrah: *“˹This is˺ a Book sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺— do not let anxiety into your heart about it—so with it you may warn ˹the disbelievers˺, and as a reminder to the believers. Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not take others as guardians besides Him. How seldom are you mindful!”* (7:2–3), and Sūrat al-Naḥl's affirmation of the divine oneness closes with a similar question (16:51–52).

**The Wind That Ended Them**

The end of ʿĀd is described in al-Ḥāqqah in terms that complete the sūrah's account: *“as for ’Ȃd, they were destroyed by a furious, bitter wind”* (69:6), *“which Allah unleashed on them non-stop for seven nights and eight days. That you would have seen its people lying dead like trunks of uprooted palm trees.”* (69:7)

The image answers the stature described in al-Fajr. The sūrah of al-Aʿrāf reports the same end in its own terms at 7:72, where the people are cut off to the last and the disbelievers are saved from nothing.
verses.66:
> The disbelieving chiefs of his people responded, “We surely see you as a fool, and we certainly think you are a liar.”

**The Grammar of Social Defense**

The verse is careful about who is speaking: *al-malaʾu alladhīna kafarū min qawmihi* — the disbelieving chiefs of his people. The qualifier is doing explicit work. The sūrah has already told its readers, in the account of Ṣāliḥ, that the elite and the ordinary believers were distinct groups (7:75–76); here the particle *alladhīna kafarū* marks off the notables who disbelieved from the town as a whole. The Book does not hold a people responsible for its leadership's unbelief unless the people follow them into it.

**The Qur'an's Reply to Both Charges**

The Book answers the two accusations throughout its narrative sections with weapons it never tires of using. To the charge of folly, it answers with the Criterion itself: a text whose coherence is offered as evidence, recitation whose like no human being has produced (2:23; 10:38; 11:13; 17:88), and the plain fact that the messengers' claims about the natural order — rain, dead land, resurrection — are the claims their audiences already accepted about their own agriculture. To the charge of lying, it answers with the messengers' biographies: the century of Noah's preaching, the decades of Hūd's presence among people who knew his honesty, the disinterestedness of their message. *“I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds.”* (26:109; 26:127; 26:145; 26:164; 26:180). A liar has a motive; the Book repeatedly points out that the messengers had none.

Sūrat Fuṣṣilat renders the whole exchange in a form that strips the charges of their respectability: *“The disbelievers advised ˹one another˺, ‘Do not listen to this Quran but drown it out so that you may prevail.’”* (41:26). That is the same defense in a cruder register, and the sūrah's version — fools and liars — is only the dressed-up form of the same tactic.

**The Same Two Charges in the Other Histories**

The double accusation is not particular to Hūd. Shuʿayb’s people make it in nearly the same words: *“You are simply bewitched! Also, you are only a human being like us, and we think you are indeed a liar.”* (26:185–186). Nūḥ’s chiefs put one half of it as a verdict on his guidance: *“We surely see that you are clearly misguided.”* (7:60). The Book reports the charge in its most elaborated form in Sūrah Hūd, where the chiefs add the social argument to the personal one: *“We see you only as a human being like ourselves, and we see that no one follows you except the lowliest among us.”* (11:27).

**What the Charges Assume**

Both charges assume that the messenger is to be assessed by the standards the town already uses. To call a man a fool is to say that he fails the test of practical judgment by which its own leading men are judged; to call him a liar is to say that his word fails the test of reliability by which its merchants are judged. Hūd’s reply accepts the form of the assessment and refuses its jurisdiction: *“O my people! I am no fool! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds,”* (7:67), *“conveying to you my Lord’s messages. And I am your sincere advisor.”* (7:68).
verses.67:
> Hûd replied, “O my people! I am no fool! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds

**The Same Answer in the Same Words**

*Qāla yā qawmi laysa bī safāhatun wa-lākinnī rasūlun min rabbi al-ʿālamīn* — Hûd replied: “O my people! I am no fool! But I am a messenger from the Lord of all worlds.” (7:67) Hūd's reply is Noah's reply transposed by one letter of vocabulary: Noah denied *ḍalālah*, misguidedness; Hūd denies *safāhah*, folly. Everything else is identical, down to the address *yā qawmī* and the title *rabb al-ʿālamīn*.

The repetition is one of the sūrah's boldest compositional decisions, and it is not a stylistic failure. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ, which tells the same five narratives at greater length, organizes itself around a refrain repeated verbatim by each prophet: *“I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you. So fear Allah, and obey me. I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds”* (26:107–109, 26:125–127, 26:143–145, 26:162–164, 26:178–180). The Book's audiences were meant to hear the cadence and to draw the inference: the message has one source, and the messengers are its successive carriers rather than its authors.

**The Prophet's Own Commission**

The title *rasūl min rabbi al-ʿālamīn* is also the title the sūrah applied to Muhammad in its opening verses, and the Book links the two missions explicitly. And I am only sent with a clear warning.”* (46:9). Sūrat al-Shūrā grounds the unity more deeply: *“He has ordained for you ˹believers˺ the Way which He decreed for Noah, and what We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what We decreed for Abraham, Moses, and Jesus”* (42:13).

What the Makkan chiefs were hearing, therefore, when the Prophet recited Hūd's denial, was not a piece of ancient history. It was a mirror held up in their own assembly, in which their own accusations — *a poet, a soothsayer, a man had* (69:41–42; 52:29–30) — were shown to be the latest edition of a document that had been in use for millennia.

**Foolishness as a Charge Running Both Ways**

The charge answered in this verse is *safāhah* — foolishness, from *s-f-h*, the opposite of sound judgment in conduct rather than of intelligence. I am no fool!”* (7:67). Al-Jinn uses the same word of speech about God: *“and that the foolish of us used to utter ˹outrageous˺ falsehoods about Allah.”* (72:4).

The sūrah records the exchange from both sides. The chiefs answer Hūd at 7:66 with a charge of foolishness and a denial of his message; he answers at 7:67 by refusing the charge and stating his office.

**The Lord of All Worlds, Answered**

Hūd names his sender as *rabb al-ʿālamīn* — the Lord of all worlds. Ash-Shuʿarāʾ records what happened when the same title was used before a ruler: Pharaoh asked what the Lord of all worlds was (26:23), and Mūsā answered, *“˹He is˺ the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, if only you had sure faith.”* (26:24).

The answer defines the title by its scope. *ʿĀlam* is the collective of all that is other than God — the worlds of men, of jinn, of angels — and 26:24 gives the definition in the terms of creation: heavens, earth, and what is between. That is the same scope 7:54 describes when it lists what God created and what He subjected.

Hūd’s use of the title is therefore not a formula but a claim about jurisdiction. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the messengers of this sūrah all use *rabb al-ʿālamīn* — Nūḥ (7:61), Hūd (7:67), Mūsā (7:104) — and that the repetition is the sūrah’s way of stating that the five towns were addressed by one Lord.

When his people drove him from al-Ṭāʾif, the tradition reports that he prayed for them rather than against them. And Sūrat al-Qalam, addressing the accusations of the Makkan chiefs point by point, ends with an instruction to patience and a reminder of the man of the whale, who called out in the darkness (68:48).
verses.68:
> conveying to you my Lord’s messages. And I am your sincere advisor

**The Counsel and the Commission**

*Uballeghukum rasālāti rabbī wa-anā lakum nāṣiḥun amīn* — conveying to you my Lord’s messages, and I am your sincere advisor. Hūd's sentence repeats Noah's double duty with one addition at the end: *amīn*, trustworthy. The word crowns the verse, and it belongs to the vocabulary of deposit and return. *Amīn* is the person entrusted with something — a caravan's goods, a household's stores, a secret — who returns it whole. The messenger is a trustee of the message, and the term claims for the transmission the reliability the towns were denying him in the previous verse.

The slogan is the same one that the Qur'an uses for the Prophet himself: *“I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you”* (26:107, 26:125, 26:143, 26:162, 26:178), and the sequence in Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ shows it deliberately repeated by each prophet in the sūrah's own cadence. Trustworthiness is the one quality the Book insists on for its messengers: not brilliance, not eloquence, not miracles, but the faithful return of what was entrusted to them.

**What Trustworthiness Is For**

The Qur'an's arguments for revelation lean heavily on this attribute, and the way it uses it is nearly forensic. A message is only as good as its carrier; a messenger who alters the text to suit his audience destroys the evidence he is bringing. So the Book's repeated insistence that the Prophet recite without adjustment — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘I do not say to you that I have Allah’s treasuries or know the unseen, nor do I claim to be an angel. I only follow what is revealed to me.”* (6:50) — and its equal insistence that the message be delivered whole, including the parts that are inconvenient to its own community: *“What is revealed to me is that I am only sent with a clear warning.’”* (38:70). *“Say, ‘I am not the first messenger ever sent, nor do I know what will happen to me or you. I only follow what is revealed to me. And I am only sent with a clear warning.’”* (46:9).

**Sincerity Without Return**

*Nāṣiḥ* — the sincere adviser — reappears here, the second use of the word in the sūrah's sequence, after Noah's. What the messengers do not receive for it is left unrecorded. Nowhere in the sūrah's narratives does the sincere adviser of a town profit in any way from his counsel; the Qur'an's prophets are poor, mocked, boycotted, and in most cases driven out. Hūd's audience will end the story by asking him to justify himself with a miracle and will then call for the destruction he warned them of (7:70). The Book's prophets are, by design, without leverage.

Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ' formula makes this explicit in the messenger's own voice: *“I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the Lord of all worlds.”* (26:127). The repeated phrase means that any account of religion as a profession of self-interest must fail against the Book's own description of its prophets, and ʿĀd's charges — fool and liar — collapse against a man with nothing to gain.

**The Word for Sincere Counsel**

The second clause is built on *naṣīḥah*, which is not a sentiment but an activity. The root *n-ṣ-ḥ* carries the sense of purifying a thing of what adulterates it — honey strained of wax, cloth cleared of a flaw — and the counsellor is the one who hands over something undiluted. The sūrah uses the word of Nūḥ in the same construction: *“conveying to you my Lord’s messages and giving you ˹sincere˺ advice. And I know from Allah what you do not know.”* (7:62), and Nūḥ returns to it when the advice has failed: *“My advice will not benefit you—no matter how hard I try—if Allah wills ˹for˺ you to stray.”* (11:34).
verses.69:
> Do you find it astonishing that a reminder should come to you from your Lord through one of your own so he may warn you? Remember that He made you successors after the people of Noah and increased you greatly in stature. So remember Allah’s favours, so you may be successful.”

*Udkhurū idh jaʿalakum khulafāʾa min baʿdi qawmi Nūḥ* — remember that He made you successors after the people of Noah. The verse turns from the messenger's credentials to the audience's history, and it uses a word that occurs at several key points in the sūrah: *khulafāʾ*, successors, deputies, the ones who come after. The Qur'an uses it for humanity's viceregency on the earth (2:30), for the generations that inherit a land after its inhabitants (7:74, 7:100, 10:14, 27:62), and for David's succession (38:26).

**"And Increased You Greatly in Stature"**

*Wa-zādakum fī al-khalqi basṭatan* — and He increased you in the creation, in stature. The phrase has been read as referring to physical size, and the tradition of commentary preserves reports about the height and strength of ʿĀd; it has also been read more broadly as increase in means — the stretch and abundance of their possessions, the grandeur of their buildings. Both readings fit the Book's account of the town, which elsewhere stresses their monuments and their boasts. Sūrat al-Fajr's description of the pillar-city, *the like of which was never created in the lands* (89:8), and Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ's reproof about the palaces built as though their makers would live forever (26:129), support the wider sense.

**"So Remember the Favours of Allah"**

*Fa-dhkurū ālāʾa Allāh laʿallakum tufliḥūn* — so remember the favours of Allah, so that you may succeed. *Ālāʾ* is the Qur'an's word for the successive gifts of God, and the sūrah will use the same instruction in the next narrative, from Ṣāliḥ (7:74). The command to remember is not an invitation to sentimentality. In the Book's usage, remembrance is the act of tracing a good thing back to its source, which is why it is so closely bound up with gratitude — the faculty the sūrah named at the close of the parable about the soils (7:58).

The connection between remembering and success is stated here as a chain: the town's prosperity is a fact, the source of the prosperity is a knowable fact, and the outcome of acknowledging the second depends on what the town does with the first.

**The Test of Blessing in the Book**

The Qur'an uses prosperity as a trap and as a mercy with a consistency that has always unsettled comfortable readers. Sūrat al-Anʿām describes a people showered with everything they desired until they became proud of what they were given and were cut off (6:44). Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ describes Qārūn, who said his wealth was due to knowledge he had, and was swallowed by the earth (28:78–81). And Sūrat al-Aʿrāf itself will shortly tell of the towns whose security was taken from them *while they were sleeping* (7:97–98).

**The Refrain of Wonder**

The question opening this verse — do you find it astonishing — is the sūrah’s refrain, put first to Nūḥ’s people (7:63) and then to ʿĀd here. Outside the sūrah the same wonder is named and answered at the opening of Sūrah Yūnus: *“Is it astonishing to people that We have sent revelation to a man from among themselves?”* (10:2), a verse that goes on to report what the disbelievers called the man who brought it.

The same word is used elsewhere of an endowment of another kind, when the prophet of the Banū Isrāʾīl answers the objection to Ṭālūt’s kingship: *“Allah has chosen him over you and blessed him with knowledge and stature.”* (2:247).
verses.70:
> They said, “Have you come to us so that we would worship Allah alone and abandon what our forefathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if what you say is true!”

**The Demand for the Punishment**

*Qālū a-jiʾtanā li-naʿbuda Allāha waḥdahu wa-nadhara mā kāna yaʿbudu ābāʾunā* — they said: have you come to us so that we worship Allah alone and give up what our fathers used to worship? The response is the sūrah's clearest statement of the towns' real objection, and it is not a religious one. The chiefs of ʿĀd are not denying that a single God might exist; they are objecting to a proposal that would require them to abandon the religion of their ancestors.

The objection is answered in the Book with a consistency that repays attention. Sūrat al-Zukhruf puts it in the words of every town in history: *“We found our forefathers following a ˹particular˺ way. We are following in their footsteps.”* (43:22) — and the Book supplies God's answer to all such claims: *“Even if what I brought you is better guidance than what you found your forefathers practicing?” They said, “Even if what I brought you is better guidance than what you found your forefathers practicing?” They replied, “We totally reject whatever you have been sent with.”* (43:22–24). Sūrat al-Baqarah's account of the same reflex is sharper still: when the people of Israel were told to follow what God had revealed, they answered, *“We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.”* — and they too were asked whether their fathers had understood anything at all (2:170).

**"Then Bring Us What You Threaten Us With"**

*Fa-ʾtinā bimā taʿidunā in kunta mina al-ṣādiqīn* — bring us what you threaten us with, if what you say is true. The challenge converts the argument into a test of strength, and the sūrah's towns use it repeatedly: Thamūd demands the punishment from Ṣāliḥ (7:77), the Makkans demand it of the Prophet (8:32; 46:22), and the Qur'an records the formula on the lips of the impatient in nearly every era: *“Our Lord! Hasten for us our share ˹of the punishment˺ before the Day of Reckoning.”* (38:16).

The Book's answer to the taunt is not a scheduled miracle but a statement about the purpose of delay. *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Perhaps some of what you seek to hasten is close at hand.’”* (27:72), and Sūrat Yūnus explains why the postponement exists: *“If Allah were to hasten evil for people as they wish to hasten good, they would have certainly been doomed. But We leave those who do not expect to meet Us to wander blindly in their defiance.”* (10:11; see also 16:61, 35:45). The towns treat the absence of the penalty as evidence of impunity; the Book treats the gap as the mercy that keeps them alive.

**The Fathers as an Argument**

The sūrah's question at 7:71 will name that warrant with a single word — *sulṭān*, authority — and its absence is the whole case against the gods of ʿĀd. Verse 38 of the sūrah has already staged the end of the argument in the Hereafter, where communities curse their predecessors as they enter the Fire, and where the excuse of following others is refused (7:39).

**Rain Stones Upon Us: The Demand Elsewhere**

The verse of al-Anfāl shows the assumption in its plainest shape, since the people ask for stones from the sky as the condition of believing. In al-Aʿrāf the same assumption appears in the demand at 7:70 and in the refusal at 7:132, where the court declares that no sign will move it; both are statements that the evidence offered is not the evidence required.

The Book states the principle when the Makkans demand signs: *“Signs are only with Allah. And I am only sent with a clear warning”* (29:50), and it points out that the demanders would not believe even after them (6:109; 2:145).

The first half of the question at 7:70 restates the call the sūrah puts to every people, and the Book states that call as the content of every message: *“There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Me, so worship Me ˹alone˺.”* (21:25)
verses.71:
> He said, “You will certainly be subjected to your Lord’s torment and wrath. Do you dispute with me regarding the so-called gods which you and your forefathers have made up—a practice Allah has never authorized? Then wait! I too am waiting with you.”

**"Wrath and Anger Have Already Fallen"**

*Qāla qad waqaʿa ʿalaykum min rabbikum rijzun wa-ghaḍab* — he said: wrath and anger from your Lord have already descended upon you. The tense is the verse's startling feature. Hūd does not say that punishment *will* come; he says it has *fallen* — a past-tense verdict pronounced on a town that is still standing, still trading, still strong, and still mocking. The sūrah's doctrinal point is that the judgment of a people begins before the sky changes colour: the decision has been made in the record, and ʿĀd's prosperity is the interval between the sentence and its execution.

*Rijz* is the Qur'an's word for the punishment that is also a pollution — the same term the Book uses for the plagues that fell on Egypt (7:133, 2:59), for the filth God casts on those who refuse to use their reason (10:100). For the torment that follows the unjust. *Ghaḍab*, anger, is God's displeasure stated in the human vocabulary of a personal response; the Book uses it for those who have earned it (2:61; 5:60; 8:16). The combination names both the fact and the response: a penalty that is a defilement, and a judgment that is a relation.

**The Radical Critique of Idols: "Only Names"**

*A-tujādilūnanī fī asmāʾin sammaytumūhā antum wa-ābāʾukum mā nazzala Allāhu bihā min sulṭān* — do you dispute with me about the so-called gods which you and your forefathers have made up, a practice Allah has never authorized? The verse is the Qur'an's most complete statement of what idols are, and the Book repeats it in exactly these terms at two other points: *“Whatever ˹idols˺ you worship instead of Him are mere names which you and your forefathers have made up—a practice Allah has never authorized. That is the upright faith, but most people do not know.”* (12:40, spoken by Yūsuf in prison, and 53:23).

The second term is *sulṭān*: authority, evidence, a warrant. The Book's argument against the town is not that the practice is old, or unpopular, or socially damaging, but that it can produce no authorization from the one whose prerogative it invades. The same word appears throughout the sūrah at the exact points where the towns' positions are tested — *“He said, ‘You will certainly be subjected to your Lord’s torment and wrath. Do you dispute with me about the so-called gods which you and your forefathers have made up —a practice Allah has never authorized? Then wait! I too am waiting with you.’”* (7:71; see also 3:151, 10:68), *“They follow nothing but assumptions, and do nothing but lie.”* (6:116). In the Book's account of knowledge, a claim about God without a warrant from God is not a theology; it is a name.

**Mere Names: The Same Charge in an-Najm**

The dispute at 7:71 is about names, and the Book states the same charge in an-Najm: *“These ˹idols˺ are mere names that you and your forefathers have made up—a practice Allah has never authorized.”* (53:23). The two verses share their object, their agents, and the ground of the objection.

**Beliefs Ordained Without Authorization**

The absence of authorization at 7:71 is stated elsewhere as a question about its source: *“do they have associate-gods who have ordained for them some ˹polytheistic˺ beliefs, which Allah has not authorized?”* (42:21). The verse of ash-Shūrā asks where the beliefs came from if not from Allah, and the question implies that an ordaining requires an ordainer with standing.

The Book's messengers use this formula when their arguments are exhausted — Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ's Prophet is told to say, *“Say ˹to them, O Prophet˺, ‘Each ˹of us˺ is waiting, so keep waiting! You will soon know who is on the Straight Path and is ˹rightly˺ guided.’”* (20:135), and Sūrat al-Sāffāt records Noah's townsmen being told the same.

The summons precedes the sentence, and the delay is not indecision but opportunity: *“Be patient ˹O Prophet˺ with what they say”* (38:17) is addressed to the last of the messengers, whose own people were being given exactly the interval the earlier towns had wasted.
verses.72:
> So We saved him and those with him by Our mercy and uprooted those who denied Our signs. They were not believers

**Saved by Mercy, Cut Off for Denial**

*Fa-anjaynāhu wa-lladhīna maʿahu bi-raḥmatin minnā* — so We saved him and those with him by Our mercy. The rescue is attributed, as in Noah's case, to a rescue rather than to merit: *bi-raḥmatin minnā*, by mercy from Us. The sūrah's narrative has so far shown towns punished and remnants spared, and it takes care each time to name the mechanism. Ḥūd's people are not saved because they had proven their case or exceeded their accusers in virtue they could measure; they are saved because mercy reached them, and the mercy is the reason given.

Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own scene of the entry into Paradise has the saved confess that they would never have been guided had God not guided them (7:43), and the Prophet's hadith places the same fact in a single sentence: *none of you will be saved by his deeds* (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816).

**"We Uprooted Those Who Denied Our Signs"**

*Wa-qaṭaʿnā dābira alladhīna kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā* — and We uprooted those who denied Our signs. The verb is one of the Book's grimmest images of destruction: *qaṭaʿa dābira* means to cut off the rear, to leave no successor behind, to end a line. The Qur'an uses it for nations (6:45, 8:7, 15:66, 7:72 here) and the image is agricultural in origin — the cutting of a stem so that nothing regrows from the base.

What makes the phrase pointed in ʿĀd's case is the Book's account of their civilization elsewhere. This is the town of the lofty pillars, of the buildings that imitated eternity (26:129), of the boast *who is stronger than us in might?* (41:15). Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah's description of the wind makes the physical shape of the sentence explicit: *“a furious, bitter wind which Allah unleashed on them non-stop for seven nights and eight days, so that you would have seen its people lying dead like trunks of uprooted palm trees.”* (69:6–7). Sūrat al-Qamar adds the morning-after detail: *“Indeed, We sent against them ˹only˺ one ˹mighty˺ blast, leaving them like the twigs of fencebuilders.”* (54:31).

**The Remnant and the Mercy**

The other half of the verse — *him and those with him* — returns to the pattern established in Noah's account, and the sūrah will keep it. The Book's later chapters add the detail of how the remnant was preserved. Sūrat al-Ḥūd records that they were saved *by a mercy from Us* from a punishment that came as a cry and an earthquake (11:58, 11:67 in the two accounts), and Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ has the town ask, at the last moment, whether there is any remnant to be spared (26:139 in its wording).

**Saved by a Mercy From Us**

The parallel fixes the shape of every deliverance the sūrah reports. Lūṭ and his household are saved except the wife (7:83); Hūd and the believers are saved by a mercy (11:58); Ṣāliḥ and the believers are saved “by a mercy from Us” (11:66); Shuʿayb and the believers are saved (7:93). In each case the salvation is stated as given, and in each case the destruction is stated as earned: the sūrah’s summaries attach the outcome to the people’s denial (7:72, 7:78, 7:92).

That asymmetry is the verse’s doctrinal content and the reason it is placed where it is. The cycle of towns opens at 7:59 with a messenger’s fear for his people and closes at 7:93 with the last of them buried; 7:72 stands early enough to establish the rule that governs all of them.

The most remarkable detail of ʿĀd's destruction in the Book appears in Sūrat al-Aḥqāf, where the punishment arrives in the form of what they had been waiting for all along: *“Then when they saw the torment as a ˹dense˺ cloud approaching their valleys, they said ˹happily˺, ‘This is a cloud bringing us rain.’ ˹But Hûd replied,˺ ‘No, it is what you sought to hasten: a ˹fierce˺ wind carrying a painful punishment!’ It destroyed everything by the command of its Lord, leaving nothing visible except their ruins.”* (46:24–25).
verses.73:
> And to the people of Thamûd We sent their brother Ṣâliḥ. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. A clear proof has come to you from your Lord: this is Allah’s she-camel as a sign to you. So leave her to graze ˹freely˺ on Allah’s land and do not harm her, or else you will be overcome by a painful punishment

**Ṣāliḥ's Address and Its Additions**

Ṣāliḥ's opening speech is the same as Noah's and Hūd's — the call to the worship of the One God — with the addition of the sign and the warning of the punishment to follow its violation. The sūrah gives him no new doctrine. What the account adds is the mechanism of the town's doom: not a philosophical error, not a failure of argument, but a collective decision to kill a particular animal to show that the messenger's God could not protect it.

Sūrat al-Shams tells the same story in its own way and supplies the reason the refusal became fatal: *“when the most wicked of them was roused ˹to kill the she-camel˺.”* (91:12). The warning is given in the next verse (91:13), and its answer in the one after: *“Still they defied him and slaughtered her. So their Lord crushed them for their crime, levelling all to the ground.”* (91:14). The Book's analysis locates the sin in the act of hamstringing and in the rejection that made it deliberate. The town had been given a sign that was also a daily ordinance, and it chose to destroy the ordinance in public.

**The Geography of Thamūd**

The sūrah's next verse will describe the town's achievements, but the Book supplies its own portrait in several places, and the archaeological details are consistent: the carving of dwellings in the rock, and the trading of security for wealth. Sūrat al-Ḥijr records that the people *“They carved their homes in the mountains, feeling secure.”* (15:82), and Sūrat al-Fajr names Thamūd with the people who *hollowed out the rock in the valley* (89:9). This sūrah's own memory of the tribe is Ṣāliḥ's reminder of their carved homes in the next verse (7:74), and the Qur'an returns to the empty houses of Thamūd as a lesson: *“So their homes are there”* (27:52).

**The Sign’s Terms: A Share of Water and of Grazing**

Ṣāliḥ’s sign arrives with conditions. The sūrah states the first of them here — *“So leave her to graze ˹freely˺ on Allah’s land and do not harm her, or else you will be overcome by a painful punishment!”* (7:73) — and ash-Shuʿarāʾ’s parallel account states the second: *“Here is a camel. She will have her turn to drink as you have yours, each on an appointed day.”* (26:155). The she-camel is given grazing and a scheduled share of water; the town is given the same schedule and told not to touch her.

**The Command Not to Harm Her, and Its Breach**

The prohibition in 7:73 is *lā tamassūhā bi-sūʾ* — literally do not touch her with harm — which the translation renders *“do not harm her”* (7:73). The preposition makes the harm an instrument: not merely do not harm her, but do not come at her with harm. 11:64 states the sanction for breach, and ash-Shams states the command in its shortest form: *“But the messenger of Allah warned them, ‘Do not disturb Allah’s camel and her turn to drink!’”* (91:13) — where the thing protected is not only the animal but her share.

The sūrah reports the breach and its consequence in the verse that follows this one: the hamstrung camel, the defiance of the command, the punishment (7:77–78). Ash-Shams adds the detail that the act was undertaken by the town’s most wretched (91:12).

Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ states the arrangement in the town's own hearing: *“Ṣâliḥ said, ‘Here is a camel. And do not ever touch her with harm, or you will be overtaken by the torment of a tremendous day.’”* (26:155–156).

Sūrat al-Qamar compresses the whole affair into four verses: the warning, the consultation, the hamstringing, and the cry (54:23–31).

The sūrah does not yet say what will happen, but its audience had heard the story in the markets and the Book has told it elsewhere: the she-camel was hamstrung, the town was given three days, and the cry took them (11:65, 54:31).
verses.74:
> Remember when He made you successors after ’Âd and established you in the land—˹and˺ you built palaces on its plains and carved homes into mountains. So remember Allah’s favours, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”

**Palaces on the Plains and Homes in the Mountains**

*Tabnūna bi-suhūlihā qaṣūran wa-tanḥitūna al-jibāla buyūtan* — you build palaces on its plains and carve the mountains into homes. The description is precise and it matches the Book's other accounts: Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ has Ṣāliḥ asking, *“˹Why˺ do you build a landmark on every high place in vanity. Construct castles, as if you are going to live forever,”* (26:128–129), and Sūrat al-Ḥijr records the practice of carving dwellings from the rock *“feeling secure”* (15:82). The two halves of the verse's image — the tower on the plain and the chamber in the cliff — form a catalogue of defensive achievement, and the Book's readers have always recognized the picture: an architecture designed to make attack impossible and time irrelevant.

The Qur'an's treatment of this architecture is consistently religious. The stones are not criticized as luxury; the Book's objection is to what such building expresses about its builders' estimate of their own permanence. Sūrat al-Fajr's description of Iram's pillars is framed by the same thought — *the like of which was never created in the lands* — and immediately followed by the account of a people who thought their strength made them immune to judgment (89:6–13). What Thamūd had converted into self-confidence was, in the Book's account, a loan by which it was being tested.

**"So Remember the Favours of Allah"**

*Fa-dhkurū ālāʾa Allāh* — so remember the favours of Allah. The instruction is repeated verbatim from Hūd's address (7:69), and the sūrah's towns are shown to receive identical counsel from identical messengers. The word *ālāʾ* covers the whole inventory the verse has just listed: the succession, the settlement, the plains, the cliffs, and the skill to use them. Nothing in the list is described as a product of Thamūd's own creative power; the city is presented as a set of gifts that happens to be inhabited by people with names.

The Book's later verses about Thamūd make the same point from the ruins: *“So their homes are there”* (27:52). Whatever the town thought its architecture was for, the Book's epitaph is empty buildings — an inventory of materials with the tenants gone. The verse's instruction to remember is so the only defence the sūrah offers against that outcome, and it is offered at the last moment before the town's refusal is sealed.

**"Do Not Spread Corruption in the Land"**

The verse ends with the prohibition that the sūrah placed at the head of its practical instructions at 7:56: *wa-lā taʿthaw fī al-arḍ mufsidīn* — and do not go about the land spreading corruption. The verb *ʿathā* adds to *fasād* the sense of violent, ruinous action — the destruction that leaves wreckage behind — and the Book uses it for those whose conduct goes beyond mere disobedience into devastation (2:27, 2:60, 26:151–152, 29:36).

**The Carving in Two Other Accounts**

The sūrah reports Thamūd’s building as a fact about their skill, and the two other accounts add the quality of the work and the state of mind behind it. Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ puts the question to them directly: *“to carve homes in the mountains with great skill?”* (26:149). Sūrah al-Ḥijr supplies the motive in a single participle: *“They carved their homes in the mountains, feeling secure.”* (15:82).

The Book uses it for Israel in the promised land (10:93) and for the settlement of the believers after their trials (22:41).
verses.75:
> The arrogant chiefs of his people asked the lowly who believed among them, “Are you certain that Ṣâliḥ has been sent by his Lord?” They replied, “We certainly believe in what he has been sent with.”

**The Question the Elite Ask the Poor**

*Qāla al-malaʾu alladhīna istakbarū min qawmihi li-lladhīna istuḍʿifū li-man āmana minhum* — the arrogant chiefs of his people said to the weak ones among them who had believed. The town is divided into two vocabularies: the *malaʾ* who are *mustakbirūn*, arrogant, and the *mustaḍʿafūn*, those treated as weak.

Sūrat Sabaʾ records the exchange between the arrogant and the weak in the Hereafter and has the weak say to the arrogant, *“The disbelievers vow, ‘We will never believe in this Quran, nor in those ˹Scriptures˺ before it.” If only you could see when the wrongdoers will be detained before their Lord, throwing blame at each other! The lowly ˹followers˺ will say to the …’* (34:31–33). If only an angel had been sent down with him to be his co-warner,”* (25:7) — the objection of those who expected the message to arrive with attendants.

**The Answer of the Lowly**

The reply has been quoted by Muslims in every generation facing official pressure. The Book itself prepares the reader for it earlier in the sūrah: the reader has already heard the divine voice describe the saved of the end times as those who *“As for those who believe and do good—We never require of any soul more than what it can afford—it is they who will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever.”* (7:42), and has already watched the lowly appear on the sūrah's wall of separation while the tyrants stand in the Fire (7:48–49).

**The Poor as the Book's Constant Constituency**

The Qur'an's sociology of belief is one of its least fashionable and most consistent features. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ's version of the towns' objection is explicit: *“How can we believe in you, when you are followed ˹only˺ by the lowest of the low?”* (26:111; see also 11:27, where the chiefs say that no one follows Noah except the lowliest, and note that Noah refuses to drive them away).

Sūrat al-Anʿām's instruction to the Prophet is the doctrine in action: *“˹O Prophet!˺ Do not dismiss those ˹poor believers˺ who invoke their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure.”* (6:52), and Sūrat al-Kahf repeats it: *“Patiently stick with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure. Do not let your eyes look beyond them, desiring the luxuries of this worldly life.”* (18:28). Both verses were revealed in a Makkah where the Prophet was under pressure to send away the poor to attract the notables — the same pressure the sūrah's Thamūd applies from below.

**The Chiefs Counted, and the Adjectives Added**

*Al-malaʾ* is not a loose word for important people in this sūrah. It occurs eight times, counted from the translation, and every occurrence is the same institution: Noah’s opponents (7:60), Hūd’s (7:66), Ṣāliḥ’s (7:75), Shuʿayb’s twice (7:88, 7:90), Pharaoh and his chiefs as the object of the mission (7:103), and Pharaoh’s chiefs twice more (7:109, 7:127). Five prophetic careers, one ruling assembly. The modifiers are the finer evidence. The noun stands bare where the chiefs address a prophet — “We surely see that you are clearly misguided.” (7:60) — and takes *kāfir* where the sūrah wants the rejection on record: “We surely see you as a fool, and we certainly think you are a liar.” (7:66). It takes *mustakbir* only twice, at 7:75 and 7:88, and those are the two verses where the chiefs are not arguing with a prophet but disposing of believers — interrogating the lowly about their certainty, and threatening expulsion. The arrogance the sūrah names is social before it is religious.

The object of the belief is not the man but the message, and the Book states the same object in its fullest form: *“The Messenger ˹firmly˺ believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. They ˹all˺ believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers.”* (2:285)
verses.76:
> The arrogant said, “We surely reject what you believe in.”

**"We Reject What You Believe In"**

*Qāla al-ladhīna istakbarū innā bi-mā āmantum bihi kāfirūn* — the arrogant said: we reject what you have believed in. The reply is a sentence about the believers rather than about God, and its grammar reveals how religious rejection actually works in the sūrah's towns. The chiefs do not say *we disbelieve in the messenger* or *we deny the Lord of all worlds*; they say they are *kāfirūn* about the faith of the lowly. The object of their denial is another group's confidence.

The Book records this structure repeatedly, and it is one of its sharpest psychological observations. Sūrat al-Baqarah's accounts of the prophets' audiences show the leaders' objections moving from the message to the messenger to the messenger's followers. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ's Noah narrative has the chiefs objecting that *only the lowest of the people follow him*, as though the composition of a community were evidence about its God (26:111; see also 11:27). And the Qur'an's description of the disbelievers' own logic at the Judgment places exactly this sentence in a larger diagnosis: *“And they will lament, ‘If only we had listened and reasoned, we would not be among the residents of the Blaze!’”* (67:10).

**What the Sentence Concedes**

What the chiefs' sentence quietly grants is the point. They do not dispute that the believers exist, nor that their belief is sincere, nor that Ṣāliḥ has been with them. Their objection is neither evidential nor moral; it is social. Sūrat al-Zukhruf catches the same concession at the highest level, where the Makkans, unable to attack the message, attack the recipient: *“And they exclaimed, ‘If only this Quran was revealed to a great man from ˹one of˺ the two cities!’”* (43:31) — a sentence that presumes the Qur'an might be genuine and objects only to its address.

The Book's later sūrahs preserve the end of this argument at the Judgment, when the elite and their followers exchange recriminations. Sūrat Sabaʾ reports the followers' answer to their leaders — *“No! It was your plotting by day and night — when you ordered us to disbelieve in Allah and to set up equals with Him”* (34:33) — and their final plea is preserved in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb: *“Our Lord! We obeyed our leaders and elite, but they led us astray from the ˹Right˺ Way. Our Lord! Give them double ˹our˺ punishment, and condemn them tremendously”* (33:67–68). Verse 76's sentence — *we surely disbelieve in what you believe in* — will therefore be spoken twice in the Book's history: once by Thamūd's elite in the town's assembly, and once on the Day when the order of speakers is reversed.

The arrogant and the lowly argue in the Fire (7:38–39); each side blames the other; the Book's verdict is that the leaders carry the teaching-load and the followers carry the imitation-load, and neither gets to transfer the bill.

Sūrat al-Baqarah's refutation of the same habit is aimed at a different community but makes the identical point: *“And when they are told, ‘Believe as others believe,’ they reply, ‘Will we believe as the fools believe?’ Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know” (2:13)* (2:13).
verses.77:
> Then they killed the she-camel—defying their Lord’s command—and challenged ˹Ṣâliḥ˺, “Bring us what you threaten us with, if you are ˹truly˺ one of the messengers.”

**From Argument to Slaughter**

*Fa-ʿaqarū al-nāqata wa-ʿataw ʿan amri rabbihim* — then they killed the she-camel, defying their Lord’s command. The sūrah's third town now crosses the line its predecessors approached, and the verb the Book chooses is significant: *ʿaqara* — to hamstring, to cut the tendon that makes a creature useless. It is not a description of a general massacre; it is the precise act of crippling an animal. The crime of Thamūd, in the Book's account, is an act of deliberate vandalism against a sign left among them.

Sūrat al-Qamar names the town's own agent: *“But they roused a companion of theirs, so he dared to kill ˹her˺”* (54:29), and Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ records the outcome: *“But they killed her, becoming regretful”* (26:157). Sūrat al-Shams names the demagogue: *“when the most wicked of them was roused ˹to kill the she-camel˺.”* (91:12). The Book's account of the events shows a division of responsibility that the sūrah's narrative has already prepared: a designated agent performs the deed, and the town consents — the Qur'an reports that they were all pleased with it — and so the punishment falls on all of them (91:14).

**"Defying Their Lord’s Command"**

The second clause, *wa-ʿataw ʿan amri rabbihim* — defying their Lord’s command — states the religious content of the act. *ʿAtā* is to overstep the limit placed in front of a person; the phrase is used throughout the Book for the violation of an explicit divine prohibition (2:61, 5:78, 7:166). What makes Thamūd's act different from the pagan rites of their neighbours is that the command they defied was not a general moral law they had never heard; it was the specific instruction attached to the sign visible in their pasture: *do not touch her with harm*.

For Thamūd it was an animal; for Adam it was one tree; for the people of the sabbath it was the fishing net (7:163); for Abraham's people there was no such command but a fire.

**"Bring Us What You Threaten Us With"**

The Book records the taunt at several points with a consistency that shows how central the challenge was to the prophetic experience: *“Our Lord! Hasten for us our share ˹of the punishment˺ before the Day of Reckoning.”* (38:16); *“They said, ‘Have you come to us so that we would worship Allah alone and abandon what our forefathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if what you say is true!’”* (7:70); *“Bring us then whatever you threaten us with”* (46:22). And the Book's replies repeat the fact that the demanded item has already been scheduled: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘A Day has ˹already˺ been appointed for you, which you can neither delay nor advance by a ˹single˺ moment.’”* (34:30; see also 71:4). The sūrah's audience, hearing verse 77 read aloud, already knows what follows in the next verse. So did Thamūd, in principle.

**Saved From the Disgrace of That Day**

The verse of Hūd reports the outcome in two clauses: *“When Our command came, We saved Ṣâliḥ and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us and spared them the disgrace of that Day.”* (11:66). Al-Aʿrāf reports it in one: *“Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them, and they fell lifeless in their homes.”* (7:78).

This is the inversion the sūrah keeps. The challenge at 7:77 asked for the threatened thing to be brought, and it was brought to the ones who asked. The verse’s own phrase — defying their Lord’s command — describes the act as defiance rather than as doubt, and 11:66 supplies the counterparty: a prophet and those with him, saved by a mercy and spared a disgrace whose name is the same word the sūrah used of the disgraced at 7:13.
verses.78:
> Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them, and they fell lifeless in their homes

**The Tremor**

*Fa-akhadhat-humu al-rajfatu fa-aṣbaḥū fī dārihim jāthimīn* — so the tremor seized them, and they became, in their homes, fallen on their knees. The sūrah's account of Thamūd's end is one sentence long, and every word of it is chosen to close an argument. The instrument of destruction is *al-rajfah*: the quake, the shudder — the punishment that arrives through the ground the town had built its palaces on.

The Book uses different instruments for different towns, and the variation is a teaching device. Noah's people drowned (7:64); ʿĀd's were carried off by a wind (69:6–7); Thamūd's were shaken; the people of Lot were overwhelmed by a rain of stones and a deafening cry (7:84, 15:73–74); Madyan's were seized by the quake and the day of the shadow (7:91, 26:189). The sūrah's list of penalties matches the towns' accounts of their own invulnerability: a maritime people would not have feared a quake, a mountain people would not have feared a flood. The Book gives each town a destruction that its own pride had ruled out.

**"In Their Homes"**

The details deserve the attention the sūrah gives them. The town of carved mountains is destroyed *in their home* — inside the buildings that were supposed to be shelter from exactly this kind of judgment. The Book's earlier verse has just listed their architecture as evidence of their blessings; the next sentence cancels it. The Qur'an repeats the formula for ʿĀd and Madyan (46:25; 7:91; 11:94) and uses it again in Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt: *“So their homes are there”* (27:52), and in Sūrat Hūd: *“And the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook the wrongdoers, so they fell lifeless in their homes,”* (11:67).

*Jāthimīn* is a precise posture-word: kneeling, fallen on the chest, crouched. Every community will be summoned to its record ˹of deeds˺.”* (45:28).

**What the Book Says About the Warnings**

The Book's repeated judgments on the towns are not only narrative; they are evidence in the sūrah's argument about the Hereafter. Or did they feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by day while they were at play?”* (7:97–98).

**Rajfah and Ṣayḥah: Two Words for Thamūd’s End**

This sūrah gives Thamūd the shaking; three other accounts give them a blast. Hūd states it as the thing that overtook them: “And the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook the wrongdoers, so they fell lifeless in their homes,” (11:67). Al-Qamar reduces it to a single act: “Indeed, We sent against them ˹only˺ one ˹mighty˺ blast, leaving them like the twigs of fencebuilders.” (54:31). Al-Ḥāqqah names the mode without the scene: “As for Thamûd, they were destroyed by an overwhelming blast.” (69:5).

**Jāthimīn: Prone and Lifeless**

The word rendered lifeless here is *jāthimīn*, and it occurs in five destruction accounts — this verse, 7:91, 11:67, 11:94 and 29:37 — never anywhere else in the corpus, and always with the same phrase for the place where the bodies were left. It describes a posture rather than a state: crouched or pressed to the ground, motionless. The consistency of the five uses is what makes the word legible; a body *jāthim* is one that fell where it stood and did not move again.

**The Ruins as Address**

Al-ʿAnkabūt repeats the sentence and then turns it into an argument: “But they rejected him, so an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them and they fell lifeless in their homes.” (29:37). What follows addresses the Qurʾān’s first hearers directly — the fate of ʿĀd and Thamūd, “which must be clear to you ˹Meccans˺ from their ruins.” (29:38). The ruins are offered as visible evidence on the road the Meccans travelled, which is the same argument this sūrah makes at 7:92 for the town Shuʿayb left behind.

Al-Ḥāqqah pairs the two peoples before naming one of their ends: Thamūd and ʿĀd both denied the Striking Disaster (69:4), and the verse that follows gives Thamūd the overwhelming blast (69:5).
verses.79:
> So he turned away from them, saying, “O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice, but you do not like ˹sincere˺ advisors.”

**The Eleventh Hour and the Eleventh Verse**

*Fa-tawallā ʿanhum wa-qāla yā qawmi laqad ablaghtukum risālata rabbī wa-naṣaḥtu lakum wa-lākin lā tuḥibbūna al-nāṣiḥīn* — so he turned away from them, saying: “O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord’s message and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice, but you do not like ˹sincere˺ advisors.” (7:79)

**"I Have Conveyed the Message"**

That claim is important in the Book's moral economy. The sūrah's reader is repeatedly shown that the messengers are not blamed for the outcome of their preaching, and the Book's instruction to the last Prophet repeats the principle: *“So, ˹continue to˺ remind ˹all, O Prophet˺, for your duty is only to remind. You are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺.”* (88:21–22; see also 42:48). Verse 79 teaches the same lesson with the town's corpse as the visual aid.

**"Sincere Advice" for the Third Time**

The word *naṣaḥtu* — I gave sincere advice — appears in the sūrah's sequence now for the third time, after Noah (7:62) and Ḥūd (7:68), and it is used again by Shuʿayb (7:93). The repetition is the sūrah's way of defining the prophetic office through the term that the towns most thoroughly misread. The messenger's counsel had been free, patient, uninterested in reward, and addressed to the town's own interest; the town experienced it as interference.

**The Role of Reproach in the Book**

The sūrah's messenger does not curse the town in this verse and does not invoke punishment upon it; he reports his own conduct and the town's dislike. The Book's other farewells supply a comparison: Shuʿayb's in the same sūrah ends with *“We would surely be fabricating a lie against Allah if we were to return to your faith after Allah has saved us from it. It does not befit us to return to it unless it is the Will of Allah, our Lord. Our Lord has encompassed everything in ˹His˺ knowledge. In Allah we trust. Our Lord! Judge between us and our people with truth. You are the best of those who judge.”* (7:89), and Noah's prayer over his people in Sūrat Nūḥ is recorded at length — *“My Lord, do not leave a single disbeliever on earth”* (71:26). The Qur'an's messengers are not uniformly gentle, and they are not uniformly severe; what the Book's portraits share is that none of them takes the town's answer personally. Their reproach is always directed at the refusal of the message, and their grief is always for the people, not for themselves.

The verb means both a refusal and a departure, and the Book gives it to the Prophet ﷺ as a command in the same form: *“So turn away from them ˹O Prophet˺.”* (54:6), followed by an instruction to wait for a Day whose summons will be a horrifying one.

The Book states the right order of loves and treats a reversal of it as the thing to be feared: *“If your parents and children and siblings and spouses and extended family and the wealth you have acquired and the trade you fear will decline and the homes you cherish”* (9:24) — if these are dearer than God, His Messenger and struggle in His way, then wait for God’s command.
verses.80:
> And ˹remember˺ when Lot scolded ˹the men of˺ his people, ˹saying,˺ “Do you commit a shameful deed that no man has ever done before

**Lot and the Crime Without Precedent**

*Wa-Lūṭan idh qāla li-qawmihi a-taʾtūna al-fāḥishata mā sabaqakum bihā min aḥadin mina al-ʿālamīn* — and ˹remember˺ when Lot rebuked ˹the men of˺ his people: *“You certainly commit a shameful deed that no man has ever done before you.”* (29:28) The sūrah's fourth town is introduced without the word *brother*. The omission is itself a comment: Lot's relationship to Sodom is one of residence rather than kinship, and the Book's account elsewhere notes that he was a stranger among them (21:74; 29:26).

The phrase the verse uses for the crime is *al-fāḥishah* — the sūrah's standard term for sexual immorality, used at 7:28 for the circumambulation, at 6:151, and at 4:22. What distinguishes Sodom's offense in the Book's telling is the qualifier: *mā sabaqakum bihā min aḥadin mina al-ʿālamīn* — no one before you among the worlds had done it. Whether the clause means that no people before them had committed this particular act, or that no one had committed an indecency of this brazenness in public, the effect is the same: Sodom's crime is presented as historically unprecedented, which is to say that the town had reached a refinement of transgression its neighbours had not imagined.

**The Crime in the Book's Other Accounts**

Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ has Lot name the deed and its inversion of creation: *“Why do you ˹men˺ lust after fellow men, leaving the wives that your Lord has created for you? In fact, you are a transgressing people.’”* (26:165–166). Sūrat al-Naml's version has the town's own view of the matter: *“And ˹remember˺ Lot, when he rebuked ˹the men of˺ his people, ‘Do you commit that shameful deed while you can see ˹one another˺?’”* (27:54). Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt adds the detail of their public councils: *“Do you really lust after ˹other˺ men, abuse the travellers, and practice immorality ˹openly˺ in your gatherings?” His people’s only response was to say ˹mockingly˺: “Bring Allah’s punishment upon us, if what you say is true.’”* (29:29). The picture the Book builds is not of a private vice but of a town that had made the deed part of its public culture.

**The Difference Between Sodom and Its Neighbours**

The sūrah's towns have so far at least argued with their messengers. ʿĀd demanded proof, Thamūd killed a sign, Noah's chiefs pronounced a verdict. Sodom's response, recorded in the next verse, will contain no religious content at all — no gods are defended, no ancestors are cited, no claim is made about the messenger's truthfulness. What the town says is that the messenger and his household must leave.

Sūrat al-Qamar preserves the town's atmosphere with the same emphasis: *“He had already warned them of Our ˹crushing˺ blow but they disputed the warnings.”* (54:36), and the Book repeatedly describes the towns as being destroyed *while they were still in their transgression, asleep at dawn* (15:66; 15:73; 7:97–98). The sūrah of al-Aʿrāf gives the town one verse of speech in the next lines, and the whole town has nothing to say about God.

**Fāḥishah: The Word and Its Range**

The word is therefore not specific to one act but describes a class: a deed that exceeds a limit in a way that is visible as excess. 17:32 adds the prohibition of approach — *lā taqrabū*, do not go near — which is the same form of address the sūrah gives about the tree (2:35, 7:19). The prohibition is placed before the act rather than at it.

This is why 7:80 can put the charge as a question about precedent and still be a statement about a limit. The people are asked whether they do something no one did before, and the word used for it names excess rather than novelty. 17:32 supplies the range of the word, and the two verses together describe the deed as an approach forbidden and an excess committed.
verses.81:
> You lust after men instead of women! You are certainly transgressors.”

**The Specification of the Charge**

*Innakum la-taʾtūna al-rijāla shahwatan min dūni al-nisāʾ* — you approach men with desire, instead of women. Lot's opening address continues with the detail that makes the town's crime specific: the substitution. The Book's phrasing is careful. It is not a general accusation of sexual disorder; it names the act, the object, and the perversion of the design — *min dūni al-nisāʾ*, to the exclusion of women. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ's version adds the created order to the charge: *“leaving the wives that your Lord has created for you? In fact, you are a transgressing people.’”* (26:166). The argument in the Book is so about authorship: the pairing of male and female was a creation, and the town's practice was a repudiation of the arrangement in favour of an invention.

The Qur'an records the same indictment against Sodom across six sūrahs, and its constancy is itself part of the teaching: this is not a prohibition the Book is embarrassed about, and it never softens the account under pressure. Sūrat al-Naml puts the accusation in the mouth of the town rather than of the prophet — *“And ˹remember˺ Lot, when he rebuked ˹the men of˺ his people, ‘Do you commit that shameful deed while you can see ˹one another˺?’”* (27:54) — and Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt expands the catalogue with the town's other practices: the cutting of the road, the shameful assembly (29:29).

**The Town's Public Dimension**

Several of the Book's accounts of Sodom place the crime in the street or in an assembly. Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt's version has the town's own question — *“Do you really lust after ˹other˺ men, abuse the travellers. Practice immorality ˹openly˺ in your gatherings?” His people’s only response was to say ˹mockingly˺: “Bring Allah’s punishment upon us, if what you say is true.’”* (29:29) — and Sūrat al-Naml has the deed performed with the knowledge of the community, which is what its rhetorical question about *seeing* implies (27:54). Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ records the response of the townsmen to Lot's guests as a mob action (26:165). The Book's picture is of a vice that had become an institution, defended as a culture, and enforced by the town's collective will.

That is the context in which the next verse is to be read. When a community arranges itself around an inversion, the presence of a man who will not conform becomes a scandal rather than an eccentricity. The Book's judgment against Sodom, in its own framing, is not pronounced on private acts discovered in the dark; it is pronounced on a public order that had decided to define itself by them.

**The Comparative Context**

The Qur'an's severity on this subject has been noted by every generation of its readers, and the Book's own comparative treatment is instructive. Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, in legislating against an unrelated sexual offense, uses a term that connects the two: *“And the two among you who commit this sin—discipline them. If they repent and mend their ways, relieve them.”* (4:16, read by the majority of the commentators as a general indecency). Sūrat al-Nūr establishes the evidentiary and penal structure for illicit sexual conduct and closes the door on slander (24:4). The Book's approach to sexual ethics is so consistent and structural: a fixed boundary, a heavy penalty, and a strong guard against accusation.
verses.82:
> But his people’s only response was to say, “Expel them from your land! They are a people who wish to remain chaste!”

**"Drive Them Out — They Want To Be Pure"**

*Wa-mā kāna jawāba qawmihi illā a qālū akhrijūhum min qaryatikum innahum unās yataṭahharūn* — but his people’s only response was to say: “Expel them from your land! They are a people who wish to remain chaste!” (7:82) The sentence is the sūrah's finest specimen of the rhetoric of resentment, and its cruelty lies in the last word.

**Purity as an Accusation**

The word *yataṭahharūn* is the fifth form of the root *ṭ-h-r*, with the reflexive and intensive sense: they seek to purify themselves, they make a show of purity. The town's sentence treats moral cleanliness as an affectation — something a person pretends to, something that embarrasses a honest community, something to be expelled for. The sūrah's reader already knows how the Book regards that reversal, because its opening had made purity of heart a defining mark of the saved (7:42–43), and because the Book's own community would spend its history being told that *“Allah loves those who purify themselves”* (9:108).

There is a further indictment in the grammar. The townspeople do not say *Lot is a hypocrite*; they say the household *wants* to be pure, as though the desire itself is the offense. What Sodom objected to was not the performance of virtue — a town can accommodate a few performers — but its presence as a standing contradiction of their own order. Sūrat al-Muṭaffifīn's picture of the mockers at the gate — *“Indeed, the wicked used to laugh at the believers,”* (83:29) — is the same social mechanism at a smaller scale; the sūrah's verse is the mechanism with a decree attached.

**The Town That Could Not Tolerate a Neighbour**

That is why the Book's account of Sodom has always been read by its communities as a description of something more than a sexual history. Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt's version adds the crime of highway robbery (29:29); the sūrah of Hūd records the town's assembly proposing to the guests (11:78–79); the Book's overall portrait is of a walled community whose walls were its main achievement. Verse 82 tells the reader what such a community does when something on the inside refuses to match the outside.

**A Town That Expelled What It Needed**

The final observation on the verse belongs to the Book's use of Sodom as a warning to the towns of its own audience. The sūrah has described the town's answer to the messenger as an expulsion — *akhrijūhum min qaryatikum* — and it is not incidental that the Qur'an's account of the migration that follows, in other sūrahs, makes Lot's departure from Sodom the one journey that saved his family (29:26; 51:35).

The Book's narratives of the towns are full of such reversals, and the sūrah's audience in Makkah had its own version of them under way. The verse of the Aʿrāf records the formula in the mouths of Sodom: *they are people who want to be pure*.

**The Same Answer in al-Naml**

The reply of Lūṭ’s people is reported twice, and the two versions agree word for word in the charge: *“Expel Lot’s followers from your land! They are a people who wish to remain chaste!”* (27:56). Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ gives the same demand with the threat attached: *“If you do not desist, O Lot, you will surely be expelled.”* (26:167).
verses.83:
> So We saved him and his family except his wife, who was one of the doomed

**The Family and the One Who Stayed**

*Fa-anjaynāhu wa-ahlahu illā imraʾatahu kānat mina al-ghābirīn* — so We saved him and his family, except his wife, who was one of the doomed. The rescue is stated in the sūrah's familiar form, and one clause alters the pattern that Noah's and ʿĀd's towns had established. In the earlier narratives, the remnant was defined by belief; here the household itself is named as the saved unit, and the exception is spelled out.

The Book's other accounts supply the drama the sūrah leaves out. Sūrat al-Ḥijr and Sūrat Hūd record the angels arriving at Lot's door and the instruction that he should travel by night with his family and that no one should look back (15:65; 11:81). Sūrat al-Dhāriyāt has them leave before dawn (51:35), and 11:76 records the negotiation over the guests. The wife's sympathy for the town's order is named only in the phrase *who was one of the doomed* — *al-ghābirīn*, literally those who stayed behind. The word's root carries both the sense of remaining and of delay, and the Book uses it for those left inside a punishment when the righteous are extracted.

**The Doctrine of the Household**

The exception is one of the Book's clearest statements about the limits of kinship. The Qur'an's teaching that ties of blood do not transmit faith is not a side note. It is stated in several places, and this verse is one of its canonical instances: *“Indeed, some of your spouses and children are enemies to you. Beware of them.”* (64:14); *“You will never find a people who ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day loyal to those who defy Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their parents, children, siblings, or extended family. For those ˹believers˺, Allah has instilled faith in their hearts and strengthened them with a spirit from Him. He will admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever. Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him. They are the party of Allah. Indeed, Allah’s party is bound to succeed.”* (58:22). Sūrat al-Taḥrīm makes the point with two examples and both of them are women married to prophets: *“Allah sets forth an example for the disbelievers: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. Each was married to one of Our righteous servants, yet betrayed them. So their husbands were of no benefit to them against Allah whatsoever. Both were told, ‘Enter the Fire, along with the others!’”* (66:10).

The Book's prophets are so shown to be without a special power over their own households. Noah's son drowned (11:42–43); Abraham's father died in his error (9:114); the Prophet's uncle was condemned in a sūrah named for him (111:1–5). The sūrah's narrative keeps the record honest, and verse 83's exception — one woman in a rescued house — is the scripture's protection against treating a believing household as a charm.

**The Rescue and Its Terms**

*Anjaynā* — the verb that has closed each narrative in the sūrah — appears again, and the Book's consistent account of the deliverances is that they are accomplished by mercy and by the faithful transmission of instructions. In the fuller versions, the rescued are given a deadline, a direction, and a prohibition against looking back; the Book's narrative interest is in the fact that the rescue was arranged in advance and announced as an event. Sūrat al-Ḥijr's version is the most vivid: the angels tell Lot that the town's term is the morning, *“We revealed to him this decree: ‘Those ˹sinners˺ will be uprooted in the morning.’”* (15:66; see also 11:81).

**A Rain Poured on Them**

The verse that follows reports what befell those who remained: *“We poured upon them a rain ˹of brimstone˺. See what was the end of the wicked!”* (7:84). The verb is *amṭarnā*, to rain, and the sūrah uses the same verb of the rain sent on the towns as a sign of mercy (7:57).
verses.84:
> We poured upon them a rain ˹of brimstone˺. See what was the end of the wicked

**The Rain and the End**

*Wa-amṭarnā ʿalayhim maṭaran fa-nẓur kayfa kāna ʿāqibatu al-mujrimīn* — and We rained down upon them a rain; then see what was the end of the criminals. The sūrah's fourth town closes with the shortest and harshest of its endings, and the sequence of verbs is exact: the rain is sent, and the reader is addressed directly.

The Book's other accounts of the event supply the materials of that rain. Sūrat al-Dhāriyāt names the stones: *“To send upon them stones of ˹baked˺ clay, marked by your Lord for the transgressors.”* (51:33–34). Sūrat al-Ḥijr records the hour and the direction: *“So the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook them at sunrise. And We turned the cities ˹of Sodom and Gomorrah˺ upside down and rained upon them stones of baked clay.”* (15:73–74). Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ and Sūrat al-Qamar describe the morning and the overturned place (26:172–173; 54:37–38); and the Book's characteristic evaluation of the rain is stated at 25:40: *“They have certainly passed by the city ˹of Sodom˺, which had been showered with a dreadful rain ˹of stones˺.”*.

**"See What Was the End of the Criminals"**

*Fa-nẓur* — then look, consider, see. The imperative is directed at the sūrah's reader and it turns the narrative into evidence. This is the same move the sūrah made after Noah's rescue, where the blindness of the town was named as its own verdict, and it is the move the Book makes repeatedly in the Makkan sūrahs: the ruins of the prophetic age are presented as available, inspectable data. Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt's account of the same history ends with the same address to the reader: *“You ˹Meccans˺ certainly pass by their ruins day and night. Will you not then understand?”* (37:137–138).

The term for the town is *al-mujrimīn*: the criminals, from the root *j-r-m*, which carries the sense of cutting off and of a harvest of guilt. The sūrah has used it in its own verdicts before (7:40, 7:41) — the residents of the Fire and the wrongdoers.

**Rain, Water, and the Sūrah's Own Imagery**

There is a final resonance in the word *maṭar* that ties the narrative to the sūrah's earlier verses. In 7:57 the sūrah described God driving clouds to a dead land and sending down water as mercy, and it drew the argument for the resurrection from the rain that brings a barren place to life. Here the same vocabulary is used for the punishment: a rain that kills rather than revives. The Book's imagery is deliberately capable of either direction, and what determines whether water is mercy or judgment is the same thing that determines whether Hūd's cloud is a season's hope or a wind of destruction.

The sūrah's parallels fill out what this verse compresses. Sūrat Hūd describes the instrument and its maker: *“When Our command came, We turned the cities upside down and rained down on them clustered stones of baked clay, marked by your Lord ˹O Prophet˺. And these stones are not far from the ˹pagan˺ wrongdoers!”* (11:82–83). Sūrat al-Dhāriyāt states the same with the economy of this verse (51:33–34). And Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt records that the site was left as evidence: *“And We did leave ˹some of˺ its ruins as a clear lesson for people of understanding”* (29:35) — ruins on the route the sūrah's first audience travelled north on its trade journeys. The command *then see* is therefore not rhetorical: it points to a road the reader had walked and to remains that outlived the town's laughter.
verses.85:
> And to the people of Midian We sent their brother Shu’aib. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah—you have no other god except Him. A clear proof has already come to you from your Lord. So give just measure and weight, do not defraud people of their property, nor spread corruption in the land after it has been set in order. This is for your own good, if you are ˹truly˺ believers

**The Prophet of the Market**

*Wa-ilā Madyana akhāhum Shuʿayban* — and to Madyan, their brother Shuʿayb. The sūrah's last town before Moses is a trading city, and the crime it is charged with is the one its economy makes possible: *fa-awfū al-kayla wa-l-mīzān* — so give full measure and weight — *wa-lā tabkhasū al-nāsa ashyāʾahum* — and do not defraud people of their goods.

The Book's association of prophecy with commercial honesty is one of its most distinctive features, and this verse states the connection at its strongest: the messenger's first duty after the call to worship is the correction of the scales. Those who take full measure ˹when they buy˺ from people, but give less when they measure or weigh for buyers.”* (83:1–3). Sūrat al-Isrāʾ lists the honest scale among the commandments of the Decalogue tradition: *“Give in full when you measure, and weigh with an even balance. That is fairest and best in the end.”* (17:35). And Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ records Shuʿayb's version of this verse with an addition about the danger of the practice: *“and do not defraud people of their property. Nor go about spreading corruption in the land.”* (26:183).

**The Order of the Commandments**

The verse's arrangement repays attention. Surely Allah is ever Merciful to you.”* (4:29), and Sūrat al-Baqarah's catalogue of the people of the Book includes the crime of consuming wealth unjustly and of devouring the property of the weak (2:188).

The Madyan narrative in Sūrat Hūd records the town's own understanding of Shuʿayb's demand, and their objection is revealing: *“They asked ˹sarcastically˺, ‘O Shu’aib! Indeed, you are such a tolerant, sensible man!’”* (11:87).

**"Do Not Spread Corruption in the Land"**

*Wa-lā taʿthaw fī al-arḍ mufsidīn* — and do not spread corruption in the land — this is the third time the sūrah has used the prohibition, after its general instruction at 7:56 and Ṣāliḥ's warning at 7:74, and in this town it acquires a sharp economic meaning. The verb *ʿathā* names destructive action, and its objects in the Book's usage are crops, property, and people.

The Qur'an's later treatment of Madyan states the outcome in the Book's own phrase: *“So they rejected him, and ˹so˺ were overtaken by the torment of the day of the ˹deadly˺ cloud. That was really a torment of a tremendous day.”* (26:189), and Sūrat Hūd records the cry and the quake that took them (11:94–95).

**"That Is Better for You, If You Are ˹Truly˺ Believers"**

*Dhālikum khayrun lakum in kuntum muʾminīn* — that is better for you, if you are ˹truly˺ believers. The Book makes the same move in the story of Madyan's fuller version, where Shuʿayb urges his people with a reminder of God's own largesse: *“He has blessed me with a good provision from Him”* (11:88).

The Book's economic doctrine will be stated in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's later verse: *“O believers! Do not devour one another’s wealth illegally, but rather trade by mutual consent.”* (4:29), and its view of the market is that a working economy is a form of the trust the sūrah has been describing since its first pages. The hadith the tradition received on the same point is among the shortest and sharpest in the corpus: the Prophet ﷺ passed a heap of grain, put his hand into it, found its lower part damp, and said, *“Whoever cheats is not one of us”* (Muslim 102, from Abū Hurayrah).
