**An Even Balance: The Same Command in al-Isrāʾ**

Shuʿayb’s address begins with a proof: *“A clear proof has already come to you from your Lord.”* (7:85), and then turns to measure and weight. That is fairest and best in the end.”* (17:35).

The commentators read the two verses as one instruction given twice. 55:9 states the negative form — weigh with justice and do not give short measure — and 17:35 states the positive.

Hūd gives the same three commands in the same messenger’s mouth: *“O my people! Do not defraud people of their property, nor go about spreading corruption in the land.”* (11:85).

Al-Muṭaffifīn is named for it, and its opening states the asymmetry that defines the offence: “Woe to the defrauders!” (83:1) — “Those who take full measure ˹when they buy˺ from people,” (83:2) “but give less when they measure or weigh for buyers.” (83:3).

Ash-Shuʿarāʾ gives the same commands to the residents of the Forest in a form that omits two of this verse’s elements: “Give full measure, and cause no loss ˹to others˺.” (26:181) “Weigh with an even balance,” (26:182).
verses.86:
> And do not lie in ambush on every road—threatening and hindering those who believe in Allah from His Path and striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked. Remember when you were few, then He increased you in number. And consider the fate of the corruptors

**"Remember When You Were Few"**

*Wa-dhkurū idh kuntum qalīlan fa-kaththarakum* — and remember when you were few and He multiplied you. The verse turns from the crime to the town's history, and it uses the same argumentation as Ḥūd's address to ʿĀd and Ṣāliḥ's to Thamūd: the community's present standing is a gift with a history. Madyan had been small, marginal, and dependent; it had grown into a settled trading center; and the measure of its growth is also the measure of its obligation.

The Book's use of demographic history as a religious argument is consistent from its earliest sūrahs. Sūrat al-Takāthur mocks the city's pride in numbers (102:1–2); Sūrat al-Anfāl reminds the first Muslim community in Madinah of its weakness and God's protection: *“Remember when you had been vastly outnumbered and oppressed in the land, constantly in fear of attacks by your enemy, then He sheltered you.”* (8:26). Verse 86's instruction to Madyan is so part of a general pattern: the Book reads a community's success as a ledger entry, not as a trophy.

**"See What Was the End of the Corrupters"**

The term *mufsidūn* — corrupters — is the sūrah's own word for what the towns were (7:74, 7:85, 7:86). The verse binds the whole sequence together: the crime of Madyan, in the Book's framework, is the same crime as the crime of the towns before it, committed in a different department of life. The cheated customer, the threatened believer, and the bribed official are the same phenomenon in the sūrah's moral grammar — a community treating what does not belong to it as its own.

**Crookedness, and the Law the Verse Gave the Jurists**

The verse’s third charge uses a word the Book reserves for a defect in a road and in a book. The crookedness the ambushers strive to give the path is *ʿiwaj*, and the same word is denied of the revelation in the opening of Sūrah al-Kahf: Allah *“has revealed the Book to His servant, allowing no crookedness in it”* (18:1). The pairing sets the two operations against one another. The Book is straight and admits no bending; the work of the ambushers is to bend the road people take to it — not by arguing against it, but by making the way to it unsafe.

The jurists read the first clause as a legal text and not only as a moral one. Lying in wait on the roads to threaten and to take is what the tradition calls *ḥirābah*, brigandage. Its ruling is given in Sūrah al-Māʾidah: *“Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and spread mischief in the land is death, crucifixion, cutting off their hands and feet on opposite sides, or exile from the land.”* (5:33). The connection drawn between the two verses is that the ambush here is against the path of God rather than against a traveller’s purse, and that the corruption named in this verse’s last clause is the same *fasād* the ruling in al-Māʾidah punishes.

**The Refrain of Increase**

The verse’s second sentence is one of three in this sūrah built on the same pattern, addressed to three different towns. To ʿĀd: *“Remember that He made you successors after the people of Noah and increased you greatly in stature.”* (7:69). To Thamūd: *“Remember when He made you successors after ’Âd and established you in the land.”* (7:74). To Midian, here: remember when you were few, and He increased you in number. In each case the increase is given as a fact to be remembered before the charge is made, and in each case it is the fact that converts the town’s confidence into evidence against it.

The three increases differ in kind, and the difference is exact. That is why the verse closes on the fate of the corrupters, and why the sūrah turns next to the rule of the towns — that none was taken without first being tried with hardship and then with ease (7:94–95).
verses.87:
> If some of you do believe in what I have been sent with while others do not, then be patient until Allah judges between us. He is the Best of Judges.”

**The Argument Against Compulsion**

The Qur'an's most famous statement on coercion is Sūrat al-Baqarah's *“Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood. So whoever renounces false gods and believes in Allah has certainly grasped the firmest, unfailing hand-hold. And Allah is AllHearing, All-Knowing.”* (2:256), and verse 87 is one of the places where the principle is displayed in the conduct of a prophet. The Book's messengers do not enforce; they convey, warn, and leave the verdict to its owner. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ gives the same logic to Noah: *“So judge between me and them decisively, and save me and the believers with me”* (26:118), and this sūrah gives Shuʿayb the prayer it prepares: *“Our Lord! Judge between us and our people with truth. You are the best of those who judge”* (7:89).

**The Community in Transit**

The verse also gives a picture of a community in the middle of a decision, and the picture is unsparing in its realism: some believe, some do not, and both groups are standing in the same marketplace, trading with one another, sharing the same wells. The Book does not describe the believers of Madyan as a separate enclave; the sūrah's earlier narrative of Ṣāliḥ showed the believers as the town's underclass (7:75), and Shuʿayb's town has its own version of the split.

That realism is the basis of the sūrah's instruction to patience. A community that must live beside its opponents for years needs a discipline that does not depend on the outcome of the argument. The Book names it in the sūrah of the Cave: *“And patiently stick with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening”* (18:28), and in Sūrat al-ʿAṣr's summary of salvation: *“except those who have faith, do good, and urge each other to the truth, and urge each other to perseverance.”* (103:3). The verse of the Aʿrāf supplies the same discipline to a merchant town that has just been told its scales are crooked.

**"He Is the Best of Judges"**

*Wa-huwa khayru al-ḥākimīn.* The phrase is one of the Qur'an's recurring doxological formulas. It appears at points where human judgment is being contrasted with divine: Sūrat Yūnus has the Prophet told to follow what is revealed and to be patient *until Allah judges. He is the best of judges* (10:109); Sūrat Yūsuf puts the phrase in the mouth of Jacob's sons (12:80); Sūrat al-Tīn closes with the same question: *“Is Allah not the most just of all judges?”* (95:8).

In the sūrah's narrative, the phrase has a practical edge: the town has judges of its own — the elite who will shortly threaten Shuʿayb with expulsion (7:88) — and the verse is relocating the case to a higher court. The messenger's patience is not passivity; it is the transfer of a case that the local bench cannot try fairly. The Book's audiences have always read this verse as the charter of a community that does not take the law into its own hands, and the Madyan narrative remains its canonical exhibit.

**The Same Sentence to Two Other Messengers**

The instruction to wait for a judgment is given to the Prophet ﷺ in the same words: *“And follow what is revealed to you, and be patient until Allah passes His judgment. For He is the Best of Judges.”* (10:109). Shuʿayb states the same position from inside a confrontation that has already failed: *“O my people! Persist in your ways, for I ˹too˺ will persist in mine.”* (11:93).

The Book's instruction to its Prophet in the middle of the persecution uses the same verb and the same limit: *“So endure patiently, as did the Messengers of Firm Resolve. And do not ˹seek to˺ hasten ˹the torment˺ for the deniers.”* (46:35).

The Book distinguishes this waiting from mere endurance by attaching it to a decree: *“So be patient with your Lord’s decree, for you are truly under Our ˹watchful˺ Eyes.”* (52:48).
verses.88:
> The arrogant chiefs of his people threatened, “O Shu’aib! We will certainly expel you and your fellow believers from our land, unless you return to our faith.” He replied, “Even if we hate it

**The Word Millah**

*Millah* is the Book's term for a community's religion regarded as a shared way of life — the word used of Abraham's way (2:130, 3:95, 16:123), of the idolaters’ religion in Joseph’s prison (12:37). Of the Prophet’s own faith in Sūrat al-Kāfirūn (109:6, *“You have your way, and I have my Way.”*). That Shuʿayb's opponents call their system a *millah* shows what they are defending: not a doctrine but a community's inheritance, the package of customs that made Madyan Madyan. The verse's threat is therefore an identity claim: conform, or leave.

**"Even If We Detest It?"**

Sūrat al-Baqarah forbids compulsion in religion (2:256); Sūrat al-Naḥl's command to the Prophet to invite to the way of the Lord *with wisdom and good counsel* (16:125) rules out the alternative; Sūrat al-Ghāshiyah tells the Prophet, in the same sūrah, that he is not a controller over them (88:22). And the Book's own account of the hypocrites in Madinah makes the same point from the other side: a profession produced by pressure has no spiritual content, and the Book treats it as worse than the honest rejection because it corrupts the community's integrity.

**Millah, Dīn, and Sharīʿah**

The chiefs’ demand is phrased with the word *millah* — return to our *millah* — and the choice is not incidental. The Book distinguishes three words that English collapses into religion. *Dīn* is religion as a way of judgment and obedience. *Sharīʿah* and *minhāj* are the ordained way given to a particular community: *“To each of you We have ordained a code of law and a way of life.”* (5:48). *Millah* is the creed as inherited and followed, and it nearly always takes a personal genitive — the *millah* of Ibrāhīm.

That genitive is what gives the chiefs’ phrasing its significance. They do not say return to the truth, or return to our *dīn*; they say *our millah*, the way of our fathers, which is a claim of descent rather than of evidence. The Book uses the same construction of the true path, and so exposes the argument actually being made. The answer given to those who say follow our faith is that the faith followed is defined by its founder: *“We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright—who was not a polytheist.”* (2:135). And the community of the Prophet ﷺ is told to hold to a *millah* likewise defined by a father — *“the way of your forefather Abraham”* (22:78). The grammar is the same in both cases. What differs is whether the father was upright.

**Expulsion in the Sūrah’s Other Histories**

The threat to drive Shuʿayb and those who believed with him out of the town is not particular to Midian. It is the second move in the sūrah’s histories, and the Book records it in nearly the same words to other messengers. Nūḥ’s people threaten him with stones: *“If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be stoned ˹to death˺.”* (26:116). Lūṭ’s people threaten him with precisely what Midian threatens here: *“If you do not desist, O Lot, you will surely be expelled.”* (26:167). The threat reaches the Prophet ﷺ himself: *“They were about to intimidate you to drive you out of the land ˹of Mecca˺, but then they would not have survived after you ˹had left˺ except for a little while.”* (17:76).

**The Other Expulsion in This Sūrah**

The sūrah has already staged this scene, and the comparison is exact. At the close of Lot’s story the demand comes from the whole community and carries no condition: “Expel them from your land! They are a people who wish to remain chaste!” (7:82). Here it comes from a named subset — “The arrogant chiefs of his people threatened” — and it is issued as a bargain: “We will certainly expel you and your fellow believers from our land, unless you return to our faith.” (7:88). Lot’s neighbours expel for a virtue and say so; Midian’s chiefs expel for a belief and attach a price to stopping.
verses.89:
> We would surely be fabricating a lie against Allah if we were to return to your faith after Allah has saved us from it. It does not befit us to return to it unless it is the Will of Allah, our Lord. Our Lord has encompassed everything in ˹His˺ knowledge. In Allah we trust. Our Lord! Judge between us and our people with truth. You are the best of those who judge.”

**"After Allah Has Saved Us From It"**

The clause *baʿda idh najjānā Allāhu minhā* adds a second layer: what the town offers as a homecoming, Shuʿayb describes as a rescue already accomplished. The Book's vocabulary for conversion in several places uses this language of deliverance: Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own account of the followers of the messengers, Sūrat al-Māʾidah's promise that God will bring a people whom He loves, and Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt's description of the one who says, *“I was among the heedless”*.

The Book's later sūrahs make the refusal the duty of the community and the point of its identity: *“Whoever disbelieves in Allah after their belief—not those who are forced while their hearts are firm in faith. Those who embrace disbelief wholeheartedly—they will be condemned by Allah and suffer a tremendous punishment”* (16:106).

**"Unless Allah Wills"**

*Wa-mā yakūnu lanā a naʿūda fīhā illā a yashāʾa Allāhu rabbunā* — and it does not befit us to return to it unless it is the Will of Allah, our Lord. The exception is one of the Book's characteristic qualifications, and it is a statement about the limits of the human will rather than a loophole in the refusal. The Qur'an places the clause on the believer's tongue in matters of resolve: *“you cannot will ˹to do so˺ unless Allah wills”* (76:30; see also 81:29), and it teaches the community to say *God willing* about its own plans.

**"Our Lord Has Encompassed Everything in Knowledge"**

*Wasiʿa rabbunā kulla shayʾin ʿilman* — our Lord has encompassed everything in ˹His˺ knowledge. The Book's omniscience verses typically appear at decisive moments, and this one is placed where the town's leaders are weighing a private calculation and the messenger is declaring that no calculation is private. Sūrat al-Talāq's famous verse uses the same concept: *“Allah is the One Who created seven heavens ˹in layers˺, and likewise for the earth. The ˹divine˺ command descends between them so you may know that Allah is Most Capable of everything and that Allah certainly encompasses all things in ˹His˺ knowledge.” (65:12). Sūrat al-Anʿām states it in a form that would make any conspiracy absurd: *“With Him are the keys of the unseen—no one knows them except Him. And He knows what is in the land and sea. Not even a leaf falls”* (6:59).

**"In Allah We Put Our Trust"**

*ʿAlā Allāhi tawakkalnā* — in Allah we have placed our trust. The Book's *tawakkul* is the disposition of a person who has done what can be done and then released the outcome, and the sūrah of the family of ʿImrān explains the sequence: *“And consult with them in ˹conducting˺ matters. Once you make a decision, put your trust in Allah. Surely Allah loves those who trust in Him.”* (3:159). Shuʿayb's community had delivered its case, refused the coercion, and been told to wait; the trust is the state in which the waiting is possible.

The declared trust is also the community's answer to the threat of expulsion. What Madyan controlled was a place in Madyan, and the verse's sentence says that the believers' security is held elsewhere. The Book's later account of the believers' answer to Pharaoh uses the same formula: *“Your rage toward us is only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance, and let us die while submitting ˹to You˺.’”* (7:126; see also 10:85).

**Guidance Not Owned: Why a Return Would Be a Lie**

The refusal at 7:89 is stated as a claim about fabrication: returning to the rejected faith after being saved from it would be a lie against Allah. The ground of the claim is that the guidance was not the speakers' own achievement, and the Book states that ground plainly: *“You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺, but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills”* (28:56)

The prayer of 7:89 asks for a judgment between the two parties with truth, and the Book records the same prayer on the Prophet's tongue: *“My Lord! Judge ˹between us˺ in truth.”* (21:112).
verses.90:
> The disbelieving chiefs of his people threatened, “If you follow Shu’aib, you will surely be losers!”

**"If You Follow Shu’aib, You Will Surely Be Losers"**

*Wa-qāla al-malaʾu alladhīna kafarū min qawmihi la-in ittabaʿtum Shuʿayban innakum idhan la-khāsirūn* — and the disbelieving chiefs of his people threatened: “If you follow Shu’aib, you will surely be losers!” (7:90) The town's last argument is not about God, revelation, or the resurrection. It is about the price of conversion, and the sūrah reports it in the plainest commercial grammar Madyan knew.

The word *khāsirūn* — losers — belongs to the ledger that this town's narrative has been about since its first verse: short measure, honest weight, defrauded goods, ambushed caravans. They are simply lying.”* (29:12). The leadership’s own dismissal is recorded in the same sūrat al-Zumar: *“Worship then whatever ˹gods˺ you want instead of Him.”* (39:15).

**The Cost of Conversion in a Trading Town**

Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt describes the mechanism as a test: *“Do people think once they say, ‘We believe,” (29:2) that they will be left without being put to the test? … We certainly tested those before them. And ˹in this way˺ Allah will clearly distinguish between those who are truthful and those who are liars.’* (29:2–3). They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were so ˹violently˺ shaken that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried out, ‘When will Allah’s help come?’ Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near.”* (2:214; see also 2:155).

**The Book's Answer: a Different Ledger**

The Qur'an's rebuttal of the town's arithmetic is not that losing money does not matter; it is that the town's ledger omits its largest column. Shall I guide you to an exchange that will save you from a painful punishment?”* (61:10) — followed by faith, struggle. The promise of forgiveness, gardens, and noble dwellings (61:11–13); Sūrat al-Tawbah uses the language of purchase outright: *“Allah has indeed purchased from the believers their lives and wealth in exchange for Paradise.”* (9:111).

The sūrah of al-Baqarah states the failure of the alternative with the same metaphor: *“They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided.”* (2:16). Against that, the Book's promise to those who pay the price of following is stated in the sūrah of al-Aʿrāf's own later chapters and in Sūrat al-Naḥl: *“Whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah will find many safe havens and bountiful resources throughout the earth. Those who leave their homes and die while emigrating to Allah and His Messenger—their reward has already been secured with Allah.”* (4:100); *“Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life”* (16:97). The chiefs' threat at 7:90 declares the followers of Shuʿayb to be losers, and the sūrah answers it two verses later in the same terms: *“Those who rejected Shu’aib were ˹wiped out˺ as if they had never lived there.”

A people destroyed leave ruins, and the sūrah treats the ruins as instruction at 7:100; a people wiped out as if they had never lived there leave nothing to be instructed by.

**The Word’s Six Occurrences, and Who Speaks It**

The word the chiefs use is the sūrah’s verdict-word, and it occurs six times — counted from the translation: 7:23, 7:90, 7:92, 7:99, 7:149 and 7:178. Twice penitents apply it to themselves, in sentences so nearly identical that they differ only in the order of their two requests: Adam and his wife ask to be forgiven and then shown mercy (7:23), while those who took the calf ask to be shown mercy and then forgiven (7:149). Three times it is God’s own verdict — on the town that rejected Shuʿayb (7:92), on whoever feels secure from His planning (7:99), and on whoever is left to stray (7:178).

Sūrat al-Anʿām's version puts the challenge and the answer in a single exchange: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘O my people! Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed.’”* (6:135).

The threat of 7:90 is a prediction made by one party about another, and the Book records a prediction made in the other direction: *“I and My messengers will certainly prevail.”* (58:21).
verses.91:
> Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them and they fell lifeless in their homes

**The Earthquake at Madyan**

*Fa-akhadhat-humu al-rajfatu fa-aṣbaḥū fī dārihim jāthimīn* — so the tremor seized them, and they became, in their homes, fallen on their knees. The sūrah closes Madyan with the exact formula it used for Thamūd at 7:78: same instrument, same posture, same morning. The towns have been presented to the reader as a series of variations on a theme, and the two identical endings bind Madyan and Thamūd into a single lesson.

The Qur'an's other accounts of Madyan's end preserve details the sūrah leaves out. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ describes the instrument as a shadow and a day: *“So they rejected him, and ˹so˺ were overtaken by the torment of the day of the ˹deadly˺ cloud. That was really a torment of a tremendous day.”* (26:189). Sūrat Hūd has the cry and the quake together and adds that the town's dwellings were left uninhabited: *“When Our command came, We saved Shu’aib and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us. And the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook the wrongdoers, so they fell lifeless in their homes, as if they had never lived there. So away with Midian as it was with Thamûd!”* (11:94–95). The Book's use of several terms for one event — cry, blast, quake, shadow — is characteristic: the destruction is described from the viewpoint of the people who experienced its different phases. *Rajfah* is the shudder, the violent trembling of the ground; the Book uses it for Thamūd (7:78), for the punishment that seized the people of Shuʿayb here (7:91), and for the quake at the destruction of the town in Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt (29:37). Its choice for a trading city is deliberate in a Book that matches penalties to settings: Madyan's wealth was stored in stone and mud-brick, its caravans were somewhere on the road, and its people were confident in the solidity of the ground they had built on.

**"In Their Homes" and the Morning**

*Fa-aṣbaḥū* — and they became in the morning — is a favourite construction of the sūrah's narratives and the Book's warnings more generally. The ending of a people is typically reported at dawn: Sūrat al-Ḥijr gives Sodom the sunrise and the cry (15:73). Sūrat Hūd has Madyan's destruction by the cry, its people left lifeless in their homes (11:94); the sūrah's own 7:97 will ask the Makkans whether they feel secure from a punishment that arrives *by night while they sleep*, or *by day while they play*. The morning is the hour when a community is most confident of the day ahead; the Book's verdicts arrive there.

**Why Ash-Shuʿarāʾ Omits “Their Brother”**

Three accounts introduce Shuʿayb as his people’s brother: “And to the people of Midian ˹We sent˺ their brother” (29:36), and the same formula in this sūrah at 7:85 and in Hūd at 11:84. Ash-Shuʿarāʾ does not. It says that the residents of the Forest rejected the messengers (26:176), and then that Shuʿayb spoke to them, with no relation named (26:177). Ibn Kathīr’s explanation is that the name ties them to a tree they revered, so that account cuts the brotherhood off in the telling even though he was their brother in lineage. The omission is therefore deliberate, and it is only visible when the four introductions are read together.

**26:157: The Killing and the Regret**

Ash-Shuʿarāʾ records the breach and its immediate consequence in one clause: “But they killed her, becoming regretful.” (26:157). The regret precedes the punishment in that account, so the shaking reported here is not what produced the remorse. Read with the terms of the sign at 26:155 and the warning at 26:156, the sequence is fixed: a share of water allotted, harm forbidden, harm done, regret felt, and then the day.
verses.92:
> Those who rejected Shu’aib were ˹wiped out˺ as if they had never lived there. Those who rejected Shu’aib were the true losers

**"As If They Had Never Lived There"**

The image is the sūrah's most complete statement of what the destruction of a society means. *Ka-a lam yaghnaw fīhā* — as if they had never been settled there, never prospered there, never been at home. The verb *ghaniya* carries dwelling and sufficiency at once: it is the word for being settled in a place and the word for being well off in it. Madyan's disappearance erases both at the same time.

The Book uses the phrase for other destroyed towns and gives it additional weight each time. Sūrat Hūd's account of Thamūd ends with the same formula — *as if they had never lived there* (11:68) — and its account of Madyan repeats it (11:95). In both cases the phrase follows the observation that the towns' messengers had delivered their warnings and that the towns had had every material reason to listen. The Book's choice of words makes the erasure total: not conquered, not merely defeated, but unwritten — their buildings, names, and generations absorbed into a landscape that no longer remembered them.

**Why the Book Erases**

Modern readings of the sūrah sometimes take the verse for a piece of poetry about history's indifference. The Book's own framing of the same image is religious and, in its phrase, exact. Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ states the principle that the erasure is a judgment: *“˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed that had been spoiled by their ˹comfortable˺ living! Those are their residences, never inhabited after them except passingly. And We ˹alone˺ were the Successor.”* (28:58). Sūrat al-Naml's version states the ruin plainly: *“So their homes are there, ˹but completely˺ ruined because of their wrongdoing.”* (27:52; see also 29:38).

**The Loss That the Word Names**

The final clause's construction — *humu al-khāsirūn*, they are the true losers — is emphatic and restrictive in Arabic: the pronoun separates the subject and the definite noun claims the category. The sūrah's scale has already provided the definition: whoever comes to the Day with a light scale has lost himself (7:9). The elite of Madyan spent their political capital trying to prove that devotion to a prophet would bankrupt their city; the sūrah's answer is that the city's actual bankruptcy was recorded in a different account, under a different entry, and on a day when its notables had nothing left to protect.

**A Merchant’s Word for Ruin**

The verdict of the verse is *khasirū* — they lost — and the root *kh-s-r* is commercial before it is moral. To lose, in the Qurʾān’s usage, is to come out of a transaction holding less than one put in: the capital is gone and the goods never arrived. The sūrah’s first audience were traders who would have heard the word as a ledger entry, and the Book argues with them in that register throughout: *“They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided.”* (2:16).

**The Erasure Formula and the Ruins Left Behind**

The Book does not leave the ruins merely empty; it makes them evidence and asks the reader to go and look. *“And the people of ’Ȃd and Thamûd ˹met a similar fate˺, which must be clear to you ˹Meccans˺ from their ruins.”* (29:38). The invitation is put as a command to travel: *“Have they not travelled throughout the land so their hearts may reason, and their ears may listen? Indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind.”* (22:46). The erasure of verse 92 is so double. The town is removed from the present, and what remains of it is placed where a traveller can verify the removal — the ruins are the verse’s footnote, left standing on the trade routes the sūrah’s audience actually used.
verses.93:
> He turned away from them, saying, “O my people! Indeed, I have delivered to you the messages of my Lord and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice. How can I then grieve for those who chose to disbelieve?”

**Shuʿayb's Farewell**

*Fa-tawallā ʿanhum wa-qāla yā qawmi laqad ablaghtukum risālāti rabbī wa-naṣaḥtu lakum fa-kayfa āsā ʿalā qawmin kāfirīn* — he turned away from them, saying: “O my people! Indeed, I have delivered to you the messages of my Lord and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice. How can I then grieve for those who chose to disbelieve?” (7:93)

The sūrah's fifth town closes with the third of its farewells, and the differences between them measure the sūrah's composition. Noah left a drowned world for an ark; Ṣāliḥ left a city prostrate and spoke to it of counsel that was disliked; Shuʿayb leaves a town erased from the ground, and his final sentence is not about the town's response but about his own grief, ending in a question he answers himself. The Book's account of Madyan in Sūrat Hūd closes with the same erasure: *“as if they had never lived there. So away with Midian as it was with Thamûd!”* (11:95). The Hūd narrative also gives Shuʿayb a last line that is not grief but a warning: *“And watch! I too am watching with you!”* (11:93).

**"I Have Delivered the Messages of My Lord"**

The point is one the Book returns to in its instruction to the Prophet: *“So, ˹continue to˺ remind ˹all, O Prophet˺, for your duty is only to remind. You are not ˹there˺ to compel them ˹to believe˺.”* (88:21–22); *“Respond to evil with what is best. We know well what they claim. And say, ‘My Lord! I seek refuge in You from the temptations of the devils. And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, that they ˹even˺ come near me.’”* (23:96–98). The sūrah's own narrative has now shown five messengers fulfilling a duty whose results were not their property, and the farewells are the sūrah's way of setting the record straight about what a prophetic career is measured by.

**"Sincere Advice" — the Fourth Occurrence**

*Wa-naṣaḥtu lakum* — and I gave you sincere advice. The word *nāṣiḥ* has now appeared in the sūrah's sequence for the fourth time, after Noah (7:62), Ḥūd (7:68), and Ṣāliḥ (7:79), and its repetition across five towns is the sūrah's deliberately monotonous answer to the towns' accusations of folly. The messengers were not rulers, miracle-workers, or tribal champions; the Book's one-word summary of their function is the term for the man who mends what is torn without leaving a seam.

**Messages Plural: Delivery and What Is Delivered**

Shuʿayb says *risālāt rabbī* — the messages of my Lord — in the plural. The plural is used in the sūrah of a delivery made over time and more than once, and the same plural appears in his other address (7:85). Al-Māʾidah states the duty in the singular and in the imperative: *“O Messenger! Convey everything revealed to you from your Lord. If you do not, then you have not delivered His message.”* (5:67).

The sūrah’s own record of that repetition is in its structure. Shuʿayb speaks at 7:85, is answered at 7:88, speaks again at 7:93 in the past tense — *balaghtu*, I have delivered — and the narration ends. The plural *risālāt* is therefore not a general phrase but a count: the messages were delivered more than once, and the verse reports the last of those deliveries as complete.

The Book teaches the same discipline to the Prophet repeatedly. Its most reassuring form is in Sūrat al-Kahf: *“Now, perhaps you ˹O Prophet˺ will grieve yourself to death over their denial, if they ˹continue to˺ disbelieve in this message.”* (18:6), followed by the sūrah's answer that the message is not the messenger's to enforce.
verses.94:
> Whenever We sent a prophet to a society, We afflicted its ˹disbelieving˺ people with suffering and adversity, so perhaps they would be humbled

**The Law of Adversity**

*Wa-mā arsalnā fī qaryatin min nabiyyin illā akhadhnā ahlahā bi-l-baʾsāʾi wa-l-ḍarrāʾi laʿallahum yaḍḍarraʿūn* — and We never sent a prophet to any town without seizing its people with suffering and hardship, so that they might humble themselves. With this verse the sūrah stops telling the stories of towns and begins to state the law that governed them all.

The two nouns are a fixed pair in the Qur'an's language of trial: *baʾsāʾ* is the hardship that touches property and circumstances — poverty, hunger, loss — and *ḍarrāʾ* is the hardship that touches the body and the self — illness, pain, injury. The Book uses them together whenever it describes the afflictions by which a message is brought home: *“Indeed, We have sent messengers before you ˹O Prophet˺ to other people who We put through suffering and adversity ˹for their denial˺. Perhaps they would be humbled”* (6:42), and the sūrah's own verse states the same purpose in the same pair of nouns (7:94). Sūrat al-Baqarah applies the pair to the Prophet's community: *“They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were so ˹violently˺ shaken”* (2:214).

**The Purpose Stated in the Verse**

*Laʿallahum yaḍḍarraʿūn* — so that they might humble themselves — the clause is the verse's whole doctrine, and its verb is one of the Qur'an's most precise religious terms. *Taḍarruʿ* is the self-abasement of a creature who has run out of resources. It is the root the sūrah used for the manner of supplication in its instruction at 7:55: *call upon your Lord humbly and secretly*. The Book's teaching here is that the hardships that visit a society are not random and not only retributive; they are summonses, and their intended outcome is the posture of a person who has stopped relying on his own strength.

Sūrat al-Anʿām's parallel passage uses the same word with the same purpose and adds a lament: *“so perhaps they would be humbled. Why did they not humble themselves when We made them suffer? Instead, their hearts were hardened, and Satan made their misdeeds appealing to them”* (6:42–43). The sūrah's verse hides the rest of the story in its optative form — *so that they might humble themselves* — and the next verse will show what actually happened in the towns the sūrah has been describing.

**The Second Movement of the Test**

The verse states the first movement of the sūrah’s law — a town seized with hardship so that it might be humbled — and the verse after it states the second: *“Then We changed their adversity to prosperity until they flourished”* (7:95). The towns then offer the argument the verse records: *“Our forefathers ˹too˺ had been visited by adversity and prosperity.”* (7:95).

**The Same Purpose Clause Elsewhere**

The clause *so perhaps they would be humbled* is the sūrah’s, and the Book uses the same construction elsewhere with the same end in view. Of the corruption people have made on land and sea: *“Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people’s hands have done, so that Allah may cause them to taste ˹the consequences of˺ some of their deeds and perhaps they might return ˹to the Right Path˺.”* (30:41). Of the punishment before the punishment: *“We will certainly make them taste some of the minor torment ˹in this life˺ before the major torment ˹of the Hereafter˺, so perhaps they will return ˹to the Right Path˺.”* (32:21).

Sūrat Yūnus states the response that saves: *“When We give people a taste of mercy after being afflicted with a hardship, they swiftly devise plots against Our revelations! Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Allah is swifter in devising ˹punishment˺. Surely Our messengerangels record whatever you devise.’”* (10:21).

**Hardship at the Personal Scale**

The law this verse applies to nations, the Prophet ﷺ applied to individuals: "No fatigue, nor disease, nor sorrow, nor sadness, nor hurt, nor distress befalls a Muslim — not even the prick of a thorn — but that Allah expiates some of his sins for it" (al-Bukhārī 5641; Muslim 2573, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and Abū Hurayrah). The two teachings run at different scales and say the same thing about pain in the Qur'an's world: hardship is not proof of abandonment, and it can be a mercy that turns a person back before the final account.
verses.95:
> Then We changed their adversity to prosperity until they flourished and argued ˹falsely˺, “Our forefathers ˹too˺ had been visited by adversity and prosperity.” So We seized them by surprise, while they were unaware

**"Our Fathers Had Both"**

The argument the towns construct is the argument from normalcy, and the Book names it as the last stage of the deception. Its Qur'anic parallel appears in Sūrat al-Anʿām, where the sequence is stated almost as a law: *“When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired. But just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise, then they instantly fell into despair!”* (6:44). The same pattern is repeated in Sūrat al-Muʾminūn, where the sūrah describes a community receiving mercy after hardship and using it as an argument for security (23:75–77 in the sequence).

**The Suddenness**

*Fa-akhadhnāhum baghtatan wa-hum lā yashʿurūn* — so We seized them by surprise while they were unaware. The adverb *baghtatan* — suddenly — is the Book's standard attribute of the seizure that ends a heedless generation. The pairing with *lā yashʿurūn*, while they were not aware, is stated at several points in the Makkan sūrahs: Sūrat al-Aʿrāf will repeat the formulation in its account of the Hour (7:187). Sūrat Yūsuf asks whether people feel secure that the Hour will not take them by surprise when they least expect it (12:107). Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt's version of the punishment of the towns uses the same logic (29:53); and Sūrat al-Naḥl's series of questions states the doctrine plainly: *“Do those who devise evil plots feel secure that Allah will not cause the earth to swallow them? Or that the torment will not come upon them in ways they cannot understand? Or that He will not seize them while they go about ˹their day˺, for then they will have no escape?”* (16:45–46).

The wording is not only picturesque. The Book's teaching is that the timing of judgment is a deliberate concealment: the generation that has made its peace with a warning cannot see the hour of the settlement, and the warning itself becomes part of the ordinary furniture of its life. Sūrat Yūnus gives the reason the delay exists: *“If Allah were to hasten evil for people as they wish to hasten good, they would have certainly been doomed. But We leave those who do not expect to meet Us to wander blindly in their defiance.”* (10:11; see also 16:61, 35:45).

**Prosperity as the Heavier Test**

The verse's most important claim is that the good condition after the bad was the actual trial, and the sūrah's own earlier material supports it. The rain that revives a dead land was described at 7:57 as a sign; the good soil's yield at 7:58 was an argument; and the sūrah's address to ʿĀd at 7:69 named *the favours of Allah* as the thing to remember.

Sūrat Luqmān puts the same thought in the mouth of its warning: *“So do not let the life of this world deceive you, nor let the Chief Deceiver deceive you about Allah.”* (31:33) — and Sūrat al-Anʿām's verse about the opening of the gates of everything is followed by the sūrah's own explanation: *“So the wrongdoers were utterly uprooted. And all praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds.”* (6:45).

**Until They Increased: The Growth That Sealed the Term**

7:95 describes a substitution and then a growth. The verb of increase is the hinge of the verse. The Book states the same hinge in a test whose two forms are mistaken for verdicts: *“whenever a human being is tested by their Lord through ˹His˺ generosity and blessings”* (89:15) the person boasts of honour, and *“when He tests them by limiting their provision”* (89:16) the person protests at humiliation. The two verses of al-Fajr name the error that 7:95 narrates, namely the reading of a change in circumstances as a statement about the person rather than as a test.

The growth is what makes the argument possible. The sūrah states the same mechanism at 7:94–95 in sequence: the messenger is sent, the people are afflicted, then they are relieved, and the relief is what generates the false reading.
verses.96:
> Had the people of those societies been faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, We would have overwhelmed them with blessings from heaven and earth. But they disbelieved, so We seized them for what they used to commit

**Faith and Mindfulness**

The condition the verse attaches to the promise is a pair of terms the sūrah has used throughout: *āmanū*, they believed — trust in the message and the messenger — and *ittaqaw*, they were mindful — the practical restraint that the sūrah's prophets kept demanding, the honest scale at Madyan, the untouched she-camel at Thamūd, the undefiled sign at Sodom. The Book's grammar of blessing is consistently conditional in this way, and its statements are equally consistently corporate: the covenant is with a community, and so is the consequence.

Sūrat al-Naḥl's parable of the town states the two conditions under a single image: *“And Allah sets forth the example of a society which was safe and at ease, receiving its provision in abundance from all directions. But its people met Allah’s favours with ingratitude, so Allah made them taste the clutches of hunger and fear for their misdeeds.”* (16:112). The verse is the sūrah's own theology in narrative form, and its details — security, ample provision, the denial of favour, the garment of hunger and fear — are the exact reversal of verse 96's promise. Sūrat Sabaʾ's account of the people of Sheba makes the same point with garden imagery: *“Indeed, there was a sign for ˹the tribe of˺ Sheba in their homeland: two orchards—one to the right and the other to the left. ˹They were told:˺ ‘Eat from the provision of your Lord. Be grateful to Him. ˹Yours is˺ a good land and a forgiving Lord.’”* (34:15) — until the town turned away and was given, in place of its gardens, a flood and bitter fruit (34:15–17).

**The Doctrine of Blessing in the Book**

And the Book's warnings about the alternative are equally corporate. Sūrat al-Anʿām's verse about the opening of every gate and the sudden seizure (6:44) is followed by the sūrah's statement of the purpose: *“So the wrongdoers were utterly uprooted. And all praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds.”* (6:45). The sūrah's own 7:96 states the terms of the exchange, and the next three verses will ask the reader the only question that remains: whether he has considered the alternative.

**From Heaven and Earth: The Two Sources Described**

The blessings the verse promises come from two directions: *“We would have overwhelmed them with blessings from heaven and earth.”* (7:96). Al-Muʾminūn describes the two movements: *“We send down rain from the sky in perfect measure, causing it to soak into the earth. And We are surely able to take it away.”* (23:18) and *“With it We produce for you gardens of palm trees and grapevines, in which there are abundant fruits, and from which you may eat.”* (23:19).

**Seized for What They Used to Earn**

The verse’s second half reports the seizure: they disbelieved, so they were taken for what they used to earn. Ar-Rūm states the same relation between conduct and consequence: *“Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people’s hands have done, so that Allah may cause them to taste ˹the consequences of˺ some of their deeds and perhaps they might return ˹to the Right Path˺.”* (30:41).

The verse supplies the purpose 7:96 leaves implicit — the tasting is partial and is meant to produce a return. The sūrah’s own histories follow exactly this shape: years of shortage given so that they might come back (7:130), signs sent in succession so that they might humble themselves (7:133). In every case the seizure is a taste and not the whole.
verses.97:
> Did the people of those societies feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by night while they were asleep

*A-fa-aminu ahlu al-qurā a yaʾtiyahum baʾsunā bayātan wa-hum nāʾimūn* — did the people of those societies feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by night while they were asleep?

Sodom was destroyed at dawn (15:66); Thamūd's punishment came in the morning (15:83); the sūrah's own accounts of the townships mostly arrive at the beginning of a day.

Sūrat al-Mulk's address to the secure is the purest instance: *“Do you feel secure that the One Who is in heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you up as it quakes violently? Or do you feel secure that the One Who is in heaven will not unleash upon you a storm of stones. Only then would you know how ˹serious˺ My warning was!”* (67:16–17). Sūrat al-Naḥl's list of possibilities — swallowing, seizure from beneath, confusion, a wasting punishment, an enemy — is followed by its own warning: *“But your Lord is truly Ever Gracious, Most Merciful.”* (16:47), which is the verse's way of saying the delay in all those scenarios is mercy, not immunity.

**The Sense of the Hour**

There is one more layer in the verse's composition. The night and its sleep are the Book's standing symbols of heedlessness in this world — Sūrat al-Furqān describes the believing servants as those who *“spend ˹a good portion of˺ the night, prostrating themselves and standing before their Lord.”* (25:64), Sūrat al-Sajdah commends those *“They abandon their beds, invoking their Lord with hope and fear. Donate from what We have provided for them.”* (32:16), and the sūrah of al-Muzzammil opens with the command to *“Stand all night ˹in prayer˺ except a little”* (73:2). The sūrah's question asks what the sleeping town thought was protecting it during the hours when the faithful are described as awake.

The contrast is between two ways of passing a night: the town that sleeps in the confidence of its walls, and the believer who rises in the confidence of his Lord. The Qur'an's instruction to the Prophet about the Day's nearness uses the same imagery of the night and its end: *“So be patient ˹O Prophet˺ with what they say. And glorify the praises of your Lord before sunrise and before sunset”* (20:130), and the sūrah of al-ʿAṣr's warning about humanity in loss is preached against the background of time's march. Verse 97 is so the sūrah's invitation to a discipline, in the form of a question that no city can answer for itself.

**The Pattern Announced in the Fourth Verse**

The pattern this verse questions is announced before any town has been named: “Our torment took them by surprise ˹while sleeping˺ at night or midday.” (7:4). One clause there carries both hours, and the sūrah spends ninety-three verses turning it into two questions — the night and its sleep here, the day and its play in the verse that follows. The word for surprise occurs three times in the sūrah, at 7:4, 7:95 and 7:187, and the third applies it to the Hour itself: the timing is withheld but the manner is not, since “It is too tremendous for the heavens and the earth and will only take you by surprise.” (7:187). What the towns are asked about is therefore not a feature of their history but the sūrah’s stated rule for every society, including the one being addressed.

The question of 7:97 asks whether the people of the towns felt secure against a punishment arriving at night. The Book puts the same question in al-Mulk with two images attached: *“Do you feel secure that the One Who is in heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you up as it quakes violently?”* (67:16), *“Or do you feel secure that the One Who is in heaven will not unleash upon you a storm of stones.”* (67:17)
verses.98:
> Or did they feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by day while they were at play

**The Daytime and Its Confidence**

The pairing of night with day means that the sūrah's question covers the whole human clock. There is no hour of the day or night at which a society is, by its own arrangements, safe. The two conditions the verses name — sleep, the absence of consciousness, and play, the absence of seriousness — are the two modes of heedlessness, and both are described as the normal activity of the well-off.

The Book uses this double question elsewhere, and its versions are worth setting side by side. Sūrat al-Naḥl's series of possibilities covers seizure from above, from below, in confusion, or by a slow wasting (16:45–47). Sūrat al-Mulk's questions come in a pair with the earth's swallowing and the storm of stones (67:16–17). And Sūrat al-Isrāʾ's account of the towns destroyed uses the night explicitly: *“Whenever We intend to destroy a society, We command its elite ˹to obey Allah˺ but they act rebelliously in it. So the decree ˹of punishment˺ is justified, and We destroy it utterly.”* (17:16). In every version, the point is the same: the destruction arrives in the middle of a routine.

**The Play of the Prosperous**

*Yalʿabūn* is the Book's word for what a community does when it confuses the interval of mercy with a permanent concession. The Qur'an's use of the term is not confined to recreation; it covers the serious business of societies that have decided that the questions the prophets raise can be deferred indefinitely. Sūrat al-Anʿām's confrontation with the townspeople who made a game of their religion (6:70's *lahw wa-laʿib*) and Sūrat al-Ḥadīd's description of the world's own texture — amusement, play, adornment, boasting, competition in wealth and children (57:20) — express the same judgment.

Verse 98's question so belongs with the sūrah's earlier diagnosis of the towns. The elites of Madyan and ʿĀd and Thamūd were not frivolous people; they were serious about their trade, their monuments, and their standing. What the Book calls play is the seriousness of a person who has excluded the one serious question from the ledger. Sūrat al-Muʾminūn's summary of the contrast puts the two lives side by side: the believers who turn away from idle talk (23:3) and the heedless who are described by the sūrah's recurring image of play (21:1–3; 44:9; 52:12).

**Why the Questions Have No Answer**

The sūrah is also, in these verses, completing the work it began at 7:94. That verse established that hardship was the summons; 7:95 showed the towns misreading relief; 7:96 stated the counterfactual; and 7:97–98 ask whether the survivors of history have understood the lesson of those who have not survived. The Book's addressee has now been given the law, the case, the evidence, and the question. The verses that follow close the argument with one sentence about the only disposition that can be called sane.

**The Blessedness of Not Feeling Secure**

Read in the context of the sūrah's earlier teachings, the questions are not an accusation aimed at the reader; they are an invitation to a state of mind the Book calls *taqwā*. The faithful are described elsewhere as those who *fear their Lord unseen* and as those whose hearts tremble when His name is mentioned (22:35; 8:2).

Sūrat al-Zumar leaves the door of that interval open in the widest terms: *“O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah's mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins”* (39:53).

Of those whose faith is not mixed with wrongdoing: *“It is ˹only˺ those who are faithful and do not tarnish their faith with falsehood who are guaranteed security and are ˹rightly˺ guided.”* (6:82).

The Book also reports a security given as a provision, and asks what it obliges: *“Have they not seen how We have made ˹Mecca˺ a safe haven, whereas people ˹all˺ around them are snatched away?”* (29:67).
verses.99:
> Did they feel secure against Allah’s planning? None would feel secure from Allah’s planning except the losers

**"Did They Feel Secure From Allah's Plan?"**

*A-fa-aminū makra Allāh* — did they feel secure from the plan of Allah? The third question of the series introduces the sūrah's sharpest religious term, and its sharpness has troubled readers for centuries. *Makr* in Arabic is the word for a stratagem, a scheme, a plan worked out with cunning. The Qur'an applies it to human scheming when it reports the plots of the disbelievers, and it applies it to God when it describes the counter-plot by which their schemes are undone.

*“And the disbelievers made a plan ˹against Jesus˺, but Allah also planned —and Allah is the best of planners.”* (3:54). Sūrat al-Naml's account of the plot against Ṣāliḥ states the principle in the sūrah's own terms: *“And ˹so˺ they made a plan, but We too made a plan, while they were unaware.”* (27:50).

**The Believer's Fear and the Prophet's Prayer**

The Book's positive doctrine of fear appears throughout the Makkan sūrahs and is stated most fully in the sūrah of the Cave and the sūrah of al-Raʿd: *“and those who maintain whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained, stand in awe of their Lord. Fear strict judgment.”* (13:21); *“and those who fear the punishment of their Lord—”* (70:27). The Prophet's own practice is recorded in the hadith, where fear and hope are held together in his instruction: the Companions heard him say, *“None of you should wish for death because of a calamity befalling him; but if he has to wish for death, he should say: ‘O Allah! Keep me alive as long as life is better for me, and let me die if death is better for me’”* (al-Bukhārī 5671; Muslim 2680, from Anas ibn Mālik). The sūrah's own earlier instruction — call upon God *with hope and fear* (7:56) — is the positive form of the same discipline.

**The Passage Complete**

With verse 99 the sūrah's meditation on the towns is complete, and its shape can be seen whole: the law of adversity (7:94), the misread relief (7:95), the counterfactual (7:96), the two questions about night and day (7:97–98), and the question about the plan itself (7:99). The five towns of the earlier narrative are the evidence, and the passage's four general verses are the sūrah's doctrine of history.

What follows will apply the doctrine to the sūrah's own readers with two more questions about inheritance and the seal on the heart (7:100–101), then draw the moral of the nations (7:102) and turn the page toward Moses and Pharaoh (7:103). The sūrah's reader, having been asked whether he feels secure, is about to be asked whether he has understood what he is standing on.

**The Losers Named**

The sūrah uses the same participle at its own turning points. It is the word of the first confession — *“we will certainly be losers”* (7:23) — and of those whose scales are light (7:9), and it appears in the histories of the towns (7:92). In each case the loss is stated by the ones who suffer it or by God about them, never as an accusation thrown at an opponent. 7:99 is the sūrah’s summary use: the security that is not faith is a loss, and the people who feel it are the losers.

39:15 supplies the measure of the loss 7:99 names. The verse calls this *al-khusr al-mubīn*, the clear loss — the same adjective the sūrah uses of the warning at 7:184.

Sūrat al-Mulk's questions about the security of the heaven-dwellers are answered with the observation that gratitude and walking humbly are the alternatives (67:16–22).

Sūrat al-Rūm's account of the cycles of fortune warns that the alternation is by design (30:34–36) and Sūrat Fāṭir's passages on the same theme conclude with the phrase that sums up the sūrah's theology: *“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, ‘Have you considered your associate-gods which you invoke besides Allah?’”* (35:40).

Abraham’s visitor asks the identical question from the other side: “Who would despair of the mercy of their Lord except the misguided?” (15:56).
verses.100:
> Is it not clear to those who take over the land after ˹the destruction of˺ its former residents that—if We will—We can punish them ˹too˺ for their sins and seal their hearts so they will not hear ˹the truth˺

**The Book's Doctrine of Succession**

The Qur'an consistently treats the succession of peoples as an office and not an accident. *“Then We made you their successors in the land to see how you would act.”* (10:14) (Yūnus 10:14). *“Have they not seen how many ˹disbelieving˺ peoples We destroyed before them? We had made them more established in the land than you. We sent down abundant rain for them and made rivers flow at their feet. Then We destroyed them for their sins and replaced them with other peoples.”* (6:6) (Anʿām 6:6). The Book's formula — establishment, abundance, destruction, replacement — is the same sequence the sūrah has just narrated in five instalments, and 6:6 states it as a general law addressed to the Prophet's contemporaries.

The doctrine cuts the other way as well. Sūrat al-Nūr makes the succession a promise to the faithful — *“Allah has promised those of you who believe and do good that He will certainly make them successors in the land, as He did with those before them”* (24:55) — and Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ states the condition plainly: *“Surely, following the ˹heavenly˺ Record, We decreed in the Scriptures: ‘My righteous servants shall inherit the land.’”* (21:105).

**The Seal on the Heart**

*Wa-naṭbaʿu ʿalā qulūbihim fa-hum lā yasmaʿūn.* The verse's second threat is graver than the first, and it names the penalty that makes the whole meditation on the towns intelligible. The Book's vocabulary of the sealed heart appears in several forms — *khatama* (2:7), *ṭabaʿa* (7:101, 10:74, 40:35), *rān* (83:14), *ghulf* (4:155) — and in each place it is the settled result of a person's own persistence rather than a sentence imposed from outside. In fact, their hearts have been stained by all ˹the evil˺ they used to commit!”* (83:14).

The Prophet's teaching preserved the same image in one of the best-known explanations of that verse. Abū Hurayrah reported him saying: *“When the servant commits a sin, a black spot appears in his heart. If he repents and desists, his heart is polished clean. But if he returns, it increases until it covers his heart — and that is the covering (rān) which Allah mentions: 'No indeed, what they used to earn has covered their hearts.'”* (al-Tirmidhī 3334, from Abū Hurayrah; graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ by al-Tirmidhī and ḥasan by Dār al-Salām).

**"So They Will Not Hear"**

The verse's consequence is stated in hearing rather than punishment, and the choice is deliberate in a sūrah that has been about speech and its reception from its first page. The Book's own description of the loss appears at 7:179, where the condemned have eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, and at 7:198, where the idols' claimants are called and do not hear the call. Sūrat Yā Sīn states the same condition in the form of a barrier: *“and have placed a barrier before them and a barrier behind them and covered them ˹all˺ up. They fail to see ˹the truth˺”* (36:9), followed immediately by the Book's own summary — *“It is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe”* (36:10).

Sūrat al-Anʿām gives the same loss a first-person form: *“We turn their hearts and eyes away ˹from the truth˺ as they refused to believe at first”* (6:110). The sūrah's 7:100 therefore states, in one conditional sentence, the whole arithmetic of the Book's warnings: the punishment a nation fears may take away its cities, but the punishment that ends its possibility is the closing of the organ by which the message is received.

**Left to Stray Knowingly: The Sealing as an Act**

The question at the end of 45:23 completes the warning: who can guide them after Allah. The sūrah's own question at 7:100 is put in the same form, asking whether it is not clear to the inheritors that the same could be done to them.

Sūrat Ṭāhā's formulation is the closest parallel: *“Is it not yet clear to them how many peoples We destroyed before them, whose ruins they still pass by? Surely in this are signs for people of sound judgment.”* (20:128).

Sūrat al-Sajdah's version adds the Book's own lament: *“Is it not yet clear to them how many peoples We destroyed before them, whose ruins they still pass by? Will they not then listen?”* (32:26) — and the verse ends with the very faculty that 7:100's seal removes.
verses.101:
> We have narrated to you ˹O Prophet˺ some of the stories of those societies. Surely, their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but still they would not believe in what they had already denied. This is how Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers

**"These Are the Societies Whose Stories We Relate to You"**

*Tilka al-qurā naquṣṣu ʿalayka min anbāʾihā* — those are the towns; We relate to you some of their tidings. The verse is the sūrah's own caption on the narrative block that has just concluded, and it states the purpose of the material: the account of the five communities has been transmitted to the Prophet as information, for him first of all.

The Book gives the same caption to its stories in several places, and the repeated formula deserves attention because it defines what kind of book the Qur'an claims to be. *“And We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ the stories of the messengers to reassure your heart. And there has come to you in this ˹sûrah˺ the truth, a warning ˹to the disbelievers˺, and a reminder to the believers.”* (11:120). *“This is how We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ some of the stories of the past. And We have certainly granted you a Reminder from Us.”* (20:99). *“We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ the best of stories”* (12:3). *“We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ their story in truth.”* (18:13). *“We narrate to you ˹O Prophet˺ part of the story of Moses and Pharaoh in truth for people who believe.”* (28:3).

**"They Were Not To Believe What They Had Already Denied"**

*Fa-mā kānū li-yuʾminū bimā kadhdhabū bihi min qabl.* This is the verse's hardest clause, and the Book repeats it in nearly identical form elsewhere: *“Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wrongfully rejected them. See what was the end of the corruptors!”* (7:103). *“So We plagued them with floods, locusts, lice, frogs. Blood—all as clear signs, but they persisted in arrogance and were a wicked people.”* (7:133); and the clause that closes the same pattern in Sūrat Yūnus: *“Then after him We sent ˹other˺ messengers to their ˹own˺ people and they came to them with clear proofs. This is how We seal the hearts of the transgressors.”* (10:74).

The clause states the Book's doctrine of settled disbelief. The refusal the towns were practicing at the moment of the messenger's arrival was not a fresh decision. It was the continuation of a posture already adopted, and Sūrat al-Anʿām identifies the process in God's own voice: *“We turn their hearts and eyes away ˹from the truth˺ as they refused to believe at first, leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance”* (6:110). Sūrat al-Baqarah's opening states the same verdict in its starkest form: the disbelievers are those whom warning and its absence leave equally unmoved, hearts, hearing, and sight alike covered (2:6–7).

**"Thus Allah Seals the Hearts of the Disbelievers"**

*Kadhālika yaṭbaʿu Allāh ʿalā qulūbi al-kāfirīn.* the teaching about the seal is not a blot on the Book's justice; it is the explanation of why the towns' stories repeat with such monotony. The Qur'an's own remedy for a heart that is hardening is stated repeatedly in the imperative: remember, turn back, seek forgiveness, recite. Sūrat al-Zumar leaves the door open in the widest terms: *“Say, ˹O Prophet, that Allah says,˺ ‘O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah’s mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins.”* (39:53), and Sūrat al-Furqān's verse on repentance promises the substitution of good deeds for bad: *“As for those who repent, believe, and do good deeds, they are the ones whose evil deeds Allah will change into good deeds.

The Prophet's own practice shows what the seal's alternative looks like in a life. Umm Salamah reported that he used to say in his supplication: *“O Turner of hearts, keep my heart firm upon Your religion”* (al-Tirmidhī 3522, from Umm Salamah; graded ḥasan by al-Tirmidhī).

The verse closes: *“This is how Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers.”* (7:101). They will suffer a tremendous punishment.”* (2:7).
verses.102:
> We did not find most of them true to their covenant. Rather, We found most of them truly rebellious

**Which Covenant?**

The Qur'an's language of *ʿahd* and *mīthāq* refers to more than the agreements made with particular prophets. The Book describes a covenant taken from every human being before their earthly life: *“And ˹remember˺ when your Lord brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam their descendants and had them testify about themselves. ˹Allah asked,˺ ‘Am I not your Lord?’ They replied, ‘Yes, You are! We testify.’”* (7:172) — the verse belongs to this very sūrah, and it is the reason the sūrah's summaries can speak of a covenant that every people has broken. Sūrat Yā Sīn restates the same primordial undertaking: *“Did I not command you, O Children of Adam, not to follow Satan, for he is truly your sworn enemy, but to worship Me ˹alone˺? This is the Straight Path.”* (36:60–61).

The Book also speaks of covenants with the prophets (33:7), with the People of the Book (3:187, 5:12–14). With the Prophet's community *“Surely those who pledge allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ are actually pledging allegiance to Allah.”* (48:10), and it gives the ordinance its general form in Sūrat al-Isrāʾ: *“Do not come near the wealth of the orphan—unless intending to enhance it—until they attain maturity. And honour ˹your˺ pledges, for you will surely be accountable for them.”* (17:34).

**The Anatomy of Transgression**

*Fāsiqīn* is the Book's precise term for that condition, and its root meaning is instructive: *fisq* in Arabic describes a date emerging from its skin, the fruit leaving the husk that should have contained it. The Qur'an's own definitions show the term operating in the realm of conduct rather than doctrine. It is they who are ˹truly˺ rebellious.”* (59:19). Sūrat al-Nūr treats the slanderer's offense as transgression (24:4), and Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt warns that a careless report may be a transgression with consequences (49:6–7).

Most telling for this verse is Sūrat al-Baqarah's linkage of transgression to covenant-breaking in a single passage: the sūrah's parable of the gnat misleads by it *many*. The ones it misleads are defined immediately as those who break the covenant of Allah after ratifying it, sever what Allah commanded to be joined, and spread corruption in the earth (2:26–27). The Book's own sequence — covenant, breach, corruption, loss — is the sūrah's sequence in miniature, and the towns of al-Aʿrāf have just enacted it five times.

**The Weight of "Most"**

The verse's word *aktharihim*, most of them, prevents two errors. Some among them are upright, yet many do nothing but evil.”* (5:66), and Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's own later passage promises that *“And among those We created is a group that guides with the truth and establishes justice accordingly.”* (7:181).

The sūrah's earlier verse on the towns' accounting made the same point with different words: the blessings were available to the faithful and mindful, and the record says that most preferred otherwise. The Qur'an returns to the theme insistently — *“most people will not believe”* (12:103); *“most people do not believe”* (13:1); *“most of them do not know”* (6:37 and elsewhere), *“We have indeed established you on earth and provided you with a means of livelihood. ˹Yet˺ you seldom give any thanks.”* (7:10) — because the reader's instinct is to infer truth from numbers, and the Book's histories are written to sever that inference.

**Covenant Violated After It Was Affirmed**

The three acts belong together and correspond to what 7:102 summarises. The covenant is the testimony taken from the descendants of Ādam (7:172); the ties ordered to be maintained are the relations that testimony established; and the corruption in the land is what the sūrah’s histories report town by town. The verse of ar-Raʿd gives the sequence, and 7:102 gives the verdict on it.

The comparison also fixes the meaning of *most*. 13:25 describes a class by its acts; 7:102 quantifies a finding.

The Book states the same verdict about communities that have gone before and the generations that inherit them: *“That was a community that had already gone before. And you will not be accountable for what they have done”* (2:134; the same sentence closes 2:141).
verses.103:
> Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wrongfully rejected them. See what was the end of the corruptors

**"Then After Them We Sent Moses"**

*Thumma baʿathnā min baʿdihim Mūsā bi-āyātinā ilā Firʿawna wa-malaʾihi fa-ẓalamū bihā fa-nẓur kayfa kāna ʿāqibatu al-mufsidīn* — then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wrongfully rejected them; see what was the end of the corruptors!

**The Chain of Prophecy**

*Min baʿdihim* — after them — places Moses in the succession the sūrah has been tracing. The Book's own sense of prophetic history is genealogical and continuous: *“Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers.”* (2:87); *“We already sent messengers before you. We have told you the stories of some of them, while others We have not.”* (40:78); *“Indeed, We have sent revelation to you ˹O Prophet˺ as We sent revelation to Noah and the prophets after him”* (4:163). The sequence is not a series of isolated episodes but one message entrusted to a chain of bearers, and the sūrah's five towns have been its first five links of the Arab world's portion.

**"They Wrongfully Rejected Them"**

*Fa-ẓalamū bihā* — they did injustice to the signs — the phrase is the Book's standing analysis of the psychopathology of denial. Its fullest form appears in Sūrat al-Naml: *“And, although their hearts were convinced the signs were true, they still denied them wrongfully and arrogantly. See then what was the end of the corruptors!”* (27:14). The Qur'an's claim is so not that the deniers lacked evidence; it is that they suppressed an evidence they had. Sūrat al-Aʿrāf states the same mechanism at 7:146, where the Book announces that it will turn away from its signs those who behave arrogantly on the earth without right, and even if they see every sign they will not believe it.

The verb also exposes what the denial costs. The signs Moses brought are described in Sūrat al-Naml as *nine* clear signs (27:12) and in Sūrat al-Isrāʾ as the same nine (17:101); the Book's account of the Egyptian court's response is that it called them *magic* and attributed them to the skills of a professional class. The injustice in *ẓalamū bihā* is therefore directed at the signs themselves — the court denied what it had seen — and the Book's narrative treats the lying interpretation as a further offense rather than a mere error of judgment.

**"The End of the Corrupters"**

*Fa-nẓur kayfa kāna ʿāqibatu al-mufsidīn.* The closing command is the sūrah's refrain and the age of the audience is invited into it: the ruins of the Egyptian world were still visible in the Book's own account — *“And ˹so˺ We made the oppressed people successors of the eastern and western lands, which We had showered with blessings.”* (7:137) — and the story's later outcomes were known to its listeners. It is they who are the ˹true˺ losers”* (2:27).

Sūrat al-Rūm's statement of the consequences is one of the Book's most quoted: *“Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people’s hands have done. That Allah may cause them to taste ˹the consequences of˺ some of their deeds and perhaps they might return ˹to the Right Path˺.”* (30:41). Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ adds the Book's standard for the office of the land: *“That ˹eternal˺ Home in the Hereafter We reserve ˹only˺ for those who seek neither tyranny nor corruption on the earth. The ultimate outcome belongs ˹only˺ to the righteous”* (28:83). The sūrah's verdict on Pharaoh is so a verdict on a category, stated in verse 103 before the narrative has begun to describe his deeds — a technique the Book uses to tell the reader in advance what kind of story he is about to hear.

Sūrah Yūnus does the same at the same point in its own account: *“Then after these ˹messengers˺ We sent Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and his chiefs with Our signs. But they behaved arrogantly and were a wicked people.”* (10:75).
verses.104:
> And Moses said, “O Pharaoh! I am truly a messenger from the Lord of all worlds

**The Claim Made in the Belly of the Beast**

The Qur'an's Moses stories vary in detail and share this opening: the messenger walks into the seat of supreme power and names the authority that sent him. In Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ the conversation expands into a dialogue between two claims of lordship: Moses says *Lord of the worlds* (26:23), the court calls for the other gods of Moses' ancestors, and Moses answers with the Lord of the east and the west and all that lies between (26:28). Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt reports the verse that explains the exchange: *“I am your lord, the most high!”* (79:24); Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ gives the same claim in the words *“I know of no other god for you but myself.”* (28:38). Pharaoh's politics was a claim of divinity, and Moses' first sentence in the sūrah is the direct refusal of it.

**"The Lord of All Worlds"**

The Qur'an's uses of the title carry the same political charge wherever they appear. Sūrat al-Fātiḥah opens with it before making any other statement about God. Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt's account of Abraham uses it in his confrontation with a people who took their kings' traditions as law (37:87). And the sūrah's own structure sets 7:104 against 7:54 much as the prayer of the saved in the hereafter — *“Praise be to Allah for guiding us to this”* (7:43) — answers every claim of lordship that preceded it.

**The Messenger and the Man**

The Book insists that Moses is also one of the earthly powerless, and the narrative will make much of it. He had been raised in Pharaoh's palace and had fled it (28:14–21), he is described as a man who killed accidentally and who returned speaking with a tongue that his brother's fluency must support (28:33–34). The Book's account of his confrontation in Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ has the court try to discredit him with the fact that he was raised among them (26:18–19). The verse's claim so rests on the office rather than the person: the authority of the speaker comes completely from *rabbi al-ʿālamīn*, a Lord whose claim over Egypt had nothing to do with Egypt's gods or its king's edicts.

**The Pattern of the Sūrah's Narratives**

Preached to the Prophet's Makkan congregation, the sentence had an obvious double edge. Their own interlocutors were men of standing and lineage who treated the traditions of their city as law, and the sūrah's Moses cycle is the Book's fullest dramatization of what happens when a message arrives at an established order and the order tries to outlast it. The Prophet's own practice in this regard is preserved in the tradition: when he came to Madīnah and found the Jews fasting on ʿĀshūrāʾ, he asked what the day meant. When told that it was the day Allah saved Moses and drowned Pharaoh, he said, *“We have a greater right to Moses than you,”* and commanded the fast (al-Bukhārī 2004; Muslim 1130, from Ibn ʿAbbās). The Book's use of Moses as the emblem of deliverance from a tyrannical power is so continuous with the community's own memory.

**The Address by Name**

The address is also the fulfilment of the commission as the Book records it: *“Go to Pharaoh, for he has truly transgressed ˹all bounds˺.”* (79:17). The instruction names the man and states his condition, and the sūrah shows the messenger beginning his speech at exactly that point — the name and the office, before the message.

Verse 105 will complete Moses' opening speech: *“obliged to say nothing about Allah except the truth. Indeed, I have come to you with clear proof from your Lord. Let the children of Israel go with me.”* (7:104–105) This is the Qur'an's characteristic ordering of the message — the truth about God, then the proof, then the demand for the concrete wrong to be undone — and the sūrah will develop the confrontation through signs, magicians, the plagues, the sea. The deliverance of Israel, before returning once more to the law of the towns.
verses.105:
> obliged to say nothing about Allah except the truth. Indeed, I have come to you with clear proof from your Lord, so let the children of Israel go with me.”

**"Let the Children of Israel Go With Me"**

The verse completes Moses' opening speech, and its three parts are the Qur'an's whole theory of prophethood in miniature: a statement of the messenger's constraint, a statement of his evidence, and a concrete demand. *Ḥaqīqun ʿalā a lā aqūla ʿalā Allāhi illā al-ḥaqq* — "obliged to say nothing about Allah except the truth." (7:105) The word *ḥaqīq* is stronger than a moral preference; it is the vocabulary of an incumbent obligation, of something owed.

**A Claim That Arrives as a Demand**

> *“So go to him and say, ‘Indeed we are both messengers from your Lord, so let the Children of Israel go with us, and do not oppress them. We have come to you with a sign from your Lord. And salvation will be for whoever follows the ˹right˺ guidance.’”* (20:47)

**Why the Demand Belongs in the Message**

Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ gives the confrontation its sharpest political edge. When Pharaoh reminds Moses of the favour of having been raised in the palace, Moses refuses the ledger: *“How can that be a ‘favour,’ of which you remind me, when ˹it was only because˺ you ˹have˺ enslaved the Children of Israel?”* (26:22).

**Truth, Proof, and Demand**

The order of the three clauses is the Book's standard sequence for prophecy. And say, ‘Would you ˹be willing to˺ purify yourself, and let me guide you to your Lord so that you will be in awe ˹of Him˺?’”* (79:17–19).

Moses' evidence is the *bayyinah*, the clear proof that the next two verses will produce. The Qur'an's later summary counts the signs he carried: *“We surely gave Moses nine clear signs. ˹You, O Prophet, can˺ ask the Children of Israel. When Moses came to them, Pharaoh said to him, ‘I really think that you, O Moses, are bewitched’”* (17:101). Verse 105 announces the proof; verses 107 and 108 exhibit the first two of the nine.

**What the Reader Is Meant to Carry Away**
