**The Book's Honesty About Israel**

The Qur'an's narratives of the Children of Israel are remarkable for their refusal of hagiography. The Book records the complaints about food in the desert, the refusal to enter the Holy Land — *“we will never ˹be able to˺ enter it”* (5:22) — and the worship of the calf while Moses was on the mountain (20:85). The sūrah's readers are being given a community they can recognize.

*Yastakhlifakum fī al-arḍ* — He may make you successors in the land. The root *khalafa* is the Qur'an's term for the transfer of stewardship. The Book uses it for individuals, communities, and generations: *“Then We made you their successors in the land to see how you would act”* (10:14); *“He can do away with you and replace you with whoever He wills”* (6:133); and the promise to the believers of succession with security (24:55).

**The Clause That Tests Everything**

The Qur'an supplies the answer to that question in its later narratives of the same people: a generation that saw the sea split asks for an idol like the ones they had seen (7:138), refuses to enter the land that had been promised (5:21–22). Needs prophets and kings to be reminded of the covenant.

**A Community Between Two Statements**

The sūrah will report what the community did with its deliverance in the very next chapter of the narrative, including the request for a visible god and Moses' rebuke (7:138–141). Verse 129's "to see how you will do" is therefore answered within the same sūrah, and the answer is not flattering.

**Succession Promised and Succession Held**

The answer’s second promise uses the sūrah’s word for succession. The Book states the same promise to this community with its conditions attached: *“Allah has promised those of you who believe and do good that He will certainly make them successors in the land, as He did with those before them”* (24:55). The verse goes on to name the establishment of their religion and the replacement of their fear with security, and it attaches all of it to worship without association.

The parallel makes the answer in verse 129 legible as a rule rather than as a comfort. Succession in the land is something God does and something that has conditions, and the sūrah’s own account of Israel shows what follows when the succession is received and the conditions are not kept: the land is inherited (7:137), the favours are enumerated, and the enumeration becomes the ground of a charge. The clause the sūrah appends to its own promise — that God will see how they act — is the clause the promise in al-Nūr carries, and it is what makes a deliverance a beginning.
verses.130:
> Indeed, We afflicted Pharaoh’s people with famine and shortage of crops so they might come back ˹to their senses˺

**Hardship as Summons**

The Book's doctrine is that afflictions are addressed to a community's attention rather than merely to its treasury. Sūrat al-Anʿām states the mechanism and its typical failure: *“When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired”* (6:44) — and the sūrah's earlier passage in al-Aʿrāf records how often the summons was refused. Egypt's famine is one more instance of the same summons.

The Qur'an knows another famine in Egypt, and it was survived by foresight. Sūrat Yūsuf reports the king's dream of seven fat cows and seven lean ones (12:43) and Joseph's interpretation, which included seven years of hardship to be provisioned against (12:48). The state in that story listened to a prisoner; the state in this one is busy commissioning magicians.

**The Plagues That Follow**

The sūrah expands the affliction into a series: *“So We plagued them with floods, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood — all as clear signs, but they persisted in arrogance and were a wicked people”* (7:133). The Book's list runs from the agricultural to the domestic, and its last item, blood, touches the Nile itself — the substance of Egypt's life and of its religion.

Egypt's gods presided over the river, the sun, the harvest, and the household, and the plagues are chosen to reach each domain. Sūrat al-Zukhruf notes that the signs surpassed one another as the sequence continued (43:48), and the sūrah's own account shows the court's response varying between panic and amnesia. When the plagues become intolerable, the court asks Moses to pray: *“O Moses! Pray to your Lord on our behalf, by virtue of the covenant He made with you. If you help remove this torment from us, we will certainly believe in you and let the Children of Israel go with you”* (7:134).

The sūrah's next verse records the outcome of that plea, and it is the pattern the Book applies to the whole sequence: *“But as soon as We removed the torment from them — until they met their inevitable fate — they broke their promise”* (7:135).

**The Narrative's Next Move**

With the purpose clause stated and the afflictions named, the sūrah turns to the two responses the plagues produced — the court's self-serving interpretation (7:131) and its outright refusal of signs (7:132) — before it reaches the sea.

**The Word for Omen**

The court’s reading of the famine is reported in the next verse, and its vocabulary is worth holding. In prosperity they claim the good as their due; in adversity they take it as an omen against Mūsā and those with him — and the Book’s comment is flat: *“Surely all is destined by Allah. Yet most of them did not know.”* (7:131). The word behind the omen is *ṭāʾir*, from the root for a bird, and it carries the practice it came from: omen taken from the flight of birds.

The same word is used elsewhere of the answer to that practice. The messengers in Sūrah Yā Sīn are told they are a bad omen and reply: *“Your bad omen lies within yourselves.”* (36:19). And the Book states the doctrine against omen in an image: *“We have bound every human’s destiny to their neck.”* (17:13) — the *ṭāʾir* is not in the sky but attached to the person, which is to say that what befalls him is his own record. Verse 131 applies the same correction to a court that had just been through a famine: the omen they find in the messenger is the thing they should have found in themselves, and the sūrah’s histories are full of towns that made the same substitution.
verses.131:
> In times of prosperity, they said, “This is what we deserve,” but in adversity, they blamed it on Moses and those with him. Surely all is destined by Allah. Yet most of them did not know

**"This Is What We Deserve"**

*Fa-idhā jāʾat-humu al-ḥasanatu qālū lanā hādhihi wa-in tuṣibhum sayyiʾatun yaṭṭayyarū bi-Mūsā wa-man maʿahu alā inna-mā ṭāʾiruhum ʿinda Allāhi wa-lākinna aktharahum lā yaʿlamūn* — in times of prosperity they said, "This is what we deserve," (7:131) but in adversity they blamed it on Moses and those with him. Surely all is destined by Allah. Yet most of them did not know.

The verse describes a disposition the Qur'an returns to repeatedly: a person reads good fortune as a verdict on his own worth and misfortune as evidence about someone else's. Sūrat al-Fajr states the pair almost in so many words: *“Now, whenever a human being is tested by their Lord through ˹His˺ generosity and blessings, they boast, ‘My Lord has ˹deservedly˺ honoured me!’ But when He tests them by limiting their provision, they protest, ‘My Lord has ˹undeservedly˺ humiliated me!’”* (89:15–16).

**The Claim of Ownership**

*Lanā hādhihi* — literally *this is ours* — is a claim about entitlement rather than gratitude. Sūrat Fuṣṣilat reports the same sentence in response to relief: *“And if We let them taste a mercy from Us after being touched with adversity, they will certainly say, ‘This is what I deserve’”* (41:50). Sūrat al-Zumar gives it in the first person singular of prosperity — *“I have been granted all this only because of ˹my˺ knowledge”* (39:49) — and Sūrat Hūd names the tone: *“totally prideful and boastful”* (11:10).

*Yaṭṭayyarū bi-Mūsā* — they took an evil omen from Moses — is the Book's term for the transfer of blame onto a person or a group in hard times. The Qur'an reports the same reflex in other towns: the people of the messengers said *“We definitely see you as a bad omen for us”* (36:18), and the reply to them was *“Your bad omen lies within yourselves”* (36:19). The Egyptian court blames its own failed harvest on foreigners.

**The Pattern the Sūrah Established**

The rules had already been stated. *“Whenever We sent a prophet to a society, We afflicted its ˹disbelieving˺ people with suffering and adversity, so perhaps they would be humbled”* (7:94); the next verses described the substitution of good days for bad and the people's conclusion that their fathers had been touched by the same things (7:95). Egypt is the sūrah's demonstration case, and the court's reaction of verse 131 is the reaction the earlier verses predicted.

The Qur'an's constant warning is that ease tests a person as much as hardship. But just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise, then they instantly fell into despair!”* (6:44) — and the court's confident reading of its own prosperity is exactly the condition described.

**Both Have Been Destined by Allah**

The verse’s corrective is a single clause: *“Surely all is destined by Allah.”* (7:131). An-Nisāʾ records the same exchange with the same correction, in the mouth of people who assign good to God and evil to the messenger: *“When something good befalls them, they say, ‘This is from Allah,’ but when something evil befalls them, they say, ‘This is from you.’”* (4:78).

This is the verse’s place in the sūrah’s account of the wilderness. The alternation of good and bad years (7:130) is described as an occasion for return; 7:131 reports what the people did with it instead — credit taken in prosperity, blame assigned in adversity — and the corrective clause restores the attribution that makes the alternation meaningful.

The Book's teaching is stated in similar terms about the believers' own battles: *“Say, ‘Nothing will ever befall us except what Allah has destined for us’”* (9:51).

The Qur'an repeats the formulation in many forms — *“To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And to Allah ˹all˺ matters will be returned ˹for judgment˺.”* (3:109) — and its function in narratives of famine and plague is to close the conversation about proximate causes.
verses.132:
> They said, “No matter what sign you may bring to deceive us, we will never believe in you.”

**"No Matter What Sign You Bring, We Will Never Believe"**

*Wa-qālū mahmā taʾtinā bihi min āyatin li-tasḥaranā bihā fa-mā naḥnu laka bi-muʾminīn* — they said: "No matter what sign you may bring to deceive us, we will never believe in you." (7:132) The sentence is the court's final position on evidence. The Book preserves it for what it reveals about the logic of refusal.

*Li-tasḥaranā* — to bewitch us — is the label the Book's unbelievers attach to revelation in sūrah after sūrah. The people of Noah called the messenger's message sorcery (54:9), Pharaoh's court described the sign as *clear magic* (10:76), and Qur'anic towns reached for the same word when they could find no other. The Egyptian court's version is stated in the register of formal refusal: the signs are tricks by definition.

**The Shape of Unconditional Rejection**

The sentence does not say *we will not believe in this sign* It says, *“we will never believe in you”* (7:132) — that no sign, however presented, will produce belief. And even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe in them.”* (7:146).

The Qur'an records countless versions of the sentence for the Prophet's own audience. *“They challenge ˹the Prophet˺, ‘We will never believe in you until you cause a spring to gush forth from the earth for us’”* (17:90). The passage continues through gardens, a house of gold, and a book brought down from heaven (17:91–93). *“They say, ‘Our hearts are veiled against what you are calling us to, there is deafness in our ears, and there is a barrier between us and you’”* (41:5).

**The Sūrah's Own Precedent**

The pattern had been established in the sūrah's earlier narratives. The people of the towns had also seen the signs: ʿĀd's leaders had asked for a punishment to be brought (7:70), the people of Lot had demanded the same (7:82's sequel). The sūrah's own summary of them all — *“So We seized them by surprise, while they were unaware.”* (7:95) — applies to a refusal of exactly this kind. What Egypt adds is the machinery of the state and the record of a policy.

The verse is the compound voice of palace and people: the translation's "they said" covers the same crowd that had been organized for the contest (26:39–40). The sūrah's narratives never distinguish the ruler's refusal from the population's; the Book treats a state's official position and a people's settled disposition as one phenomenon when both have access to the same signs.

**Never: The Particle and Its Uses**

Al-Jumuʿah uses the same particle in a case the Book describes as unfulfilled: *“But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done.”* (62:7).

The parallel shows what *lan* is doing in both places. 62:7 gives the reason in a clause — because of what their hands have done — and 7:132’s refusal arrives after the same history: signs given, promises made and broken, and a hardening recorded in the verse that follows.

**Nine Clear Signs Already Given**

The sūrah’s own account lists the signs in detail: the staff and the hand (7:107–108), then the years of shortage (7:130), then flood, locusts, lice, frogs and blood (7:133). The refusal at 7:132 is made in the middle of that sequence, after several signs and before the rest, and it is made in terms that no further sign could satisfy.

This is the verse’s point about the shape of the refusal. 17:101 supplies the measure — nine clear signs — and the sūrah supplies the record of what happened after each of them: a promise made, a reprieve granted, and the promise broken (7:134).

Sūrat al-Anʿām anticipates every variation of the demand and closes the door: *“Had We sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ a revelation in writing and they were to touch it with their own hands, the disbelievers would still have said, ‘This is nothing but pure magic!’”* (6:7).
verses.133:
> So We plagued them with floods, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood—all as clear signs, but they persisted in arrogance and were a wicked people

**"Floods, Locusts, Lice, Frogs, and Blood"**

*Fa-arsalnā ʿalayhim al-ṭūfāna wa-l-jarāda wa-l-qummal wa-l-ḍafādiʿa wa-l-dama āyātin mufaṣṣalātin fa-stakbarū wa-kānū qawman mujrimīn* — so We plagued them with floods, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood — all as clear signs, but they persisted in arrogance and were a wicked people.

The Qur'an typically summarizes the Egyptian signs: *“We surely gave Moses nine clear signs”* (17:101); *“˹These are two˺ of nine signs for Pharaoh and his people”* (27:12). This verse is the sūrah's enumeration, and it is the most concrete of the accounts. The Egyptian prostration of the sūrah's first narrative and the court's stubbornness here are the two poles the signs produced.

Sūrat al-Zukhruf supplies the pattern within the sequence: *“although every sign We showed them was greater than the one before. Ultimately, We seized them with torments so that they might return ˹to the Right Path˺”* (43:48). Sūrat Ṭāhā states the outcome in one line — *“And We certainly showed Pharaoh all of Our signs, but he denied them and refused ˹to believe˺”* (20:56) — and Sūrat al-Muʾmin's long narrative supplies the court's deliberations (40:23–46).

**Signs Addressed to Egypt's World**

The purpose clause of the previous verse — that they might remember (7:130) — governs the list, and the Qur'an's framing of the sequence as a summons rather than a simple punishment is consistent across the accounts.

**Pharaoh's Own Appeal to Signs**

Sūrat al-Aʿrāf had already recorded the court's demand for proof (7:106), and Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ shows the king being shown the staff and the hand and calling them magic (26:30–33). The plagues are the answer to a court that had asked for evidence and had never intended to treat it as evidence, and the sūrah's phrasing — "clear signs" — is the Book's verdict on the bad faith of the request.

*Istakbarū* — they grew arrogant — is the Book's diagnosis of the refusal rather than an accusation about intelligence. The Qur'an consistently connects the rejection of signs to the will's self-exaltation: *“I will turn away from My signs those who act unjustly with arrogance in the land. And even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe in them. If they see the Right Path, they will not take it. But if they see a crooked path, they will follow it. This is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.”* (7:146), and Sūrat al-Muʾmin's account of the court's debate has a believer among Pharaoh's own people warning them against exactly this posture (40:28).

**Five Things Named: The Signs Inside Egypt's Own World**

The verse's structure is a list followed by two clauses about the response: they persisted in arrogance and were a wicked people. The persistence is stated with the same verb the sūrah uses at 7:132 and 7:146, and the wickedness is the verdict that follows from it. This is the pattern of the sūrah's accounts throughout: signs given in detail, a refusal stated in general terms, and a verdict attached to the refusal. What distinguishes 7:133 is the detail, since the other accounts of the plagues in the Book summarise them, and the sūrah's list is what allows the reader to see the sequence as an address to a specific world.

The intervals between the signs are supplied by the verses around this one. At 7:134 the court pleads for removal and promises belief, and the promise is broken when the torment is lifted; at 7:132 the court declares that no sign will move it.

**All the Signs Rejected: The Seizing That Followed**

The Book summarises the same episode from the side of the rejection: *“And indeed, the warnings ˹also˺ came to the people of Pharaoh”* (54:41), and *“they rejected all of Our signs, so We seized them with the ˹crushing˺ grip of the Almighty, Most Powerful”* (54:42)
verses.134:
> When tormented, they pleaded, “O Moses! Pray to your Lord on our behalf, by virtue of the covenant He made with you. If you help remove this torment from us, we will certainly believe in you and let the Children of Israel go with you.”

**"Pray to Your Lord on Our Behalf"**

*Wa-lammā waqaʿa ʿalayhimu al-rijzu qālū yā Mūsā udʿu lanā rabbaka bimā ʿahida ʿindaka la-in kashafta ʿannā al-rijza la-nuʾminanna laka wa-la-nursilanna maʿaka Banī Isrāʾīl* — when tormented, they pleaded: "O Moses! Pray to your Lord on our behalf, by virtue of the covenant He made with you. If you help remove this torment from us, we will certainly believe in you and let the Children of Israel go with you." (7:134)

The men who had commissioned magicians, threatened crucifixion, and declared that no sign would ever be believed now request the prophet's intercession. The Book's analysis of this posture is given in several places: *“When one is touched with hardship, they cry out to Us ˹alone˺. Then when We shower Our blessings upon them, they say, ‘I have been granted all this only because of ˹my˺ knowledge’”* (39:49). The sūrah's court shows the first half of the verse.

**The Same Plea in the Other Account**

Sūrat al-Zukhruf preserves the scene with an added detail that must be read in full to be appreciated: *“˹Then˺ they pleaded, ‘O ˹mighty˺ magician! Pray to your Lord on our behalf, by virtue of the covenant He made with you. We will certainly accept guidance’”* (43:49) — followed immediately by the Book's report that they reneged (43:50). The court asks the man it calls a sorcerer to pray for it, and the Book lets the insult stand beside the request.

The Qur'an treats the cry of the distressed as evidence of something the prosperous person denies: the knowledge of where help actually comes from. Sūrat al-Anʿām states the fact without endorsing the speaker — *“When people are touched with hardship, they cry out to their Lord, turning to Him ˹alone˺. But as soon as He gives them a taste of His mercy, a group of them associates ˹others˺ with their Lord ˹in worship˺”* (30:33) — and Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt describes the same shipwreck scene: *“If they happen to be aboard a ship ˹caught in a storm˺, they cry out to Allah ˹alone˺ in sincere devotion. But as soon as He delivers them ˹safely˺ to shore, they associate ˹others with Him once again˺”* (29:65). The Book records broken promises of this exact type throughout its histories: here a court that swore belief under every plague and withdrew the oath the moment it lifted (7:130–134), the Sodomites' fear when the angels arrived, and Israel's own repeated pledges in the wilderness.

The sūrah had opened the Egyptian narrative with the demand for that release (7:105), and the plagues bring the state to the point of conceding it.

The Qur'an's prophets are described as men who intercede for their communities — Abraham for Sodom (11:74–76), Noah for his people (71:26–28's contrast), the Prophet for his — and the deliverance narrative requires the state's release of Israel to be given, however cynically, before the crossing of the sea.

The covenant invoked is the one stated at 7:134 in the court's own words and at 7:135 in the report of its breaking.

**Obedience Rather Than Intercession: What a Messenger Is Sent For**

The plea asks Mūsā to act on the court's behalf, and the Book states what a messenger's act consists of. He is sent to be obeyed, and the command to obey is put in the plainest form: *“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger.”* (24:54)

Sūrat Ghāfir states the rule for the nations: *“But their faith was of no benefit to them when they saw Our torment.”* (40:85), and Sūrat Yūnus reports the drowning king's confession and its refusal (10:90–91).

The Book's instructions about prayer place intercession with the living and prayers of the community for one another, and it forbids reliance on intermediaries who cannot answer (6:51; 39:43–44).

Sūrat Yūnus's account of the one town whose faith was accepted — the people of Jonah — notes that their belief came while they could still see (10:98), a distinction the Qur'an uses consistently against deathbed conversions.
verses.135:
> But as soon as We removed the torment from them—until they met their inevitable fate—they broke their promise

**"They Broke Their Promise"**

*Fa-lammā kashafnā ʿanhumu al-rijza ilā ajalin hum bālighūhu idhā hum yankuthūn* — but as soon as We removed the torment from them — until they met their inevitable fate — they broke their promise. The verse is the sūrah's verdict on the court's faith, and it records the interval between the relief and the reckoning.

Sūrat al-Zukhruf reports the same sequence in the same words: *“But as soon as We removed the torments from them, they broke their promise.”* (43:50). The Book repeats the sentence because the pattern is the point: a promise made under affliction and broken under relief is one of the Qur'an's standard portraits of the unrepentant, and it appears in the sūrahs with a regularity that makes it a law.

The Qur'an's descriptions of this pattern are many and precise. *“Then as soon as He removes the hardship from you, a group of you associates ˹others˺ with their Lord ˹in worship˺”* (16:54); *“But when He delivers you ˹safely˺ to shore, you turn away. Humankind is ever ungrateful”* (17:67); *“If We give people a taste of Our mercy then take it away from them, they become utterly desperate, ungrateful”* (11:9). The verses map a cycle the sūrah's court illustrates at the scale of a state.

**The Pattern's Repetition Within the Story**

The plagues came in a series, and the sūrah's narrative implies that the plea and the betrayal happened more than once. Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's list of the signs (7:133) and Sūrat al-Zukhruf's note that each sign surpassed the last (43:48) leave no room for a single, isolated incident. The court's promise was broken as often as it was made, which is why the sūrah needs only one clause to dismiss the state's faith.

The Book grants relief repeatedly and does not treat the repetition as weakness in the divine government. But He delays them for an appointed term.”* (35:45).

**The Transition to the Sea**

The verse reports the breaking: *“But as soon as We removed the torment from them—until they met their inevitable fate—they broke their promise.”* (7:135). Ar-Raʿd describes the opposite class: *“˹They are˺ those who honour Allah’s covenant, never breaking the pledge.”* (13:20).

The commentators read 13:20–21 as the description of whom the sūrah’s histories exclude. Those who honour the covenant also join what God has commanded to be joined and fear the reckoning; the people of 7:135 do the opposite in each case, and the verse that follows their breaking reports the destruction of what they had built (7:136–137).

**The Promise in Their Own Words**

The verse says they broke their promise without quoting it. The verse before records it: *“O Moses! Pray to your Lord on our behalf, by virtue of the covenant He made with you. If you help remove this torment from us, we will certainly believe in you and let the Children of Israel go with you.”* (7:134).

The promise has three parts and each is broken in the narrative that follows. The belief promised is not given, since the refusal stated at 7:132 remains in force; the release of the Children of Israel is not made until after the drowning; and the appeal to the covenant made with Mūsā is answered by a breaking the verse describes in the same word.

*Yankuthūn* is the tearing of a woven thing, and the Qur'an uses it for the violation of pledges in several places, including the instruction to Israel not to be like the woman who unravels her thread after spinning it (16:92).

Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn states the tone of that warning in an address to the heedless — *“And donate from what We have provided for you before death comes to one of you, and you cry, ‘My Lord! If only You delayed me for a short while’”* (63:10) — and the sūrah's court receives its extension and spends it on further refusal.
verses.136:
> So We inflicted punishment upon them, drowning them in the sea for denying Our signs and being heedless of them

**"Drowning Them in the Sea"**

*Fa-ntaqamnā minhum fa-aghraqnāhum fī al-yammi bi-annnahum kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā wa-kānū ʿanhā ghāfilīn* — so We inflicted punishment upon them, drowning them in the sea for denying Our signs and being heedless of them. The verse ends the Egyptian narrative's central conflict in a single clause.

*Intiqām* in the Qur'an is the recompense of a wrong that has been carried past warning, and the Book uses it for the sea in the other account as well: *“So when they enraged Us, We inflicted punishment upon them, drowning them all. And We made them an example and a lesson for those after them”* (43:55–56). The punishment's function in the Book is not only retribution; it is the production of a sign for later generations.

Sūrat al-Baqarah records it as Israel's memory: *“And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea, rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh's people before your very eyes”* (2:50). Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ gives the sequence in four verses, ending with *“Then We drowned the others”* (26:66). Sūrat Ṭāhā narrates the pursuit and the waters (20:77–79), Sūrat al-Dukhān records the command to leave the sea parted because *“they are certainly an army bound to drown”* (44:24). Sūrat al-Isrāʾ summarizes the whole: *“So Pharaoh wanted to scare the Israelites out of the land ˹of Egypt˺, but We drowned him and all of those with him”* (17:103).

**The Nation That Was Not Destroyed Unwarned**

The Book is explicit that the pattern requires warning first: *“your Lord would never destroy a society for their wrongdoing while its people are unaware ˹of the truth˺”* (6:131). Egypt had been warned through a messenger, a contest, and a campaign of signs, and the sūrah's account of the plagues records the warnings precisely so that this verse's verdict can be read as the last step of a sequence rather than an arbitrary act of power.

Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ supplies the human scene the sūrah only implies: the two groups face to face and the companions of Moses crying *“We are overtaken for sure”* (26:61), and Moses' answer — *“Absolutely not! My Lord is certainly with me — He will guide me”* (26:62). The drowning is the answer to the state's pursuit, and the Book gives the reassurance in the same breath as the event.

**Enraged and Punished: The Word for Retribution**

The verse reports the punishment and its instrument: *“So We inflicted punishment upon them, drowning them in the sea”* (7:136). Az-Zukhruf describes the same event with the cause named first: *“So when they enraged Us, We inflicted punishment upon them, drowning them all.”* (43:55).

Read together the two verses separate the event from its instrument. That is why the sūrah can describe the sea in this verse as the place of the punishment and two verses later as a road crossed (7:138) — the same water performs both functions inside one narrative, and neither is the point of the sentence.

**Left Behind and Awarded to Another People**

The drowning is followed in the Book by an inventory. Ad-Dukhān lists what the departing party left: *“˹Imagine˺ how many gardens and springs the tyrants left behind, as well as ˹various˺ crops and splendid residences, and luxuries which they fully enjoyed.”* (44:25–27), and then states the transfer in five words: *“So it was. And We awarded it ˹all˺ to another people.”* (44:28).

The inventory is the measure of what the verse calls heedlessness. 7:137 states the same transfer for this sūrah’s account: the land was inherited by those who had been held down.

When the king confessed as the water closed over him, the answer came: *“˹He was told,˺ ‘Now ˹you believe˺? But you always disobeyed and were one of the corruptors. Today We will preserve your corpse so that you may become an example for those who come after you’”* (10:91–92).

The Book's use of the drowning in its address is explicit elsewhere: *“Surely in this is a lesson for whoever”* (79:26), and the sūrah's narration leaves its audience to apply the lesson to their own situation.
verses.137:
> And ˹so˺ We made the oppressed people successors of the eastern and western lands, which We had showered with blessings. ˹In this way˺ the noble Word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel for what they had endured. And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people constructed and what they established

**The East and the West**

*Mashāriqa al-arḍi wa-maghāribahā* — the eastern and western reaches — is the Book's way of describing a land whose extent is known to God rather than fixed on a map. The Qur'an uses the pair for the range of the earth and the created order generally (26:28; 55:17; 70:40), and here it measures the territory from the Nile valley to the lands beyond it, with the note that the region had been blessed.

The Qur'an refers to the region's blessing in several places: the land around the Sacred House (21:71), the Holy Land assigned to Israel (5:21), and the *“land We had showered with blessings for all people”* (21:71). The sūrah's own phrase — *which We had showered with blessings* — attributes the prosperity the Israelites were about to inherit to a prior divine act, not to Egypt's gods or the throne's management.

**The Ruin of the Constructors**

*Wa-dammarnā mā kāna yaṣnaʿu Firʿawnu wa-qawmuhu wa-mā kānū yaʿrishūn* — We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people made and what they erected. The Book elsewhere describes the estate that was left behind: *“˹Imagine˺ how many gardens and springs the tyrants left behind, as well as ˹various˺ crops and splendid residences, and luxuries which they fully enjoyed.”* (44:25–27), followed by the verse that names the transfer of ownership (44:28). Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ states it as the dispossession of the gardens, springs, treasures, and noble stations (26:57–58) awarded to Israel (26:59).

**A Pattern the Book Applies Repeatedly**

The Qur'an turns the inheritance of the arrogant into a general law. *“Then We made you their successors in the land to see how you would act”* (10:14). *“He can do away with you and replace you with whoever He wills”* (6:133); *“He is the One Who has placed you as successors on earth and elevated some of you in rank over others, so He may test you with what He has given you”* (6:165). The Prophet's community receives the same law in its own promise of succession (24:55) and its own warning (7:129).

The sūrah does not treat Israel's inheritance as a charter. The narrative's next verses report the community's request for a visible god (7:138), and the sūrah's later chapters record the calf, the refusal to enter the Holy Land, and the breaking of the covenant (7:148–152; 5:20–26). The Book's gift and its test arrive together by design.

**Inherited by the Righteous: The Decree in the Scriptures**

The verse reports an inheritance given to the oppressed: *“We made the oppressed people successors of the eastern and western lands”* (7:137). Al-Anbiyāʾ states the same inheritance as a decree recorded before it: *“Surely, following the ˹heavenly˺ Record, We decreed in the Scriptures: ‘My righteous servants shall inherit the land.’”* (21:105).

**Surroundings Blessed**

The two verses therefore describe one region from two directions: the blessing given and the constructions raised inside it. 17:1 names the blessing in connection with a journey of signs; 7:137 names it in connection with a transfer of ownership.

The Book's language of the "word" is the language of a decree that cannot fail. The Qur'an applies it to this promise elsewhere: the deliverance narrative in Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ was introduced as the realization of what the oppressors feared (28:6), and Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ states the transfer in a single line: *“So it was. And We awarded it ˹all˺ to the Children of Israel”* (26:59).

The Qur'an's references to the Egyptian state's constructions are consistently about their fate rather than their grandeur, and the later sūrahs treat the king's boast about the rivers beneath his palace (43:51) as the epitome of a confidence that did not survive him.
verses.138:
> We brought the Children of Israel across the sea and they came upon a people devoted to idols. They demanded, “O Moses! Make for us a god like their gods.” He replied, “Indeed, you are a people acting ignorantly

**"Make for Us a God Like Their Gods"**

*Wa-jāwaznā bi-Banī Isrāʾīla al-baḥra fa-atā ʿalā qawmin yaʿkufūna ʿalā aṣnāmihim qālū yā Mūsā ijʿal lanā ilāhan ka-mā lahum ālihatun qāla innakum qawmun tajhalūn* — We brought the Children of Israel across the sea and they came upon a people devoted to idols. They demanded: "O Moses! Make for us a god like their gods." (7:138) He replied: "Indeed, you are a people acting ignorantly!" (7:138)

**The Request's Logic**

The Israelites had left a country of temples and arrived among a people with visible gods, and they wanted the visibility. The Book's narratives show this preference repeatedly: the demand to see Allah with their own eyes (2:55), the demand for a sign on paper (4:153), and the calf manufactured during Moses' absence (20:88).

**The Book's Critique of Inherited Religion**

The demand's premise is the practice it observed, and the Qur'an meets that premise head-on in sūrah after sūrah. *“When it is said to them, ‘Follow what Allah has revealed,’ they reply, ‘No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing’”* (2:170). Sūrat al-Zukhruf reports the same formula in four consecutive verses: *“We found our forefathers following a ˹particular˺ way. We are following in their footsteps”* (43:22), with the warner's question — *“Even if what I brought you is better guidance than what you found your forefathers practicing?”* — and the elite's answer that they reject it (43:23–24).

The Qur'an's longest treatment of this logic is placed on Abraham's lips. The sūrah of al-Shuʿarāʾ records the question and the reply — *“They replied, ‘No! But we found our forefathers doing the same’”* (26:74) — followed by Abraham's demolition of the position: *“Have you ˹really˺ considered what you have been worshipping — you and your ancestors? They are ˹all˺ enemies to me, except the Lord of all worlds”* (26:75–77). The same scene in al-Anbiyāʾ has Abraham say to the people and their forefathers: *“Indeed, you and your forefathers have been clearly astray”* (21:54).

**The Footsteps Metaphor**

Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt uses the image of walking in another's tracks to describe the mechanism of inherited idolatry: *“Indeed, they found their forefathers astray, so they rushed in their footsteps!”* (37:69–70). The Book's complaint is not that tradition exists but that it is being used as a substitute for judgment, and its sentence about the majority is stated without qualification: *“If you were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead you away from Allah's Way”* (6:116).

The verse's request is made by people who had been spared, fed, and freed. The Book recalls the sequence for them directly: *“O Children of Israel! We saved you from your enemy, and made an appointment with you on the right side of Mount Ṭûr, and sent down to you manna and quails”* (20:80). Israel's pattern of response to blessing is one of the Qur'an's most persistent themes, and the sūrah's narrative does not soften it.

**Deeds Made Void**

Read with 39:65 the request has a cost that the requesters did not calculate. A deliverance had just been given (7:138), and the response was to ask for a god like the gods of a people they had just passed. The diagnosis and az-Zumar’s rule belong together: the voiding is not a punishment added to the act but a property of it.

Al-Baqarah uses the same word of a legitimate attachment: *“And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺.”* (2:125).
verses.139:
> What they follow is certainly doomed to destruction and their deeds are in vain.”

**"Doomed to Destruction"**

*Inna hāʾulāʾi mutabbarun mā hum fīhi wa-bāṭilun mā kānū yaʿmalūn* — what they follow is certainly doomed to destruction, and their deeds are in vain. The verse is Moses' second answer to the request for an idol, and it dismantles the model the Israelites wanted to imitate.

*Mutabbar* is the Qur'an's term for complete ruin, and its root appears in the sūrah of al-Isrāʾ in the prediction about the temple's desecration: the enemy would enter and *“utterly destroy whatever would fall into their hands”* (17:7). Moses' sentence about the idolaters' religion uses the same vocabulary, and the Book's choice of so absolute a word is deliberate.

**The Book's Doctrine of Falsehood's End**

The Qur'an states the principle in the form of a promise and an image: *“Say, ‘The truth has come. Falsehood will vanish, never to return’”* (34:49); *“In fact, We hurl the truth against falsehood, leaving it crushed. It quickly vanishes”* (21:18); and the sūrah of al-Ḥajj gives the doctrinal summary — *“That is because Allah ˹alone˺ is the Truth and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood”* (22:62, repeated at 31:30). Moses' verdict on the idolaters' religion is the Book's general verdict applied to a particular people.

The verse's second clause, *their deeds are in vain*, introduces a theme the Qur'an develops at length. Sūrat al-Kahf asks: *“Shall we inform you of who will lose the most deeds? ˹They are˺ those whose efforts are in vain in this worldly life, while they think they are doing good!”* (18:103–104). Sūrat al-Furqān states what becomes of such labor — *“Then We will turn to whatever ˹good˺ deeds they did, reducing them to scattered dust”* (25:23) — and Sūrat al-Nūr compares it to a mirage in a desert (24:39).

**Work That Is Not Necessarily Evil**

The Book's verdict here is not that the idolaters did nothing; it is that their activity lacked a foundation. The Qur'an's phrase for the condition is that their deeds have no weight on the Day of Judgment because the deeds were performed for what does not exist (18:105). Moses' sentence therefore distinguishes between effort and achievement, a distinction the sūrah's readers would need in evaluating the impressive civilization they had just left behind.

The response's logic is worth noticing: Moses does not begin by forbidding the request, he begins by removing its attraction. The Qur'an's persuasion in these passages works by exposure rather than command, and the sūrah's narrative of Abraham destroyed the idols before arguing about them (21:57–58). The prophet's answer to the Israelites follows the same method in words.

**Idols and Their Worshippers in the Book**

The Qur'an's idols are consistently described as beings that cannot hear, see, or profit their worshippers: *“They are ˹all˺ enemies to me, except the Lord of all worlds”* (26:77) is Abraham's verdict, and Sūrat Maryam records his question to his father about worshipping what cannot hear or see (19:42). The sūrah's sentence about the adherents' state — what they are in is doomed — extends the verdict from the object to the practice.

The verse in al-Aʿrāf states the same structure in the language of a ledger — the object followed is destroyed, the work is void — and the two together describe the position of a person whose effort is real and whose return is not.
verses.140:
> He added, “Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, while He has honoured you above the others?”

**"While He Has Honoured You Above the Others"**

*Qāla a-ghayra Allāhi abghīkum ilāhan wa-huwa faḍḍalakum ʿalā al-ʿālamīn* — he added: "Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah. He has honoured you above the others?" (7:140) The third and last of Moses' answers turns from the worthlessness of the model to the position of the people asking for it.

*A-ghayra Allāhi abghīkum ilāhan* repeats a construction the Qur'an puts in the Prophet's own mouth: *“Should I seek a lord other than Allah while He is the Lord of everything?”* (6:164). Sūrat al-Zumar states it with the Book's sharpest adjective — *“Are you urging me to worship ˹anyone˺ other than Allah, O ignorant ones?”* (39:64) — and Sūrat Ghāfir records the Prophet's declaration that he has been forbidden to worship what others invoke besides Allah (40:66).

**A Prophet Cannot Manufacture a God**

The request had asked Moses to be the author of a deity, and the Book's answer to that demand is stated categorically elsewhere: it is not for a person blessed with scripture, wisdom, and prophethood to say to people, "Worship me instead of Allah" (3:79). The verse's question therefore does more than reply to an insult; it defines the limit of the prophetic office. A messenger's task is to convey, not to invent.

*Wa-huwa faḍḍalakum ʿalā al-ʿālamīn* — while He has honoured you above the others. The Qur'an repeats this reminder to Israel in several places as an argument against ingratitude: *“O Children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you and how I honoured you above the others”* (2:122, also 2:47), and Sūrat al-Jāthiyah lists the content of the favour — scripture, wisdom, prophethood, good provision, and precedence (45:16–17). Sūrat al-Dukhān states it as election: *“And indeed, We chose the Israelites knowingly above the others”* (44:32).

**What the Favour Consisted Of**

Sūrat al-Māʾidah's Moses speech names the elements: *“O my people! Remember Allah’s favours upon you when He raised prophets from among you, made you sovereign, and gave you what He had never given anyone in the world”* (5:20). The Book's account of Israel's distinction is therefore institutional and historical — messengers, kingship, scripture — rather than a claim about blood, and its purpose in the narrative is to show what the request for an idol would be throwing away.

The same sūrah that records the honour records its condition. Abraham's elevation is followed by the sentence that the covenant does not extend to wrongdoers (2:124), and the Book's reminders to Israel always accompany a demand for loyalty: *“O children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you. Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil”* (2:40). Verse 140's reminder is therefore an appeal to obligation as much as to privilege.

**The Past Is Not an Inheritance**

The Surah's own narrative denies that the distinction can be inherited automatically: the community that crossed the sea will ask for an idol in this very verse, and later chapters record its failures. Sūrat al-Baqarah states the principle for the descendants of Israel and, by extension, for everyone: *“That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done.”* (2:134).

Read together, the prophet's answer covers the whole ground of the request: the requesters are ignorant of what they are asking (7:138); what they want to imitate is doomed and its works are void (7:139); and what they already have is a favour that the imitation would abandon (7:140).

**The Book's Remedy for Idolatry**

The Qur'an's cure for the inclination the Israelites displayed is the rehearsal of what God has done — the sūrah's own repeated command: *“remember Allah’s favours, so you may be successful”* (7:69; see also 2:231).

The narrative immediately repeats the favour in the form of a command: *“And ˹remember˺ when We rescued you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment—killing your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord.”* (7:141).
verses.141:
> And ˹remember˺ when We rescued you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment—killing your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord

**"Rescued From the People of Pharaoh"**

*Wa-idh anjaynākum min āli Firʿawna yasūmūnakum sūʾa al-ʿadhābi yuqattilūna abnāʾakum wa-yastaḥyūna nisāʾakum wa-fī dhālikum balāʾun min rabbikum ʿaẓīm* — and ˹remember˺ when We rescued you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment — killing your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord.

The narrative has just reported the drowning and the inheritance of the land (7:136–137), and it now returns to Israel's memory with a command to remember. The sūrah's placement is deliberate: the reminder of the persecution is given at the moment the community is about to be summoned to the mountain and given the law, so that the covenant to come is grounded in what has been done for them.

The Qur'an's address to Israel is built on the verb of remembrance: *“O children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you. Fulfil your covenant and I”* (2:40); *“Remember My favours upon you and how I honoured you above the others”* (2:122); *“Remember Allah's favours upon you when He raised prophets from among you”* (5:20). The sūrah's verse belongs to that series, and the Book treats memory as the discipline that steadies a community between deliverance and obedience.

**The Test Named**

*Balāʾun min rabbikum ʿaẓīm* — a severe test from your Lord. Sūrat al-Baqarah states the same verdict in the same words (2:49), and Sūrat Ibrāhīm's Moses prayer adds the words of the community itself: *“Remember Allah's favour upon you when He rescued you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment”* (14:6).

The verse's first word is *We*: the rescue is attributed to God, and Moses appears only as the messenger through whom it happened. The Book's exodus narrative consistently presents the crossing as a divine act performed on behalf of an enslaved people, and the narrative's later episodes — the manna, the quails, the water from the rock (2:60) — continue the attribution.

The command to remember is given in the middle of the sūrah's narrative about the building of a community. The generation that had been freed now had to be formed, and the Qur'an's account of the mountain, the tablets, and the covenant (7:142–145) is the institution of that formation.

**The Same Reminder in the Prophet's Community**

The Qur'an's method with Israel became its method with the Muslims: *“So remember Me, and I will remember you; and be grateful to Me and never deny Me”* (2:152). The sūrah's readers in Makkah were being told to do with their own history what Israel was told to do with Egypt's — to treat the record of deliverance as the ground of loyalty.

The reminder is also a warning to a community that had not yet entered its own tests. The generation that sang at the sea would manufacture a calf within weeks (20:85–88), and the sūrah's reminder of the persecution is placed where the reader knows what is coming.

The verse names the persecution a severe test, and the sūrah's narrative will shortly name a second test at the mountain (7:143's vision) and a third in the wilderness (7:148's calf). The Book's account of Israel is a series of examinations, and the answer to each is recorded — including the answers that failed.

**Remember the Favour: The Same Rescue in Ibrāhīm**

Ibrāhīm records the same event in the mouth of Mūsā, as a favour to be remembered — *“who afflicted you with dreadful torment—slaughtering your sons and keeping your women.”* (14:6). The wording is almost identical to 7:141, and the two verses differ in the verb given to the people — remember.

The two words together describe the sūrah’s method with its readers. The verse holds both, and the histories that follow show what happens to a people given both — the manna and the quails, the water from the rock, the land inherited, and the ingratitude recorded at 7:160.
verses.142:
> We appointed for Moses thirty nights then added another ten—completing his Lord’s term of forty nights. Moses commanded his brother Aaron, “Take my place among my people, do what is right, and do not follow the way of the corruptors.”

**"Thirty Nights and Ten More"**

*Wa-wāʿadnā Mūsā thalāthīna laylatan wa-atmamnāhā bi-ʿashrin fa-tamma mīqātu rabbihi arbaʿīna laylatan wa-qāla Mūsā li-akhīhi Hārūna akhlufnī fī qawmī wa-aṣliḥ wa-lā tattabiʿ sabīla al-mufsidīn* — We appointed for Moses thirty nights then added another ten — completing his Lord's term of forty nights. Moses commanded his brother Aaron, "Take my place among my people, do what is right, and do not follow the way of the corruptors." (7:142)

**"Do What Is Right"**

*Wa-aṣliḥ* — the command's verb is the Book's term for setting a matter right, and it establishes Aaron's mandate as reform rather than mere maintenance. The Qur'an's vocabulary opposes *iṣlāḥ* to *ifsād*, and the same sūrah uses both terms in its narratives: Shuʿayb's counsel in Madyan (7:85), and the destroyers' label for their crimes (7:127).

*Wa-lā tattabiʿ sabīla al-mufsidīn* — the prohibition names the sūrah's recurring category. The corruptors (*mufsidūn*) are those whose activity degrades the moral order of a community, and the sūrah has just recorded the destruction of the towns for exactly this (7:103). Moses' instruction anticipates the specific failure that will occur: a population ready to follow a maker of idols (20:88).

The Qur'an's account of Aaron during the absence is unsparing and sympathetic at once. You are only being tested by this, for indeed your ˹one true˺ Lord is the Most Compassionate. So follow me and obey my orders”* (20:90); they answered that they would persist until Moses returned (20:91). The Book's verdict on his performance arrives when Moses questions him, and Aaron answers, *“O son of my mother! I really feared that you would say, ‘You have caused division among the Children of Israel, and did not observe my word.’”* (20:94).

**Three Nights and Three Days: One Sign in Two Registers**

The Book uses the same convention for the same kind of term in Maryam, where Zakariyyā asks for a sign: *“Your sign is that you will not be able to speak to people for three nights, despite being healthy.”* (19:10). Āl ʿImrān reports the identical sign counted in days: *“Your sign is that you will not be able to speak to people for three days except through gestures.”* (3:41). The two verses describe one event in the two registers, and the commentators cite the pair as evidence that “three nights” and “three days” denote the same period — nights with their days.

**Al-Baqarah’s Account and the Word for the Term**

The two versions therefore do different work. 7:142 gives the term and the delegation left behind: thirty nights, ten added, the charge to Hārūn, the warning against the way of the corruptors. 2:51 gives the term and the breach: forty nights, the calf, the absence, the wrongdoing. Read together they supply the appointment and its outcome, and the sūrah’s own account of the outcome follows at 7:148.

The comparison also fixes the word the verse uses for the term. *Ajal* — *“completing his Lord’s term of forty nights”* (7:142) — is the sūrah’s standing word for an appointed end: the nations’ term at 7:34, the day’s fixed hour. The appointment of the forty nights is an *ajal* like those, and the phrase *fa-lammā jāʾa Mūsā li-mīqātinā* uses *mīqāt*, the same word the sūrah uses at *“When Moses came at the appointed time”* (7:143) and, for the delegation, *“for Our appointment”* (7:155).

Moses arrives ahead of his people and is asked why: *“˹Allah asked,˺ ‘Why have you come with such haste ahead of your people, O Moses?’ He replied, ‘They are close on my tracks. And I have hastened to You, my Lord, so You will be pleased’”* (20:83–84).

The Qur'an's Moses had asked for his brother from the beginning, and Sūrat Ṭāhā records the request and its answer: *“And grant me a helper from my family — Aaron, my brother”* (20:29–30), granted in 20:36.

The appointment's location is fixed in several sūrahs: Moses is called at the sacred valley of Ṭuwā (20:12), from the bush on the right side of the valley (28:30), and blessed is the fire and those around it (27:8).
verses.143:
> When Moses came at the appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he asked, “My Lord! Reveal Yourself to me so I may see You.” Allah answered, “You cannot see Me! But look at the mountain. If it remains firm in its place, only then will you see Me.” When his Lord appeared to the mountain, He levelled it to dust and Moses collapsed unconscious. When he recovered, he cried, “Glory be to You! I turn to You in repentance and I am the first of the believers.”

**"My Lord! Reveal Yourself to Me"**

*Wa-lammā jāʾa Mūsā li-mīqātinā wa-kallamahu rabbuhu qāla rabbi arinī anẓur ilayka qāla lan tarānī wa-lākini anẓur ilā al-jabali fa-in istaqarra makānahu fa-sawfa tarānī fa-lammā tajallā rabbuhu li-l-jabali jaʿalahu dakkan wa-kharra Mūsā ṣaʿiqan* — when Moses came at the appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he asked: "My Lord! Reveal Yourself to me so I may see You." (7:143) Allah answered: "You cannot see Me! But look at the mountain. If it remains firm in its place, only then will you see Me." (7:143) When his Lord appeared to the mountain, He levelled it to dust and Moses collapsed unconscious.

The Book places the request at the summit of Moses' career: after forty nights, at the appointed meeting, in the middle of a conversation. The Qur'an's other requests of this kind — the people's demand to see Allah with their own eyes (2:55) and the challenge of those who do not expect to meet Him (25:21) — are answered differently, and the difference lies in who is asking and how.

*Lan tarānī* — you will never see Me — is the Book's categorical statement about the vision of God in this world, and the Qur'an supports it elsewhere: *“No vision can encompass Him, but He encompasses all vision. For He is the Most Subtle, All-Aware”* (6:103), and the declaration that nothing is like Him (42:11).

**The Mountain as the Proof**

The clause has been read in several ways, and the readings agree on its humility: the first among his people to believe, or the first to believe the truth of what he had just learned about God's transcendence. The sūrah's narrative gives the same phrase to the Egyptian magicians after the contest (26:51) and to Abraham in the matter of pure monotheism (6:79's sense), and the Book consistently places it on the lips of those who have just been corrected.

The sūrah's readers have been given the mountain's history: the call from the fire at the sacred valley (20:11–14), the blessing pronounced at the bush (27:8–9), and the direct speech the Book names as Moses' distinction — *“And to Moses Allah spoke directly”* (4:164). Verse 143 is the culmination of that series: the man who had been addressed by God asks to see Him and is shown the limit of the creature.

**Falling on the Face: The Collapse and What Follows It**

The commentators read the two verses as describing one disposition. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the collapse at 7:143 is followed immediately by glorification and repentance, and that the sequence — overwhelming, falling, then turning — is the form the Book gives to an encounter with a manifestation. 17:109 describes the same form in the ordinary reception of revelation, with weeping in place of the mountain.

**The Request and What Would Have Followed**

The answer is absolute: *“You cannot see Me!”* (7:143). Al-Anʿām describes what would happen if a comparable request were granted to the deniers: *“They say, ‘Why has no ˹visible˺ angel come with him?’ Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have certainly been settled ˹at once˺, and they would have never been given more time ˹to repent˺.”* (6:8).

**The Miʿrāj Report as the Counter-Witness**

Abū Dharr asked the Prophet ﷺ whether he had seen his Lord on the night of the ascent, and the answer, in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 178a, is that He is light, and how could I see Him. The variant at Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 178b, through ʿAbdullāh b. Shaqīq, is shorter: I saw light.

The Qurʾān’s own counter-evidence is at 10:26: “Those who do good will have the finest reward and ˹even˺ more.” (10:26). The report of Jarīr b. ʿAbdullāh in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 7436 supports the reading: the Prophet ﷺ came out to his companions on the night of the full moon and told them they would see their Lord on the Day of Resurrection as they saw that moon, with no difficulty in seeing Him.

A line of the interpretive tradition holds that Mūsā did not ask for himself alone. The seventy were chosen for the same appointment — “Moses chose seventy men from among his people for Our appointment” (7:155) — and the sūrah uses one word for the meeting in both places: the *mīqāt* of 7:143 and the appointment of 7:155.
verses.144:
> Allah said, “O Moses! I have ˹already˺ elevated you above all others by My messages and speech. So hold firmly to what I have given you and be grateful.”

**"Elevated You Above All Others by My Messages and Speech"**

*Qāla yā Mūsā innī iṣṭafaytuka ʿalā al-nāsi bi-risālātī wa-bi-kalāmī fa-khudh mā ātaytuka wa-kun mina al-shākirīn* — Allah said: "O Moses! I have ˹already˺ elevated you above all others by My messages and speech. So hold firmly to what I have given you and be grateful." (7:144)

The sūrahs that narrate the call supply the atmosphere the abbreviation retains: the voice from the fire in the sacred valley of Ṭuwā (20:12), the blessing at the bush on the right side of the valley (27:8). The nearness the Book states in its own words: *“We called him from the right side of Mount Ṭûr, and drew him near, speaking ˹with him˺ directly”* (19:52). The verse's *speech* is the content of those nights and this appointment.

**The Choice of a Messenger**

*Iṣṭafaytuka* — I have chosen you — is the Book's verb for the selection of messengers, and the Qur'an uses it of the families chosen above their peoples: *“Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of ʾImrān above all people ˹of their time˺”* (3:33). The honour of verse 144 is therefore not personal superiority but commission: Moses had been selected for a task, and the sūrah's earlier chapters have shown the scale of it — a court, a kingdom, a sea, and a community to be formed.

*Khudh mā ātaytuka* — take what I have given you — is the same charge given to Israel at the mountain: *“Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you”* (2:63; 2:93), and it recurs in the sūrah's own instruction about the tablets (7:145). The Book's reception of revelation is consistently described as an act of grasping, and obedience is presented as the strength to hold.

**Gratitude as the Response to Elevation**

*Wa-kun mina al-shākirīn* — and be grateful. The Qur'an's treatment of gratitude is a whole theology: *“If you are grateful, I will certainly give you more. But if you are ungrateful, surely My punishment is severe.”* (14:7), *“whoever is grateful, it is only for their own good”* (31:12). Solomon's court hears the same principle stated in the middle of a miracle: *“whoever is grateful, it is only for their own good”* (27:40), and the Book's summary command to the believers — *“remember Me; I will remember you. And thank Me, and never be ungrateful”* (2:152). The honour of verse 144 arrives with an obligation to acknowledge its source.

**Spoken to Directly**

An-Nisāʾ records the second of the two in its own terms: *“And to Moses Allah spoke directly.”* (4:164). The adverb *taklīmā* makes the speech explicit rather than reported.

The commentators note that the sūrah’s account of the speech is careful about its form. Mūsā came at the appointed time and his Lord spoke to him (7:143); the request to see is refused (7:143); the elevation is then stated as already given. 4:164 supplies the term for what happened on the mountain without describing it, which is the same restraint the sūrah observes.

**Be Grateful: The One the Gratitude Benefits**

The sūrah’s own first statement of the relation is at 7:10, where establishment and provision are followed by a complaint about thanks. 7:144 inverts the case: the elevation is stated, the command to be grateful follows, and the one addressed is a prophet rather than a people.

Yet the Book's account of his elevation keeps the gift tied to a mission, and his failure to enter the Holy Land (5:23–26) is reported without exemption.

The Book refers to the mountain by name and by oath (95:2; 52:1's Mount), and the sūrah's account of this appointment is the reason.
verses.145:
> We wrote for him on the Tablets ˹the fundamentals˺ of everything; commandments and explanations of all things. ˹We commanded,˺ “Hold to this firmly and ask your people to take the best of it. I will soon show ˹all of˺ you the home of the rebellious

**"We Wrote for Him on the Tablets"**

*Wa-katabnā lahu fī al-alwāḥi min kulli shayʾin mawʿiẓatan wa-tafṣīlan li-kulli shayʾin khudhhā bi-quwwatin wa-mur qawmaka yaʾkhudhū bi-aḥsanihā sa-urīkum dāra al-fāsiqīn* — We wrote for him on the Tablets ˹the fundamentals˺ of everything; commandments and explanations of all things. ˹We commanded,˺ "Hold to this firmly and ask your people to take the best of it. I will soon show ˹all of˺ you the home of the rebellious." (7:145)

The verse is the Qur'an's most concrete statement about the material transmission of revelation: writing, tablets, and a text. The Book elsewhere names the scripture given to Moses as a guide and a mercy (17:2), a completion of the favour detailing everything (6:154), and *“the Book of Moses was ˹revealed as˺ a guide and mercy.”* (46:12). The guidance which could not be seen on the mountain had been written down instead.

The phrase claims comprehensiveness for the revelation given to Moses: commandments, explanations, and the principles of conduct. The Qur'an makes a similar claim for its own book — *“We have revealed to you the Book as an explanation of all things, a guide, a mercy. Good news for those who ˹fully˺ submit.”* (16:89) — and the sūrah's formulation belongs to the Book's consistent doctrine that divine guidance is enough for the life of a community. What is given is not a set of hints but a constitution.

**The Command to Hold Firmly**

*Khudhhā bi-quwwatin* — take it with strength — is addressed to Moses, and it repeats the charge of the previous verse (*hold firmly to what I have given you*, 7:144). The Book's language for receiving revelation is physical and demanding, and the same verb is used for Israel at the mountain: *“Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you”* (2:63; 2:93).

The command extends the obligation to the community: the prophet is to require his people to adopt the best of what has been revealed. The Qur'an's description of the guided uses the same idea — *“those who listen to what is said and follow the best of it. These are the ones ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah”* (39:18) — and the sūrah's phrasing makes the community's reception of the law a matter of deliberate choice rather than inheritance.

**The Warning That Accompanies the Gift**

The sūrah has used the word *fāsiqīn* for those who broke their covenants (7:102) and it will use it for the dwellings of the disobedient, and the Book's later verses supply the meaning: *“But as for those who are rebellious, the Fire will be their home”* (32:20). The warning is attached to the gift, so that the giving of the tablets is accompanied by the statement of what refusal costs.

**Written, Thrown Down, Taken Up: The Tablets Across the Sūrah**

The tablets appear three times in al-Aʿrāf, and the three appearances form a sequence. They are written at 7:145, thrown down at 7:150 when Mūsā returns to find the calf, and taken up at 7:154 after the earthquake. The sequence is a narrative about a community's relation to a text rather than about the text itself: the same object is given, dropped in anger at those who abandoned it, and recovered.

The recovery is what allows the verse's command to stand. A law given once and lost would be a gift withdrawn; a law given, dropped, and taken up again remains in force, and the sūrah's account of the generations that follow at 7:169–170 describes people who inherited the writing and held it differently.

The Qur'an's moral universe is built on that bifurcation, and the sūrah's narrative will supply both examples within a few verses — the calf-worshippers and those who repented (7:148–153).
verses.146:
> I will turn away from My signs those who act unjustly with arrogance in the land. And even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe in them. If they see the Right Path, they will not take it. But if they see a crooked path, they will follow it. This is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them

**The Arrogance Without Right**

The verse's condition for the blindness is a specific one: *those who act unjustly with arrogance in the land*, without any legitimate claim. The Book uses the phrase for Pharaoh and his army — *“And so he and his soldiers behaved arrogantly in the land with no right”* (28:39) — and it connects the posture to the reward that is excluded from the arrogant: *“That ˹eternal˺ Home in the Hereafter We reserve ˹only˺ for those who seek neither tyranny nor corruption on the earth”* (28:83). What the sūrah's verse describes is a self-elevation that has no basis in anything but the self.

The verse gives three symptoms of a refused revelation, and they form a sequence: signs seen and not believed; guidance recognized and not taken; error chosen as a road. The Qur'an states the same triple incapacity elsewhere — *“Had We sent down this Quran upon a mountain, you would have certainly seen it humbled and torn apart in awe of Allah. We set forth such comparisons for people, ˹so˺ perhaps they may reflect.”* (59:21) is the counter-image; the sealed heart is the same phenomenon in different words (7:100–101; 30:59). The Book's grammar of unbelief is consistently about direction rather than information.

**The Crooked Path**

*Sabīl al-ghayy* — the road of error — is contrasted with *sabīl al-rushd*, the path of right judgment. The Qur'an uses the language of crookedness for the deliberate distortion of guidance: the sūrah's Shuʿayb warned Madyan against lying in ambush on every road and *“striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked”* (7:86). Sūrat Āl ʿImrān asks the People of the Book why they turn believers away from the Way of Allah, *“striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked, while you are witnesses ˹to it˺”* (3:99). The verse's travelers who prefer the bent road are the Book's image of a will that has stopped looking for the straight one.

**The Sūrah's Own Diagnosis Repeated**

The verse's final clause is the exact charge that closed the Egyptian narrative: *“so We inflicted punishment upon them, drowning them in the sea for denying Our signs and being heedless of them”* (7:136). The sūrah is telling Israel, at the mountain, that the sentence which destroyed the state that had enslaved them describes a conduct rather than a nation, and that the conduct is available to anyone — including the people who had just been delivered.

The Book presents the sealing from both directions without embarrassment. Verse 146 is spoken by God about those who behave in a certain way. The sections preceding it (7:100–102) stated the law in general terms about generations that inherit a land; and the Book's other statements place the same reality in the language of abandonment — *“Allah left them to stray knowingly, sealed their hearing and hearts”* (45:23). The Qur'an's theology treats human choice as real and its consequences as authoritative.

**Every Sign Seen and Not Believed**

The verse describes a turning away imposed on a class: *“I will turn away from My signs those who act unjustly with arrogance in the land.”* (7:146).

The two verses agree that the condition is not a lack of evidence. Every sign is granted in the conditional, and belief does not follow. The commentators read this as the sūrah’s answer to the demand for signs recorded at 7:132: the sign is not what is missing, and a further sign would not supply it.

**Hearts and Eyes Turned Away**

The Qur'an's use of the teaching in its own address to the Muslims is explicit — *“And who does more wrong than those who, when reminded of their Lord's revelations, turn away from them and forget what their own hands have done?”* (18:57) — and the sūrah's readers are meant to hear the caution in their own case.
verses.147:
> The deeds of those who deny Our signs and the meeting ˹with Allah˺ in the Hereafter will be in vain. Will they be rewarded except for what they have done?”

**What Makes Deeds Void**

The verse names two denials: the signs and the meeting in the Hereafter. The Qur'an's pairing is consistent — the moral quality of an act depends on the horizon against which it is performed — and the Book states the consequence in closely parallel verses: *“Losers indeed are those who deny the meeting with Allah until the Hour takes them by surprise”* (6:31). *“Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us, being pleased and content with this worldly life, and who are heedless of Our signs”* (10:7).

Sūrat al-Jāthiyah reports the verdict spoken to the negligent: *“This Day We will neglect you as you neglected the meeting of this Day of yours! Your home will be the Fire”* (45:34).

**The Justice Formula**

*Hal yujzawna illā mā kānū yaʿmalūn* — will they be rewarded except for what they have done? The Qur'an repeats this principle in several forms: *“Whoever does good, it is to their own benefit. And whoever does evil, it is to their own loss”* (45:15; 41:46), and *“Is there any reward for goodness except goodness?”* (55:60). The Book's doctrine of recompense is consistently proportionate, and it sets limits that the sūrah's readers are meant to notice: *“Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold. But whoever comes with a bad deed will be punished for only one”* (6:160).

Sūrat al-Kahf states the other half of the ledger immediately after describing the futile: *“As for those who believe and do good, We certainly never deny the reward of those who are best in deeds”* (18:30). The Qur'an's God is described as neither wasting the effort of the good nor allowing the deeds of the heedless to provide them with standing. Verse 147 is the second clause of that pairing in the sūrah's own words.

**The Record That Cannot Be Lost**

The Book's description of the final accounting makes the verse's premise concrete: the record will be laid open, and the wicked will be shown what is written in it (18:49); *“whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it”* (99:7); and the one whose scale is light *“have doomed themselves”* (7:9). The sūrah's declaration that deeds become worthless therefore means worthless for reward, not that they go unrecorded.

**Deeds Reduced to Dust**

The voidness of 7:147 is described elsewhere with an image: *“We will turn to whatever ˹good˺ deeds they did, reducing them to scattered dust.”* (25:23). The verse of al-Furqān does what 7:147 does not: it shows the deeds being handled and then dispersed. Both verses attach the outcome to the same ground, namely the denial of the signs and of the meeting, and both state the result as an absence of value rather than as a punishment added to the record.

The image of scattered dust explains what void means in this context. This is why the sūrah's reckoning at 7:8–9 is the relevant frame: the scales measure weight, and a deed that has been scattered has none.

Sūrat Ibrāhīm compares such deeds to ashes on a stormy day, blown away with nothing gained (14:18). Sūrat al-Nūr compares them to a mirage that a thirsty traveler takes for water (24:39); Sūrat Āl ʿImrān compares them to a harvest struck by a bitter wind that destroys it completely (3:117); and Sūrat al-Baqarah compares them to a smooth rock with dust on it which heavy rain leaves bare (2:264).

The sūrah's own image of the Day is a scale, and the Book states the outcome of the weighing in the same terms: *“as for those whose scale is heavy ˹with good deeds˺”* (101:6), *“they will be in a life of bliss”* (101:7)
verses.148:
> In the absence of Moses, his people made from their ˹golden˺ jewellery an idol of a calf that made a lowing sound. Did they not see that it could neither speak to them nor guide them to the ˹Right˺ Path? Still they took it as a god and were wrongdoers

**The Rubric the Book Uses for Idols**

The Qur'an's tests for divinity are consistently functional: speech, guidance, benefit, harm, creation, provision. Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ's Abraham states the standard and then applies it — *“They are ˹all˺ enemies to me, except the Lord of all worlds”* (26:77) — after questioning the worship of what his ancestors had served. The sūrah's question about the calf is that rubric in a single sentence, and it is framed as something the people could have checked for themselves.

*Did they not see* — the question identifies the moment of refusal as one of attention rather than of evidence. The sūrah's earlier verdict on the idolaters the Israelites admired — *doomed to destruction* (7:139) — now applies inside the camp.

**Aaron's Warning Ignored**

Sūrat Ṭāhā records that the deputy did his duty: *“Aaron had already warned them beforehand, ‘O my people! You are only being tested by this, for indeed your ˹one true˺ Lord is the Most Compassionate. So follow me and obey my orders’”* (20:90). The people's answer was to wait for Moses (20:91). The sūrah's narrative of the episode is so a study in collective responsibility: a warning given, a community that preferred to wait for a leader, and an offense committed in the meantime.

The Qur'an returns to the calf in sūrat after sūrah, because the episode became the archetype of Israel's covenant-breaking: *“And ˹remember˺ when We appointed forty nights for Moses, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully”* (2:51). The repetition is the Book's method of training its own community to recognize the pattern — an idol made while the guidance is being received.

**What the Calf Scene Says About Leadership**

The episode's real drama is about the interval between a leader's departure and his return. Moses had provided a deputy, a charge, and a criterion (7:142); the community had the guidance and asked for a spectacle. The strength of a community's institutions is tested precisely when leadership is absent.

The report of the calf is followed by the people's remorse and prayer (7:149), by Moses' furious return (7:150), and by the punishment and forgiveness that follow (7:152–153). The sūrah treats the sin as a real offense with real consequences and real repentance, and it records all three rather than allowing the episode to end in either despair or indulgence.

**They Took It Up: The Verb of Adoption**

The verse’s verb is *ittakhadhū*, form VIII of *a-kh-dh*, to take — in this form, to take something up as one’s own, to adopt it. The sūrah uses the same verb of the same act in its verdict: *“Those who worshipped the calf will certainly be afflicted with Allah’s wrath as well as disgrace in the life of this world.”* (7:152), and of the taking of devils as masters (7:30).

The verb describes an act of choosing rather than an act of being given. What was taken up was made from the people’s own jewellery (7:148), and the sūrah’s phrase for it is *min ḥuliyyihim*, from their ornaments. The object is therefore described as originating with them, and the verb describes them as adopting it.

Sūrat Ṭāhā names the maker and the community's excuse: *“‘We did not break our promise to you of our own free will. We were made to carry the burden of the people’s ˹golden˺ jewellery, then we threw it ˹into the fire˺, and so did the Sâmiri.”* (20:87), followed by the molding of the calf and the claim that it was the god of Moses (20:88).
verses.149:
> Later, when they were filled with remorse and realized they had gone astray, they cried, “If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will certainly be losers.”

*Wa-lammā nadimū ʿalā mā faʿalū wa-raʾaw annahum qad ḍallū qālū la-in lam yarḥamnā rabbunā wa-yaghfir lanā la-nakūnanna mina al-khāsirīn* — later, when they were filled with remorse and realized they had gone astray, they cried: “If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will certainly be losers.” (7:149)

The sūrah has recorded this formula before, and its first appearance was on the lips of Adam and Eve after the fall: *“They replied, ‘Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers’”* (7:23).

**The Condition's Grammar**

*La-in lam yarḥamnā rabbunā wa-yaghfir lanā* — if our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us. The sentence hangs the outcome completely on God's action, and the Book's repentance formulas are built that way: the supplicant contributes the acknowledgment, and the remedy belongs to God. The Qur'an's answer to despair is stated in the same register: *“O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah's mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins”* (39:53).

The Qur'an treats repentance as a standing offer with stated conditions, and the sūrah itself supplies them in the next verse: *“But those who commit evil, then repent and become ˹true˺ believers, your Lord will certainly be All-Forgiving, Most-Merciful”* (7:153). The Book's other formulations add detail: *“Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord.
