He accepted his repentance”* (2:37); *“I am truly Most Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, and does good, then persists on ˹true˺ guidance”* (20:82); *“He is the One Who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons ˹their˺ sins”* (42:25).

**The Scope of the Remedy**

The sūrah's promises are not limited to forgiveness. Sūrat al-Furqān states the exchange that the Book offers the repentant — *“they are the ones whose evil deeds Allah will change into good deeds”* (25:70) — and the sūrah's own narrative reports that Moses' prayer for the community included both forgiveness and mercy (7:151). The Book's treatment of repentance is architectural rather than cosmetic: the structure of the person's record is rebuilt.

*Mina al-khāsirīn* is the Book's term for those whose loss is total, and it appears in its own distinct contexts: *“Whoever Allah guides is truly guided. And whoever He leaves to stray, they are the ˹true˺ losers”* (7:178); *“they have doomed themselves for wrongfully denying Our signs”* (7:9); and the sūrah of al-Kahf's account of those whose efforts are in vain (18:103–105). The calf-worshippers' fear is therefore precisely stated: the loss they dread is not the loss of a battle but of the self.

**Regret’s Speech in al-Furqān**

Al-Furqān records the speech of regret on the Day: *“And ˹beware of˺ the Day the wrongdoer will bite his nails ˹in regret˺ and say, ‘Oh! I wish I had followed the Way along with the Messenger!’”* (25:27), and then: *“Woe to me! I wish I had never taken so-and-so as a close friend.”* (25:28). The verse closes the speech with its cause: *“It was he who truly made me stray from the Reminder after it had reached me.”* (25:29).

Moses' anger, Aaron's defense, the punishment of the calf-makers, and the forgiveness extended to the repentant are all reported in the verses that follow (7:150–153).

Al-Qurṭubī reads the verse as the sūrah’s account of a repentance that is real but late: the words are right, the recognition is genuine, and the outcome is stated in the verses that follow — a prayer made, tablets taken up again, and forgiveness promised to those who repent (7:151–153)
verses.150:
> Upon Moses’ return to his people, ˹totally˺ furious and sorrowful, he said, “What an evil thing you committed in my absence! Did you want to hasten your Lord’s torment?” Then he threw down the Tablets and grabbed his brother by the hair, dragging him closer. Aaron pleaded, “O son of my mother! The people overpowered me and were about to kill me. So do not ˹humiliate me and˺ make my enemies rejoice, nor count me among the wrongdoing people.”

**What the Book Says About Leadership and Anger**

The episode's realism is deliberate. The Qur'an reports the fury of its own prophet toward his appointed deputy, and it reports the prayer that follows: *“My Lord! Forgive me and my brother! And admit us into Your mercy”* (7:151). The Book's model of leadership includes accountability, error, and repair, and it never presents its messengers as exempt from the emotions that make the repair necessary.

The Qur'an's narratives contain other such scenes: Noah's plea about his son and the correction it received (11:45–47), Jonah's departure and the lesson of the fish (37:139–144), and David's judgment in the case of the two litigants (38:21–25).

Sūrat Ṭāhā records what Moses said to the people themselves, and it supplies the context for the question of verse 150: *“O my people! Had your Lord not made you a good promise? Has my absence been too long for you? Or have you wished for wrath from your Lord to befall you, so you broke your promise to me?”* (20:86).

**The Samaritan and the Calf's End**

The fuller narrative names the man who made the calf and reports his sentence: the idol was burned and its ashes scattered into the sea (20:97). The sūrah's own account of the punishment belongs to the next verse (7:152), and the community's penance is reported in Sūrat al-Baqarah's charge: *“turn in repentance to your Creator and execute ˹the calf-worshippers among˺ yourselves”* (2:54).

The sūrah's account of the calf sits inside a longer record that the Book recites to the Prophet's community: the sea, the manna, the water from the rock, the mountain, the calf, the spies, and the forty years of wandering (2:57–61; 5:20–26).

With the confrontation completed, the sūrah turns to the judgment on the calf-worshippers (7:152), the offer of forgiveness to those who repent (7:153), and the recovery of the tablets (7:154). The reader of the sūrah is given the fall, the quarrel, the verdict, the mercy, and the law in the space of five verses.

**Did You Want to Hasten: The Question and the Book's Answer**

Mūsā's return at 7:150 is described in two states, furious and sorrowful, and his first words are a charge: what an evil thing you committed in my absence. The second sentence is a question, and the question identifies what the charge concerns: did you want to hasten the Lord's torment. The Book answers that question as a general fact about the human being: *“Humankind is made of haste. I will soon show you My signs, so do not ask Me to hasten them.”* (21:37). The verse of al-Anbiyāʾ names the disposition and then forbids the request that follows from it, which is exactly what the question at 7:150 puts to the people.

Hastening in this context is not impatience for a punishment but a try to bring the promised thing forward on human terms. The people had been given a term, Mūsā had gone to meet it, and the calf was made inside the interval. The sūrah states the same interval at 7:142, where the appointment is completed, and the question at 7:150 treats the making of the calf as an act performed against that interval.
verses.151:
> Moses prayed, “My Lord! Forgive me and my brother! And admit us into Your mercy. You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.”

**The Leader's Own Need**

*Ighfir lī* — forgive me — is spoken by the man who had spoken with God and received the tablets. The Qur'an's prophets are consistently depicted as supplicants: Moses himself prays elsewhere, *“My Lord! I have definitely wronged my soul, so forgive me”* (28:16), David asks forgiveness after his judgment (38:24), and Abraham includes his own errors in his prayer (26:82). The Book's doctrine of prophecy never removes the messenger's need for mercy.

The petition's second half is a model of reconciliation, and the Qur'an's narratives of brothers supply its context. Joseph's treatment of his brothers ends in the same register — *“There is no blame on you today. May Allah forgive you! He is the Most Merciful of the merciful!”* (12:92) — and the Book's instruction to the believers addresses divisions directly: *“The believers are but one brotherhood, so make peace between your brothers”* (49:10). The sūrah's Moses prays for the deputy he had just dragged by the hair.

**The Request to Enter Mercy**

*Wa-adkhilnā fī raḥmatika* — admit us into Your mercy — uses the Book's language of entry rather than of gift, and the sūrah itself states the widest form of the mercy a few verses later: *“My mercy encompasses everything”* (7:156). The Qur'an's other prayers use the same spatial vocabulary — *“Our Lord! You encompass everything in ˹Your˺ mercy and knowledge”* (40:7) — and the request places the two brothers inside a mercy that is larger than their dispute.

The phrase is one of the Qur'an's recurring supplications: Joseph's father says it when he fears for Benjamin (12:64), Ayyūb prays it in his illness (21:83), and the believers' prayer in Sūrat al-Muʾminūn closes with the same affirmation (23:109, 23:118). The Book gives this superlative to the human beings asking for mercy, which is its own statement about how the Qur'an's supplicants address God.

**The Book's Vocabulary of Mercy**

The sūrah's readers meet the mercy language repeatedly: the messengers are sent as mercy (21:107), the Book is guidance and mercy (7:154), and the divine names in the prayer open the sūrah's own account of God's letters to His servants (7:156). Verse 151 therefore sits inside the sūrah's most sustained treatment of mercy, and it uses the vocabulary that treatment establishes.

The episode gives leaders three things in three verses: the accountability of a deputy (7:150), the reconciliation of those who lead (7:151), and the community's punishment and forgiveness (7:152–153). The Book's editorial arrangement of the scene turns a family quarrel into a pattern, and the sūrah's next chapter of Israel's history begins from the repaired relationship between the two brothers.

**Nūḥ, Ibrāhīm, and the Prayers for Family**

The inclusion of another in a prayer for oneself is not a routine of prophetic speech in the Qurʾān, and where it occurs it marks a bond. Nūḥ prays, *“My Lord! Forgive me, my parents, and whoever enters my house in faith, and ˹all˺ believing men and women.”* (71:28) — the same petition widened from self to parents to household to the whole community of believers. Ibrāhīm prays for his father: *“Forgive my father, for he is certainly one of the misguided.”* (26:86).

The three prayers form a scale. Nūḥ’s runs outward through kinship and faith and stops at the believers, because the prayer for an unbelieving son is refused him (11:46). Ibrāhīm’s is for a father whose case he later abandons on instruction (9:114).

**The Answer Given Five Verses Later**

The sūrah answers the request five verses later, in the widest statement of mercy it contains: *“I will inflict My torment on whoever I will. But My mercy encompasses everything.”* (7:156). The prayer asked to be admitted into mercy; the answer declares that mercy encompasses all things and then specifies who will be given it — those who follow the Messenger (7:157).

Moses had asked for his brother's assistance (20:29–36), had left him in charge (7:142), and had returned to find the community in the worst condition imaginable.
verses.152:
> Those who worshipped the calf will certainly be afflicted with Allah’s wrath as well as disgrace in the life of this world. This is how We reward those who invent falsehood

**"Wrath and Disgrace in This World"**

*Inna alladhīna ittakhadhū al-ʿijla sa-yanāluhum ghaḍabun min rabbihim wa-dhillatun fī al-ḥayāti al-dunyā wa-kadhālika najzī al-muftarīn* — those who worshipped the calf will certainly be afflicted with Allah's wrath as well as disgrace in the life of this world.

The sūrah announces the penalty for the calf-worshippers in a sentence. The Book's other accounts supply the details: Moses commanded the community to carry out the execution of the offenders among themselves (2:54), and the maker of the calf received his own sentence — his idol was burned and its ashes scattered into the sea (20:97).

Sūrat al-Ḥajj describes those who turn away in pride: *“They will suffer disgrace in this world. On the Day of Judgment We will make them taste the torment of burning”* (22:9); Sūrat al-Aḥzāb states the general rule about those who offend God and His Messenger: *“condemned by Allah in this world and the Hereafter”* (33:57). Verse 152 is the sūrah's instance of the pattern.

**"Those Who Invent Falsehood"**

*Al-muftarīn* — the fabricators — is the Book's term for those who attribute to God what is not His, and the Qur'an's challenge to them is repeated in almost identical words across the sūrahs: *“Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah?”* (6:21; 11:18; 29:68; 39:32). The calf was not merely an object of bad taste; the sūrah names it as a fabrication, an invention presented as the god of Moses (20:88).

The Book's designation of the offense clarifies what the sūrah considers the gravest element of the episode: the community did not simply lapse into an old habit; it manufactured a claim about God. Sūrat al-Nisāʾ states the act's character in a single clause — *“See how they fabricate lies against Allah — this alone is a blatant sin”* (4:50) — and the Qur'an's strong reproach to whoever persists in such claims closes with, *“they will be the ˹true˺ wrongdoers”* (3:94).

**Stricken With Disgrace and Misery**

The parallel is close enough to be read as one event described twice. 7:152 states the wrath and the disgrace as a present consequence, in this world, before describing the penance that follows (7:153); 2:61 states the disgrace and misery and the displeasure as a standing condition, with the reasons listed. Neither verse confines the consequence to the hereafter, which is what makes this case different from the sūrah’s destroyed towns.

**A Fitting Home: Lying About Allah**

The verse ends with the same formula used at 7:41: so are the inventors of falsehood rewarded. Az-Zumar puts the invention as a question about comparison: *“Who then does more wrong than those who lie about Allah and reject the truth after it has reached them? Is Hell not a ˹fitting˺ home for the disbelievers?”* (39:32).

This is what the formula is doing in the sūrah. At 7:41 it closes a description of the Fire; at 7:152 it closes a description of a sin committed inside the covenant. In both cases the sentence is not a threat but a statement of proportion, and 39:32 supplies the term the sūrah leaves implicit: the home is *fitting*, which is why the wrong is measured rather than inflicted.
verses.153:
> But those who commit evil, then repent and become ˹true˺ believers, your Lord will certainly be All-Forgiving, Most-Merciful

**The Order of the Conditions**

The verse names evil, repentance, and faith in sequence, and the Book's other formulations expand the list. Sūrat al-Furqān states the exchange offered to those who meet the conditions — *“As for those who repent, believe. Do good deeds, they are the ones whose evil deeds Allah will change into good deeds”* (25:70) — and Sūrat Ṭāhā's promise includes persistence in guidance: *“I am truly Most Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, and does good, then persists on ˹true˺ guidance”* (20:82). The Qur'an's repentance is consistently a program rather than a sentiment.

The Book's other statements of the same promise emphasize amendment of conduct. *“As for those who repent, mend their ways, and let the truth be known, they are the ones to whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺”* (2:160); *“As for those who repent afterwards and mend their ways, then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”* (3:89). The vocabulary of mending in these verses shows that the Qur'an's door is open to the person who changes course, not to the person who merely regrets the consequences.

**The Two Names**

*Ghafūr* and *Raḥīm* — All-Forgiving, Most-Merciful — are the Book's most frequently paired divine names. The sūrah has used them for the remedy throughout: the sūrah's own statement of the widest mercy, *“My mercy encompasses everything”* (7:156), stands a few verses later, and the promise attached to it names those who shun evil, pay alms, and believe. The sūrah's God is described neither as indifferent nor as unforgiving, and the pairing is the Book's way of holding judgment and mercy together.

The verse's subject is Israel at the foot of the mountain. The Book's later reports show the promise was taken up: Sūrat al-Baqarah's account of the penance ends with God's acceptance of the community's repentance (2:54), and the sūrah's own narrative continues with the seventy chosen for the appointment and the grant of mercy that followed (7:155–156). The Book treats the calf episode as closed by both judgment and forgiveness. The Qur'an's warnings about repentance arriving too late are as clear as its promises: Sūrat al-Nisāʾ distinguishes the repentance of those who sin in ignorance and turn quickly from the repentance of those who persist until death (4:17–18). Sūrat Āl ʿImrān states that those who disbelieve after believing and increase in disbelief will not have their repentance accepted (3:90).

The Qur'an instructs its readers to hold the two together: *“Inform My servants ˹O Prophet˺ that I am truly the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful, and that My torment is indeed the most painful”* (15:49–50's pairing).

**Hope Not Lost: The Door the Verse Leaves Open**

7:153 covers those who did evil, repented and believed, and then names the two names that receive them: Forgiving, Merciful. Yūsuf states the same openness from the other side, in a father’s instruction to his sons: *“And do not lose hope in the mercy of Allah, for no one loses hope in Allah’s mercy except those with no faith.”* (12:87). Despair is there classified as a form of disbelief — not as a weakness of mood but as a statement about God.

The sūrah’s own first confession supplies the form the promise takes in practice: *“Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers.”* (7:23). The two requests are the two names of 7:153, and the confession is the repentance the verse describes. Nothing in 7:153 requires a prior record of virtue; it requires the sequence, and the sequence begins with an admission.

Al-Burūj states the case in which the interval is not filled: *“Those who persecute the believing men and women and then do not repent will certainly suffer the punishment of Hell and the torment of burning.”* (85:10)
verses.154:
> When Moses’ anger subsided, he took up the Tablets whose text contained guidance and mercy for those who stand in awe of their Lord

**The Tablets Recovered**

The sūrah had reported the tablets' casting down in the moment of grief (7:150), and it now reports their recovery. The Book's symbol is exact and its sequence deliberate: the written guidance is knocked from a community's hands by that community's failure, and it is taken up again after the punishment and the repentance. What survives the crisis is the text.

The verse describes the tablets' contents with the pairing the Qur'an uses for revelation throughout: *“This is an insight to humanity — a guide and a lesson to the God-fearing”* (3:138). *“We send down the Quran as a healing and mercy for the believers”* (17:82); *“a warning from your Lord, a cure for what is in the hearts, a guide. A mercy for the believers”* (10:57); *“This ˹Quran˺ is an insight for humanity — a guide and mercy for people of sure faith”* (45:20). The sūrah's own earlier statement — the Book is *“a guide and mercy for those who believe”* (7:52) — belongs to the same series.

**For Those Who Stand in Awe**

The verse's final clause restricts the benefit: *li-lladhīna hum li-rabbihim yarhabūn*, for those who stand in awe of their Lord. The Book's statements about its own guidance are consistently conditioned in this way — *“a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺”* (2:2). *“˹It is˺ a guide and mercy for the good-doers”* (31:3); *“it is truly a guide and mercy for the believers”* (27:77) — and the Qur'an states the reason elsewhere: *“Of all of Allah's servants, only the knowledgeable ˹of His might˺ are ˹truly˺ in awe of Him”* (35:28). The tablets guide the people disposed to be guided. The sūrah's use of *rahba* rather than a milder term for reverence sets the tone for the passage's conclusion, and the Qur'an attaches forgiveness and reward to the same disposition: *“Indeed, those in awe of their Lord without seeing Him will have forgiveness and a mighty reward”* (67:12).

The Qur'an's presentation of its own book in relation to earlier scripture follows the same logic: *“We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ this Book with the truth, as a confirmation of previous Scriptures and a supreme authority on them”* (5:48).

**The Scripture and the Standard**

The comparison is instructive on the difference between the two verses. 2:53 is addressed to the descendants and ends with *laʿallakum*, perhaps you will be guided; 7:154 describes the tablets as containing guidance and mercy *for those who stand in awe of their Lord*, and the relation is stated as fact rather than as expectation. The awe is what makes the contents available.

**The Record and What It Contains**

This is the sūrah’s own contrast, and it is why the verse follows the episode of the calf. The tablets were thrown down (7:150), the brother was seized (7:150), the prayer was made (7:151), and the text is taken up again — with its contents stated for the first time in the narrative. 18:49 describes the other book that will be taken up, and the two together frame what the sūrah means by a written thing.
verses.155:
> Moses chose seventy men from among his people for Our appointment and, when they were seized by an earthquake, he cried, “My Lord! Had You willed, You could have destroyed them long ago, and me as well. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done? This is only a test from You—by which You allow whoever you will to stray and guide whoever You will. You are our Guardian. So forgive us and have mercy on us. You are the best forgiver

**"Seventy Men for Our Appointment"**

*Wa-khtāra Mūsā qawmahu sabʿīna rajulan li-mīqātinā fa-lammā akhadhathumu al-rajfatu qāla rabbi law shiʾta ahlaktahum min qablu wa-iyyāya a-tuhlikunā bimā faʿala al-sufahāʾu minnā* — Moses chose seventy men from among his people for Our appointment and, when they were seized by an earthquake, he cried: "My Lord! Had You willed, You could have destroyed them long ago, and me as well. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?" (7:155)

The verse opens with a selection: seventy men, drawn from the community, chosen for the appointment Moses himself had already attended. The sūrah's narrative of the mountain had ended with the law recovered and the community's repentance accepted (7:153–154); the delegation belongs to the community's effort to approach what its prophet had been granted.

Sūrat al-Baqarah records the demand that produced the earthquake, and it is the raw claim of people who had watched the sea open: *“And ˹remember˺ when you said, ‘O Moses! We will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes,’ so a thunderbolt struck you while you were looking on”* (2:55). The sūrah's seventy are the representatives of that demand, and their seizure is the answer to it.

**The Prophet as Intercessor**

The number matters in the Book's memory: the tradition of Israel's leaders is twelve, and the Qur'an's account of the covenant with the Children of Israel names twelve chiefs (5:12). The seventy here are a delegation rather than an institution, and the sūrah treats them as representatives — which is why their failure is the community's failure and their restoration is the community's mercy.

The sūrah has now described two gatherings at the mountain: the appointment of Moses alone, where he asked for the vision and the mountain was levelled (7:143), and the appointment of the seventy, where an earthquake seized the representatives.

**Rajfah: The Towns’ Word Used of the Delegation**

The seventy are seized by a *rajfah* — an earthquake, a shaking, from the root *r-j-f*, which describes violent motion and the trembling that accompanies dread. *Rājifah* is the first of the two blasts in an-Nāziʿāt (79:6). The word is used in this sūrah of the punishment that destroyed two other communities: of Midian, *“Then an overwhelming earthquake struck them, and they fell lifeless in their homes.”* (7:78); and of the people of Lot, *“Then an overwhelming earthquake struck them and they fell lifeless in their homes.”* (7:91).

**Forgiveness Then Mercy: The Pair at 7:23**

Mūsā asks two things and asks them in the order the sūrah’s first confession used: forgiveness, then mercy. Ādam and his wife said, *“Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers.”* (7:23). Mūsā says, *“My Lord! Had You willed, You could have destroyed them long ago, and me as well. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?”* (7:155) and then, in the verse’s closing petition, asks forgiveness and mercy for himself and for the people.

It is also a communal prayer. Mūsā includes the seventy in the petition, as he included his brother at 7:151. The sūrah’s leaders ask for others, and the sūrah’s destroyed towns are the ones whose leaders asked only for themselves. That contrast, unremarked in the verse, is available to any reader who has followed the histories from 7:59 onward.

Sūrat al-Baqarah gives the sequel to the thunderbolt: *“Then We brought you back to life after your death, so that perhaps you would be grateful”* (2:56).
verses.156:
> Ordain for us what is good in this life and the next. Indeed, we have turned to You ˹in repentance˺.” Allah replied, “I will inflict My torment on whoever I will. But My mercy encompasses everything. I will ordain mercy for those who shun evil, pay alms-tax, and believe in Our revelations

**"My Mercy Encompasses Everything"**

*Wa-ktub lanā fī hādhihi al-dunyā ḥasanatan wa-fī al-ākhirati innā hudnā ilayka qāla ʿadhābī uṣību bihi man ashāʾu wa-raḥmatī wasiʿat kulla shayʾin fa-sa-aktubuhā li-lladhīna yattaqūna wa-yuʾtūna al-zakāta wa-lladhīna hum bi-āyātinā yuʾminūn* — "Ordain for us what is good in this life and the next. Indeed, we have turned to You ˹in repentance˺." (7:156) Allah replied: "I will inflict My torment on whoever I will. But My mercy encompasses everything. I will ordain mercy for those who shun evil, pay alms-tax, and believe in Our revelations." (7:156)

*Wa-ktub lanā* — decree for us, write for us — asks for good in this world and the next in a single sentence. The Book's prayers characteristically join the two, and the Qur'an states the contrast: *“Yet there are others who say, ‘Our Lord! Grant us the good of this world and the Hereafter, and protect us from the torment of the Fire’”* (2:201), against the petition of those who want only this life (2:200). Moses' sentence asks for both.

**The Return to God**

*Innā hudnā ilayka* — we have turned to You in repentance — closes the prayer with the word the sūrah used for Israel's remorse at the calf (7:149). The Book's repentance formulas make the turning the condition of the request, and the sūrah's placement of the clause after the plea for mercy keeps that order intact.

*Wa-raḥmatī wasiʿat kulla shayʾ* — My mercy encompasses everything. The sentence is the Book's most expansive statement of divine mercy, and the Qur'an states its logic elsewhere: *“Our Lord! You encompass everything in ˹Your˺ mercy and knowledge”* (40:7). Here the phrase answers the interrogation of a people whose representatives had just been struck down.

**The Three Marks in the Qur'an's Law**

The triple — God-consciousness, alms, and faith in the signs — describes the Qur'an's standard of the believer's life: the inner disposition, the social duty, and the doctrinal commitment. Sūrat al-Baqarah's definition of righteousness makes the same move from ritual to substance (2:177), and the sūrah's own later verse about abiding by the Scripture and establishing prayer repeats the structure (7:170).

The answer joins the widest mercy in the Book to a specific list of obligations, and the sūrah's readers are meant to hold both. Sūrat al-Ḥijr states the pairing as a command to the Prophet: *“Inform My servants ˹O Prophet˺ that I am truly the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful, and that My torment is indeed the most painful”* (15:49–50). Verse 156 is the same pairing in the form of an answer to prayer.

**Zakah Named Before the Law Was Quantified**

The second of the three marks is named here without specification. This is a Meccan passage, and the alms-tax it makes a condition of mercy carries no rate, no threshold and no list of recipients; those come later, when the community has a treasury. “Alms-tax is only for the poor and the needy” (9:60) opens the enumeration of the eight categories, and the fifth of the spoils is assigned at 8:41. The sequence is the point. The obligation is attached to the mercy before its administration exists, so what the verse conditions is the disposition to give rather than compliance with a schedule — not an anachronism in a Meccan verse but the same obligation at an earlier stage of its disclosure.
verses.157:
> “˹They are˺ the ones who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whose description they find in their Torah and the Gospel. He commands them to do good and forbids them from evil, permits for them what is lawful and forbids to them what is impure, and relieves them from their burdens and the shackles that bound them. ˹Only˺ those who believe in him, honour and support him, and follow the light sent down to him will be successful.”

**"Whose Description They Find in Their Torah and Gospel"**

The verse claims that the earlier scriptures name him. The Qur'an makes the claim elsewhere: *“And ˹remember˺ when Jesus, son of Mary, said, ‘O children of Israel! I am truly Allah's messenger to you, confirming the Torah which came before me, and giving good news of a messenger after me whose name will be Aḥmad’”* (61:6), and Sūrat Āl ʿImrān's covenant with the prophets states the same pattern (3:81). The new revelation fulfils a text already in their hands.

**"He Commands Them to Do Good and Forbids Them from Evil"**

The formula *al-maʿrūf* and *al-munkar* — the recognized good and the repudiated evil — becomes one of the Book's standard descriptions of prophetic office and of the Muslim community's public duty: *“Let there be a group among you who call ˹others˺ to goodness, encourage what is good. Forbid what is evil — it is they who will be successful”* (3:104). The sūrah presents it as a continuation rather than an innovation.

*Wa-yuḥillu lahum al-ṭayyibāti wa-yuḥarrimu ʿalayhim al-khabāʾith* — he permits the good things and forbids the foul. The Qur'an's moral vocabulary distinguishes things by their quality rather than by arbitrary decree, and the sūrah's readers have just been told about the adornments of God and the question of who forbade them (7:32).

**What the Verse Relieves and What It Confirms**

The sūrah's charges against the earlier communities had been about concealment, distortion, and the abandoning of the Book (7:162, 7:169). The verse's answer is not a severance from them but a restoration of what they had been given — the good things made lawful, the impurities forbidden, and the burdens lifted.

The verse's final clause makes success conditional on the four responses, and the sūrah's readers hear the condition in a passage that has just described Israel's failures. The Book's promises attach to conduct throughout, and the sūrah's earlier verse about Israel's favoured position (7:140) shows how the Book uses such claims.

**The Unlettered Prophet and the Description in the Earlier Books**

The Book states the condition plainly elsewhere: *“You ˹O Prophet˺ could not read any writing ˹even˺ before this ˹revelation˺, nor could you write at all. Otherwise, the people of falsehood would have been suspicious.”* (29:48). It also reports that the earlier scriptures contain the description referred to here, and puts the announcement in the mouth of ʿĪsā: *“giving good news of a messenger after me whose name will be Aḥmad”* (61:6). The knowledge of those who received the Book is described as intimate rather than technical: *“Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children.”* (2:146) — a recognition that the same verse says a group of them then concealed knowingly.

**The Burdens, and What the Tradition Reports of Them**

The clause that the Prophet ﷺ relieves them of their burdens and the shackles that were upon them is the verse’s summary of a legal history, and the commentators supply instances. Among those they report from the earlier law are a repentance that required the killing of the self, as in the command to Israel after the calf — *“turn in repentance to your Creator and execute ˹the calf-worshippers among˺ yourselves”* (2:54) — the cutting away of a garment that had been soiled, and the confinement of worship to designated places.

The Book says the same of the religion given to this community: *“He ˹Who˺ has chosen you, and laid upon you no hardship in the religion”* (22:78).

**The Description as the Tradition Reports It**

Ibn Kathīr, under this verse, transmits from ʿAṭāʾ b. Yasār a description of the Prophet ﷺ as the earlier books give it: sent as a witness over the nations, a bearer of good tidings to the righteous and a warner to the wrongdoers, named *al-Mutawakkil*, the one who trusts God. Not harsh of temperament, not quarrelsome, not crying out in the markets, and not returning evil for evil but forgiving it. Al-Fatḥ states the claim this verse makes — “This is their description in the Torah.” (48:29) — and describes his company: “And those with him are firm with the disbelievers and compassionate with one another.” (48:29). Āl ʿImrān gives the temperament: “Had you been cruel or hard-hearted, they would have certainly abandoned you.” (3:159).

The Qur'an describes its messenger in several verses as a mercy, a warner, and a light, and elsewhere as the seal of the prophets (33:40).
verses.158:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O humanity! I am Allah’s Messenger to you all. To Him ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. He gives life and causes death.” So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, who believes in Allah and His revelations. And follow him, so you may be ˹rightly˺ guided

**"I Am Allah's Messenger to You All"**

*Qul yā ayyuhā al-nāsu innī rasūlu Allāhi ilaykum jamīʿan alladhī lahu mulku al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi lā ilāha illā huwa yuḥyī wa-yumīt* — Say, ˹O Prophet˺: "O humanity! I am Allah's Messenger to you all. To Him ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. He gives life and causes death." (7:158)

The Qur'an states the same universality in several sūrahs: *“We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a deliverer of good news and a warner to all of humanity, but most people do not know”* (34:28), and *“We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a mercy for the whole world”* (21:107). The sūrah's verse belongs to that series, and its placement after the Sinai narrative gives the universality a historical argument.

**The Authentication of the Message**

The Book's messengers argue from the sovereignty of the One who sent them, and the sūrah has already used the same reasoning in Moses' opening speech to the court of Egypt (7:104) and in the magicians' confession (7:121).

Sūrat al-Anʿām records the Prophet's instruction to state that God is witness between him and his people, and that the Qur'an was revealed to him so that he might warn with it (6:19). Verse 158's declaration is the same testimony in the form of a public announcement, and its content — one God, one messenger, one humanity — is the sūrah's summary of its own message.

**The Scope of the Address in the Book’s Other Statements**

The address *O humanity* is the verse’s claim about the mission’s reach, and the Book states the same reach in three other places with three emphases. Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ states it as the mission’s character: *“We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a mercy for the whole world.”* (21:107). Sūrah al-Anʿām states it as the reach of the Book itself: *“this Quran has been revealed to me so that, with it, I may warn you and whoever it reaches.”* (6:19).

**The Kingdom Clause and What It Settles**

Between the address and the command to believe, the verse inserts three statements about God: the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, there is no god but He, and He gives life and causes death. The order is an argument. Ownership of the kingdom is the premise; its exclusivity is the first consequence; the disposal of life and death is the demonstration, being the one act no rival claimant can perform and every claimant must concede.

The premise is what makes the address universal. A messenger sent by the owner of a province speaks to that province; a messenger sent by the one to whom the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs cannot be sent to a part of it only. The Book puts the same premise in the mouth of the Day itself: *“Who does all authority belong to this Day? To Allah—the One, the Supreme!”* (40:16). The sūrah has already stated the reach of the mercy that follows from such ownership: *“But My mercy encompasses everything.”* (7:156). Verse 158 is where that reach becomes an address, and where the sūrah’s argument about the towns closes by opening onto everyone who hears it.
verses.159:
> There are some among the people of Moses who guide with the truth and establish justice accordingly

**Guidance with the Truth**

*Yahdūna bi-l-ḥaqq* — they guide by the truth — names the standard rather than the community. The Book's definition of a guided group is not its lineage, its history, or its claims, but the truth by which it guides others, and the same word *al-ḥaqq* has been the sūrah's term for what prevailed in Egypt's courtyard (7:118).

*Wa-bihi yaʿdilūn* — the second clause converts guidance into administration. The Qur'an's righteous communities are described as those who establish justice, and the sūrah's earlier narratives measured the destroyed towns by the same standard: Madyan's fraud, ʿĀd's oppression, and Sodom's violence were failures of justice rather than of ritual.

The Qur'an states the same doctrine about the earlier communities in several places. *“Yet they are not all alike: there are some among the People of the Book who are upright, who recite Allah's revelations throughout the night, prostrating ˹in prayer˺. They believe in Allah and the Last Day, encourage good and forbid evil, and race with one another in doing good”* (3:113–114), and the verses that follow promise that their good will not be denied (3:115).

**The Verse's Comfort for the Sūrah's Prophet**

Addressed to the Prophet at the end of a narrative about Israel's failures, the sentence is also an encouragement. The Qur'an's narratives of rejection are consistently accompanied by statements that the rejection is not universal: Sūrat al-Anʿām's instruction to follow the guidance given to the earlier messengers (6:90) rests on the same idea, and Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ's promise of a believing remnant follows a similar pattern.

The verse does not say that the group is many, and the Book's statements about the righteous are consistently quantitative-minimal: *“except for a few”* (11:40's phrasing), *“˹Only˺ a few of My servants are ˹truly˺ grateful”* (34:13). The point of the sentence is not the size of the remnant but the possibility of guidance within a community that has otherwise failed.

**The Book's Rejection of Two Errors**

Read with the sūrah's surrounding verses, the sentence refuses two symmetrical errors. It denies that a community's failures justify a blanket verdict on every individual in it, and it denies that membership in a favoured lineage substitutes for conduct. The Book's doctrine of responsibility, stated earlier in the sūrah (6:164) and in its covenant passages, is applied here to a people with the longest record of signs.

The pairing of guidance with justice in the verse is not accidental. The sūrah's narratives about the towns had ended with the destruction of communities whose religion had become a screen for fraud, and its accounts of Israel's failures had included the unlawful gains of the generations who inherited the Scripture (7:169). The test of a guided group in this sūrah is therefore whether its guidance reaches its scales.

**The Group in the Book's Later History**

The Qur'an's address to the People of the Book elsewhere commands the community to compete in good and notes that among them are believers (5:48's command, 3:199's statement about those who truly believe in what was revealed to them and to the Muslims). The sūrah's verse is the first statement of that theme in this sūrah, and the later verses of the Qur'an develop it.

The Book's answer is given here in a clause about the people of Moses, and it is repeated later in the sūrah for humanity as a whole (7:181).
verses.160:
> We divided them into twelve tribes—each as a community. And We revealed to Moses, when his people asked for water, “Strike the rock with your staff.” Then twelve springs gushed out. Each tribe knew its drinking place. We shaded them with clouds and sent down to them manna and quails, ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided for you.” They ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves

**"Twelve Tribes, Twelve Springs"**

*Wa-qaṭṭaʿnāhum ithnatay ʿashrata asbāṭan umaman wa-awḥaynā ilā Mūsā idhi stasqāhu qawmuhu ani iḍrib bi-ʿaṣāka al-ḥajara fa-nbajasat minhu ithnatā ʿashrata ʿaynan* — We divided them into twelve tribes — each as a community. And We revealed to Moses, when his people asked for water, "Strike the rock with your staff." (7:160) Then twelve springs gushed out. Each tribe knew its drinking place.

The verse treats Israel's social organization as a divine arrangement: *We divided them into twelve tribes, each as a community*. The Qur'an's account of the covenant with the Children of Israel names twelve leaders appointed from among them (5:12), and the Book's administrative vocabulary here matches the structure of the event at the rock in which each group received its own water.

Sūrat al-Baqarah preserves the same scene in nearly the same words: *“And ˹remember˺ when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said, ‘Strike the rock with your staff.’ Then twelve springs gushed out, ˹and˺ each tribe knew its drinking place”* (2:60). The Book's repetition of the scene at the head of its longest sūrah and again here, in the middle of its narrative of the wilderness, marks it as one of the founding signs of Israel's formation.

**"They Did Not Wrong Us, but Wronged Themselves"**

The verse's final clause is one of the Book's most quoted statements of the logic of wrongdoing: *wa-mā ẓalamūnā wa-lākin kānū anfusahum yaẓlimūn*. The Qur'an states the principle in several forms — *“Whoever does good, it is to their own benefit. And whoever does evil, it is to their own loss”* (41:46) — and its function in this narrative is to strip the community's complaints of any claim against God.

The complaint about the provision has already been recorded, in the account of the demand for a change of diet: *“O Moses! We cannot endure the same meal ˹every day˺”* (2:61). The Book reports the complaint in the same breath as the gift, and verse 160's closing clause is its verdict on the exchange.

The wilderness provisions belong to the sūrah's doctrine of testing: the same gifting that forms a community can expose its dispositions, and the Book's narratives about manna include the gathering on the Sabbath and the community's discontent. Sūrat al-Baqarah states the pattern in its own account of the same years (2:57–61), and the two are meant to be weighed against each other.

**Peoples and Tribes: The Word for a Division**

The contrast is what makes the verse more than an administrative detail. 49:13 describes divisions given at creation and ordered toward knowledge of one another; 7:160 describes divisions made in the wilderness and ordered toward a supply of water.

**Created From Water: The Gift and Its Use**

The manna and the quails come with an instruction to eat, and the instruction is followed by the report of ingratitude — *“They ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves”* (7:160). A provision given at the scale of 21:30 and answered with ingratitude is the sūrah’s sharpest instance of the pattern it has been describing since 7:59: the gift is real, the demand attached to it is small, and the refusal damages the one who refuses.

Sūrat Ṭāhā's account of the same incident adds a warning — *“Eat from the good things We have provided for you, but do not transgress in them, or My wrath will befall you”* (20:81) — and the Book's pairing of provision with accountability is the sūrah's own doctrine.

The verse sits between the acknowledgement of a righteous remnant among the people of Moses (7:159) and the account of the city whose inhabitants changed what they had been told (7:161–162).

The Qur'an comments on ingratitude as a disposition rather than an act, and its formal statement appears repeatedly: *“Whatever blessings you have are from Allah. Then whenever hardship touches you, to Him ˹alone˺ you cry ˹for help˺”* (16:53).
verses.161:
> And ˹remember˺ when it was said to them, “Enter this city ˹of Jerusalem˺ and eat from wherever you please. Say, ‘Absolve us,’ and enter the gate with humility. We will forgive your sins, ˹and˺ We will multiply the reward for the good-doers.”

**"Enter This City and Eat Freely"**

*Wa-idh qīla lahumu skunū hādhihi al-qaryata fa-kulū minhā ḥaythu shiʾtum wa-qūlū ḥiṭṭatun wa-dkhulū al-bāba sujjadan naghfir lakum khaṭīʾātikum sa-nazīdu al-muḥsinīn* — and ˹remember˺ when it was said to them: "Enter this city ˹of Jerusalem˺ and eat from wherever you please. Say, 'Absolve us,' and enter the gate with humility. We will forgive your sins, ˹and˺ We will multiply the reward for the good-doers." (7:161)

Sūrat al-Baqarah reports the same instruction almost word for word: *“And ˹remember˺ when We said, ‘Enter this city and eat freely from wherever you please; enter the gate with humility, saying, “Absolve us.” We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward for the good-doers’”* (2:58). The Book's repetition of the command fixes it as one of Israel's defining moments, and the sūrah's readers meet it here at the end of the wilderness narrative.

**The Command and the Coming Rebellion**

What the community actually did is left to the next verse to state: the wrongdoers among them changed the words they had been commanded to say (7:162). The Book's arrangement of command and disobedience in consecutive verses is its standard method for showing how a community loses a gift, and the sūrah's narrative continues in this pattern.

The verse's final clause introduces the doctrine the Qur'an states elsewhere in precise terms: *“Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold”* (6:160). The entry into the land was not simply a political event but an opportunity for reward, and its conditions were a request for pardon and a bowed head.

The Book's address to its own community uses the vocabulary of covenant and entry in its own way, and the command to remember the favour and the covenant when the believers said *“We hear and obey”* (5:7) is the parallel formula. The sūrah's narrative is so instructive rather than merely historical: the terms on which a community receives a gift have not changed.

**Enter Egypt, in Security**

The command recorded in this verse is to enter a city with two conditions attached. Yūsuf records a different entering, and its words are quoted: *“Enter Egypt, Allah willing, in security.”* (12:99). The two verses describe the same act — an arrival at a settled place — with opposite conditions.

The commentators read the two conditions as the terms of a favour that could be received badly. The word commanded is a request for forgiveness, and the manner commanded is humility — the two things the sūrah’s later account reports as altered (7:162)

**A Good Life and a Reward Measured by the Best**

The verse’s promise has two parts: forgiveness of sins and an increase for the doers of good. An-Naḥl states the same promise in general terms: *“Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life, and We will certainly reward them according to the best of their deeds.”* (16:97).

The verse supplies the measure 7:161 leaves implicit. The reward is not an average of what was done but is taken from its best, and the good life is stated as part of the reward rather than as a separate gift. The condition named is belief, which is the same condition the sūrah attaches to its blessings at 7:96.
verses.162:
> But the wrongdoers among them changed the words they were commanded to say. So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their wrongdoing

**"They Changed the Words They Were Commanded to Say"**

*Fa-baddala alladhīna ẓalamū minhum qawlan ghayra alladhī qīla lahum fa-arsalnā ʿalayhim rijzan mina al-samāʾi bimā kānū yaẓlimūn* — but the wrongdoers among them changed the words they were commanded to say. So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their wrongdoing.

The Qur'an's accusations against the People of the Book concentrate on this kind of alteration. *“Some Jews take words out of context and say, ‘We listen and we disobey’”* (4:46). *“They distorted the words of the Scripture and neglected a portion of what they had been commanded to uphold”* (5:13); *“There are some among them who distort the Book with their tongues to make you think this ˹distortion˺ is from the Book — but it is not what the Book says”* (3:78). The sūrah's verse is the first entry in that dossier.

**The Formula They Were Given**

The verse's phrase *the wrongdoers among them* repeats the sūrah's persistent care not to condemn a whole community for the acts of its members. The sentence immediately before it had reported a righteous group within the people of Moses (7:159) and a multiplied reward for the good-doers (7:161), and the Book's verdict here falls on the specific agents of the change.

**The Punishment From the Heavens**

*Rijz mina al-samāʾ* — a punishment from the heaven — is the Book's term for the affliction that came upon the Israelites in the wilderness, and the same word appears in the sūrah's account of the plagues of Egypt (7:134's *al-rijz*). The Qur'an's narratives of Israel and Egypt share the vocabulary because they share the diagnosis: a community that alters what it has been given is answered from above.

*Bimā kānū yaẓlimūn* — for the wrongdoing they persisted in — the imperfect verb marks a practice rather than an incident. The sūrah's earlier verse about the wilderness generation had said the same thing in almost the same words (7:160's *they wronged themselves*), and the Book's reading of the community's history is that the failures were habitual.

Sūrat al-Baqarah reports the substitution and its consequence in one verse: *“But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say. So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their rebelliousness”* (2:59). The two sūrahs give the same sentence, which is the Book's way of fixing the event in the community's memory as a warning rather than a curiosity.

**Two Kinds of Alteration**

The tradition distinguishes two operations on a revealed word, and the Book uses a different verb for each. One is distortion of the sense while the text stands: *“though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it?”* (2:75). The other is displacement, the moving of a word from the place it was given: *“Some Jews take words out of context”* (4:46). This verse reports a third, the plainest of the three — the substitution of a different word for the one that had been commanded.

The three are worth holding together because they describe a descending order of difficulty. Substitution is the easiest to detect and the hardest to defend; displacement is subtler, since the words remain and their arrangement is changed; distortion of the sense is the subtlest of all, because nothing visible has been touched.
verses.163:
> Ask them ˹O Prophet˺ about ˹the people of˺ the town which was by the sea, who broke the Sabbath. During the Sabbath, ˹abundant˺ fish would come to them clearly visible, but on other days the fish were never seen. In this way We tested them for their rebelliousness

**"Ask Them About the Town by the Sea"**

*Wa-sʾalhum ʿani al-qaryati allatī kānat ḥāḍirata al-baḥri idh yaʿdūna fī al-sabti idh taʾtīhim ḥītānuhum yawma sabtihim shurraʿan wa-yawma lā yasbitūna lā taʾtīhim kadhālika nablūhum bimā kānū yafsuqūn* — ask them ˹O Prophet˺ about ˹the people of˺ the town which was by the sea, who broke the Sabbath. During the Sabbath, ˹abundant˺ fish would come to them clearly visible, but on other days the fish were never seen. In this way We tested them for their rebelliousness.

*Wa-sʾalhum* — ask them — addresses the Prophet and turns the sūrah's narrative into an interrogation of the People given the Book, standing in front of him. The Qur'an uses the same device elsewhere when it asks the Prophet to consult the People of the Book about what their scriptures contain, and the story about to be told is deliberately one the addressed community already knows.

**The Test Named Explicitly**

The Book's teaching about the Sabbath appears in several places: it was a sign for a people who disputed, and the Qur'an's own verse in Sūrat al-Naḥl says *“˹Honouring˺ the Sabbath was ordained only for those who disputed about Abraham”* (16:124). Israel's obligations here are treated as a specific charge laid on a specific community, and the sūrah's account of its violation is presented as an affair between that community and its Lord.

**The Charge in the Other Accounts**

Sūrat al-Baqarah reports the episode and its sentence: *“You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, ‘Be disgraced apes!’”* (2:65), and Sūrat al-Nisāʾ includes the Sabbath breach in its account of the covenant's violation (4:154–155). What is being recited, then, is a story their own scriptures and the Qur'an share.

The fish arrived on the day when fishing was forbidden and vanished on the days when it was permitted, which put the community's obedience on a permanent knife-edge. The Book's presentation of the test exposes the character of legalistic evasion: the community had the letter of a prohibition and immediately looked for a way around its intent, and the sūrah's narrative treats the innovation as rebellion rather than cleverness.

*Yafsuqūn* — the same word the sūrah has used for those who broke their covenants (7:102) and for the wicked of Egypt (7:133) — closes the verse. The Book's moral vocabulary is consistent across its narratives: transgression is a departure from a commitment, and the sabbath-breakers had a covenant that made their cleverness a violation.

**The Device, and the Ruling It Occasioned**

The ruling drawn from it is that a device does not make lawful what the law forbade, because the law addresses the outcome as well as the form. The sūrah supplies the consequence in the verses that follow, and the Book supplies it earlier, recalling the same people and reporting the sentence spoken over them: *“Be disgraced apes!”* (2:65). The two accounts differ in what they report and agree in what they judge: the transgression was in the arrangement, and the arrangement was not a defence.
verses.164:
> When some of ˹the righteous among˺ them questioned ˹their fellow Sabbath-keepers˺, “Why do you ˹bother to˺ warn those ˹Sabbath-breakers˺ who will either be destroyed or severely punished by Allah?” They replied, “Just to be free from your Lord’s blame, and so perhaps they may abstain.”

**"Why Do You Warn a People Whom Allah Will Destroy?"**

*Wa-idh qālat ummatun minhum lima taʿiẓūna qawman Allāhu muhlikuhum aw muʿadhdhibuhum ʿadhāban shadīdan qālū maʿdhiratan ilā rabbikum wa-laʿallahum yattaqūn* — when some of ˹the righteous among˺ them questioned ˹their fellow Sabbath-keepers˺: "Why do you ˹bother to˺ warn those ˹Sabbath-breakers˺ who will either be destroyed or severely punished by Allah?" (7:164) They replied: "Just to be free from your Lord's blame, and so perhaps they may abstain." (7:164)

**The Qur'an's Insistence on Warning**

The Book repeatedly makes warning a communal obligation. *“Let there be a group among you who call ˹others˺ to goodness, encourage what is good. Forbid what is evil — it is they who will be successful”* (3:104). The believers are described as those who “encourage good and forbid evil” (9:112, 3:114); and the Qur'an's criticism of the People of the Book includes the failure to forbid one another: *“They did not forbid one another from doing evil. Evil indeed was what they did!”* (5:79). Sūrat al-Baqarah states the duty's inner contradiction in an address to the community: *“Do you preach righteousness and fail to practice it yourselves, although you read the Scripture? Do you not understand?”* (2:44), and Sūrat al-Ṣaff's warning is even sharper: *“O believers! Why do you say what you do not do? How despicable it is in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do!”* (61:2–3).

**An Excuse Before Allah: The Word for the Discharge**

The warners’ answer contains the word *maʿdhira*, rendered here as *“Just to be free from your Lord’s blame”* (7:164), from the root *ʿ-dh-r*, which gives *ʿudhr* (an excuse, a plea that removes blame) and *maʿdhira* (the plea itself, or the act of offering it). The commentators read the noun in two ways: as an excuse offered to God for having warned a people whose outcome is fixed, and as an admonition offered to the warned.

An-Nisāʾ states the principle that makes the answer necessary: *“˹All were˺ messengers delivering good news and warnings so humanity should have no excuse before Allah after ˹the coming of˺ the messengers. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”* (4:165)

Read with 4:165 the warners’ answer is not a hedge but a statement of the office. The warning is given so that no plea remains — for the warned, who will have been told, and for the warners, who will have discharged what was asked of them.

**Delivery Is the Duty, and the Judgment Is Not**

The separation is what makes 7:164 an answer rather than a resignation. If delivery is the duty, then a delivery made to people who will be destroyed is a complete performance and not a wasted one. The warners’ second clause — *“and so perhaps they may abstain.”* (7:164) — is then not the ground of the duty but a hope attached to it, which is why it is introduced by *laʿalla* rather than by a promise.

The sūrah states the same structure elsewhere without the dialogue. Its messengers are told that their office is delivery (7:93), that the reckoning belongs to God (7:7), and that the outcome of the towns is already written (7:34). 13:40 gathers these into one sentence, and 7:164 shows a group of ordinary believers inside a town reasoning their way to it.
verses.165:
> When they ignored the warning they were given, We rescued those who used to warn against evil and overtook the wrongdoers with a dreadful punishment for their rebelliousness

**The Reason the Punishment Gives**

The same practice governs the timing. *“Your Lord would never destroy a society until He had sent to its capital a messenger, reciting Our revelations to them. Nor would We ever destroy a society unless its people persisted in wrongdoing.”* (28:59). Read with verse 165, the two statements give the sūrah’s whole account of judgment: a messenger sent and reciting, a warning given and ignored, a departure persisted in, and then a punishment whose description names the departure as its cause. Nothing in the sequence is arbitrary, and the rescue of the warners is its other half — the one group that spoke when speaking had stopped being useful.

**"When They Ignored the Warning"**

*Nasū mā dhukkirū bihi* — the verb the sūrah uses is forgetting. The Book's use of it for the rejection of reminders is a consistent theme: the sūrah's own charge against the Sabbath-breakers is *being heedless of them* (7:136's clause about the Egyptians), and the Qur'an's warnings about forgetting the reminder recur throughout. The verse's grammar marks a settled refusal rather than a single lapse.

*Anjaynā alladhīna yanhawna ʿani al-sūʾ* — We rescued those who used to forbid evil. The Book's narratives of destroyed towns frequently report a saved party, and the pattern is by now familiar: Lot's household was brought out of the doomed town (11:81), and this sūrah has already said that a group among the people of Moses guided with truth (7:159).

**The Punishment's Word**

*Bi-ʿadhābin baʾīs* — a dreadful, miserable punishment — and the closing clause, *bimā kānū yafsuqūn*, for their rebelliousness. The sūrah's diagnosis has not changed since the town was introduced: the offense is transgression against a covenant, and the punishment is named as the consequence of the same conduct the fish were sent to test (7:163).

The verse does not describe the warners' reward beyond rescue, and the Book's restraint here is characteristic. Its narratives of the saved frequently leave their future undescribed, and the Qur'an's promises for those who command good are stated elsewhere: the community that calls to goodness is described as successful (3:104), and the sūrah's own promise of multiplied reward for the good-doers (7:161) covers the same ground.

The Qur'an frequently describes a community's destruction in terms that exempt a party: Noah's family and the believers with him, Lot's household, the people of Jonah, and here the warners of the town by the sea. The pattern is one of the Book's most consistent narrative features, and it serves the doctrine that judgment in the Qur'an is individual even when it arrives collectively.

**The Third Group, and the Question They Put**

The verse cannot be read without the one before it, which introduces a third party in the town: those who asked the warners why they were addressing people already marked for destruction — *“Why do you ˹bother to˺ warn those ˹Sabbath-breakers˺ who will either be destroyed or severely punished by Allah?”* (7:164). The warners answer with two motives, an excuse before God and the hope that the warned might become mindful, and the sūrah then reports an outcome for two groups only: those who warned were rescued, and the wrongdoers were overtaken.
verses.166:
> But when they stubbornly persisted in violation, We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”

**"Be Disgraced Apes"**

*Fa-lammā ʿataw ʿan mā nuhū ʿanhu qulnā lahum kūnū qiradatan khāsiʾīn* — but when they stubbornly persisted in violation, We said to them: "Be disgraced apes!" (7:166)

Sūrat al-Baqarah reports it identically: *“You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, ‘Be disgraced apes!’”* (2:65). Sūrat al-Māʾidah's catalogue of the cursed among the Children of Israel names those who incurred condemnation and were turned into apes and pigs (5:60), and Sūrat al-Baqarah's next verse states the purpose: *“So We made their fate an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing”* (2:66).

**The Charge of Persistence**

*Fa-lammā ʿataw ʿan mā nuhū ʿanhu* — when they persisted in what they were forbidden. The Book's word *ʿataw* is obstinacy, and the verse's opening clause establishes that every stage before the verdict had been completed: the law, the temptation, the warnings, the argument, and the refusal. The punishment is not the response to a surprise offense but to a settled course.

Sūrat al-Baqarah's commentary names the purpose of the punishment in words the sūrah's readers are meant to carry: an example to those present and those after them, and a lesson to the God-fearing (2:66). The Book's narratives of destroyed towns all serve that function in the sūrah, and the metamorphosis is its most vivid instance.

**The Meaning of the Curse**

The Qur'an's other reference to the transformation places it inside a catalogue of the condemned: *“Say, ˹O Prophet˺, ‘Shall I inform you of those who deserve a worse punishment from Allah ˹than the rebellious˺? It is those who earned Allah's condemnation and displeasure—some being reduced to apes and pigs and worshippers of false gods. These are far worse in rank and farther astray from the Right Way.’”* (5:60). The Book's formulation there and here treats the punishment as the visible form of a condition the community had already chosen.

The verse closes the account of the town by the sea with the same word the sūrah has used for the wicked of Egypt (7:133's *mujrimīn*) and for the offenders at the gate (7:162's *yaẓlimūn*). The Book's moral vocabulary in this sūrah is deliberately repetitive, and the sabbath-breakers are filed in the same drawer as the other communities whose conduct had made judgment necessary.

**The Contrast With Mercy**

The sūrah's closing verses return to the widest language of mercy — the names of God, the group that guides with truth (7:180–181), and the call to seek refuge (7:200) — and the metamorphosis of verse 166 stands inside that context. The Book's arrangement of judgment and mercy in a single sūrah is its standing method, and the reader of this passage is given both accounts of the same community.

**The Grammar of the Decree**

The sentence spoken over the transgressors is an imperative addressed to bodies: be apes, disgraced. The same construction is the Book’s word for creation — God is the originator of the heavens and the earth, and *“When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it”* (2:117), and it is — and the commentators note that a command in this form does not request but effects. What is told to be a thing is by this made that thing.
verses.167:
> And ˹remember, O Prophet,˺ when your Lord declared that He would send against them others who would make them suffer terribly until the Day of Judgment. Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, but He is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**"He Would Send Against Them Others Until the Day of Judgment"**

*Wa-idh taʾadhana rabbuka la-yabʿathanna ʿalayhim ilā yawmi al-qiyāmati man yasūmuhum sūʾa al-ʿadhābi inna rabbaka la-sarīʿu al-ʿiqābi wa-innahu la-ghafūrun raḥīm* — and ˹remember, O Prophet,˺ when your Lord declared that He would send against them others who would make them suffer terribly until the Day of Judgment. Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, but He is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

*Taʾadhana* — the Book's verb for a solemn announcement — opens a sentence that runs to the end of history. The verse is the sūrah's account of a decree binding on the people of Israel until the Day of Judgment, and its placement after the punishment of the town by the sea extends the narrative's scope from a single community to a people's political fate.

Sūrat al-Isrāʾ gives the decree its historical form: *“And We warned the Children of Israel in the Scripture, ‘You will certainly cause corruption in the land twice. You will become extremely arrogant’”* (17:4), followed by the account of the two visitations — the servants of great might who ravaged their homes (17:5), the restoration of their power after repentance (17:6), and the second warning with its consequences (17:7). The sūrah's verse is the same decree stated as a permanent condition.

**Dispersion as the Decree's Shape**

The next verse reports the consequence: *“We dispersed them through the land in groups”* (7:168). The tradition read the two verses together as the Qur'an's account of Israel's exile and continuing subjection, and the Book's own narrative of the people from this point is a narrative of communities scattered among nations rather than a kingdom with a capital.

The sūrah's readers have met the theme before: the Qur'an says of the Children of Israel that they were struck with disgrace and drew wrath upon themselves (2:61). Sūrat Āl ʿImrān's account of their condition — *“They will be stricken with disgrace wherever they go, unless they are protected by a covenant with Allah or a treaty with the people”* (3:112) — states the same law and adds its exception.

**Swift in Punishment, Forgiving and Merciful**

The verse closes with the Book's paired names, and the pairing is the sūrah's own refrain for the destruction narratives: *swift in punishment* and *All-Forgiving, Most Merciful*. The Qur'an places the two attributes side by side in this way repeatedly — *“Inform My servants ˹O Prophet˺ that I am truly the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful, and that My torment is indeed the most painful”* (15:49–50) — and the sūrah declines to leave either attribute alone with the reader.

The sūrah's following verses report the generations who inherited the Scripture, seized unlawful gains, and claimed forgiveness (7:169), and they also report those who firmly abide by the Book (7:170).

**Swift in Punishment, and the Pair It Keeps**

The verse ends on a formula the Book repeats: your Lord is swift in punishment, and He is forgiving and merciful. The same pairing closes a statement about succession and testing: *“Surely your Lord is swift in punishment”* (6:165). Sūrah al-Raʿd puts the two halves under a different emphasis, answering those who ask for the torment to be hurried: *“Surely your Lord is full of forgiveness for people, despite their wrongdoing”* (13:6).
verses.168:
> We dispersed them through the land in groups—some were righteous, others were less so. We tested them with prosperity and adversity, so perhaps they would return ˹to the Right Path˺

**"We Dispersed Them Through the Land in Groups"**

*Wa-qaṭṭaʿnāhum fī al-arḍi umaman minhumu al-ṣāliḥūna wa-minhum dūna dhālika wa-balawnāhum bi-l-ḥasanāti wa-l-sayyiʾāti laʿallahum yarjiʿūn* — We dispersed them through the land in groups — some were righteous, others were less so. We tested them with prosperity and adversity, so perhaps they would return ˹to the Right Path˺.

*Qaṭṭaʿnāhum fī al-arḍi umaman* — the verb is the same one the sūrah used for the division into tribes (7:160), and its repetition here marks a change of scale: the community is now scattered among nations rather than settled as a single people. The Qur'an's account of Israel's history after the kingdom is a history of communities, and the verse states it as the consequence of the decree in the previous sentence.

The Book's insistence on the mixed character of Israel appears here again, and it has accompanied every stage of the narrative: the group that guides with truth (7:159), the wrongdoers who changed the words (7:162), the warners and their questioners (7:164), and now the dispersed communities.

*Wa-balawnāhum bi-l-ḥasanāti wa-l-sayyiʾāt* — We tested them with good and evil. The sūrah has stated this law in general terms earlier in the same narrative — *“We afflicted its ˹disbelieving˺ people with suffering and adversity, so perhaps they would be humbled”* (7:94), and the exchange of hardship for prosperity that followed (7:95) — and the verse applies it to the scattered people. The Book's doctrine of history is a doctrine of examination.

**The Purpose Clause**

*Laʿallahum yarjiʿūn* — so perhaps they would return. The sūrah's uses of the same clause cluster around its narratives of punishment and provision (7:130, 7:174), and the Book's grammar keeps the outcome open. The verse does not say the test succeeded or failed; it states the intent, and the sūrah's following verses supply the record.

The Book states the laws of communal rise and fall in several sūrahs: *“Indeed, Allah would never change a people's state ˹of favour˺ until they change their own state ˹of faith˺”* (13:11); *“Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your own hands have committed. And He pardons much”* (42:30); *“Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people's hands have done”* (30:41). The sūrah's verse is that doctrine in narrative form.

**Succession and Its Conditions**

The Qur'an's statements about the inheritance of the earth attach it to conduct: *“He is the One Who has placed you as successors on earth and elevated some of you in rank over others. He may test you with what He has given you”* (6:165); *“Then We made you their successors in the land to see how you would act”* (10:14); *“My righteous servants shall inherit the land”* (21:105). The sūrah's readers are told that Israel's dispersion is the reverse image of the same law.

**The Remnant Within the Dispersed People**

The Book's use of prosperity as a test is as prominent as its use of adversity, and the sūrah's readers have already watched Egypt misread its good fortune as a verdict on its own merit (7:131). The dispersion's test comprises both conditions, and the Qur'an's statements about wealth and ease as dangers belong to the same teaching.
verses.169:
> Then they were succeeded by other generations who inherited the Scripture. They indulged in unlawful gains, claiming, “We will be forgiven ˹after all˺.” And if similar gain came their way, they would seize it. Was a covenant not taken from them in the Scripture that they would not say anything about Allah except the truth? And they were already well-versed in its teachings. But the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter is far better for those mindful ˹of Allah˺. Will you not then understand

**"Generations Who Inherited the Scripture"**

*Fa-khalafa min baʿdihim khalfun warithū al-kitāba yaʾkhudhūna ʿaraḍa hādhā al-adnā wa-yaqūlūna sa-yughfaru lanā wa-in yaʾtihim ʿaraḍun mithluhu yaʾkhudhūhu a-lam yuʾkhadh ʿalayhim mīthāqu al-kitābi a lā yaqūlū ʿalā Allāhi illā al-ḥaqqa wa-darasū mā fīhi wa-l-dāru al-ākhiratu khayrun li-lladhīna yattaqūn* — then they were succeeded by other generations who inherited the Scripture. They indulged in unlawful gains, claiming: "We will be forgiven." (7:169) And if similar gain came their way, they would seize it. Was a covenant not taken from them in the Scripture that they would not say anything about Allah except the truth? And they were already well-versed in its teachings. But the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter is far better for those mindful ˹of Allah˺.

*Khalafa min baʿdihim khalfun warithū al-kitāba* — the Book's word for a successor generation is used elsewhere for the heirs of a land (7:100) and for the generations that came after the messengers. The verse's subject is therefore not a break in transmission but a decay within it: the Scripture was inherited, read, and taught, and the life around it was arranged differently.

*Yaʾkhudhūna ʿaraḍa hādhā al-adnā* — they indulged in unlawful gains: the passing goods of this lower world. The Qur'an uses the phrase for what the earlier communities traded their covenants for, and the Book's accusations against them are consistently financial in this sūrah: Madyan's scales (7:85), the town's fish (7:163), and now the inherited Book's revenue.

**The Covenant About Speech**

*An lā yaqūlū ʿalā Allāhi illā al-ḥaqqa* — that they would not say about Allah anything but the truth. The Book's covenant passages include this clause among their terms, and the sūrah's readers have already met the offense in its narrative form: the substitution of the words at the gate (7:162) and the distortion of the Scripture with the tongue (3:78).

*Wa-darasū mā fīhi* — they studied what was in it. Sūrat al-Baqarah's reproach to those who preach righteousness and do not practice it uses the same move (2:44).

**The Rulers Who Looked Away**

The sūrah's account is completed by Sūrat al-Māʾidah's parallel charge, which names the scholars' silence: *“You see many of them racing toward sin, transgression, and consumption of forbidden gain. Evil indeed is their inaction!”* (5:62–63).

The next verse answers the record of the generations with a statement about those who hold fast to the Book: *“As for those who firmly abide by the Scripture and establish prayer — surely We never discount the reward of those acting righteously”* (7:170).

**Desires Made Appealing**

The commentators read 3:14 as the explanation of how an inherited Scripture is traded. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the appeal is what makes the trade seem reasonable, and that the claim of forgiveness recorded at 7:169 is the reasoning of a person who has already made it.

The Book's condemnations of the People of the Book include this expectation in almost the same words: *“˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, ‘The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days’”* (2:80). *“This is because they say, ‘The Fire will not touch us except for a few days.’ They have been deceived in their faith by their wishful lying”* (3:24).

The Qur'an's condemnation of this commerce is stated in its sharpest form in Sūrat al-Baqarah: *“So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, ‘This is from Allah’ — seeking a fleeting gain! So woe to them for what their hands have written and woe to them for what they have earned”* (2:79).

Sūrat al-Baqarah states the consequence with the same vocabulary: *“Indeed, those who hide Allah's revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them; and they will suffer a painful punishment”* (2:174).

Al-Māʾidah describes what the Scripture was: *“Indeed, We revealed the Torah, containing guidance and light, by which the prophets, who submitted themselves to Allah, made judgments for Jews.”* (5:44).
verses.170:
> As for those who firmly abide by the Scripture and establish prayer—surely We never discount the reward of those acting righteously

**"We Never Discount the Reward"**

*Innā lā nuḍīʿu ajra al-muṣliḥīn* — the sentence is a divine guarantee in the form of a negative, and the Book states it repeatedly: *“As for those who believe and do good, We certainly never deny the reward of those who are best in deeds”* (18:30). The qualifications of lineage and history do not enter the accounting, and the reward follows the conduct.

The verse's final noun, *al-muṣliḥīn* — those who act rightly, who put things right — echoes the sūrah's earlier use of the same root in Moses' charge to Aaron: *do what is right, and do not follow the way of the corruptors* (7:142). The Book's vocabulary pairs reform with corruption throughout, and the verse identifies the faithful among the People of the Book with the first of the two. The Qur'an's statements of reward are stated in deeds rather than identity: *“But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good will have their reward with their Lord”* (2:112). *“But those who do good — whether male or female — and have faith will enter Paradise and will never be wronged ˹even as much as˺ the speck on a date stone”* (4:124); *“Indeed, those who believe, do good, establish prayer. Pay alms-tax will receive their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve”* (2:277).

**Hold Firmly to the Rope**

The verse describes a group by two acts: holding firmly to the Scripture and establishing prayer. Āl ʿImrān commands the first act in the same terms: *“And hold firmly to the rope of Allah and do not be divided.”* (3:103). The verb is the same — *iʿtaṣama*, form VIII of *ʿ-ṣ-m*, to take hold of something for protection.

The two verses differ in what is held. 3:103 names a rope, which the commentators read as the Book, the covenant, or the community itself; 7:170 names the Scripture directly. Both attach a second term to the holding: 3:103 forbids division, and 7:170 adds the establishing of prayer.

**The Generation Before**

The verse that precedes this one describes the alternative: *“Then they were succeeded by other generations who inherited the Scripture. They indulged in unlawful gains”* (7:169), claiming that they would be forgiven after all. The verse then asks whether a covenant had not been taken from them that they would say nothing about Allah except the truth.

The comparison is the verse’s argument. Inheritance of a book is not the same as holding firmly to it, and the claim of forgiveness in 7:169 is precisely the claim 7:170 answers by describing what the reward is given for. The one group inherits and takes; the other holds and establishes.

The Qur'an's description of those who truly believe in the Book is stated with the same idea: *“Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it”* (2:121).
verses.171:
