> And ˹remember˺ when We raised the mountain over them as if it were a cloud and they thought it would fall on them. ˹We said,˺ “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”

**"We Raised the Mountain Over Them"**

*Wa-idh nataqnā al-jabala fawqahum ka-annahu ẓullatun wa-ẓannū annahu wāqiʿun bihim khudhū mā ātaynākum bi-quwwatin wa-dhkurū mā fīhi laʿallakum tattaqūn* — and ˹remember˺ when We raised the mountain over them as if it were a cloud and they thought it would fall on them. ˹We said,˺ "Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺." (7:171)

The mountain is described as a *ẓullah* — a canopy, a shade — and the people's assumption is that it is about to fall. The Book's narrative of the covenant at Sinai uses the image of the mountain's suspension in several places. Sūrat al-Baqarah's account is the most compact: *“And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, ‘Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you’”* (2:63).

**The Same Scene in the Other Covenant Accounts**

Sūrat al-Baqarah's second account adds the community's answer: *“they answered, ‘We hear and disobey’”* (2:93). Sūrat al-Nisāʾ reports the same event as a warning attached to the breaking of the covenant: *“We raised the Mount over them ˹as a warning˺ for ˹breaking˺ their covenant and said, ‘Enter the gate ˹of Jerusalem˺ with humility’”* (4:154). The sūrah's readers are therefore hearing a scene their own Book reports three times, each with a different emphasis.

The Book does not present the raised mountain as a threat for its own sake; it presents it as the visible form of the covenant's weight. The sūrah's earlier account of the same mountain had described Moses' request to see God and the leveling of the peak to dust (7:143). The Qur'an's use of the mountain as an image of awe runs through its revelation theology — *“Had We sent down this Quran upon a mountain, you would have certainly seen it humbled and torn apart in awe of Allah”* (59:21).

**The Command Repeated**

*Khudhū mā ātaynākum bi-quwwatin* — hold firmly to what We have given you — the same charge given to Moses on the mountain (7:144–145) is now given to the community. The Book's language of reception is consistent: what is revealed is to be grasped, and the grasping is a matter of strength rather than sentiment.

*Wa-dhkurū mā fīhi* — remember what is in it — the command the sūrah's Israel has been failing since the narrative began. The Book's repeated charge to the People of the Book about remembering the covenant appears in Sūrat al-Māʾidah with the community's own formula of acceptance: *“Remember Allah's favour upon you and the covenant He made with you when you said, ‘We hear and obey’”* (5:7).

*Laʿallakum tattaqūn* — so that you may become mindful. The sūrah has used the same clause for the towns' testing (7:94's *humbled*), for the plagues of Egypt (7:130), and for the dispersion of Israel (7:168). Its repetition in this verse closes the sūrah's account of the covenant with the same stated purpose: the entire sequence of signs, gifts, warnings, and punishments exists so that a community might become mindful.

**The Word for Canopy, and Its Other Appearances**

The mountain is likened to a *ẓullah* — a canopy, a thing that shades — and the word is used elsewhere in the Book of both a protection and a punishment. God shaded Israel in the wilderness: *“And ˹remember when˺ We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quails”* (2:57). Paradise is described by a shade that does not end: *“eternal is its fruit as well as its shade”* (13:35). The same word names the destruction that overtook Shuʿayb’s people, in the story this sūrah has just told: *“So they rejected him, and ˹so˺ were overtaken by the torment of the day of the ˹deadly˺ cloud.”* (26:189).
verses.172:
> And ˹remember˺ when your Lord brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam their descendants and had them testify regarding themselves. ˹Allah asked,˺ “Am I not your Lord?” They replied, “Yes, You are! We testify.” ˹He cautioned,˺ “Now you have no right to say on Judgment Day, ‘We were not aware of this.’

**"Am I Not Your Lord?"**

*Wa-idh akhadha rabbuka min banī Ādama min ẓuhūrihim dhurriyyatahum wa-ashhadahum ʿalā anfusihim a-lastu bi-rabbikum qālū balā shahidnā a taqūlū yawma al-qiyāmati innā kunnā ʿan hādhā ghāfilīn* — and ˹remember˺ when your Lord brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam their descendants and had them testify about themselves. ˹Allah asked,˺ "Am I not your Lord?" (7:172) They replied: "Yes, You are! We testify." (7:172) ˹He cautioned,˺ "Now you have no right to say on Judgment Day, 'We were not aware of this.'" (7:172)

**The Self as Witness**

*An taqūlū yawma al-qiyāmati innā kunnā ʿan hādhā ghāfilīn* — so that you cannot say on the Day of Judgment: we were unaware of this. The clause states the doctrine's function, and the sūrah's next verse completes it with the second excuse to be prevented: that the ancestors had associated others with God and the descendants merely followed (7:173). The Book closes both doors in advance.

**The Book's Appeal to Universal Knowledge**

The Qur'an appeals to the same knowledge elsewhere: *“Did I not command you, O Children of Adam, not to follow Satan, for he is truly your sworn enemy, but to worship Me ˹alone˺? This is the Straight Path”* (36:60–61), and the Book's address to an ungrateful humanity assumes a knowledge it should not need to be told again. The verse in this sūrah is the doctrinal ground for that assumption.

The Book's whole doctrine of accountability rests on capacity, and this verse establishes the capacity at the most basic level. The Qur'an's statements that no soul is burdened beyond its strength (2:286) and that no one will be wronged (4:40) belong with the primordial testimony: the creature cannot plead that it was never given the means to know.

The Book's account of Iblīs's refusal states the principle from the opposite side when the devil admits that he will not be able to mislead God's chosen servants (15:39–40). The Qur'an's narratives consistently present the human being as capable of both directions, and the covenant of the loins is the Book's statement that the capacity for the first is native.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Structure**

The sūrah's narrative has moved from the creation of Adam and the refusal of Iblīs (7:11–18) through the history of the messengers, the towns, Egypt, and Israel. The covenant of verse 172 returns to the human being at the root, and the sūrah's later verses — the parable of the dog, the names of God, and the closing instructions about the Qur'an and remembrance — address the community on that foundation.

**The Disposition the Covenant Presupposes**

The Book describes what this verse narrates as an original condition rather than as an event left behind. Sūrah al-Rūm: *“So be steadfast in faith in all uprightness ˹O Prophet˺—the natural Way of Allah which He has instilled in ˹all˺ people. Let there be no change in this creation of Allah. That is the Straight Way, but most people do not know.”* (30:30). The phrase *let there be no change in this creation* is the same prohibition the covenant in al-Aʿrāf makes unnecessary to argue for: what was taken from the descendants of Adam is what they were made with.
verses.173:
> Nor say, ‘It was our forefathers who had associated others ˹with Allah in worship˺ and we, as their descendants, followed in their footsteps. Will you then destroy us for the falsehood they invented?’”

**"It Was Our Forefathers Who Associated Others"**

*Aw taqūlū innamā ashraka ābāʾunā min qablu wa-kunnā dhurriyyatan min baʿdihim a-fatuhlikunā bimā faʿala al-mubṭilūn* — nor say: "It was our forefathers who had associated others ˹with Allah in worship˺ and we, as their descendants, followed in their footsteps. Will you then destroy us for the falsehood they invented?" (7:173)

**The Argument the Qur'an Meets Everywhere**

The plea of inherited practice is the Qur'an's most frequently answered objection. *“When it is said to them, ‘Follow what Allah has revealed,’ they reply, ‘No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing’”* (2:170); *“What we found our forefathers practicing is good enough for us”* (5:104); *“We found our forefathers following a ˹particular˺ way, and we are following in their footsteps”* (43:22). The sūrah's verse states the argument in its most vulnerable form: the plea of people who admit the error and plead the precedent.

The Qur'an's most sustained demolition of the argument is placed on Abraham's lips: *“Have you ˹really˺ considered what you have been worshipping — you and your ancestors? They are ˹all˺ enemies to me, except the Lord of all worlds”* (26:75–77), and his summary verdict on the people and their forefathers: *“Indeed, you and your forefathers have been clearly astray”* (21:54). The same logic governed the catalogue of the patriarchs' faith a few verses earlier.

**The Descendants and Their Own Acts**

The Book's doctrine of individual responsibility is stated in the sūrah's own earlier narratives — no soul bears another's burden (6:164's clause) — and in the Qur'an's address to the descendants of Israel: *“That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done”* (2:134). The verse's implicit answer to *will You destroy us for what they invented* is that the descendants are not being destroyed for their fathers' deeds but for their own.

**No Soul Bears Another’s Burden**

The Book answers that question with a rule stated repeatedly: *“No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another.”* (6:164). The rule is not a concession to the excuse-makers; it is the ground on which their excuse fails.

For the rule cuts both ways, and the verse’s speakers use only one half of it. If no soul bears another’s burden, then the ancestors’ association is not transferred to their descendants — which is what the excuse claims. But the same rule means that whatever the descendants themselves did is theirs, and the act the excuse describes is the act of following. The verse says so in its own words: *“we, as their descendants, followed in their footsteps.”* (7:173). Following is an act, and under 6:164 it is carried by the one who follows.

**The Formula at 34:25**

The sūrah’s answer is put in the mouth of the Prophet at another point in the Book: *“Say, ‘You will not be accountable for our misdeeds, nor will we be accountable for your deeds.’”* (34:25). The formula separates two parties and assigns each its own account. It is the same structure as 6:164 stated as an address rather than a rule.

The verse therefore closes the covenant argument the sūrah began at 7:172.
verses.174:
> This is how We make our signs clear, so perhaps they will return ˹to the Right Path˺

**"This Is How We Make Our Signs Clear"**

*Wa-kadhālika nufaṣṣilu al-āyāti wa-laʿallahum yarjiʿūn* — this is how We make our signs clear, so perhaps they will return ˹to the Right Path˺.

*Nufaṣṣilu* — the Book's word for setting out in detail, distinguishing one thing from another — appears in the sūrah's account of the tablets as well: *commandments and explanations of all things* (7:145). The Qur'an's self-description is that of a text that separates and clarifies rather than one that leaves matters ambiguous, and the verse's use of the verb follows a passage that has distinguished the covenant of the loins from the excuse of ancestry.

The Book uses the formula repeatedly at the close of argumentative passages: *“This is how We make Our signs clear, so the way of the wicked may become distinct”* (6:55); *“That is your Lord's Path — perfectly straight. We have already made the signs clear to those who are mindful”* (6:126); *“We have certainly brought them a Book which We explained with knowledge — a guide and mercy for those who believe”* (7:52). The sūrah's own earlier verses used the same phrase, and the reader is meant to recognize it as a cadence.

**The Purpose: That They May Return**

*Laʿallahum yarjiʿūn* — so that they may return. The sūrah has used the same clause for the plagues of Egypt (7:130) and for the dispersion of Israel (7:168), and the Book's stated purpose for its signs is consistently remedial rather than merely informational. The Qur'an's God is described as making things clear to bring people back, not to convict them.

**Signs Varied and Aversion Increased**

The verse states the method: *“This is how We make our signs clear, so perhaps they will return ˹to the Right Path˺.”* (7:174). Al-Isrāʾ reports what the same method produced: *“We have surely varied ˹the signs˺ in this Quran so perhaps they may be mindful, but it only drives them farther away.”* (17:41).

The two verses share a purpose clause and differ in its outcome. 7:174 states the intention — return; 17:41 states the intention and then the result — remembrance tried, distance increased. The variation is the same in both: the signs are presented in more than one form so that no single form can be dismissed.

**Signs Made Clear So the Way Is Distinct**

The pair explains the sūrah’s procedure in the passage this verse closes. The covenant is described (7:172), the excuses are blocked (7:172–173), and the signs are detailed (7:174). What the detailing produces depends on the hearer, and 6:55 supplies the case 7:174 leaves open: for some, clarity is what makes their way visible as theirs.

This is the verse’s function as a hinge. It ends the covenant passage and precedes the example — a man given the signs who casts them off and is followed by Satan (7:175). The example is the case 6:55 describes, and the verse that introduces it is the method by which it became possible to see.

The parable of the man who was given the signs and abandoned them (7:175–176) is placed directly after this verse, and the arrangement is a further statement of the same purpose clause: the sign was clear, the man had it, and the choice was his.
verses.175:
> And relate to them ˹O Prophet˺ the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he abandoned them, so Satan took hold of him, and he became a deviant

**"Satan Took Hold of Him"**

*Fa-atbaʿahu al-shayṭānu* — the phrase describes pursuit and attachment, and the Book's accounts of the devil's work use the same vocabulary: whoever turns away from the Reminder finds a companion set for him (43:36). The verse presents the sequence in its actual order: the abandonment came first, and the attachment followed. The sūrah's narrative is careful about where agency lies.

The verse treats the signs as a possession that can be given and abandoned, and the Qur'an's instruction about revelation elsewhere is that it must be held firmly and conveyed (7:145, 7:171). The parable's man failed in both directions at once: he had the signs and neither kept them for himself nor delivered them to others.

**The Knowledge Without Practice**

The sūrah is full of figures who had knowledge and no practice: the generation who inherited the Scripture and traded it for gain (7:169), the scholars who did not forbid wrong (5:63), the inheritors of the Book who changed its words (7:162). The parable's man is the individual form of that collective portrait, and the Book tells his story to a community already familiar with the type.

**The Book's Parables of the Individual**

The Qur'an's parables of individuals are relatively few — the man of the two gardens (18:32–44), the owner of the vineyard (68:17–33), and this figure — and each of them concerns the same thing: the use of a gift in a life. The sūrah's readers are given one of the Book's most compact statements of that theme, and its outcome is stated in the next verse.

**The Word for Stripping Out**

The verb at the centre of the verse is *insalakha* — he stripped himself out of them — and the root *s-l-kh* is the word for taking a skin off an animal or a husk off a seed. The Book uses the same root of a cosmic stripping: *“There is also a sign for them in the night: We strip from it daylight, then —behold!—they are in darkness.”* (36:37).

**The Parallels the Book Draws for Knowledge Not Carried**

Two other passages give the same case a picture, and both are addressed to communities rather than to a single man. Of those who were given the Torah and did not carry it: *“The example of those who were entrusted with ˹observing˺ the Torah but failed to do so, is that of a donkey carrying books.”* (62:5). The image is precise — the load is carried, the load is worth carrying, and the carrier takes nothing from it. Of believers whose speech outran their conduct: *“O believers! Why do you say what you do not do?”* (61:2), *“How despicable it is in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do!”* (61:3).

**Three Candidates and Their Transmitters**

The identification the tradition debates has three candidates, and each comes with named transmitters rather than as a bare assertion. Balʿam b. Bāʿūrāʾ: Ibn Masʿūd, in a report ʿAbd ar-Razzāq recorded and Ibn Kathīr transmits under this verse; Ibn ʿAbbās through al-ʿAwfī, who places him in Yemen; ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥah, who describes a man in a city of tyrants who knew the Greatest Name; Mālik b. Dīnār, whose account has a scholar whose supplication was answered, sent to the king of Madyan and apostatising for his gifts; and Ibn Isḥāq, who makes him a man of Banū Kānān in ash-Shām. Umayyah b. Abī ṣ-Ṣalt: ʿAbdullāh b. ʿAmr and Zayd b. Aslem, describing a man who studied the scriptures, hoped to be the messenger, and envied Muḥammad ﷺ when the office went elsewhere. Sayfī b. Ar-Rāhib: Qatādah.

The sūrah's imagery of clothing had appeared earlier in the narrative of Adam's fall (7:26–27), where the garment of God-consciousness was named; here a man divests himself of revelation, and the Book's choice of the verb supplies the image.
verses.176:
> If We had willed, We would have elevated him with Our signs, but he clung to this life—following his evil desires. His example is that of a dog: if you chase it away, it pants, and if you leave it, it ˹still˺ pants. This is the example of the people who deny Our signs. So narrate ˹to them˺ stories ˹of the past˺, so perhaps they will reflect

**The Ability That Was Not Used**

*Wa-law shiʾnā la-rafaʿnāhu bihā* — the verse states what could have happened and did not. The Book's parallel constructions typically name God's capacity rather than a withheld decree, and the Qur'an's teaching about guidance is stated in the same register elsewhere: *“It is not for any soul to believe except by Allah's leave”* (10:100). The man's failure is not attributed to a deficiency in what he was given.

**"Following His Evil Desires"**

*Wa-ttabaʿa hawāhu* — the Book's term for desire as a ruling principle appears in sūrah after sūrah, and the Qur'an's warning about it is among its most frequent: *“Have you seen ˹O Prophet˺ those who have taken their own desires as their god? ˹And so˺ Allah left them to stray knowingly”* (45:23). The verse places the man in that category, and what is displayed is a knowledgeable person whose appetite set his course.

The simile's point is persistence without aim: the animal pants whether driven off or left alone, which is to say that its condition is unaffected by the treatment it receives. The Book uses animals as measures of human condition in several places — the donkey carrying books (62:5), the cattle that do not understand (25:44), and the dog in this verse — and each of them makes the same point about an incapacity that no external change can remedy.

**The Book's Attitude to Reflection**

The verb *yatafakkarūn* belongs to the Qur'an's moral anthropology: human beings are addressed as creatures capable of thinking their way to conclusions, and the Book's reproaches are aimed at those who have stopped. The sūrah's earlier verse about eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear (7:179, soon following) states the failure from the other side.

The Book's treatment of this man is one of the Qur'an's clearest statements that knowledge alone does not save, and the application is intended to be personal. The Qur'an's rebuke of the earlier communities for knowing and not acting uses the same logic, and Sūrat al-Baqarah's parable of the mosquito and what is even smaller (2:26) states the general principle that the Book's teachings sort people rather than inform them.

**The Root of Clinging**

The same word is used earlier in this sūrah of what the tempter offered, and the offer is the same one in both cases: *“O Adam! Shall I show you the Tree of Immortality and a kingdom that does not fade away?”* (20:120). The first man was promised a permanence he could not have and lost a place he had; the man of this verse was given signs he could have risen by and chose a permanence in the earth instead. The sūrah sets the two failures beside each other at a distance of a hundred and fifty verses, and both turn on the same word.

**This Life as the Book Describes It**

The object of the clinging is described elsewhere in terms that explain why it could not hold: *“The life of this world is just like rain We send down from the sky, producing a mixture of plants which humans and animals consume.”* (10:24). The parable continues to the point where the earth looks its best and its people believe they have command of it, and then to the command that reduces it to stubble.
verses.177:
> What an evil example of those who denied Our signs! They ˹only˺ wronged their own souls

**The Book's Sentences on the Deniers**

The Qur'an describes the condition of those who deny the signs in several registers: they are the losers whose works are void (18:103–105), they trade guidance for misguidance (2:16), and they will find no helper (3:177). The verse's formulation is the most compact of these and it belongs to the sūrah's own vocabulary of debt and loss.

The Book's reasoning about the self-inflicted nature of wrongdoing is grounded in its doctrine of God's self-sufficiency: *“Your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, Full of Mercy”* (6:133), and the Qur'an states explicitly that neither obedience nor disobedience adds anything to Him. The whole register of profit and loss in the Book therefore operates on the human side of the transaction.

**The Vocabulary of Loss in the Sūrah**

The theme of loss runs through the passage and the sūrah: the elites of the towns called their prophet's followers the losers (7:90), the calf-worshippers feared being among the losers (7:149), and the sūrah's later verse states the law that whoever God leaves to stray are the true losers (7:178). The verse's ending belongs to that chain, and its placement prepares the reader for the next verse's statement about guidance.

**The Example's Function in the Address**

The verse's severity is bounded by the sūrah's repeated statements that the door remains open: the signs are detailed so that people may return (7:174), the stories are told so that they may reflect (7:176), and the guidance of whoever God guides follows immediately (7:178). The Book's arrangement keeps judgment and possibility in view at once.

**The Verse in the Sequence**

The sūrah's narratives of destroyed towns served the same purpose, and the Book states the function explicitly elsewhere — *So We made their fate an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing* (2:66).

The Book's other statements of the doctrine use the same grammar — *Whoever does good, it is to their own benefit. And whoever does evil, it is to their own loss* (41:46) — and the two clauses of verse 177 are to be heard as a single verdict.

**The Example Set Down for Others**

The verse’s first clause calls the case an example, and the Book states the practice that makes examples of such cases: *“We have certainly set forth every ˹kind of˺ lesson for people in this Quran.”* (30:58). A case narrated in scripture is not a record kept for its own sake; it is a form others can be shown to fit.

That is the function of this verse at the end of its passage. The man’s story was told at length, with the parable of the dog attached to it, and the verdict then converts the narrative into a *mathal* — a thing to be compared against. The sūrah’s command to narrate the story (7:176) and its verdict on the story here are the two halves of one operation: tell it, then state what it is an example of. The clause naming the wronged souls completes the operation by telling the reader where to look when he compares — not at the man’s knowledge, which was real, but at what he did with it, which is the only part of the case that transfers.
verses.178:
> Whoever Allah guides is truly guided. And whoever He leaves to stray, they are the ˹true˺ losers

**"Whoever Allah Guides Is Truly Guided"**

*Man yahdi Allāhu fa-huwa al-muhtadī wa-man yuḍlil fa-ulāʾika humu al-khāsirūn* — whoever Allah guides is truly guided. And whoever He leaves to stray, they are the ˹true˺ losers.

The verse presents the sūrah's doctrine of guidance in a single pair of clauses, and it does so immediately after the parable of the man who lost the signs.

The sūrah states the law again in almost the same words a few verses later — *“Whoever Allah allows to stray, none can guide, leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance”* (7:186) — and the repetition frames the passage about the signs and the names of God.

**The Parallel Statements in the Qur'an**

The Book states the same doctrine in several sūrahs: *“Whoever Allah guides is truly guided. And whoever He leaves to stray, you will find no guardians for them besides Him”* (17:97); *“And whoever Allah guides, none can lead astray”* (39:37); *“And whoever Allah leaves to stray will have no guide after Him”* (42:44). The Qur'an's repeated insistence on the point makes it one of the load-bearing sentences of its theology.

The sentence does not remove human responsibility, and the sūrah's surrounding verses are the evidence: the same passage commands the Prophet to narrate the stories, warns the deniers, and instructs the Prophet to seek refuge with God (7:200). The Book's doctrine of divine guidance is stated in a text that addresses people as agents, and the two levels of the account are held together throughout the Qur'an.

**The Vocabulary of Loss**

*Al-khāsirūn* — the losers — is the sūrah's recurring term for those whose end is ruin. Its use here closes a sequence: the towns' elites called the believers losers (7:90), Madyan's people used the same word for Shuʿayb's followers (7:92's account), the calf-worshippers feared that they would be among the losers (7:149), and the verse now states who those losers actually are. The Book's irony in this sūrah is structural, and the term's migration is its clearest example.

The Qur'an's accounts of guidance present it as a gift that follows a person's own orientation: *“We turn their hearts and eyes away ˹from the truth˺ as they refused to believe at first”* (6:110), and the sūrah's earlier verse about turning away the arrogant (7:146) states the same law. The verse's first clause is so a promise rather than an arbitrary distribution.

**The Turn to the Signs of the Heedless**

The next verses describe those who have hearts that do not understand and eyes that do not see (7:179) and then name the remedy in the Beautiful Names of God (7:180). The verse's law is so immediately illustrated from the human side, and the reader is carried from the teaching about guidance to its visible effects and then to the invocation that belongs with it.

**Guidance in Its Two Senses**

The tradition distinguishes two things called guidance, and the distinction is what keeps this verse from being read as a statement about arbitrary favour. One is direction: the showing of a road, which the messengers perform and which the Book performs. The other makes the heart accept what has been shown, which the Book assigns to God alone: *“You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺, but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills, and He knows best who are ˹fit to be˺ guided.”* (28:56).
verses.179:
> Indeed, We have destined many jinn and humans for Hell. They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with. They are like cattle. In fact, they are even less guided! Such ˹people˺ are ˹entirely˺ heedless

**The Same Triple Elsewhere**

The Qur'an uses the formula in sūrah after sūrah: *“They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb. Blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺”* (2:18); *“Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered”* (2:7); and the account of those who listen to the recitation with veils over their hearts (6:25). The theme of the sealed heart is by now familiar from this sūrah (7:100–101, 7:146), and the verse states it as a description of a class.

*Dharaʾnā li-jahannama* — the Book's statement of the destination follows the same logic as its statements about guidance: the instrument is given, the use of it is what fixes the end, and the Qur'an describes the outcome as the purpose for which such people exist. The Book's other formulations of the doctrine use the same register — the sūrah's own statement that God guides whom He wills and leaves to stray whom He wills (7:178).

**"Like Cattle, Even Less Guided"**

*Ka-l-anʿāmi bal hum aḍallu* — the comparison to animals is one the Qur'an uses repeatedly: *“They are only like cattle — no, more than that, they are astray from the ˹Right˺ Way!”* (25:44). The point is not a contempt for animals but a contrast between an animal's perfect conformity to its nature and a human being's failure to conform to his. The animal cannot be anything other than what it is; the human being is the creature capable of turning away.

**The Word for Heedlessness**

*Al-ghāfilūn* — the heedless — closes the verse, and the sūrah has used the same term for the Egyptians who drowned (7:136) and for the audience of the signs. The Qur'an's diagnosis of heedlessness is not that people lack information but that they do not attend; the verse's list of idle faculties is the same charge in three parts.

**The Comparison to Cattle, Elsewhere**

The verse’s comparison is not unique to it, and the other occurrences show what is being claimed. Sūrah al-Furqān puts it as a question about the faculties: *“Or do you think that most of them listen or understand? They are only like cattle—no, more than that, they are astray from the ˹Right˺ Way!”* (25:44). Sūrah al-Jāthiyah describes the same state from the inside, as a sealing: *“˹And so˹ Allah left them to stray knowingly, sealed their hearing and hearts, and placed a cover on their sight. Who then can guide them after Allah?”* (45:23).

**The Verb of the First Clause**

The opening clause is usually rendered as a destination — We have destined for Hell many of the jinn and humankind — and the verb behind it, *dharaʾnā*, carries the sense of bringing forth in abundance or of scattering. The commentators read the clause accordingly: not that a number was fixed before any conduct occurred, but that many were brought forth toward that end, and the verse’s own next sentence explains the bringing by describing what the many do with their faculties.

The verse says *many*, not all, and the sūrah has just stated the scope of the other attribute: My mercy encompasses everything (7:156).
verses.180:
> Allah has the Most Beautiful Names. So call upon Him by them, and keep away from those who abuse His Names. They will be punished for what they used to do

**"To Him Belong the Most Beautiful Names"**

*Wa-li-llāhi al-asmāʾu al-ḥusnā fa-dʿūhu bihā wa-dharū alladhīna yulḥidūna fī asmāʾihi sa-yujzawna mā kānū yaʿmalūn* — Allah has the Most Beautiful Names. So call upon Him by them, and keep away from those who abuse His Names. They will be punished for what they used to do.

The verse joins a statement about God's names to a command to use them in prayer. The Book's other formulations of the same doctrine add the instruction to call upon Him by any of them: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Compassionate — whichever you call, He has the Most Beautiful Names’”* (17:110). The names are not a subject for speculation but the vocabulary of supplication.

**The Names in the Qur'an's Theology**

The Qur'an's references to the divine names are concentrated in a few passages: *“Allah — there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. He has the Most Beautiful Names”* (20:8), and the sūrah of al-Ḥashr's closing catalogue, which names the Creator, the Inventor, and the Shaper and ends with the same formula (59:24). The sūrah's verse belongs to that set, and its placement after the account of the heedless gives it its force: the remedy for a dead heart is the invocation of God by His names.

The Prophet's statement about the names is preserved in the two most reliable collections: al-Bukhārī 2736 and Muslim 2677, from Abū Hurayrah — *Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever commits them to memory will enter Paradise*. The tradition built its literature of the names on this hadith and on the Qur'an's command to call upon God by them, and the sūrah's verse is the Book's own instruction in the practice.

**The Four Places Where the Book Names Them**

The phrase *al-asmāʾ al-ḥusnā* occurs four times in the Qurʾān, and the four divide into two pairs. Here and in Sūrah al-Isrāʾ the names come with an instruction attached: this verse commands invocation by them, and *“Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Compassionate—whichever you call, He has the Most Beautiful Names.”* (17:110) makes the same command the answer to a question about which name to use. In Sūrah Ṭā Hā and Sūrah al-Ḥashr the phrase stands in a declaration of who God is: *“Allah—there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. He has the Most Beautiful Names.”* (20:8), and *“He is Allah: the Creator, the Inventor, the Shaper.”

**The Word for Abuse, and the Niche in the Grave**

The Book describes the same practice from the other side, as invention: *“Whatever ˹idols˺ you worship instead of Him are mere names which you and your forefathers have made up—a practice Allah has never authorized.”* (12:40). A name that has not been authorised is a name that has been leaned. This sūrah makes the identical charge in its own account of the idols’ names (7:71), and the two verses together supply the test the tradition drew from them: a name of God is one God has given. Reverence for the names begins with refusing to add to them, and with refusing to bend any of them toward another object — which is the abuse the verse tells its readers to keep away from, and not merely to refrain from.
verses.181:
> And among those We created is a group that guides with the truth and establishes justice accordingly

*Wa-mimman khalaqnā ummatun yahdūna bi-l-ḥaqqi wa-bihi yaʿdilūn* — and among those We created is a group that guides with the truth and establishes justice accordingly.

The sūrah had already used this formula for the people of Moses: *there are some among the people of Moses who guide with the truth and establish justice accordingly* (7:159).

**The Group's Identity**

The tradition read the verse as a reference to the community of the Prophet. The Qur'an's own address to the believers elsewhere supplies the vocabulary: the community that calls to goodness, encourages what is good, and forbids evil is described as the successful (3:104), and the description of the righteous among the People of the Book adds the same elements (3:113–114). The verse is so a statement about the continuity of a function across communities rather than a claim about one group's privilege.

The phrase enlarges the statement beyond any single people, and the Book's theology of creation in the sūrah supplies the frame: God created humanity from a single soul (7:189) and made the descendants testify to His lordship (7:172). The group that guides with truth is so presented as an element within the created order rather than as an exception to it.

**The Parallel in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān**

The Qur'an's address to the Muslim community uses the same note: *“You are the best community ever raised for humanity — you encourage good, forbid evil, and believe in Allah”* (3:110), and its description of the upright among the People of the Book names the same activities (3:113–114). The sūrah's verse avoids the language of supremacy and uses that of function: what the group does is guide and establish justice.

**Between the Names and the Drawing On**

The verse is placed between two statements. Before it: *“Allah has the Most Beautiful Names. So call upon Him by them, and keep away from those who abuse His Names.”* (7:180). After it: *“As for those who deny Our signs, We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot comprehend.”* (7:182).

The position is the verse’s argument. A community that guides with the truth and establishes justice stands between the names by which God is called and the drawing-on by which deniers are led, and the sūrah’s closing verses admit no third option. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verse is read as an answer to the despondency of the preceding passages: after the description of a creation full of people who do not use their faculties (7:179), the Book records that a group does.

The two flanking verses also fix the terms. 7:180 concerns the names and their abuse; 7:182 concerns the signs and their denial. 7:181 describes a group defined by neither abuse nor denial but by two acts — guiding with the truth and doing justice by it — and both acts are directed outward, toward others.

**The Balance Sent Down With the Scripture**

The verse’s second act is *yaʿdilūn*, they establish justice, from *ʿ-d-l*, the root of balance and of equivalence. Al-Ḥadīd states where the balance comes from: *“Indeed, We sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and with them We sent down the Scripture and the balance ˹of justice˺ so that people may administer justice.”* (57:25).
verses.182:
> As for those who deny Our signs, We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot comprehend

**"We Will Gradually Draw Them to Destruction"**

*Wa-alladhīna kadhdhabū bi-āyātinā sa-nastadrijuhum min ḥaythu lā yaʿlamūn* — as for those who deny Our signs, We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot understand.

*Nastadrijuhum* — the Book's term for drawing a person down step by step — describes a ruin that arrives through the very conditions a man takes for comfort. The Qur'an uses the same verb in the same sentence in Sūrat al-Qalam: *“So leave to Me ˹O Prophet˺ those who reject this message. We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot understand”* (68:44), followed by the declaration that the planning is flawless (68:45).

**The Mechanism Stated Elsewhere**

The mechanism has already appeared in narrative form: Egypt read its prosperity as a verdict on its own merit (7:131), and the towns were seized after their prosperity had been granted (7:95). The Book states the law of the pattern in Sūrat al-Anʿām: *“When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired. But just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise, then they instantly fell into despair!”* (6:44).

The Qur'an addresses the same illusion about extended prosperity in a verse aimed at the deniers: *“Those who disbelieve should not think that living longer is good for them. They are only given more time to increase in sin, and they will suffer a humiliating punishment”* (3:178). The sūrah's phrase *in ways they cannot understand* adds the note of blindness: the ruin is not recognized as such while it is happening.

**The Sūrah's Own Earlier Statement**

The Book's analysis of the delusion is stated in Sūrat al-Muʾminūn's question and answer: *“Do they think, since We provide them with wealth and children, that We hasten to ˹honour˺ them ˹with˺ all kinds of good? No! They are not aware”* (23:55–56). The sūrah's verse belongs to the same teaching, and its placement after the account of the heedless gives it a diagnostic function.

**The Doctrine Tested in the Sūrah’s Histories**

The sūrah does not leave the doctrine as a statement. It narrates it. Pharaoh’s people are given years and shortages in alternation: *“so they might come back ˹to their senses˺”* (7:130). Then the signs come in detail — flood, locusts, lice, frogs, blood — and each time the respite returns, the same promise is made and the same reversal follows (7:133–135).

This is also how 7:98 and 7:99 belong to the verse. The towns that believe and keep their duty are given blessings opened from above and below; the towns that deny are seized suddenly while secure. Both outcomes are the operation of one rule, and the difference between them lies in what the people did with the interval. 7:182 states the rule for the second case and adds the one detail that makes it a warning: the interval is not visible as what it is.

**The Verified Ḥadīth on Gradual Ruin**

The doctrine has one ḥadīth that carries both a number and a grade. ʿUqbah b. ʿĀmir reported that the Prophet ﷺ said that if you see Allah giving a servant what he loves from the worldly life despite his disobedience, then it is only His luring him to destruction — and that he then recited the verse in al-Anʿām which states the mechanism: “When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired. But just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise, then they instantly fell into despair!” (6:44). The report stands in the Musnad of Aḥmad at 17311, and al-Arnaʾūṭ graded it ḥasan.

Egypt's plagues showed it operating, the relief arriving and the promise being broken (7:134–135); the verse now states the general law.
verses.183:
> I ˹only˺ delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless

**"My Planning Is Flawless"**

*Wa-umlī lahum inna kaydī matīn* — I ˹only˺ delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless.

The verse speaks in the first person, and its two clauses state a purpose and a character: the delay is granted, and the plan behind it cannot be defeated. The Book's use of the first person for these declarations in the later verses of sūrahs is a feature of its closing movements, and the phrase echoes the same declaration in Sūrat al-Qalam (68:45).

**The Sūrah's Closing Use of the Doctrine**

The remaining verses of the sūrah turn from the deniers' ruin to the Prophet's own instructions: the thought that is asked of his audience (7:184), the reflection on the heavens and the earth (7:185), the Hour (7:187), and the final commands about recitation and remembrance. The verse about the flawless plan stands at the head of that movement, and it supplies the security the messenger and his community are to carry.

The tradition's commentators connected the verse with the sūrah's earlier statements about the towns' sudden seizure and noted that the Book's accounts of destruction consistently involve an interval. The verse's contribution to the sūrah is the explicit statement of intention that the narratives had shown in action.

**Al-Qalam’s Two Verses**

7:183 is a single sentence: *“I ˹only˺ delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless.”* (7:183). Al-Qalam states the same procedure in two verses: *“So leave to Me ˹O Prophet˺ those who reject this message. We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot understand. I ˹only˺ delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless.”* (68:44–45). The second verse is word for word the verse of al-Aʿrāf; the first supplies the mechanism the second names.

*Nastadrijuhum* (we will gradually draw them) is from the same root as the sūrah’s own word for the respite at 7:182. The verb describes a step-by-step leading, and the phrase that follows fixes its character: *min ḥaythu lā yaʿlamūn* (from where they do not know). The drawn-on person does not experience the drawing as such; he experiences increase. 68:44 therefore explains what 7:182–183 states, and the pair is the Book’s fullest account of a respite that is itself an instrument.

**The Contest Between Plans**

The verse’s second clause is *wa-kaydī matīn* — rendered *“but My planning is flawless”* (7:183), literally my *kayd* is firm. *Kayd* is the word for stratagem, contrivance, the working of a plan against someone. Al-Anfāl uses it of both parties: *“They planned, but Allah also planned. And Allah is the best of planners.”* (8:30). The word is applied to the disbelievers’ contrivance and to God’s, and the comparison is settled in one clause.

The point of the shared vocabulary is that the contest is between plans, not between forces. 8:30 describes a plot to capture, kill or exile; the counter-plan is described with the same noun and declared superior. 7:183 makes the same claim in a single adjective: *matīn*, firm, unbreakable, the word used of a rope that does not fray. The contrivance of the deniers is not denied effectiveness — it is what 7:182 responds to — but it is met by a contrivance whose firmness is not subject to their knowledge.
verses.184:
> Have they not ever given it a thought? Their fellow man is not insane. He is only sent with a clear warning

*A-wa-lam yatafakkarū mā bi-ṣāḥibihim min jinnatin in huwa illā nadhīrun mubīn* — have they not ever given it a thought?

The sūrah's previous command to narrate the stories *so that they may reflect* (7:176) used the same verb, and the verse returns to the reader with the demand that the reflection be applied to the messenger himself.

The same argument appears in Sūrat Sabaʾ: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘I advise you to do ˹only˺ one thing: stand up for ˹the sake of˺ Allah — individually or in pairs — then reflect. Your fellow man is not insane. He is only a warner to you before ˹the coming of˺ a severe punishment’”* (34:46).

**The Charge Answered in Three Sūrahs**

The Qur'an answers the accusation of madness against its messenger in several places. Each formulation adds its own emphasis: Sūrat al-Qalam's *“By the grace of your Lord, you ˹O Prophet˺ are not insane”* (68:2) follows the oath of the pen. Sūrat al-Takwīr's *“And your fellow man is not insane”* (81:22) follows the account of the revelation's transmission; and the sūrah's verse answers the charge in the setting of the sūrah's own historical narratives.

**The Messenger's Humanity**

The Qur'an's insistence on the Prophet's humanity is a fixed feature of its message — *“I am only a man like you, ˹but˺ it has been revealed to me that your God is only One God”* (18:110). *“I do not say to you that I possess Allah's treasuries or know the unseen, nor do I claim to be an angel”* (6:50). The accusation of madness and the claim of divinity are both answered by the same fact, and the sūrah's verse presents the ordinary, well-known life as evidence.

**Reflection Commanded: The Question and Its Object**

Muḥammad puts the same question with its object named: *“Do they not then reflect on the Quran? Or are there locks upon their hearts?”* (47:24)

The commentators read 7:184’s question as directed at the accusation that follows it. The charge of madness is answered not by a denial alone but by an appeal to thought: a person who considers what his companion has said and done will not reach that charge.

**The Clear Book and the Clear Warner**

The verse ends: *“He is only sent with a clear warning.”* (7:184) — *nadhīr mubīn* in the Arabic. *Mubīn* is the active participle of form IV of *b-y-n*, to make clear, and it is the Book’s own adjective for itself: *“Alif-Lãm-Ra. These are the verses of the clear Book.”* (12:1). The same adjective describes the signs brought by the messengers (7:101), the proof given to Ṣāliḥ (7:73), and the warning given here.

This is the verse’s logic in its shortest form, and it is why the sūrah follows it with an appeal to the kingdom of the heavens and the earth (7:185). The clarity claimed at the end of 7:184 is a clarity about something — a warning whose content is the dominion and the term and the return. Yūsuf’s opening verse states the same claim about the book that carries it, and the two together describe a message that is intelligible on its face and a deliverer whose sanity is visible in it.
verses.185:
> Have they ever reflected on the wonders of the heavens and the earth, and everything Allah has created, and that perhaps their end is near? So what message after this ˹Quran˺ would they believe in

**The Cosmological Argument in the Qur'an**

The Book states the argument from creation in its fullest form in two famous verses: *“Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the day and night there are signs for people of reason”* (3:190). Its expansion in Sūrat al-Baqarah's catalogue of the ships, the rain, the winds, and the clouds (2:164). The sūrah's verse belongs to that family of passages, and its brevity assumes the reader's familiarity with them.

The Qur'an also directs the same reflection inward: *“Have they not reflected upon their own being? Allah only created the heavens and the earth and everything in between for a purpose and an appointed term”* (30:8). The created world and the hearer's own existence are offered as one piece of evidence, and the Book's method is to move between the two without distinguishing them.

**"Perhaps Their End Is Near"**

The second half of the verse supplies the motive for the reflection: *ʿasā a yakūna qadi iqtaraba ajaluhum* — perhaps their term has drawn near. The Qur'an states the proximity of the Hour in its own opening verses and in the sūrahs of the final revelation: *“˹The time of˺ people's judgment has drawn near, yet they are heedlessly turning away”* (21:1). *“The Hour has drawn near and the moon was split ˹in two˺”* (54:1); and the Book's counsel that the knowledge of the hour belongs to God alone with the observation that perhaps it is near (33:63).

The Qur'an's warnings about the Hour emphasize that it comes without warning: *“Are they waiting for the Hour to take them by surprise when they least expect ˹it˺?”* (43:66). The sūrah's own account of the towns had used the same note — the punishment came upon them *while they were unaware* (7:95) — and the verse attaches the created order's testimony to the possibility of an imminent end.

**The Sūrah's Argument Assembled**

The sūrah's closing verses now read as a summary of its method: the messenger is vindicated by his own life (7:184), the creation is invoked as evidence (7:185), the teaching about guidance is restated (7:186), and the Hour is named (7:187). The grounds of the summons arrive only after the long narrative of the communities that refused it.

The sūrah's own earlier statement about the guided and the straying (7:178, 7:186) supplies the answer's terms, and the reader is given the doctrine he needs to respond. The reflection commanded at 7:185 is directed at the heavens and the earth and at everything created, and the Book describes the same direction as a promise: *“We will show them Our signs in the universe and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that this ˹Quran˺ is the truth.”* (41:53).

The Book's correlative statement in Sūrat al-Anʿām describes the created order as a set of communities: *“All living beings roaming the earth and winged birds soaring in the sky are communities like yourselves. We have left nothing out of the Record”* (6:38).

The Book poses the question in similar form in Sūrat al-Jāthiyah: *“These are Allah's revelations which We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth. So what message will they believe in after ˹denying˺ Allah and His revelations?”* (45:6), and Sūrat al-Mursalāt closes with the same challenge (77:50).
verses.186:
> Whoever Allah allows to stray, none can guide, leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance

**"None Can Guide Whom Allah Leaves to Stray"**

*Man yuḍlili Allāhu fa-lā hādiya lahu wa-yadharuhum fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn* — whoever Allah allows to stray, none can guide, leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance.

The sūrah had stated the same law two verses earlier in other words (7:178), and its repetition here frames the passage about the signs of the creation and the Hour. The Book's use of such refrains gives its teaching a rhythm: the reader meets the same principle at intervals until it becomes the lens through which the sūrah's narratives are read.

The Qur'an states the doctrine in several sūrahs, each with its own emphasis: *“Whoever Allah guides is truly guided. And whoever He leaves to stray, you will find no guardians for them besides Him”* (17:97); *“And whoever Allah guides, none can lead astray. Is Allah not Almighty, capable of punishment?”* (39:37); and Sūrat al-Shūrā's *“And whoever Allah leaves to stray will have no guide after Him”* (42:44). The sūrah's verse is the Book's most compact statement of the first half of the pair.

**"Wandering Blindly"**

*Yaʿmahūn* — the verb describes the blind wandering of one who cannot tell the road from the field, and the Book uses the same image in Sūrat al-Baqarah: *“Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance”* (2:15). The verse's picture is not of a person who has chosen a wrong direction but of one who can no longer judge directions.

*Ṭughyān* — the Book's term for the overstepping that comes of prosperity, the arrogance of a creature that has forgotten the limits of its place. The sūrah uses the same root for the generation of Noah — *indeed they were a people who had gone too far* (7:64's clause at the close of that narrative) — and for the Egyptians (7:127). The blindness of the verse is the final stage of the condition the word describes.

**Whom the Book Says God Leaves to Stray**

The formula sounds absolute, and read alone it can be made to sound arbitrary. The Book does not leave it alone. Wherever it says that God leaves people astray it states the condition, and the condition is always an act of the person left astray. Sūrah al-Baqarah, introducing its parables: *“Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray, and guides many. And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious—”* (2:26). Sūrah al-Ṣaff sets out the sequence without comment: *“So when they ˹persistently˺ deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate. For Allah does not guide the rebellious people.”* (61:5).

The order of the two clauses in that verse is the interpretive point: the deviation of the people comes first, and the turning of their hearts follows it. Verse 186 states the second half of the sequence. This sūrah has been supplying the first half throughout — in the towns tried with hardship and then with ease (7:94–95), in the covenant broken after it had been accepted under the mountain (7:171), in the man who stripped himself out of the signs he had been given (7:175). Whom God leaves to stray, on the Book’s own accounting, is the one who has already taken the direction. The leaving confirms a choice; it does not stand in place of one.

**The Two Verbs of Straying, and the Matching Formula**

The Book also gives the formula’s converse, and it is the pairing that keeps either half from being read as fatalism. Sūrah al-Kahf closes the account of the sleepers with the same two clauses in the same order: *“Whoever Allah guides is truly guided. But whoever He leaves to stray, you will never find for them a guiding mentor.”* (18:17). What verse 186 adds is a description of the state that remains — wandering blindly, in defiance. That is not the portrait of a person deprived of something he wanted.
verses.187:
> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ regarding the Hour, “When will it be?” Say, “That knowledge is only with my Lord. He alone will reveal it when the time comes. It is too tremendous for the heavens and the earth and will only take you by surprise.” They ask you as if you had full knowledge of it. Say, “That knowledge is only with Allah, but most people do not know.”

**"They Ask You About the Hour"**

*Yasʾalūnaka ʿani al-sāʿati ayyāna mursāhā qul innamā ʿilmuhā ʿinda rabbī lā yujallīhā li-waqtihā illā huwa thaqulat fī al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi lā taʾtīkum illā baghtatan yasʾalūnaka ka-annaka ḥafiyyun ʿanhā qul innamā ʿilmuhā ʿinda Allāhi wa-lākinna akthara al-nāsi lā yaʿlamūn* — they ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the Hour, “When will it be?” (7:187) Say: “That knowledge is only with my Lord. He alone will reveal it when the time comes. It is too tremendous for the heavens and the earth and will only take you by surprise.” (7:187) They ask you as if you had full knowledge of it. Say: “That knowledge is only with Allah, but most people do not know.” (7:187)

**"As If You Were Well Informed About It"**

The questioners' manner is described in the verse: they press the Prophet as though the date were his to disclose.

The Qur'an's statements about what is withheld from creatures are many and consistent: *“Indeed, Allah ˹alone˺ has the knowledge of the Hour. He sends down the rain, and knows what is in the wombs”* (31:34); the Book's counsel that every community has an appointed term (10:49); and the Prophet's declaration that he does not have God's treasuries or know the unseen (6:50).

The verse follows the appeal to reflect on the heavens and the earth and precedes the command to the Prophet to state his own limits (7:188). The sequence is a single argument about the boundaries of knowledge: creation testifies, the end is hidden, and the messenger knows only what he was given.

**The Hour Drawn Near**

The verse reports a question about the Hour and refuses its answer: *“That knowledge is only with my Lord. He alone will reveal it when the time comes.”* (7:187). Al-Qamar states the position from the other side: *“The Hour has drawn near and the moon was split ˹in two˺.”* (54:1).

The two verses are not in tension but in sequence. The Hour’s nearness is announced, and its timing is withheld; the splitting of the moon is given as a sign already shown. The sūrah’s own demand for signs (7:132) is answered by a sign that was granted, and the question about the Hour is answered by a knowledge that is not given.

**The Knowledge of the Hour and the Things Withheld**

The comparison explains the verse’s closing irony. The questioners ask as though the one asked were informed (7:187), and the answer lists what no one is informed of. The commentators note that the withholding is not a withholding of information from a messenger but a description of a knowledge that belongs to the unseen, disclosed only where God chooses (72:26–27).

The Qur'an addresses the same question in Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt: *“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the Hour, ‘When will it be?’ But it is not for you to tell its time. That knowledge rests with your Lord ˹alone˺”* (79:42–44), and in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb the counsel that perhaps the Hour is near follows the same reservation (33:63).

The Qur'an's doctrine of the hidden is stated in the same terms elsewhere — *“The Hour is sure to come. My Will is to keep it hidden, so that every soul may be rewarded according to their efforts”* (20:15) — and the withholding is given a purpose in the same verse.
verses.188:
> Say, “I have no power to benefit or protect myself, except by the Will of Allah. If I had known the unknown, I would have benefited myself enormously, and no harm would have ever touched me. I am only a warner and deliverer of good news for those who believe.”

**"No Power to Benefit or Protect Myself"**

The Book states the same confession in Sūrat al-Jinn: *“Say, ‘It is not in my power to harm or benefit you’”* (72:21), and in Sūrat Yūnus with reference to the community's own appointed term (10:49). The Prophet is a creature among creatures, and the benefit and harm people seek from him are not his to dispense.

The second sentence addresses the Makkans' assumption that a prophet is a source of hidden knowledge: if the Prophet had it, he says, he would have used it for good and avoided every harm. The Qur'an states the same denial elsewhere — *“I do not say to you that I possess Allah's treasuries or know the unseen, nor do I claim to be an angel”* (6:50), and the Book's instruction in Sūrat al-Māʾidah that the messenger's duty is only to deliver the message (5:99).

**The Prophet's Humanity in the Qur'an**

The Book's insistence on the humanity of its messengers recurs throughout the Qur'an. Its most concise form is the command to the Prophet to say that he is a man like other men: *“I am only a man like you, ˹but˺ it has been revealed to me that your God is only One God”* (18:110). The sūrah's verse belongs to that set, and its portrait of the messenger is stripped of the supernatural claims made for holy men elsewhere.

*Nadhīrun wa-bashīrun* — the sūrah's earlier verse had described the Prophet as a clear warner (7:184), and the pairing of warning with good news is the Qur'an's standard description of the prophetic function. The office of a messenger is here defined by its work: he states the consequences of both courses and leaves the outcome to his hearers and to God.

**The Keys of the Unseen**

The verse disclaims a knowledge: if he had known the unseen, he says, he would have multiplied good and harm would not have touched him. Al-Anʿām states where that knowledge is: *“With Him are the keys of the unseen—no one knows them except Him. And He knows what is in the land and sea.”* (6:59).

The verse describes the unseen as locked and the keys as held, and then extends the knowledge to particulars — a leaf falling, a grain in the darkness. 7:188’s disclaimer is therefore not a statement about limits of ability but about the location of a thing: the unseen is not where a messenger can reach it, except where it is given (72:26–27).

The commentators read the two verses together as the answer to a demand. The sūrah has recorded demands for signs and for knowledge of the Hour (7:187), and 7:188 is the reply in the first person: no power over benefit or harm, no access to the unseen, an office of warning and good news. 6:59 supplies the reason the reply is not a limitation of the office but a description of reality.

**The Same Sentence in Yūnus**

The verse’s first clause is repeated almost exactly in another sūrah: *“I have no power to benefit or protect myself, except by the Will of Allah.”* (10:49). Yūnus then states what follows from it: *“For each community there is an appointed term. When their time arrives, they cannot delay it for a moment, nor could they advance it.”* (10:49).
verses.189:
> He is the One Who created you from a single soul, then from it made its spouse so he may find comfort in her. After he had been united with her, she carried a light burden that developed gradually. When it grew heavy, they prayed to Allah, their Lord, “If you grant us good offspring, we will certainly be grateful.”

**"Created You From a Single Soul"**

*Huwa alladhī khalaqakum min nafsin wāḥidatin wa-jaʿala minhā zawjahā li-yaskuna ilayhā fa-lammā taghashshāhā ḥamalat ḥamlan khafīfan fa-marrat bihi fa-lammā athqalat daʿawā Allāha rabbahumā la-in ātaytanā ṣāliḥan la-nakūnanna mina al-shākirīn* — He is the One Who created you from a single soul, then from it made its spouse so he may find comfort in her. After he had been united with her, she carried a light burden that developed gradually. When it grew heavy, they prayed to Allah, their Lord: "If you grant us good offspring, we will certainly be grateful." (7:189)

The Book's account of human origins begins with the one soul and the pair made from it, and the sūrah states the same fact in the same words as Sūrat al-Nisāʾ (4:1) and Sūrat al-Zumar (39:6). The phrase's function in the sūrah is to establish the unity of the human family before the narrative turns to the family's own prayers and, in the next verse, to its failures.

**"So He May Find Comfort in Her"**

The Qur'an's treatment of the pair belongs to its catalogues of signs: Sūrat al-Rūm names the creation of spouses among the signs and adds the compassion and mercy placed between them (30:21), and Sūrat al-Naḥl lists spouses, children, and grandchildren among God's gifts (16:72). The sūrah's verse is the same teaching in narrative form, and its placement in the sūrah's closing movement gives it the weight of a summary.

**The Shadow of the Next Verse**

The verse ends with the couple's promise, and the next verse reports what their descendants did with the gift: *“But when He granted their descendants good offspring, they associated false gods in what He has given them”* (7:190). Prayer and outcome so stand in consecutive sentences, and the passage becomes a study of how a gift is received.

The Book's narratives of the patriarchs are full of such prayers for children — Zakariyyā's plea behind the sanctuary, Abraham's supplication for righteous offspring. The believers described in Sūrat al-Furqān who ask for comfort in their spouses and offspring (25:74) — and the sūrah's verse gives the same petition in its simplest form: a good child and the gratitude that should follow.

**Sakan and Mawaddah: The Two Words for the Bond**

The verse states the making of the spouse and its purpose: *“He is the One Who created you from a single soul, then from it made its spouse so he may find comfort in her.”* (7:189). Ar-Rūm states the same arrangement as a sign: *“And one of His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves so that you may find comfort in them. And He has placed between you compassion and mercy.”* (30:21).

**One Soul and Its Mate**

The verse’s first clause is repeated in the Book’s opening address: *“O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul, and from it He created its mate, and through both He spread countless men and women.”* (4:1).

The comparison fixes the verse’s argument. The origin is one, the tie is therefore real, and the prayer recorded at 7:189 is made by both — *they both prayed*. The association that follows is described as made in the gift, and 4:1 supplies the reason a gift shared by a pair cannot be attributed to a third: the two are from one soul.
verses.190:
> But when He granted their descendants good offspring, they associated false gods in what He has given them. Exalted is Allah above what they associate ˹with Him˺

**"They Associated False Gods in What He Has Given Them"**

*Fa-lammā ātāhumā ṣāliḥan jaʿalā lahu shurakāʾa fīmā ātāhumā fa-taʿālā Allāhu ʿammā yushrikūn* — but when He granted their descendants good offspring, they associated false gods in what He has given them. Exalted is Allah above what they associate ˹with Him˺!

The sentence completes the couple's prayer from the previous verse: they had asked for a good child and promised gratitude (7:189), and the report now follows. The verse's subject is disputed among the commentators, and the translation's *they* keeps the ambiguity of the Qur'an's own pronoun, which is the Book's usual practice in such passages.

The tradition's exegetes read the pair either as Adam and Eve and their descendants, or as a generic pair whose story serves as the type of every household. The second reading is supported by the verse's plural verbs and by the presence of the same charge in the sūrah's other narratives of Israel, whose ancestors had made the calf. What the passage establishes in either reading is the pattern: a gift is given, and the giver is joined with others.

**"In What He Has Given Them"**

The phrase names the offense precisely: the association was made about the very gift that had been asked of God. The Qur'an's charge against ingratitude is consistently framed this way — the creature uses the gift as a claim against the giver — and the pattern has already run through Egypt's prosperity and Israel's abundance in the wilderness.

The Qur'an states the charge against the polytheists in several registers: *“Yet they associate the jinn with Allah ˹in worship˺, even though He created them”* (6:100). The claim of the Makkans that their gods were merely intercessors (10:18); and the declaration of Sūrat al-Zumar that sincere devotion belongs to God alone while others take lords besides Him to bring them closer to Him (39:3). The sūrah's verse names the offense at the level of the family.

**Partners in a Gift**

The offence is described in the language of property. The couple were given good offspring, and they made partners in what had been given — a share assigned to someone other than the giver, in a thing that came from him. The Book puts the same arrangement as a question about ordinary property, and the question answers itself: *“He sets forth for you an example ˹drawn˺ from your own lives: would you allow some of those ˹bondspeople˺ in your possession to be your equal partners in whatever ˹wealth˺ We have provided you”* (30:28).

**The Gift Remembered and the Gift Assigned**

The verse moves from a prayer to an answer to a misappropriation, and the Book names the middle term as the one most easily lost: *“And He has granted you all that you asked Him for. If you tried to count Allah’s blessings, you would never be able to number them.”* (14:34). The same verse ends on the character that produces the misappropriation — humankind as unjust and ungrateful.
verses.191:
> Do they associate ˹with Allah˺ those ˹idols˺ which cannot create anything, but are in fact created

**The Same Argument in Sūrat al-Naḥl**

The Book states the case in almost identical words elsewhere: *“But those ˹idols˺ they invoke besides Allah cannot create anything—they themselves are created. They are dead, not alive—not even knowing when their followers will be resurrected”* (16:20–21). The sūrah's verse is the Book's doctrine in summary form, and the two passages belong to the same argumentative tradition within the Qur'an.

Sūrat al-Furqān's version of the same charge adds the idols' inability to benefit themselves: *“Yet they have taken besides Him gods who cannot create anything but are themselves created. Nor can they protect or benefit themselves. Nor can they control life, death, or resurrection”* (25:3). The sūrah's verse and its companion in Sūrat al-Furqān together supply the full catalogue of what the associate-gods lack.

**The Book's Catalogue of the Idols' Limits**

The Qur'an returns to the theme in passage after passage: the idols have not even an atom's weight in the heavens or the earth (34:22); they can never create so much as a fly even if all assembled for the try (22:73); and they are aware of nothing their worshippers say (46:5). What accumulates here is a dossier rather than a single argument, and its consistency is the point.

The sūrah had already applied the test to the golden calf, in the account of Israel's worship in Moses' absence: *“Did they not see that it could neither speak to them nor guide them to the ˹Right˺ Path? Still they took it as a god and were wrongdoers”* (7:148), and Sūrat Ṭāhā's version states the same test in a question (20:89). The sūrah's verse now generalizes the argument to all the associate-gods of Arabia. The Book's accounts of Arab idolatry attribute to the worshipers the belief that their gods were intercessors and that they brought them closer to God (10:18, 39:3), and the verse's argument answers that claim at its base.

The Book's arguments against the idols are always accompanied by the statement of what God alone has, and the sūrah's next verses supply it in the Prophet's own declaration that his Protector is the One who revealed the Book (7:196).

**Lords Who Cannot Benefit Themselves**

The verse reduces the test from creation to self-interest. A thing that cannot benefit itself cannot be a source of benefit, and the argument does not require a claim about how it was made. 7:191 makes the larger claim and 13:16 makes the smaller one, and the sūrah uses both — the idols here, and the calf’s inability to speak or guide at 7:148.

**Originating Creation and Repeating It**

The verse’s negative claim — they create nothing — has a positive counterpart in Yūnus: *“Can any of your associate-gods originate creation and then resurrect it?”* followed by the answer given in the same breath: *“˹Only˺ Allah originates creation and then resurrects it. How can you then be deluded ˹from the truth˺?”* (10:34).

This is the argument’s place in the sūrah. The passage runs from the partners associated in a gift received (7:190) through the idols’ inability to create (7:191), to help or to be helped (7:192), and to answer a call for guidance (7:193), and ends by turning the demand back on those who make it (7:194). The sūrah does not argue from design here but from function: what the object can do, and what the one who follows it can expect.
verses.192:
> which cannot help them, or even help themselves

**"Which Cannot Help Them, or Even Help Themselves"**

*Wa-lā yastaṭīʿūna lahum naṣran wa-lā anfusahum yanṣurūn* — which cannot help them, or even help themselves?

The verse adds the test of help to the test of creation, and the order is the Book's: existence first, then the capacity to be of use. The idols fail both, and the verse's second clause is the more damaging, since it removes even the self-interest that a worshipper might attribute to his god.

The Qur'an states the two failures together in Sūrat al-Furqān — the gods who can neither protect nor benefit themselves (25:3) — and in Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ: *“Or do they have gods—other than Us—that can protect them? They cannot ˹even˺ protect themselves, nor will they be aided against Us”* (21:43). The sūrah's verse is one member of a set of formulations that the Book repeats until the point is unavoidable.

**What the Verse Implies About the Worshippers**

The sūrah's argument implies that the idolaters had transferred to their gods a capacity they themselves had in part: a human being can at least help his neighbor. The Book's satire in such passages is severe because the exchange described is a descent — the worshipper credits a stone with less than he himself can do.

The Qur'an's arguments against the idols are consistently brief in their premises and vast in their application, and this verse is an example: two clauses dismantle the claim of an entire cult. The Book's method is to assume that a hearer who knows what divinity means will draw the conclusion, and the inference is left to be drawn.

The sūrah returns to the same argument in verse 197, where the same sentence is repeated almost verbatim, and the repetition frames the passage about the Prophet's Protector (7:196). The idols' incapacity therefore frames the declaration of God's protection on either side, and the arrangement is not accidental.

The Qur'an's accounts of the Judgment include a scene in which the associate-gods themselves renounce their worshippers, and the beings invoked will not even acknowledge the invocation (10:28–29, 16:86). The present verse's silence is so a foretaste of the final rejection, and the two belong to the same discourse.

**The Next Verse's Test**

The following verse turns from capacity to response: whether the idols answer those who call on them for guidance (7:193). The sūrah's examination of the associate-gods so proceeds through creation, help, self-help, and speech before it reaches the challenge of verse 194, and the accumulation gives the passage its rhetorical force.

The Book's argument against the idols serves its positive teaching about reliance, and the sūrah's next verses declare the Prophet's own protector (7:196) and the Book that was revealed to him. A worshipper's trust is shown here from the other side, when its object is the One who creates, helps, and protects.

The verse's question is directed at those who associate and at every reader after them, and the question turns to what anyone's own reliance is placed on. The sūrah's narratives of the towns and the nations have already shown the cost of the mistake, and the verse states its anatomy in a line.
verses.193:
> And if you ˹idolaters˺ call upon them for guidance, they cannot respond to you. It is all the same whether you call them or remain silent

**"If You Call Upon Them for Guidance, They Cannot Respond"**

*Wa-in tadʿūhum ilā al-hudā lā yattabiʿūkum sawāʾun ʿalaykum a-daʿawtumūhum am antum ṣāmitūn* — and if you ˹idolaters˺ call upon them for guidance, they cannot respond to you. It is all the same whether you call them or remain silent.

The Qur'an states the same fact in several places: the idols are unaware of the calls of those who invoke them (46:5); they cannot hear; and the Book's account of the Judgment has them disowning their worshippers outright (10:28–29).

**The Book's Refusal of Compromise**

The Qur'an's monotheism does not permit the retention of the idols as intermediaries, and its arguments are framed to make the position untenable on its own terms. The polytheists' claim is met at the point where they themselves located it — the usefulness of the gods — and dismantled there.

The next verse states that the idols are created beings like their worshippers and challenges the idolaters to call upon them and see (7:194). The sūrah's examination so moves from the statement of incapacity to a direct invitation, and the case is stated in its final form.

The Book's positive teaching about supplication is placed beside its critique of the idols, and the sūrah's later instructions about calling upon God by His names (7:180) and seeking refuge with Him (7:200) supply it. Whom to call on is declared in the same passage that forbids whom not to call on.

**What the Verse Denies**

The verse denies the possibility of guidance from any source other than God, and its argument is so inseparable from the sūrah's doctrine of guidance stated earlier in the same sequence (7:178, 7:186). The idols cannot respond; the One who can has already spoken and continues to speak through the recitation.

**The Reader's Own Test**

The verse's statement about the futility of calling is also a statement about the nature of guidance, and it belongs with the sūrah's earlier declarations that guidance and straying are in God's hand (7:178, 7:186). No created thing can supply what only God bestows, and the critique of the idols is the negative form of that doctrine.

The Book's account of the idols' inability to respond is coupled throughout the Qur'an with the account of God's responsiveness, and the contrast is drawn in the same movement: the idols cannot hear, and the Book's own instruction is that God hears the suppliant (7:200's closing names). The sūrah's theology is stated by contrast as much as by assertion. The verse specifies what the idols are called for — guidance — and the Book elsewhere states the same failure with its consequence: *“And who could be more astray than those who call upon others besides Allah—˹others˺ that cannot respond to them until the Day of Judgment, and are ˹even˺ unaware of their calls?”* (46:5).

The specification matters because it narrows the argument to a case that cannot be met by concession. An idol might be granted to have some use: it can be an ornament, a marker, an inheritance, a focus for a gathering.

The scene the verse implies is described elsewhere in full: *“If you call upon them, they cannot hear your calls. And if they were to hear, they could not respond to you. On the Day of Judgment they will disown your worship ˹of them˺.”* (35:14).
verses.194:
