> Those ˹idols˺ you invoke besides Allah are created beings like yourselves. So call upon them and see if they will answer you, if your claims are true

**The Book's Challenges to the Associators**

The Qur'an states its challenges in several forms: the command to call upon those claimed besides Allah with the observation that they have not an atom's weight (34:22), and the famous comparison of the idols' inability to create even a fly (22:73). A series of such invitations follows, each asking the idolaters to show their claim.

The sūrah had already applied the test to Israel's idol in Moses' absence: the people could see that the calf made no reply and offered no guidance (7:148). The verse's challenge generalizes that scene, and The same argument operates in Israel's history and in the Arab present.

**The Intercessors' Claim and Its Refutation**

The Book's refutation of intercession is not a denial of all mediation but a denial that the idols can perform it, and the verses that follow state the positive alternative in the Prophet's declaration of God's protection (7:196). What may be relied on and what may not is the division the passage draws.

The sūrah's examination now includes creation (7:191), help (7:192), response (7:193), and now the standing of the idols as servants. Each verse removes one more claim, and the reader who follows the sequence finds himself without a case for the associate-gods at all.

The following verse examines the idols' bodies: feet, hands, eyes, and ears (7:195), and The argument is given a physical form. The Book's critique of idolatry includes this almost clinical inventory, and its effect is to make the object of worship visible as an object.

**The Reader's Own Position**

The verse's test is available to every reader, and Its application is left open: whatever is invoked besides God falls under the same test. The sūrah's closing instructions about recalling God inwardly and reciting the Qur'an (7:204–205) describe the practice that follows from the verse's conclusion, and the passage ends where the sūrah means it to.

The verse's phrase about the idols as servants places them in the same category as the angels, who are described in the sūrah's final verse as worshipers who are not too proud to serve (7:206), and the comparison is instructive: the worshipped beings of the Qur'an are worshipers themselves. The company the idols keep is not the one their worshippers imagined.

The verse's challenge also belongs to the sūrah's treatment of the demand for signs, which occupies the passage's final verses: the idolaters who asked the Prophet to produce a miracle are invited to get one from their own gods first. The demand is returned to its makers, and the sūrah's answer to the request follows soon afterwards (7:203).

**The Same Challenge in al-Aḥqāf**

The challenge to call the idols and see whether they answer is put elsewhere with demands attached: *“Have you considered whatever ˹idols˺ you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created on earth! Or do they have a share in ˹the creation of˺ the heavens?”* (46:4). The verse goes on to ask for a scripture or a trace of knowledge, so that the challenge covers what the objects made, what they hold, and what they know.

This verse states the same case in its shortest form. The objects invoked are creatures, like those invoking them, and can therefore be tested by the simplest test available: call and see. The sūrah does not need the longer version because its audience is standing in front of the objects and the test can be run where they stand. That is the difference between an argument and an experiment, and the verse’s closing conditional — if you are truthful — is the same conditional Pharaoh used when he demanded the sign (7:106). The sūrah turns the court’s demand back on the worshippers.

The Qur'an's statement of universal need is made in a verse whose audience is all of humanity: *“O humanity! It is you who stand in need of Allah, but Allah ˹alone˺ is the Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy”* (35:15).
verses.195:
> Do they have feet to walk with? Or hands to hold with? Or eyes to see with? Or ears to hear with? Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Call upon your associate-gods and conspire against me without delay

**"Do They Have Feet to Walk With?"**

*A-lahum arjulun yamshūna bihā am lahum aydin yabṭishūna bihā am lahum aʿyunun yubṣirūna bihā am lahum ādhānun yasmaʿūna bihā quli dʿū shurakāʾakum thumma kīdūni fa-lā tunẓirūn* — do they have feet to walk with? Or hands to hold with? Or eyes to see with? Or ears to hear with? Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ "Call upon your associate-gods and conspire against me without delay!" (7:195)

The verse examines the idols' anatomy and finds nothing: no feet, no hands, no eyes, no ears. The Book's critique of idolatry includes this almost clinical inventory, and its effect is to make the objects of worship visible as objects. What stands in the sanctuary is to be compared with what the word divine requires.

**The Sūrah's Earlier Use of the Same Faculties**

The sūrah had used the vocabulary of feet, hands, eyes, and ears in its description of the heedless, who have hearts, eyes, and ears and do not use them (7:179), and in the catalogue of the instruments of knowledge (7:172's testimony). The human being is made with functioning faculties and the idol with none, and the contrast is the verse's argument.

The Qur'an returns to the theme in its own comparisons: the idols who cannot respond to those who call them (46:5), the gods who cannot protect themselves (21:43), and the challenge to those who claim divine partners to produce them (34:22). The sūrah's inventory belongs to the same dossier, and its specificity gives it a rhetorical force the general statements lack. The sūrah's accounts of the towns and of Israel had repeatedly shown communities relying on what could not save them — the calf, the court of Egypt, the numbers of a tribe — and the verse now states the anatomy of that reliance.

The command to the Prophet to issue the challenge is followed immediately by his own declaration of protection (7:196), and the sequence gives the passage its shape: the idols are dismissed, the challenge is issued, and the ground of the messenger's security is named.

**The Passage's Movement**

The sūrah's final treatment of the idols now proceeds from their creation (7:191) through their help (7:192), their response (7:193), their servitude (7:194), and their bodies (7:195), and the next verses repeat and complete the examination. The Book's method in the passage is exhaustive on purpose, and the reader is meant to reach the end of the list without finding a case.

A messenger invites conspiracy against himself and then states that his Protector is the One who revealed the Book. The Book's teaching about reliance is so delivered in the form of a life rather than a proposition, and the passage's closure is a declaration of trust.

**The Book’s Other Tests for a God**

Two other passages apply the same method, and both put the test in a form the audience can run. Sūrah al-Ḥajj: *“O humanity! A lesson is set forth, so listen to it ˹carefully˺: those ˹idols˺ you invoke besides Allah can never create ˹so much as˺ a fly, even if they ˹all˺ were to come together for that.”* (22:73). Sūrah Yūnus: *“Can any of your associate-gods originate creation and then resurrect it?”* (10:34).
verses.196:
> “Indeed, my Protector is Allah Who has revealed this Book. For He ˹alone˺ protects the righteous

**The Word for Protection**

*Walī* — the Book's word for the guardian, the ally, the one who takes charge of a person's affairs — describes a relationship of both authority and care, and the Qur'an uses it for God throughout. The same word appears in the Book's account of Jacob's trust: *“But ˹only˺ Allah is the best Protector, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful”* (12:64).

The verse identifies the Protector by His act rather than by an attribute: the One Who has revealed this Book is the One who protects. The connection between the messenger's mission and his security is one authority: what commissioned him sustains him, and revelation and protection are joined in a single sentence.

**The Next Verse's Repetition**

The next verse repeats the idols' incapacity once more (7:197) before the sūrah turns to the question of hearing (7:198), and the repetition is the Book's way of concluding the argument. A final negative statement gives way to the sūrah's closing instructions, moving from refuge in God to the practice of the community.

The messenger's dependence and the idolaters' reliance differ in their object: both groups look outside themselves, and the Book's argument is about what is there when they look. The sūrah's closing instruction to seek refuge with God (7:200) applies the same reasoning to the ordinary moments of a believer's day, and the passage's doctrinal statement so becomes a practice.

**The Righteous and the Protection Promised Them**

The second clause states the protection as a fact about a class: He protects the righteous. The commentators ask whether that makes the protection conditional, and the sūrah answers by defining the class elsewhere in conduct rather than status. The towns are told what would have happened had they been faithful and mindful: *“Had the people of those societies been faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, We would have overwhelmed them with blessings from heaven and earth.”* (7:96) — a blessing attached to two acts, faith and mindfulness, and withheld when they are withheld.

The same three marks reappear in the ordaining of mercy at 7:156, and the righteousness named here is the righteousness those verses describe. The clause is therefore not a promise to a group identified in advance but a statement of where the protection is found: with the conduct, in whoever performs it. The verse’s speaker is a messenger under threat from a town that has just threatened to stone him or expel him, and the protection he claims is the one his own conduct has been described as qualifying for. The declaration has a close parallel in the sūrah of Hūd, spoken in the same situation — a prophet facing a town that has refused him and threatened him: *“I have put my trust in Allah—my Lord and your Lord. There is no living creature that is not completely under His control. Surely my Lord’s Way is perfect justice.”* (11:56).

Hūd’s uses the forelock, the hair by which a beast is led, and states that no living thing is outside that hold; the verse in al-Aʿrāf names the Book as the ground of protection, since the one who revealed it is the one who defends the messenger carrying it.
verses.197:
> But those ˹false gods˺ you call besides Him can neither help you nor even themselves.”

**The Worshippers' Position Stated Again**

The verse addresses the idolaters directly as those who call upon others besides God, and The charge is put in the second person rather than as a description. The sūrah's argument so closes as it began, with an address to the people who invoke the associate-gods.

The sūrah's readers have been told how the associate-gods will behave on the Day of Judgment: they will disown their worshippers and testify that they were unaware of the worship offered them (10:29), and Sūrat al-Naḥl reports their rebuttal of the polytheists' appeal (16:86).

The passage that began with the question about creation (7:191) now ends with the statement that the idols cannot help, and the reader is left with no attribute of divinity that the idols retain.

**The Next Verse's Change of Subject**

The following verse turns from the idols' incapacity to their deafness and their sightless appearance (7:198), and the passage's argument is extended by one more clause. The sūrah's examination of the associate-gods is so complete, and the reader is carried to the sūrah's final instructions for the community.

The sūrah's contrast between the idols and the Protector of the righteous (7:196) is the passage's positive teaching, and Here is a doctrine of reliance in which the object of trust is able to act. The sūrah's closing verses about seeking refuge with God (7:200) and remembering Him (7:205) apply that doctrine to the community's daily practice.

**The Pastoral Force of the Repetition**

The sūrah's treatment of the associate-gods now includes their creation (7:191), their help (7:192), their response (7:193), their servitude (7:194), their bodies (7:195), and their final restatement (7:197), with the Prophet's declaration (7:196) at the center. A complete dossier has been assembled, and the sūrah moves on to its closing instructions.

**The Turn to the Community**

The remaining verses of the sūrah address the Prophet and the believers: the command to be gracious and to turn from the ignorant (7:199), the instruction to seek refuge (7:200), the description of the mindful (7:201), the account of the devils' persistence (7:202), the answer about signs (7:203), the command to listen to the recitation (7:204), the remembrance morning and evening (7:205), and the prostration of the angels (7:206). The passage about the idols ends, and the sūrah's practice begins.

The verse's wording also closes the door on the possibility that the associate-gods might act on the worshippers' behalf at some future point, since the verb addresses the present and permanent condition of the objects invoked. Nothing about the idols will change, and the Book's statements about the Day of Judgment depict the same incapacity in its final form.

**The Closing Movement’s Five Steps**

The passage this verse belongs to proceeds by steps, and the steps are tests rather than assertions. The idols are asked to respond to a call for guidance and cannot (7:193). They are inventoried for organs and found without function (7:195); the messenger states whose protection he holds (7:196); they are asked to help and cannot help themselves (7:197); and they are shown facing their worshippers without seeing them (7:198).

The same pair is used where the impossibility is stated without reference to idols at all: *“And you cannot escape Him on earth or in heaven. Nor have you any protector or helper besides Allah.”* (29:22).
verses.198:
> If you ˹idolaters˺ call them to guidance, they cannot hear. And you ˹O Prophet˺ may see them facing towards you, but they cannot see

**"They Cannot Hear"**

*Wa-in tadʿūhum ilā al-hudā lā yasmaʿū wa-tarāhum yanẓurūna ilayka wa-hum lā yubṣirūn* — if you ˹idolaters˺ call them to guidance, they cannot hear. And you ˹O Prophet˺ may see them facing toward you, but they cannot see.

The Qur'an's statement about the idols' deafness appears in Sūrat al-Aḥqāf, where the gods are unaware even of the calls of those who invoke them (46:5), and in the sūrah's own earlier verse about response (7:193). The beings addressed in the sanctuaries receive nothing, and the point is made in the plainest terms.

**The Sūrah's Earlier Treatment of Sight**

The sūrah had used the vocabulary of vision and hearing in its description of the heedless who have eyes and do not see (7:179), and in the catalogue of the faculties given to the human being. Two kinds of blindness now stand in the same sūrah: the blindness of creatures who refuse to use their senses, and the blindness of objects that have none.

The idols are not only powerless but inanimate, and the Qur'an's account of the calf had made the point in Israel's history: the golden image could not speak or guide (7:148). The sūrah's final verse about the idols states the same fact for the cult of Arabia, and the two scenes belong to one teaching.

**The Three Faculties the Sūrah Names**

Two verses earlier the sūrah drew up its own inventory of the faculties and reported them as unused: *“They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, and ears they do not hear with. They are like cattle. In fact, they are even less guided!”* (7:179). Verse 198 applies the inventory to the idols, and that transfer is the passage’s argument. The organs denied function in the worshippers are denied existence in the worshipped: the idols cannot hear a call to guidance, and they cannot see the faces turned toward them.

**The Book’s Two Comparisons: the Flock and the Grave**

Elsewhere the Book makes the same charge with two images, and both are addressed to the one who calls rather than to the one who does not answer. Of the callers: *“The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd. ˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding.”* (2:171). Of the call itself: *“Nor are the dead and the living equal. Indeed, Allah ˹alone˺ makes whoever He wills hear, but you ˹O Prophet˺ can never make those in the graves hear ˹your call˺.”* (35:22).

Both images locate the failure in the receiver, and both leave the caller’s work intact, which is the instruction carried inside the argument. The shepherd goes on calling to a flock that cannot take the call as speech; the messenger goes on speaking to graves. Neither is told to stop, and neither is promised that calling will produce hearing. Verse 198 belongs to that family: it states the incapacity of the object so that the one who invites will not measure his work by its effect. The direction the sūrah gives the Prophet immediately afterwards — take what is offered, command what is right, and turn away from the ignorant (7:199) — is the conduct that follows from knowing it.
verses.199:
> Be gracious, enjoin what is right, and turn away from those who act ignorantly

**"Be Gracious, Enjoin What Is Right, and Turn Away"**

*Khudhi al-ʿafwa wa-mur bi-l-ʿurfi wa-aʿriḍ ʿani al-jāhilīn* — be gracious, command what is right, and turn away from those who act ignorantly.

*Khudhi al-ʿafwa* — the Book's phrase for taking what is easy, for accepting the surplus, for pardoning. The Qur'an's teaching about pardon appears throughout: *“The reward of an evil deed is its equivalent. But whoever pardons and seeks reconciliation, then their reward is with Allah”* (42:40); the description of the believers as those who control their anger (3:134); and the instruction to the Prophet's community to pardon and bear with the People of the Book's hostility (2:109). The verse gathers that teaching into an imperative.

**"Enjoin What Is Right"**

*Wa-mur bi-l-ʿurf* — the Book's term for what is recognized as good, the customary right that reason and revelation both acknowledge. The sūrah's own description of the Prophet includes the same charge — he commands what is good and forbids what is evil (7:157) — and the Qur'an's address to the believers names the duty as a mark of the community (3:104). The verse is so the Prophet's commission in miniature.

*Wa-aʿriḍ ʿani al-jāhilīn* — the instruction is about conduct rather than about debate. The Book's ethic of restraint is stated in similar terms elsewhere: the servants of the Most Compassionate respond to the foolish with peace (25:63), and the Book's counsel to answer evil with what is best (23:96, 41:34) belongs to the same teaching. What the verse lays down is a policy rather than a tactic.

**The Sūrah's Earlier Statements of the Same Ethic**

The sūrah had described the Prophet's community as those who command what is right and forbid what is evil (7:157) and had reported the warners of the town by the sea as the saved party (7:165). The ethic is delivered twice, in narrative and in command, and the two forms reinforce each other.

**Responding With Peace**

The verse’s third command is to turn away from those who act ignorantly. Al-Furqān describes the same posture as a mark of God’s servants: *“The ˹true˺ servants of the Most Compassionate are those who walk on the earth humbly, and when the foolish address them ˹improperly˺, they only respond with peace.”* (25:63).

A manner of walking — humility; a reception of speech — the foolish addressing them; and a reply — peace. 7:199 gives the same three in the form of commands: be gracious, command what is right, turn away from the ignorant.

**Sticking With Those Who Call Morning and Evening**

The verse’s command to turn away has a counterpart in al-Kahf, which states what the turning is toward: *“And patiently stick with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure. Do not let your eyes look beyond them, desiring the luxuries of this worldly life.”* (18:28).

Read with 7:199 the two verses describe the whole of the posture. Turning away from the ignorant is not a withdrawal into solitude but a movement toward a company defined by worship. The sūrah states the same arrangement in its closing sequence: refuge from the provocation (7:200), remembrance at the two times (7:205), and the angels who are not too proud to worship (7:206).
verses.200:
> If you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah. Surely He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing

**An Appointed Number of Your Servants**

*Fa-staʿidh bi-llāhi* — the Book's term for seeking protection, and the Qur'an returns to it in a verse almost identical in wording: *“And if you are tempted by Satan, then seek refuge with Allah. Indeed, He ˹alone˺ is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”* (41:36).

**"All-Hearing, All-Knowing"**

The two names closing the verse state why the recourse works: the One addressed hears the unspoken petition and knows the provocation that prompted it. The sūrah's earlier verse about the heedless had described ears that do not hear and hearts that do not understand (7:179), and the names at the end of this verse supply the contrast.

The Qur'an commands the same recourse in several places, and the tradition of recitation before reading the Qur'an rests on Sūrat al-Naḥl's instruction: *“When you recite the Quran, seek refuge with Allah from Satan, the accursed”* (16:98). The Book attaches this practice to recitation, to provocation, and to the moments of anger.

**The Supplication in Sūrat al-Muʾminūn**

The Qur'an also provides the words: *“My Lord! I seek refuge in You from the temptations of the devils. And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, that they ˹even˺ come near me”* (23:97–98). The refuge is sought both from the incitement and from the approach that precedes it, and the two verses together define the practice.

The Qur'an's final sūrahs consist completely of refuge-seeking, and their language — the Lord of the daybreak, the Lord of humankind (113:1, 114:1) — is the Book's most concentrated statement of the practice the sūrah's verse prescribes. The readers of the sūrah are shown the same doctrine at the beginning of the Book's closing sequence.

The following verse describes the mind of the God-conscious under the same attack: when the devils whisper to them, they remember God and begin to see clearly (7:201). Verse 200 gives the practice and verse 201 its result, and the two verses answer each other.

**No Authority Over My Servants**

The two verses describe one situation from two sides. 15:42 states the position as a fact about the enemy’s power; 7:200 states it as an instruction to the one provoked. The instruction is not to resist a force but to take refuge from a suggestion, and the reason it is enough is that the suggestion has no authority behind it.

The sūrah has already recorded the enemy’s own claim, in the verses that describe his expulsion. An-Nisāʾ reports it as part of a cursed declaration: *“I will surely take hold of a certain number of Your servants.”* (4:118). The next verse states the methods: *“I will certainly mislead them and delude them with empty hopes. Also, I will order them and they will slit the ears of cattle and alter Allah’s creation.”* (4:119).

7:200 is the answer available at each of those stages. A portion is claimed; the sūrah’s reply is not a counter-claim but an instruction — take refuge when the goading touches you. The claim in 4:118 is about a number, and the exception in 15:42 is about a kind of person: the deviant who follow. What separates the two is not strength but the act of following, which is why the instruction in 7:200 is given to the individual and in the singular.
verses.201:
> Indeed, when Satan whispers to those mindful ˹of Allah˺, they remember ˹their Lord˺ then they start to see ˹things˺ clearly

**"Then They Start to See Clearly"**

Two reactions to the same attack are set side by side: the mindful remember and see, and the devils' associates are plunged deeper (7:202). The Book's presentation of the two groups in consecutive verses makes the passage a study in contrast, and the reader is invited to locate himself in the pair.

**The Word for the Whisper**

*Ṭāʾif* — a visitation, a passing touch — describes the suggestion as something that comes and goes, and the Book's vocabulary for the devil's work consistently presents it as an approach rather than a possession. The intrusion is not the same as the intention, and the verse's grammar keeps the two apart.

*Tadhakkarū* — the Book's verb for recalling what one already knows — and the sūrah has used the same root for the community that forgot the reminder (7:165's narrative) and for the command to remember what is in the Scripture (7:171). The remedy for the whisper is a remembering, and the Book's teaching about remembrance runs through its addresses to the community.

*Fa-idhā hum mubṣirūn* — the recovered sight is stated as the immediate outcome of the remembrance, and Standing against this is the blindness of the heedless described earlier in the sūrah (7:179). The Book's use of sight for understanding is consistent, and the verse describes the restoration of a faculty rather than the acquisition of new information.

**The Sūrah's Earlier Commands to Remember**

The sūrah's community has been instructed to remember what it has been given, and the command appears at the covenant of the mountain (7:171) and in the sūrah's account of the generations who forgot. The practice recommended in verse 200 is the same faculty the earlier narratives had tested.

**The Passage's Movement Forward**

The sūrah's next verses turn to the demand for signs (7:203) and to the recitation, remembrance, and prostration that end the sūrah (7:204–206). The verse's account of the community's inner life is so the hinge of the closing passage, and the reader is carried from the devil's whisper to the angels' worship.

The verse's description of the recovery also distinguishes it from mere regret: what follows the remembrance is sight, which the Book uses for understanding the situation as it is. A person who has been disturbed is not a person who has been deceived, and the verse's sequence conveys the restoration of judgment.

**A Whisper That Passes**

The word for what reaches the mindful here is *ṭāʾif*, from a root meaning to go round a thing, and it means something that comes around and passes — a visitor, a circuit, a touch. The Book’s other word for the same operation is *waswās*, a repeated whispering: *“from the evil of the lurking whisperer—who whispers into the hearts of humankind”* (114:4–5). The two words describe different phases of one process, and the verse that uses the first is describing the earliest of them.

Sūrah al-Nās describes the whisperer as lurking and retreating, which is the same picture from the other side: the approach is intermittent, and the response that works against an intermittent approach is an intermittent readiness.
verses.202:
> But the devils persistently plunge their ˹human˺ associates deeper into wickedness, sparing no effort

**"The Devils Plunge Their Associates Deeper"**

*Wa-ikhwānuhum yamuddūnahum fī al-ghayyi thumma lā yuqṣirūn* — but the devils persistently plunge their ˹human˺ associates deeper into wickedness, sparing no effort.

The verse completes the pair begun in 7:201, and its subject is the other category of people: those whose association with the devils is reciprocal. Two conditions are described rather than two natures, and the verse's verb — the devils' persistence — means a process that continues as long as it is not interrupted.

*Ikhwānuhum* — their brothers — and the Book's use of kinship for the relation between the devils and the wicked is deliberate: What is described is a companionship rather than a servitude, and the Qur'an's language about evil presents it as a society as well as a condition.

*Yamuddūnahum fī al-ghayy* — the verb is one of extension, of stretching a rope, of drawing a thing out; the image is of a deepening that is willed from both sides. The plunging is not an assault on the unwilling, and the Book's narrative of the fall of Adam's adversary had already portrayed the devil's method as invitation (7:20).

**The Verse's Place in the Sūrah's Close**

The verse stands between the description of the mindful (7:201) and the answer about signs (7:203), and its function is to state what happens when the practice of verse 200 is not performed. Remedy and alternative now stand in consecutive lines.

The Qur'an's statements about the devil describe his activity as temptation, embellishment, and companionship, and it consistently presents his power as limited by the creature's response. The sūrah's earlier narrative of his refusal to prostrate had already stated the terms of his relation to the human being (7:11–18), and the verse's description of his persistence belongs with that account.

The sūrah had warned its readers about the communities that were overtaken while unaware (7:95) and had described the heedless who have the faculties and do not use them (7:179). The verse's image of a deepening course belongs to the same sequence of warnings, and The diagnosis is given in several registers.

**The Passage Complete**

The sūrah's account of the two responses is now complete: refuge and remembrance on one side (7:200–201), and the deepening course on the other (7:202). The Book's arrangement leaves the reader between the two, and the sūrah's final four verses supply the practice that ends the passage.

The verse's description of the devils' persistence also implies the community's part in the process, since the associates are being drawn by beings they have chosen as brothers. The companionship is the result of a prior agreement, and the sūrah's earlier narrative of the devil's refusal had stated the terms: he asked for respite and was granted it until the appointed day (7:15).

The Book states the same operation from the other side, as a respite whose purpose the recipients misread: *“Those who disbelieve should not think that living longer is good for them. They are only given more time to increase in sin, and they will suffer a humiliating punishment.”* (3:178).

On the Day, the companion is wished away by the one who had him: *“I wish you were as distant from me as the east is from the west! What an evil associate ˹you were˺!”* (43:38).
verses.203:
> If you ˹O Prophet˺ do not bring them a sign ˹which they demanded˺, they ask, “Why do you not make it yourself?” Say, “I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord. This ˹Quran˺ is an insight from your Lord—a guide and a mercy for those who believe.”

**"Why Do You Not Make It Yourself?"**

*Wa-idhā lam taʾtihim bi-āyatin qālū lawlā ijtabaytahā qul innamā attabiʿu mā yūḥā ilayya min rabbī hādhā baṣāʾiru min rabbikum wa-hudan wa-raḥmatun li-qawmin yuʾminūn* — if you ˹O Prophet˺ do not bring them a sign ˹which they demanded˺, they ask, "Why do you not make it yourself?" (7:203) Say, "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord. This ˹Quran˺ is an insight from your Lord—a guide and a mercy for those who believe." (7:203)

**The Book's Many Accounts of the Demand**

The Qur'an records the same demand in sūrah after sūrah. Each version adds a detail: the challenge to bring a sign from his Lord (6:37), the complaint that no sign had been sent (13:7), the demand that he bring one (20:133), the oath that they would believe if a sign came (6:109), and the request to produce a different Qur'an altogether (10:15). The demand's whole history is already in front of the hearer.

The Prophet's position is stated in a sentence: he is a follower of revelation before he is anything else, and the Book's accounts of the other messengers' replies to the same demand say the same thing — signs are only with Allah (6:109, 29:50). The Book states the reason in Sūrat al-Isrāʾ: the signs were not sent because the earlier peoples denied them and the demand would have been followed by the same denial (17:59). Sūrat al-Anʿām states that even the descent of the angels and the speaking of the dead would not produce belief without God's will (6:111).

*Baṣāʾiru* — the plural of insight, of clear perception — is the Book's term for what the revelation supplies, and the Qur'an's self-descriptions in this register are many: a healing and mercy for the believers (17:82), a warning, a cure for what is in the hearts, a guide and a mercy (10:57).

Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt answers the same demand by pointing to what had already been given: *“Is it not enough for them that We have sent down to you the Book, ˹which is˺ recited to them. Surely in this ˹Quran˺ is a mercy and reminder for people who believe”* (29:51).

**Only Following What Is Revealed: The Limit Stated on the Messenger**

The three refusals answer the demand of 7:203 at its root. A sign made by the messenger would require him to be an originator, and the verse of al-Aḥqāf removes that possibility; a sign produced on request would require knowledge of what is unseen, and that is removed as well.

The limit is stated without diminishing the message. The verse at 7:203 calls the Book insight, guide, and mercy, and the verse at 46:9 calls its bearer a clear warner. Both descriptions are of a thing received, and the sūrah's insistence on this is what separates its messengers from the miracle-workers its peoples demand.

The demand for a sign is recorded elsewhere with the same answer: *“Why has no ˹other˺ sign been sent down to him from his Lord?”* (10:20), and the reply is that *“˹The knowledge of˺ the unseen is with Allah alone. So wait! I too am waiting with you.”* (10:20)
verses.204:
> When the Quran is recited, listen to it attentively and be silent, so you may be shown mercy

**"So You May Be Shown Mercy"**

The command's purpose is stated in the Book's vocabulary of mercy, and Listening is not a courtesy but a means. The Qur'an attaches mercy to specific practices throughout — the sūrah's earlier commands about returning, remembering, and seeking refuge all close with a similar clause — and the verse's grammar keeps the outcome in God's hand.

The Qur'an's addresses consistently treat hearing as the first step of faith: the Book's description of the heedless is that they have ears and do not hear (7:179), and its account of the earlier communities' failure is repeatedly phrased as a refusal to listen. The command of verse 204 is the positive form of the sūrah's long indictment.

The sūrah had reported that the idols cannot hear those who call upon them (7:193, 7:198), and The contrast is exact: the objects of worship are deaf, and the worshippers of God are commanded to listen. The verse's placement at the end of the sūrah's examination of the idols makes the comparison explicit.

**The Recitation in the Prophet's Practice**

The Book's accounts of the Prophet's night recitation and of the community's prayer describe the practice the verse commands, and the Qur'an's instruction to recite in a measured manner belongs to the same discipline. A religion centred on a recited text requires silence as the condition of its reception.

The command addresses everyone present at the recitation, and The obligation is not restricted to believers: in the Prophet's city those who had not yet accepted the message were present, and the verse's requirement of silence applied to them as well.

The inward form of the command is supplied too, since the silence of the tongue is a figure for the attention of the heart, and the earlier verses had made the heart the seat of understanding (7:179). The community's tradition drew from the verse its teaching about attentiveness rather than mere quietness, and the two verbs of the verse were read together.

The verse's command assumes the Book's account of itself as a recitation that works on its hearers: The Book has been called an insight and a mercy, and elsewhere the Qur'an's recitation is said to increase the believers' humility (17:109). A text accomplishes something in the one who attends to it.

**The Same Word in the Listening of the Jinn**

The command to be silent uses a verb that appears in one other scene in the Book, and that scene is a listening. The group of jinn sent to hear the Qurʾān say to one another: *“Listen quietly!”* (46:29), using the same imperative this verse gives, and then return to their people as warners.

**The Public Listening and the Private Remembrance**

The verse that follows moves the same subject indoors: *“Remember your Lord inwardly with humility and reverence and in a moderate tone of voice, both morning and evening. And do not be one of the heedless.”* (7:205). The two verses give the sūrah’s account of hearing in two registers — one public and shared, the other inward and continual.

The pairing answers a question the first verse raises on its own. If listening is commanded when the Qurʾān is recited, what happens when it is not being recited?
verses.205:
> Remember your Lord inwardly with humility and reverence and in a moderate tone of voice, both morning and evening. And do not be one of the heedless

**"Remember Your Lord Inwardly"**

*Wa-dhkur rabbaka fī nafsika taḍarruʿan wa-khīfatan wa-dūna al-jahri mina al-qawli bi-l-ghuduwwi wa-l-āṣāli wa-lā takun mina al-ghāfilīn* — remember your Lord inwardly with humility and reverence and in a moderate tone of voice, both morning and evening.

*Fī nafsika* — The instruction turns to the interior, and the Book's teaching about the heart as the seat of understanding (7:179) gives it its setting. The Qur'an's other descriptions of remembrance make the same point: the believers remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying on their sides (3:191), and The practice described does not depend on posture or place.

**"Morning and Evening"**

*Bi-l-ghuduwwi wa-l-āṣāl* — the two ends of the day are named. The Qur'an's instructions about the times of glorification recur: the command to glorify before sunrise and before sunset (20:130, 50:39), during the night (50:40, 76:26), and the statement that the shadows of all things bow in the morning and the evening (13:15). What is prescribed is a rhythm rather than a single occasion.

**The Verse's Moderation**

The verse's command follows immediately on the instruction to listen to the Qur'an in silence (7:204), and the pair describes the community's practice as hearing and answering.

The sūrah had commanded the community to remember what it had been given at the covenant of the mountain (7:171) and had reported the generations who forgot the reminder (7:165).

**Remembrance and Supplication: Two Words for One Act**

Al-Baqarah states the nearness that makes both possible: *“When My servants ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about Me: I am truly near.”* (2:186). The verse answers a question about God in the first person, and the answer is a statement of proximity rather than of attributes — which is the same ground 7:55 and 7:205 assume when they describe an act performed inwardly and in a moderate voice.

The commentators read the two commands as one practice in two modes. Remembrance is the act that has no request in it; supplication is the act that does. Both are commanded with humility, both are performed at fixed times, and both are contrasted in this sūrah with the same fault — heedlessness, named at 7:205 and described at 7:201.

**Abandoning Their Beds**

The manner the verse specifies has a counterpart in the Book’s description of a group: *“They abandon their beds, invoking their Lord with hope and fear, and donate from what We have provided for them.”* (32:16). The verse names three acts — leaving the bed, invocation with two motives, and spending — and the first of them fixes the time: the hours when sleep is available.

This is why the verse ends with a prohibition rather than a promise: *“And do not be one of the heedless.”* (7:205). The fault excluded is not sin but inattention, and the sūrah describes its operation in the verse that follows — a provocation from Satan, a group whose hearts are made heedless by a whisper, and a remembrance that restores sight (7:201). The command to remember is therefore the sūrah’s own remedy for the condition it has been describing since its opening.
verses.206:
> Surely those ˹angels˺ nearest to your Lord are not too proud to worship Him. They glorify Him. And to Him they prostrate

**"They Glorify Him"**

*Wa-yusabbiḥūnahu* — the Book's verb of praise that accompanies the declaration of God's transcendence. The Qur'an's accounts of the angels' activity use it consistently: those near Him are not too proud to worship and do not tire (21:19), they glorify Him day and night without wavering (21:20), and the angels around the Throne glorify the praises of their Lord (39:75). The angels' occupation is the one the idolaters' gods cannot perform, because they cannot speak.

The verse's last words state the posture, and the Qur'an's prostration verses echo the same formula: whatever is in the heavens and the earth bows down to Allah, as do the angels, who are not too proud (16:49), and all things bow to Him willingly or unwillingly, as do their shadows (13:15). Prostration is the creation's common act, and the human refusal is placed against the background of the angels' practice.

**The Book's Prostration Verses**

The sūrah has just examined the associate-gods who cannot hear, cannot see, and cannot help (7:191–198), and its final verse presents the angels who listen, worship, and prostrate. Two orders of being stand at the sūrah's close, and the contrast completes the passage's argument about the true object of worship.

The Book's descriptions of creation consistently present worship as the activity of everything that exists: the stars and the trees bow (55:6), the thunder and the angels glorify (13:13), and the heavens and the earth are filled with creatures that serve. The human being's worship is a participation in an universal act rather than an isolated duty.

**Too Proud to Worship: The Same Words in Ghāfir**

The verse denies a pride: *lā yastakbirūna ʿan ʿibādatih* — rendered *“are not too proud to worship Him”* (7:206). The verb is form X of *k-b-r*, to be great; *istakbara* means to consider oneself great, and it takes *ʿan*, “from” or “away from”, so that the pride is described as turning a person away from a thing. The sūrah has already used the verb of Iblīs, whose refusal is stated in the same construction (7:13).

Al-Muʾmin states the outcome of the same pride in God’s own proclamation: *“Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Surely those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, fully humbled.”* (40:60)

7:206 is the denial of that pride, and its subject is the angels nearest to God. The verse therefore closes the sūrah with the contrast it opened with: the one who considered himself great and refused to prostrate (7:11–13), and those who are nearest and are not too proud to worship, who glorify and who prostrate.

**Prostrate and Draw Near: The Book’s Other Endings**

The sūrah ends with three acts: worship, glorification, prostration. Al-ʿAlaq ends with two of them as a command: *“Again, no! Never obey him ˹O Prophet˺! Rather, ˹continue to˺ prostrate and draw near ˹to Allah˺.”* (96:19). Ar-Raḥmān ends with a blessing: *“Blessed is the Name of your Lord, full of Majesty and Honour.”* (55:78).

The Book's negation is aimed at the very disposition the sūrah has been documenting in the human being, from Iblīs's refusal to prostrate (7:12–13) to the arrogance of the towns and of the idolaters.
